paragraphs.text: PROLOGUE.

The prophet David also sounded forth in a mystical sense, as if with the blast of a trumpet. Yet he is a great master of morals, and the whole grace of this psalm shows how far he excels in ethics. All moral teaching is sweet, but it delights the ears most of all through the sweetness of song and the pleasantness of psalm-singing, and it soothes the mind.

And rightly, in many places, he has scattered the moral sayings of the psalms like the lights of stars, which shine and stand out. But the hundred and eighteenth psalm he has set, like a sun of full light burning with midday heat, at the advanced stage of the book. So neither the half-full beginnings of its morning rising nor any aged failing of its evening setting could take anything from the brightness of its perfect splendour.

He arranged it according to the letters of the Hebrew alphabet one by one. Just as the minds of little children grow used to the practice of learning through the first elements of letters, so we too might learn the practice of living through elements of this kind.

To each letter he assigned eight verses, so as to teach two things at once. The first is unity, not plurality, for unity holds all things together and rules them, and all things are subject to it. The second is the purification of lawful sanctification. For the solemn purification comes on the eighth day, either because of the law, since it was laid down that the solemn rite of circumcision should be fulfilled on the eighth day,

or because the whole world was defiled by our sins and polluted during those seven days. But when the day of resurrection came, we were made alive together with the Lord Jesus. We rose again and were raised up in newness of life, displaying the grace of washing. And rightly we offer firstborn animals, as a figure of the firstborn Son of God, a spiritual sacrifice of chastity and simplicity acceptable to God. We do not offer them on the fourth or fifth day, lest the sacrifice be unclean or incomplete, but on the eighth day,

the day on which we were all, in Christ's resurrection, not only raised again but also confirmed. Full purification comes at once in baptism. Yet the baptized person ought to come to know the meaning of that washing and of the sacrifice. So he does not offer sacrifice until he enters the eighth day. Then, instructed in the knowledge of the heavenly sacraments and better taught, he may at last offer his gift on the holy altars, not as an untrained victim but as one capable of reason, lest the ignorance of the one offering defile the mystery of the offering.

The title of the psalm is Alleluia, that is, 'praise of God'. For God is truly praised in those hymns in which there is forgiveness of sins. Indeed, the Lord's passion was set out in the preceding psalm. That passion washed this world clean, so as to make peoples worthy to praise God with a spotless mouth. The very elements of the letters, too, like all Hebrew names, are not empty or devoid of meaningful interpretation, and we shall disclose their meanings in their proper places. In the Hebrew, the hundred and eleventh psalm is arranged by these letters at the beginnings of its verses, and it is wholly ethical. The hundred and tenth also seems to me to be written in this way. Indeed, each of them has twenty-two verses, and each verse sets out a single thought. Hence they are also said to have been composed in metre.
I. THE LETTER ALEPH.
The first letter is called 'Aleph', and its meaning is 'teaching'. So, attentive hearer, you should expect the verses that follow to be full of teaching.

Blessed, he says, are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who search his testimonies; with their whole heart they seek him. What a beautiful order, how full of teaching and grace! He did not say first, 'who search his testimonies', though by the letter that would have fitted. First he said, 'blessed are the undefiled in the way.' For life must be sought before teaching. A good life has grace even without teaching, but teaching without life lacks integrity, for wisdom will not enter a malicious soul. And so he says: The wicked will seek me and will not find me. Wickedness blinds the eye of the mind, and when iniquity darkens it, it cannot find the deep mysteries. First, then, we must practise the warfare of life and correct our conduct. When we have set these on their proper course, so that offences are corrected and the grace of purity is present, then let us come to the pursuit of knowledge in its proper order and way. Moral things, therefore, come first and mystical things second. The former hold life and the latter knowledge. So if you seek perfection, there should be neither life without knowledge nor knowledge without life; each should support the other. And so Scripture says: Sow for yourselves unto righteousness, gather the vintage unto the fruit of life, light for yourselves the light of knowledge. It does not put 'light' first, but 'sow'. And it does not say only 'sow unto righteousness' first, but also 'gather the vintage unto the fruit of life', and only then 'light the light of knowledge'. So perfection is proved not only by fruits sown but also by fruits gathered in. In the first psalm too he kept this order, teaching first that we must walk in the way and then meditate on the law. For he who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly has certainly not left the way of godliness and the path of righteousness. Rightly, then, he is declared blessed as he walks in the way, and as he meditates on the law day and night he has the grace of blessedness.

Following this pattern, Solomon wrote the book of Proverbs, in which he set out the moral part more fully. He set out the natural part in Ecclesiastes and the mystical part in the Song of Songs. Yet if you examine them carefully, you will also find much that is mystical in Proverbs, and the sweetness of moral teaching in the Song. For this is certainly mystical: Wisdom

has built herself a house and set up seven pillars; she has slain her victims, and the rest. So too in the Song, this passage is as much mystical as moral. It expresses the sweetness of endearments and the feeling of a lover: Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.

Picture, then, a maiden who has long been betrothed and burns with rightful love. She has learned of her beloved's many splendid deeds from the assurance of trustworthy witnesses. Her desires have been held in suspense and often put off, and she can no longer bear delay; she would have done anything to see her bridegroom. At last she gains her wish when he arrives unexpectedly. Flustered with joy, she does not look for the opening courtesies of greeting or an exchange of words, but at once demands what she has desired.

So too holy Church was betrothed in paradise at the beginning of the world, prefigured in the flood, announced through the law, and called through the prophets. For a long time she had awaited the redemption of mankind, the glory of the gospel, and the coming of her beloved. Impatient of delay, she rushes to his kisses, saying: Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. And delighted by the kisses, she added: for your breasts are better than wine.

To put it in more moral terms, understand by this that flesh which had been soaked in Adam with the serpent's poison and was wasting away in the stench of its crimes. Among the daughters of Zion it went about with neck stretched high and winking eyes, walking with mincing steps, trailing its tunics and playing with its feet. It had curled locks, made-up faces and ribbons, and every affected adornment only made it more unseemly. Yet this same flesh had been taught by many oracles that one would come who would shut out the serpent's allurements and pour in the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that all flesh should see the salvation of God and all flesh should come to God. It was set on fire with desire, but feared to displease by being impatient, wanton, luxurious and querulous, as it had been before. It was shaken by waiting for the Lord's coming, which was delayed longer than it could now bear. Even so, it did not murmur or transgress, but lifted up pure hands in every place without anger or dispute. It was becomingly dressed and adorned itself with modesty and sobriety, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or costly clothing, but with what befits the grace of chastity and good conduct. And it prayed, saying:

Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine. Already the flesh, which had once been a harlot's, wished to cling to Christ. Already it was hastening to marry, so as to be one spirit with him and become the flesh of Christ. Let him kiss 'me', it says. The Word of God kisses us when the Spirit of knowledge enlightens our understanding. Then, as if despising all its pleasures and delights and longing to cling to the heavenly commandments, it says: 'for the precepts of your testaments are better than every appetite of the flesh and every pleasure of the world.'

For it remembered that it had once fallen in just this way in Eve, when she preferred bodily pleasure to the heavenly commandments. Your name is ointment poured out. That is: this whole world was unclean and reeked with the impurities of all kinds of crimes; now the sweetness of chastity, the ointment of faith and the flower of integrity breathe everywhere. And from moral things it passes to mystical things, saying: The king has brought me into his chamber. Let us exult and rejoice in you; let us love your breasts more than wine. For a kiss is a simple thing, but the privacy of the chamber is a more involved matter.

In the gospel itself, too, there is a most beautiful passage on morals, teaching that each should cleanse his own vessel. The Lord says: Blind Pharisee, first cleanse the inside of the cup and the dish, so that the outside may also become clean. For unless each person cleanses himself within, he will be like whitewashed tombs, even if outwardly he seems comely and just. Outwardly he will seem just, but within he will be foul. Such is teaching without innocence of life.
Nor can teaching itself have a reward where innocence brings it no grace. For to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous acts? But let us return to the psalm before us.

Blessed, he says, are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who search his testimonies; with their whole heart they seek him. The first verse is moral, the second mystical. Who says this? The prophet, of course, who spoke as one in the flesh. And he says it after the psalm in which the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ is described.

When the divine mysteries were revealed to him, he put on the joy of the Lord's resurrection and tasted the grace of the passion. He saw the congregations of the righteous, the peoples of the redeemed, the salvation of the lost, the resurrection of the dead and the sanctification of the sacraments. Then he cried out: Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. That is: see, the earth that was cursed in Adam has begun to have blessedness, provided it does not forsake the law of the Lord; see, man who was once polluted is now undefiled. How precious it now is to keep the Lord's commandment, and how precious also to know the mystery of that commandment!

But who is undefiled? Not, surely, the one who walks in just any way, but the one who walks in Christ. For he himself said: I am the way. Whoever walks in this way cannot go astray, provided he never leaves it. The law too is a way, and so, while he is undefiled, he walks in the law of the Lord. Let him not stop walking in this way, or he will stop being undefiled. Let him not turn aside to the right or to the left;

let him not stumble, stand still or wait. Let him walk on, forgetting what lies behind and reaching out to what lies ahead. Let him pursue the goal, hasten to the prize and press on to the end, for Christ is the end of the law. Many wish to walk in the way, but not to the end. The Jews do not walk to the end, because they do not walk as far as Christ. The Manichee does not walk in the way, because he rejects the law. But true faith walks in it, for it both accepts the law and recognizes the fulfilment of the law.

If anyone, then, walks in the way, let him search the testimonies of the Lord. Though this is mystical, it also contains moral teaching, since whoever searches the Lord's testimonies can walk better in the way. Take someone utterly intemperate, seized by the heat of adulterous desire, overcome by lust or given over to shameful deeds, who will not resist the appetite of his flesh. He looks this way and that, and if he happens to see no one, he rushes into the crime. Yet even he, though the chance to gratify himself is at hand, carefully scans everything. Careless of righteousness but anxious for his reputation, he keeps turning his eyes in every direction. He who does not blush at the sin blushes at a witness to it. If he happens to notice someone watching his crime, shame puts a stop to his intemperance. Even with a slave girl or a common harlot, where there is no danger of being caught, he may set about his lustful attempts, yet out of shame he abandons what he has begun. How much more, then, if someone lifts the eyes of his mind and considers that all things are full of angels: the air, the lands, the sea, and the churches over which angels preside. For the Lord sends his angels to protect those

who are to be heirs of the heavenly promises. How much more can such a person renounce the sin he has conceived! Where does this throng of the innocent come from, if not from those very sinners? All share the same nature, but their discipline differs. Circumcision is nothing and being a Gentile is nothing, but keeping the commandments of God increases the grace of nature itself. Or does a man change what he deserves when he says: Darkness is round about me and the walls cover me; the Most High will not remember my sins?

Would you not stand in awe of the presence of angels, if you believed they were present? Would you not fear to speak, or even to think, what is wicked, let alone to do it, if divine Scripture had persuaded you that God is the judge of thoughts and the true witness of secrets? As he himself says: Be my witnesses, and I am a witness, says the Lord God, and so is my servant whom I have chosen. You stand in awe of a man who is present, and do you not stand in awe of the presence of God the Father and the Son? But you do not wish to believe, so that you need not be on your guard. When Scripture is read saying that God knows the hidden things of men, you do not wish to listen. You are afraid you might begin to know what you should fear, and then to fear sinning. Hear divine Scripture, then, so that you may be turned from the crooked and evil way.

Think of a man who is blind in his bodily eyes, or deaf. Because he cannot see or hear those around him, he believes he is alone. In a gathering of many people, thinking that no one is present, he sets about doing what he supposes is secret, for one who does not see cannot see those who see him. Do not be like him. Blinded in the eyes of your mind, do not suppose that you sin without a witness just because you managed to avoid the presence of a man. There are more who can convict you than those you were able to avoid. You cannot flee yourself, your own accuser, for your own conscience confronts you. Even if you deny it to others, you do not deny it to yourself; if you deny it to a man, you confess it to God; and if you wish to deny it, your own thoughts convict you.

Angels stood by Elisha, and he saw them, and so he did not fear the enemy's columns. But his servant, who did not see the angels, was afraid. At the prophet's word, the grace of God opened the servant's eyes. He saw the armies of angels and believed they were present, though before, because he did not see them, he had thought they were absent. You too, read the prophet so that you may see; read, so that he may open your eyes. Then the enemy legion will not terrify you, and you will not believe yourself besieged

when you are free and guarded by spiritual squadrons, provided you do not abandon the prophet. The prophet tells you that God said: I fill heaven and earth. The prophet tells you: There are more with us, for angels are round about us. When he tells you this, lift up the eyes of your mind, and you will see not only angels but God himself, who says to you: Open to me, my sister, my dear one. He knocks at the door even while you sleep. If only you wake up when roused, or open the door of your heart when called, he will come in. But suppose you shun the reading of the prophets: you do not read at home, and you will not listen in church. Some people turn their gaze aside and shut their eyes so as not to see what they could see; though they have the power of seeing, they close their eyes so as not to look. Others, in a frenzy,

have laid hands on their own eyes. Do you not do the same, turning away at first by pretending not to see rather than by outright refusal? When you come to church and declare yourself a Christian, you seem sound, and you open eyes with which you can see. But while you pretend not to hear what is read, you close them, so that you do not see for yourself, even though to others you seem to see. You even lay the hands of faithlessness and intemperance on the eyes of your soul. You bring blindness on your heart, and, what is worse, a blindness you have chosen, so that seeing you do not see and hearing you do not hear.

Do you think you are alone when you commit fornication? Do you not remember that the eyes of the Lord behold the whole world? Do you not hear him say: See, the hour is coming when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone; yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me? The Father, then, is present, and the Son of God is present. His ministers are present, and so are the Cherubim and Seraphim, who say: Holy, holy, holy; the earth is full of your majesty.

The world is full of holy powers, because it is full of wickedness. The whole earth is full of remedies, because it is full of snares. Do you think Christ does not see you in the brothel, when he sees you going into it? Do you think he does not catch you in adultery, when he sees you thinking of it? Does he who beholds errors shrink back from walls? Does he who gazes on the scene of a crime turn away from its secrecy? Or do you think you first enter the house of hire when you pass under the harlot's archway? You entered already when the harlot entered your thoughts. You entered already when you stepped in your mind into desire to possess a prostitute. You knocked at the brothel's doors when you opened the eyes of your mind to the beauty of a woman you lusted after.

And if you want to hear the truth, how could Christ fail to see you in the brothel, when he saw that by committing adultery in your heart you had made yourself a brothel? Indeed, the Lord Jesus himself says: Whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. How is it, then, that someone with such a reputation for piety is so shameful in his crime?

But I grant you that Jesus does not wish to see you, and that he who does not wish to accuse does not wish to convict. Suppose that the angels too do not wish to see. But the devil sees, for he went in with you; indeed, he led you in. His ministers see, for they surrounded you so that you would not see the angels of God. Belial sees, and the legion sees, for they drove you on so that no one would call you back or hold you. Do not think that the one who wants to share your punishment is offering you a secret pact of silence. He is eager to see many like himself, and he glories in having ruined many. He is the instigator, and he is the accuser;

he entered into Judas, drove him to betrayal and sent him to the noose. How many will say against him on that day: 'You deceived us, you drove us on!' Do you want an example? Hear Eve saying that the serpent was the author of her transgression. But in blaming him she did not clear herself, and the Lord answered her: 'Had I not commanded you not to taste of the one tree that is in the middle of paradise?' So he will answer many others as well: 'You listened to the devil urging what was harmful; could you not listen to me commanding what gives life?'

And so let us do works of righteousness. For those who work iniquity have not walked in his ways. You have commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly. O that my ways may be directed to keep your ordinances! Then I shall not be put to shame, when I look upon all your commandments.

He does not say only, 'You have commanded your commandments to be kept,' but also, 'to be kept exceedingly.' When did he command this? In paradise he did command Adam to keep the commandments, but perhaps he had not commanded him to keep them exceedingly, and that is why Adam fell. That is why he was swayed by his wife's voice and deceived by the serpent. He thought that if he departed from the commandment in some part, he would not go wholly astray. But because he once left the path of the commandments, he abandoned the whole way. The serpent found him off the way, stripped him of everything and left him naked. Because the one who was in paradise had fallen, the Lord afterwards gave warning through the law, the prophets, the gospel and the apostles that you should keep the commandments of the Lord your God exceedingly. 'For every

word that you have spoken,' it says, 'you will give account of it.' Do not pretend otherwise: not one iota or one stroke of any commandment passes away. Do not leave the way. If you are scarcely safe from the robber while walking in the way, what will you do if he finds you wandering off it? Let your steps be directed. And so that you are not too weak to direct them, pray that the Lord may direct your ways.

Here he prays: O that my ways may be directed! Elsewhere he says: I waited patiently for the Lord, and he heard me; he set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps. So you too must ask the Lord to direct the footsteps of your mind, so that you may keep the Lord's ordinances. You will not be put to shame when you look upon all the commandments, as you were once put to shame in Adam and Eve. Indeed, you were made naked; you covered yourself with leaves because you were ashamed, and you hid yourself from God's sight because you blushed. So God said to you: Adam, where are you? When he speaks to Adam, he speaks to you, for 'Adam' in Latin means 'man'. That is: 'Man, where are you?' And Adam answered: 'I was afraid because I was naked and wholly ashamed in my mind, and I did not dare to come before your sight.' So, so that we are not put to shame, let us keep the commandments of the Lord, and keep them all. If someone keeps one commandment and transgresses another, it profits him nothing. Suppose a man has kept himself from bloodshed but not from adultery. Convicted on the one count, he is surely punished, even by the laws of this world. If he has been caught in the one crime, his abstaining from the other does him no good.

I will confess to you, Lord, in uprightness of heart — do you notice what ways he directs? — when I have learned the judgments of your righteousness. I will keep your statutes; do not utterly forsake me. In this passage he testifies that he wishes to know the mysteries more fully,

so that he may enter the inner sanctuaries of the heavenly mysteries, and the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in Christ may be opened to him. That is why Solomon too says: Draw us; we will run after you in the fragrance of your ointments. The king has brought me into his chamber. And perhaps what he says earlier, Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit coming upon her, as the angel said to Mary: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. But when the king brought her into his chamber, what is declared is the time of the passion, the piercing of the side, the shedding of blood, the ointment of burial, the mystery of the resurrection. So she received the kiss as a bride, but the Church was brought into Christ's chamber no longer merely as one betrothed but as one wedded, and she not only

entered the bridal chamber but also obtained the keys of lawful union. And so, as one now placed in the bridal chamber, she says: My brother is to me a bundle of myrrh-drops; he rests between my breasts. If we ask what the chamber is, let him teach us who says: But when you pray, go into your chamber, shut the door, and pray to your Father in secret. The chamber of the Church is the body of Christ. The king brought her into all the inner mysteries and gave her the keys, so that she might open for herself the treasures of the knowledge of the sacraments, throw open doors that had been shut, and come to know the grace of rest, the sleep of the dead, and the power of the resurrection.

In that chamber the bride found the righteous deeds of the Lord Jesus. What are these righteous deeds? Surely the sacraments of baptism, as we read: when Jesus came to be baptized and John said to him, I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?, Jesus answered: Let it be so now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness.

In that chamber she learned the statutes and came to know the counsel of God, as it is written: All the people who heard, and the tax collectors, justified God, having been baptized with the baptism of John; but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the counsel of God for themselves, not having been baptized by him.

What they rejected, we have chosen, and we follow the counsel of God, for nothing can be more sublime; for this is the divine thing by which the forgiveness of sins comes about. So when she has learned the righteous ordinances of the Lord, she who fears God will not be put to shame. And Paul too says: In nothing shall I be put to shame.

And because no one can be perfect or safe without God's favour, a person must ask that God not forsake him entirely. Earlier David prayed not to be forsaken, saying: Do not forsake me, O Lord my God; here he says: Do not utterly forsake me, that is, 'too far'. Earlier, perhaps, being still imperfect and in the midst of great turmoil, he was afraid of being forsaken; but here, now stronger, he does not fear being forsaken so as to be tested, but asks not to be forsaken entirely. For God often forsakes those he wishes to be proved, but he forsakes entirely those he abandons. He utterly forsook Judas.

But he did not forsake holy Job. He gave the devil power over his property and over his body, but not over his soul; for if he had given power over his soul, he would have forsaken him entirely. Was not Job left for this very reason, that being left he might be proved, and being proved he might be crowned? Judas, then, he forsook, saying to him: What you are doing, do quickly; for he forsook him entirely when he allowed him to carry out his crime. But when he saw the other apostles troubled because he had said, Where I am going, you cannot come, he added: Let not your heart be troubled, and further on:

I am coming again and will take you to myself, so that where I am you may be also. Then Peter, troubled and afraid of being forsaken, said: Lord, where are you going? The Lord saw that he was troubled and answered him: Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterwards. So too, when Peter faltered on the sea, he cried out to Christ, and Christ stretched out his right hand to him, so that he should not perish utterly forsaken.

No one should be puffed up because he is never forsaken, nor grieve because he is sometimes forsaken, since the Son himself says that he was forsaken, as you have it: God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me? And yet he was never forsaken by the Father, for the Father is always with him; for it is written: Behold, the hour is coming when you will be scattered, each to his own, and will leave me alone; but I am not alone, because the Father is with me.

But that cry came forth in respect of the body in which he was handed over to suffering, because we seem to ourselves to be forsaken when we are placed in dangers. That is why Paul too says of God the Father: He who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all. He seems to have forsaken him, since he did not spare him but handed him over to death; but he did not utterly forsake the one to whom it is said: For you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor let your holy one see corruption.
II. THE LETTER BETH.

How shall a young man correct his way? Our discussion of the previous eight verses turned out not unreasonably, and so we have been eager to pursue what follows as well. And first we must consider the meaning of the second letter, that is, 'Beth', which when rendered into Latin is said to mean 'confusion'.

But whoever corrects his way will not be confounded. Yet since one who corrects his way was previously in error — for how is something corrected unless it had earlier swerved from the truth? — he has certainly fallen, and been captured by the excesses of adolescence and the allurements of a wanton age. When he has advanced to the threshold of youth and comes to his senses with a sober mind, he is confounded in spirit, as it were, and turns over at length within himself how he may put off what is shameful and take up what is full of uprightness. Wavering among various thoughts, forgetting what lies behind and reaching out to what lies ahead, he weighs and examines how he may correct his way and cover the offences of his younger years with the serious countenance of youth.

So that such a person may not hesitate long and remain stuck in uncertainty, the prophet gives him counsel, as though deliberating with him himself; for we consider counsels more wholesome when they appear to have been examined by more careful reflection. But the very undertaking of deliberation is marked out with a learned definition, so as to remove the clash of conflicting thoughts, when he says: How shall a young man correct his way? For this is the goal of the one deliberating: how to correct his way.

And he answers: By keeping your words. Rightly, having turned to God, he answered the one deliberating, as if, after offering up prayer and supplication, he had found this counsel by the Lord's inspiration, so that it might be believed to be a remedy not of human presumption but of divine condescension. For our mind, once sprinkled with the seeds of heavenly words, though before it was degenerating into wild growth, begins to show better cultivation and to bear fruit. Let us therefore make our paths straight and not follow the windings of the twisting serpent. For the ways of the Lord are straight, but the ways of those who go astray are crooked, and of them it is said:

O you who have forsaken the straight paths! [?] A thriving crop is laid out in rows, and vineyards are set out in lines; the course of the stag is straighter, that of the little fox winding. That is why it is said of Herod, Go, tell that fox, because he had turned aside from the straight way and had not corrected his path in his youth; he deserved the lament of Jeremiah, in which sinners are mourned who refused to take up the yoke of the word in their youth. That is why they were led away captive, that is why they are mourned as dead: because they did not know the paths of life and did not turn away from works fit for the tomb of corpses. Weeping, then, over the everlasting death of the Jews, Jeremiah says: It is good for a man when he bears the yoke in his youth; he will sit alone and keep silent, because he took it upon himself.

We ought not only to take up the yoke of the word, but to take it up in youth; for if we take it up late, we begin to have repentance for the past rather than to hold fast to grace. Let us therefore get ahead of the years of youth with fitting correction, so that each of us may rather say, God who has fed me from my youth, than remember our lapses and lament, saying: Remember not the sins of my youth and of my ignorance. The latter is a remedy for weakness, the former the strength of health.

Healing medicine is sought for a wound; grace is sought for soundness. That is why he says: It is good for a man when he bears the yoke in his youth. But for one who takes up the yoke after the years of youth have run their course, it is not at once a perfect good: his sins goad him, the habit of sinning harasses his conscience, and long practice in error makes him unstable. Such a man must struggle long to wipe out what is ingrained and of long standing. For the one, his state is perilous; for the other, it is good.

Then he will sit alone, as one who does not easily find an equal, being endowed with singular rewards; and he will keep silent, at rest and on holiday from every intrusion of worldly care and pleasure, and will be free for the divine oracles which are usually revealed to those who sit alone, as they were to holy David, who says: For you, Lord, have established me alone in hope. And he did not, indeed, sit alone in secret; but though he ruled over peoples, he stood out by a singular grace. Elijah sat alone when he was fed by an angel, or even by ravens bringing him food; alone, not only withdrawn from the crowds but also set apart from the merits of the many. Indeed, revelations of divine grace shone upon him; and he obtained the fruit of this gift as his reward, because from his youth he judged that the yoke of the word must be taken up, so that his sins should not have to be dragged along by a long rope.

This young man, who did good by taking up the yoke of the word in his youth, is not yet perfect, since he is still quite young; but by separating himself from the talk of his peers, which so often corrupts good morals, and by wishing to flee the contagion of sinners, he can be understood to sit alone and keep silent in this sense: so as not to slip through the pliancy of his inexperienced age, but to attend to the precepts of the elders, the oracles of the prophets and the teachings of the apostles. He deserves praise for this, that he wishes first to learn what ought to be said rather than

to utter what he thinks before he learns to speak, fearing that in much speaking he may incur sin. That is why I think the philosopher Pythagoras too, imitating this prophetic young man, founded his school in such a way that his disciples, by not speaking for five years, might learn to speak through so long a silence — especially as there is no doubt that David, who says, I said, I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue; I have set a guard on my mouth, lived in an earlier age than Pythagoras. And because perhaps at some time he had said something

rather incautiously, he afterwards asked God to set a guard on his mouth. And who does not know that Isaiah too was earlier than the Pythagoreans? When he heard, Cry out, he did not cry out before he heard what he ought to cry; for he answered: What shall I cry? Then it was said to him: All flesh is grass, but the word of the Lord endures for ever; and he cried out with a prophetic voice.

Both young men, then, are to be praised: the one, however, for seriousness, the other for caution. The one is content with himself and never lonely when alone; the other adopts the discipline of silence, so fitting for a slippery age, not yet having enough within himself and fearing to trust himself to others, yet seeking from his youth to gather what will profit both himself and his neighbours in old age, so that it may not be said to him: What you did not gather in youth, how will you find in old age?

Such a one, then, if he sits in the council of the elders, will lay his hand upon his mouth, so that by listening he may gather sayings to keep for himself for a riper age: just as Mary, when she heard the words of Christ, pondered them all in her heart; just as John, when he leaned his head on the breast of the Lord Jesus, drank in the deep secrets of wisdom.

Here is a young man for you who corrected his way in youth! He was a fisherman with his brother; he saw the Lord Jesus while he was folding his nets, and heard him say: Come, I will make you fishers of men; and leaving his nets and his father he followed him. He had begun to run the way of the world, but when he heard the command he abandoned the life of the world and followed Christ. He proved that a young man corrects his way by keeping the words of Christ, and said to him: Let us love your breasts more than wine — yet he drank in such a way that he was not swallowed up by the wine, but drew gladness of heart from its grace and did not stagger with bodily drunkenness.

Then, drinking this wine, he opened his eyes and saw the straight way; he left the crooked ways, saying: Uprightness has loved you, that is: 'Winding paths do not follow you; only the path of righteousness can reach you.' For whoever loves righteousness does not turn away from Christ; for how could an innocent conscience fear the judge of the just and the rewarder of merits?

In this young man, then, behold the great mysteries which holy Solomon, filled with the Spirit of the Lord, sang forth in the Song of Songs. Picture the Lord Jesus reclining at the banquet and John leaning on his breast, and the others marvelling that a servant should lean upon his master, that sinful flesh should recline upon the temple of the Word, that a soul bound in the chains of the flesh should search out the hall of the divine

fullness. To the others marvelling at this, John's soul answers: I am dark and comely, daughters of Jerusalem — dark through guilt, comely through grace. The flesh too says: I am dark and comely — dark with the dust of the world which I gathered in the contest, comely with the spiritual oil with which I wiped away the dust and grime of this world; dark through vice, but now comely through the washing that has cleansed every sin. I am dark because I have sinned, comely because Christ now loves me: he had banished me in Eve, but he took me back from the Virgin, he took me up from Mary.

The synagogue says it too, for many think that her mysteries are expressed in this passage. When she saw herself now rejected because of the impiety of the whole people, she nevertheless consoled herself, because she saw that Christ himself was from her people, and that Peter, John and James were clinging to Christ, and because she had the oracles entrusted to her; and so she said: I am dark and comely, daughters of Jerusalem — dark through unbelief,

comely through the law; dark through my fall, comely because the sun loved me and I was the first to be made the congregation of God. Do not shun me because I am dark; I am dark because the sun of righteousness, which used to give me light before, has left me. I have lost the colour of my face; the sight of my eyes, with which I once saw the sun, has grown dim; I walk in darkness because I do not know the day of Christ. Yet do not despise me, for he who has left me can look upon me again and have mercy once more.

He is wont to gather the scattered, to seek out the deserted, to gather up the destitute.' All you tribes of Israel, come together; look upon me, once comely, now forsaken. Do not look at me because I have been darkened — that is, do not look only at the fact that I have been darkened. The sun has not looked upon me, and that is why I have been darkened. But the sun shines on the just and the unjust: on the just by grace, on the unjust by mercy, granting the former the reward of their merits and forgiving the latter their sins. And it did not shine on the gentiles before; now it shines, now he rises for them who used to rise for me; he who has forgiven them will forgive me too.

Do not think, because I have been darkened, that the sun has utterly abandoned me and no longer looks upon me, that he will not seek out one who is sick. He has turned his eyes away from me because I did not keep his commandments; he will be reconciled when he sees my repentance for my sins. The sun did not see me because I did not receive him when he came; I did not open the windows for the light of life to come in. When I open them, he who came to enlighten the whole world will enlighten my eyes, so that even those who do not see may see.

The sons of my mother fought against me; they made me keeper in the vineyards: my own vineyard I have not kept. Some think this is said of those who bind the synagogue to the precepts of the law, so that she should keep the law and guard her vineyard, which she was unable to keep; indeed, he watched over it so that it might produce grapes, but it produced thorns. And as to what this vineyard is, David comes to bear witness to us, saying: You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it. The apostles too can be the sons of her mother,

for they truly assailed the synagogue, saying, Behold, we turn to the gentiles, and they began to sow the word of God among the nations. The prophets too can be understood, who by urging and warning the synagogue to keep her vineyard achieved nothing. For she, who ought to have borne rich fruits of virtue, produced the thorns of wickedness. And so she confesses that she could not keep her people, and it is fitting that she seeks too late to hold him whom she lost while she held him — very unlike the one who says: I found him whom my soul loved; I held him and will not let him go.

In short, the one invites the bridegroom into her garden, while this one, asking where he pastures his flock, says to him: Tell me, you whom my soul loved. Why do you say 'whom my soul loved' and not 'whom it loves'? Why did you let go of the one you held? You loved him through the faith of the fathers; you lost him through unbelief. You held him with the bonds of love; you lost him by the long rope of faithlessness. That is why you do not know where he pastures, where he abides; for if you knew, you would not ask.

For you say: Where do you pasture, where do you abide at noon? You know that noon is the Church which holds Christ, and do you seek him by night? Tell me, O Christ, she says; answer me at least for this reason, that you were once dear and beloved to me. Even if I have lost the privilege of so great a love, still, as one who is kind, answer me: Where do you pasture, where do you abide? You have left me, gone off to the gentiles, withdrawn far from me, and become nearer to those from whom you were far. But you have been brought near to them because they believed in your blood;

you have withdrawn from me because I did not receive your cross as the redemption of the world but as the condemnation of a guilty man. But those who received you as the author of salvation are at noon; for them you shine, for them you gleam, for them your grace is warm like the noonday. To me you were morning while I still believed, but I did not believe fully, because I was not found at noon like Joseph with his brothers, who dined at noon. You have become noon for those who feed on your riches and hope in you. Therefore, as David said, you will bring forth their righteousness as the light and their judgment as the noonday.

So you seek like a stranger, you who were nearest; like a poor woman, you who were rich. You wish to follow, you who used to go before; and would that you might at least follow those whom you ought to have gone before! You long to be a hired servant, you who once gathered in hired servants; certainly these are the words of a hired servant saying: lest I become like one veiled beside the flocks of your companions. You who once received proselytes from the gentiles now wish yourself to be received among the nations as a proselyte and gathered in like a stranger.

Jesus answers: Unless you know yourself, fair among women. What is it to know oneself, except for each to know that man was made in the image and likeness of God, capable of reason, and that he ought to cultivate his land like a good farmer with the plough, as it were, and the pruning hook of wisdom, so that hard ground may be broken up and rank growth cut back, and that he ought to govern the lower part of himself by the rule of the mind?

That is why it is also written in the Law: Take heed to yourself, lest a hidden word arise in your heart. Take heed to yourself, it says — certainly not to your money, not to your possessions, not to the strength of your body, but to your soul and your mind, from which all counsels, deeds and thoughts flow. Take heed to yourself, then, there where you know your better self to be. 'Know yourself': the gentiles ascribe this to Pythian Apollo, as if he were the author of the saying, though they have taken it from what is ours and transferred it to their own, and Moses, who wrote the book of Deuteronomy, lived long before the philosophers who made these things up.

That is why Solomon too, following the divine oracle, wrote in the Song of Songs: Unless you know yourself, fair among women. That is: unless you recognize yourself as mortal and rational, and quickly confess your sins, quickly declare your iniquities so as to be justified; unless you turn back and first accuse your own offences, the day of death comes, and then there is no longer any remedy of conversion;

you are overtaken while you are not thinking of it. Light your torch before the bridegroom's door is shut against you, for he is not wont to wait long for the negligent. Unless you know yourself, he says, fair among women, and say: I am dark and comely — dark because I have sinned, but comely because I am loved, because I am the seed of Abraham, a chosen race, beloved of God — the grace of the fathers will profit you nothing; for God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham.

And elsewhere in the gospel you have read that the devil bound a daughter of Abraham with the chains of his wickedness, and the Lord loosed her on the sabbath day. Unless, then, you know yourself, it will profit you nothing even if you say, 'I am a daughter of Abraham', you who do not believe, who do not correct your error. Abraham indeed is saved, but nobility of descent will not help you unless faith preserves you. Do not let the promise given to the fathers deceive you. I do not respect a man's person, I do not respect the privilege of descent, unless I see a nobility of conduct befitting that descent, so that the choice of a righteous race may come about.

If you know yourself and recognize that you are liable to sin, you must go out in the footsteps of the flocks. So go out barefoot and feed your kids by the tents of the shepherds. The one who is without sin feeds lambs, feeds sheep; but she who is liable to sin feeds the kids, which are on the left, for she cannot be at the right hand of the Good Shepherd. Let her rather follow the one who says to Peter: Get behind me, Satan. By following, Peter earned a place at the right hand, and so it is said to him: Feed my lambs. But where should she go out to? Listen: to the tents, it says, of the shepherds, that is, to the nations, to the dispersion.

That is why he said: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered, so that the whole world might be filled with the flock of Christ. This means that the synagogue will be saved when it too has joined itself to this dispersion that has filled the world, for the tents of the shepherds are the kingdoms of the earth. And so the prophet David, announcing that the nations would believe, says: Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God. So let the younger man know himself, so that he may correct his way.

But you say: 'How can the younger man know his way so as to correct it, when the prophet says: There are three things impossible for me to understand, and a fourth that I do not know: the tracks of an eagle in flight, the way of a serpent on a rock, the paths of a ship tossing on the sea, and the ways of a man in his youth? If Solomon admits that he does not know the ways of a man in his youth, how can the younger man know them?'

The answer will be that the ways of a man in his youth that cannot be known are the ones like the way of a serpent on a rock, the paths of a tossing ship, and the tracks of an eagle in flight, which has sharp talons, flies above the clouds, roams the air and kills fish in the sea. And yet this fourth thing is not impossible as those three are. For the Lord knows those who are his, and he wants each one to know himself, wants the people of God to know itself.

But granted that the ways of those who go astray are not known, as the Lord says: I do not know you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity. This younger man, however, who is able to correct his way, may be younger in age but not in character, and may have an old man's understanding in the first flower of his youth. Of such it says: Understanding is grey hair for men, that is, for those who have maturity and weight of counsel. Hence it is also said to Jeremiah: Do not say, I am young. And he certainly was

young in age, but God forbids him to call himself young, since he had a riper prudence. Daniel, while still a boy, received the spirit that made him worthy of the first fruits of old age, so that he could refute the elders, though he was not their senior in years but in grace. For in him there was the old age of a spotless life, and that saying of David fits him well: I have understood more than the elders. And so the divine oracle declared of him, as of a man of seasoned counsel and an old man's knowledge: Who is wiser than Daniel?

10. Now let us consider whether it is possible for the younger man to correct his way or not. If it is not, then the prophet is lying; but since he does not lie, it is possible. Yet it is possible in such a way that what seems impossible becomes possible if the younger man keeps the words of God, while if he does not keep them, it is impossible. Hence that saying in the Gospel: It is

easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. However strongly he declared this impossible, we understand it to be impossible because the rich do not keep God's commandments; but if they keep them, what seemed impossible becomes possible. This is the camel that enters by the narrow way: the way that could not admit him before, while he was covetous, now admits him as he keeps the divine commandments. Moses is chosen as an elder to keep the words of God, because he had kept them. And now those who are entrusted by the Spirit of God with the duty of choosing elders undoubtedly choose, as one of the elders, a young man who corrects his way by keeping the words of God. And if they choose a man of more advanced age, they have certainly not chosen him for his length of years but because he keeps the words of God; and if this is found in a younger man, he too should certainly be chosen. It is clear from this, then, that what is chosen is not length of years but the keeping of God's words. Indeed, Moses himself approved Joshua son of Nun and Caleb, young men, above the rest; in the choice of the land he himself followed their counsel rather than that of many elders, and God preferred it.

So too that saying of Jacob which we mentioned above, God who has fed me from my youth, is shown to have been said of one who took up the yoke of the word in his youth, and, withdrawing from Esau and those like him, sat alone, waiting within himself for the time when he could bring forth speech with discipline. For this reason he was given spiritual nourishment, still young in years but a veteran in counsel. For it is not fitting for us to believe that so great a patriarch [?] spoke of bodily food when he said, God who has fed me from my youth, since he did not long even for bodily bread when he said: If the Lord God is with me and gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear, of all that you give me I will give you a tenth. For if our fathers ate spiritual food and drank spiritual drink, how much more was holy Jacob fed on spiritual food!

Another reading is also available here, and it is not far from the truth: the younger one is the people gathered from the nations, which, before it believed in Christ, wandered along a twisting and winding road. It corrects its way in this, that it has kept the words of God which the Jewish people refused to keep, and that is why the Jewish people could not find the way of salvation. Let us consider the next verse as well.

With my whole heart I have sought you; do not drive me away from your commandments. If God drives away each person he thinks should be driven away, let us take care that he does not give an excuse to someone who claims he wanted to follow God and was driven away. First of all, how does the good God drive away someone who follows him, unless that person deserves to be driven away? As the Lord himself says: Foxes have holes, and so he drives him away as a fox. And elsewhere: To everyone who has, more will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away. To whom does he add, except to the one

who seeks him with his whole heart, so that what nature lacks he may acquire by God's working and grace? Solomon is an example: seeking God with his whole heart, he asked for wisdom, and because he requested not royal riches for himself but the gift of divine grace, he was found worthy to receive the discipline of wisdom and was filled with the Spirit of the Lord, so as to know all the commandments. But the one who does not have this, so as to seek the Lord in his heart, and who does do the work of God but does it negligently, falls under a curse, as we read: Cursed is everyone who does the work of God negligently. He is rightly driven away, then, because he deserves the curse, since he defiles and hinders the work that he thought could be carried out negligently.

Let us consider, then, whether it is kindness to remove the negligent man from the work or to keep him on, and let us take an illustration of this from other crafts. A physician is treating a sick man, but through the physician's negligence and sloth the poison of the wound spreads. How much better, then, to remove a physician of this kind, who wastes time while the wounded man feels no improvement, so that the task of treatment may be handed over to a physician who can help the sick man more quickly through his diligence! Is not the one who dismisses a man who achieves nothing more merciful than the one who keeps him on, to the peril of the sick man?

Imagine someone put in charge of builders, or of weavers, who has to bring the whole work to completion. Which seems to you more commendable? Is it the one who applies himself to it diligently, and, if he happens to notice that one of the men at work on building a house is careless, dismisses him, believing it better not to build at all than to see the building fall apart with gaping cracks, and puts in his place someone who will build with diligence? Likewise, will you not commend the overseer of a weaving shop who dismisses the negligent and replaces them with diligent workers, so that long carelessness does not ruin the weaving, more than one who lets the idle persist in their negligence?

Now turn to those who build up the commandments, weave the law, and have received the soul of each person to heal. If one of them builds the house of God with justice, weaves the garment with diligence, and heals the soul with grace, does he not do a good work?

But if someone careless and slack occupies the place of the spiritual builder, weaver, or physician, as high priest, as presbyter, as minister of the sacred altar, is it not better that no one should take on a charge he cannot fulfil, than that he should take it on and then neither discharge the office he has assumed with vigour himself, and also rob another of the place, who could guard it diligently? And what of the fact that the man who is dismissed for his slackness is himself being looked after, so that he does not incur still more guilt?

Let us consider what it means to be driven away. For we read: Like the wounded sleeping, cast down in the tombs, whom you remember no more, and indeed they have been driven away from your hand. Let us observe, then, whom he drives away, wounded and cast down in the tombs, those he will remember no more. These are the ones who are driven away from God's commandments. To the sinner God said: Why do you recite my statutes? And because they are driven away from the commandments, they are driven away from God's hand. And he took good care that no one should seem to be snatched from

God's hand, since no one can snatch anyone from God's hand. So whoever is deprived of the duty or grace of an office he has received is not snatched away but cast out, as the Lord Jesus said to Jerusalem: How often I wanted to gather your children, and you would not! Behold, your house will be left to you desolate. He took away from them their sanctuary, the altar of incense and the shrine of prayer, the mercy seat, the altar of sacrifices, the ministries of priests and Levites. And yet, though all these things that they had under the commandments of the law had been taken away, the apostle says: Has God rejected his inheritance? He has not rejected it, he says; rather, he has shut up all things in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all.

There are, then, some who are driven away from the commandments for a time for mercy's sake, just as those who are vomited out are also being cared for. For just as what ought to be vomited up grows more sour if it stays in the body, so the one who ought to be shut out, if he is kept in and does not correct himself, ulcerates the whole body. So the faithful and true witness rightly says to the angel of Laodicea: I know your works, that you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, I will begin to vomit you out of my mouth. He openly condemns negligence with a heavier judgement than ignorance. For the cold one is the one who does not know the faith; the hot one is the one set on fire by the fervour of the Holy Spirit.

So for one who lacks the warmth of faith it would have been more bearable never to have received the faith than to have neglected it. For the lukewarm is worse than the cold, like the Jew, who thinks he has a faith he does not have. How much more bearable is the case of the Gentile, who can say, 'I did not know the law, I did not hear the prophets, and so I did not believe,' than that of the one who read everything that should have led him to believe that Jesus would come, and did not believe! Neither of them, indeed, is excused, neither the one who read nor the one who refused to read; but the one who denied what he had read sins more than the one who did not do works he did not know he ought to do.

How great is the grace of faith and righteousness, that the one who holds fast to the faith and practises the works of righteousness should be in the mouth of God [?]; and how much is lost by the one whom the Lord Jesus has vomited out of his mouth and cast out of his inmost being! Yet how loving he is, who both keeps the just in his mouth and does not vomit out the unjust until he has warned them that they will be vomited out, so that, turned back by such a warning, they may at least do something worthy enough that they are not vomited out! Now let us consider the third little verse.

I have hidden your words in my heart, it says, so that I may not sin against you. This is why it is good to hide the mystery of a king; for whoever thinks that the secret mysteries entrusted to him should be made known to the unworthy sins against God. So the danger lies not only in saying what is false but also in saying what is true, if one imparts it to those to whom one ought not.

This fault takes four forms: flattery, greed, boasting, or careless talkativeness. When someone wants to flatter, he pours out the mystery to the person he is speaking to. Some, out of eagerness for gain, go after the reward of betrayal, selling by their speech what should be covered in silence. Others, to seem to know more and to show off their knowledge, disclose what they ought to conceal. Many, speaking without forethought, let slip a word they cannot take back. That is why a serious man is praised, and the man who hides his words does not babble idly,

like the apostle Paul, who knew what to say to each person and when he should say what. Hence he says to the Corinthians: I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able to take it, and even now you are not able. So he sees them only in passing, but stays among the Ephesians, because a great door had been opened to him to make known the mystery of Christ to the Gentiles. So too Solomon teaches that there is a time to speak.
But above all the Lord Jesus makes this plain in his Gospel, when he says that the kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field. Certainly not gold, nor silver, nor money can be compared

to the kingdom of heaven, but the words of the Lord, pure words, silver tried in the fire, by which the kingdom itself is gained. So when a man finds this treasure of wisdom and knowledge hidden in the field in which the words of the heavenly scriptures are planted, he hides it in his heart and does not make it known, knowing that if he makes God's treasure known to the Babylonians he will incur grave guilt, so that it will be said to him in the words of the prophet: They will take some of your offspring and make them eunuchs in the king's house. This signifies that the one who betrays the divine mysteries cannot have descendants for his soul or a seedbed of merits.

Beware, then, of betraying your riches to the faithless; even if they feign friendship, do not open the inner rooms of your house to them. Do not unlock the royal treasuries, which the Babylonians must not know about, lest they come and carry off your descendants and cut down the seedbed of virtue. This is what the Lord also says in the Gospel: Do not throw your pearls before swine.

So he does well who hides the words of the Lord in his heart, as the prophet David hid them, and as Mary did, who kept all the words of the Lord Jesus in her heart. For if it is good for a man to hide his own words, how much more ought we to cover the word of God in the bosom of our heart, how much more ought we to hide it!
In the fourth verse he says: Blessed are you, O Lord; teach me your statutes. For not everyone who says, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of God.

So this man, who has corrected his way from his youth, kept the words of God, sought the Lord his God with his whole heart, not been driven away from God's commandments, been found worthy to be entrusted with the secrets of wisdom, and hidden them in his heart so as not to sin against God, now gives thanks as one who possesses the words of God, saying: Blessed are you, O Lord. And he longs to have the Lord himself as his teacher, desiring to know the secrets of the law and how it is to be interpreted, such as: If you buy a Hebrew servant and he serves you for six years, and the rest, which are introduced by the words: These are the statutes that you shall set before the children of Israel. These things he seeks to learn from the Lord, things that men could not teach unless God had first taught them.

Once the apostles had learned these things from Christ, the Church says: The king has brought me into his chamber, that is, into that secret place of his where the treasures of his knowledge and understanding are. That is why you are told: When you pray, go into your room, which signifies the secret place of the mind and soul. Into this chamber of statutes the bride asked to be brought, after she had run in pursuit of the fragrance of the ointment, which always flows and never runs out.

So in the fifth verse the prophet, as one who has been taught the statutes, says: With my lips I have declared all the judgements of your mouth. Then how can he say elsewhere: Your judgements are like a great deep? How can the apostle say: O the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgements, and how inscrutable his ways!

For who has known the mind of the Lord? If his judgements are unsearchable, how then, says the prophet, have I declared all the judgements of your mouth? But perhaps the judgements of God are not the same as the judgements of his mouth. If they are different, it is rightly said: Who will be like your thoughts? And his judgements are unsearchable for this reason, that we know in part and prophesy in part. But what if no one says this except Christ, who can say: I and the Father are one?

Still, let us draw a distinction, and not fear that venerable Scripture contradicts itself with apparently opposing statements. Let us note that he did not say, 'the judgements of his mouth are like a great deep,' but said 'your judgements'; nor did the apostle write, 'the unsearchable judgements of his mouth,' but 'his unsearchable judgements.' For we can take the judgements of God to be

those hidden ones that he has not revealed to us, and the judgements of his mouth to be those he has announced and spoken through the mouth of the prophets. For the prophet is understood as the mouth of God; he is told, Cry out, and he says, What shall I cry? And he was inspired to say: All flesh is grass. In saying this he certainly performed the office of God's mouth, because he spoke God's judgement. So the prophetic oracles are no longer the deep itself, yet they too are like a deep, since no one in heaven or on earth could open the book except Christ. Now let us come to the sixth verse.

In the way of your testimonies I have delighted as in all riches. Some delight in gold, some in silver, some in clothes, some in property, vineyards, olive groves and crops, some in works of painting and marble; in short, each person takes his delight in different things. The spiritual man delights in the way of the heavenly testimonies as one who possesses a whole inheritance, rich in all things, as the apostle says: I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God that was given you in Christ Jesus, that in everything you have been made rich in him, in all speech and in all knowledge.

The Corinthians made such progress through the apostle's teaching that those who before could only drink milk like little children afterwards abounded in all the riches of knowledge and speech. David, then, delighted in all the riches of understanding, knowledge and wisdom, and in every deed of good works. And if anyone now, intent on divine things, drinks in that threefold discipline of wisdom, the contemplative, the practical and the logical, he will be the more beautiful for his good zeal in acquiring knowledge, holding the grace of putting rational and moral teaching into practice. Whoever has come to understand the riddles of the prophets through the revelation of God's Spirit, has grasped the depth of the Gospel in its works and counsels, and has taken note of the moral teaching in the apostle's words, will take abundant pleasure, as one rich in all things.

And because bodily pleasure is sweet, it is not set beside spiritual things as though equal in the quality of its grace, but is brought in as a witness to their sweetness, since the apostle too teaches that the invisible and eternal things of God are understood by us through the things that have been made. In the Song of Songs too we have it written: I have likened you, my love, to my mare among Pharaoh's chariots.

Here, when the Church is likened to the running of swift horses, we can gauge how rich her grace is. So do not take this as a single mare belonging to a rich king, but in a general sense, for horses as a whole, just as we often say, 'What is his sheep like?' meaning a flock of sheep. Pharaoh, then, being a most powerful and very wealthy king, had powerful horses, and so Scripture speaks of 'Pharaoh's chariots' as the most powerful force for use in war and support in battle.

Indeed, it was with these chariots that Pharaoh easily overtook the fleeing Hebrews. Just as horses yoked together pull the chariot in harmony, patiently accept the yoke, bear their load gracefully and grow tame by taking on that yoke, so too the assembly of the nations, untamed in its pagan ways, used to toss and buck. But when it took on the yoke of him who says, Take my yoke, for it is light, and my burden, for it is sweet, and the bride of Christ began to be raised high by the harmony and gentleness of the peoples and to be carried around the whole world, she was swept up above the world like a chariot drawn by swift horses and ascended to the bridegroom.

Then in the later parts of the Song she also says: I have made you like the chariots of Aminadab. The Church has many chariots within her, all of which the Lord guides with spiritual reins; and a single soul

has many thoughts, which the rein of the Lord holds back and calls back, so that this chariot of ours is not carried over some precipice. The name Aminadab means 'father of good pleasure'. In Numbers we read that his son was Nahshon, leader of the people. Understand who he is from the meaning of his name, 'serpent-like', and you will recognize this if you recall that the one who redeemed you hung on the wood like a serpent.

So the soul is God's chariot, so that its anger, lust and fear, and all worldly desires, may be reined in. The Church too is God's chariot, and it must be steered by the reins of Christ, so that the stirrings and quarrels of different peoples do not throw it into disorder. Christ is also rightly understood in that Nahshon, because the rod of Aaron, turned into a serpent, devoured the serpents of Egypt. Let us, then, have these riches and take our delight in them, so that rational horses may run for us and we may dwell on their precepts.

And so he says: I will exercise myself in your commandments, and I will consider your ways. For whoever exercises himself in the words of the apostles comes to know the commandments of the Lord Jesus and considers his ways. The end of those ways is Christ, who says: I am the way.

And I will meditate on your righteous decrees; I will not forget your words. This passage reminds us that we ought to keep the Scriptures in mind, and to meditate on his righteous decrees not only in speech but also by imitating them in deed. For it is not those who argue about the law and do not do what the law requires who are justified, but the doers of the law.
III. THE LETTER GIMEL
The third letter among the Hebrews is Gimel, which in Latin means "recompense". And indeed this is shown at once in the very first verse.

Recompense, he says, your servant. How is it that David himself said earlier: Do not repay us according to our sins, nor requite us according to our iniquities, and here asks for recompense? The former seems to be the voice of a sinner; this is the voice of one with a good conscience, asking for the rewards of good works. From this we can also understand that this psalm is composed in the person of him who, born of a virgin for the redemption of the whole world, confidently claims to sit at the right hand of the Father, as he himself says: From now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of power.

Yet it is neither out of place nor arrogant for David to ask the Lord his God for a reward for his outstanding labours: it is the privilege of faith and righteousness to lay claim to a reward from the Lord's favour. Peter, after all, is rebuked because, as he walked on the waves, he doubted with human feeling instead of being bold with apostolic authority. In the Gospel too we are taught to have faith and not to hesitate over doing things that are beyond human power. Rightly, then, did David in the earlier passages,

as one still imperfect, shrink from and turn away from being repaid according to his sins. But in this psalm, which comes later, as one now established by progress in virtue, he prays to be recompensed according to his contests of faith and works. So too Paul, who had earlier said: I am not worthy to be called an apostle, afterwards says: There is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day, and not only to me but also to all who love his coming. The apostle promises it to himself, while David here still prays more modestly. And this is surely a mark not of insolent arrogance but of an innocent conscience: to ask a reward from the one you have served. For to despair of the reward breeds sloth, while to hope for it spurs us to labour.

Ask confidently, then, if your merits support you, so that by asking for such things you may labour the more zealously and become more worthy of what you ask. What athlete would go down into the stadium if he despaired of the crown? Or what victor would give offence by claiming it? Testing produces hope, and hope confidence. Such, then, is the prayer of the righteous; the Lord delights in such a petition, that you should use authority in proportion to the purity of your conscience.

Yet, so that the petition might seem less arrogant, he aptly added: your servant. In this there is both the grace of humility and the reward of service. For whoever was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord's freedman; why should he not count on the Lord's favour, since he was bought with such precious blood? It is a great thing for you to be called my servant, as is said to a servant. If anyone, then, is a servant and serves the Lord well, and does nothing as a slave of sin, but is the kind who says: I am an unprofitable servant; I have done what I ought to have done, he rightly says: Recompense your servant.

Glorious is the service in which Christ too served for our sake. Blessed is the service in which you too serve, but only if the adversary can claim nothing of your service for himself. Christ, then, loves the freedom of a good little servant; indeed in the Song of Songs he says: How beautiful your cheeks have become, like a turtledove's, your neck like strings of ornaments! The face is freer where there is a conscience of chastity, and to bear the yoke of Christ is sweet if you think of it as ornaments for your neck, not burdens.

So lift up your eyes always to the Lord your God, and seek God, that you may find him. Raise your neck: you are wearing ornaments, not chains. Even dumb animals delight in ornaments and seem to feel that they are being decked out rather than tied up. Let your cheeks, like a turtledove's, display the marks of modesty; let the ornaments of your neck lift up the confidence of freedom. For the yoke of Christ is light, and so the neck is not weighed down by it but lifted up.

We will make you, he says, likenesses of gold with studs of silver, while the king is at his reclining. For of those who belong to the law and the prophets, only a few had believed in the glory of the Lord Jesus before; but his inheritance, spread abroad among the peoples, was proved the more fully the more often it was tested:

for the frequent persecutions of the Church have, through their victories, brought forth for us the titles of the martyrdom of the righteous. And so, like good gold, the Church suffers no loss when it is burned, but rather its brightness increases, until Christ comes into his kingdom and lays his head to rest on the faith of the Church. When he came to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, he had nowhere to lay his head; but now faith already gives off its fragrance, and so the Church says: My nard has given forth its fragrance. And she says it with confidence, awaiting her recompense.

The ointment of grace is fragrant, from which the virgin brought forth and the Lord Jesus took on the mystery of the incarnation. A bundle of myrrh-drops, she says, is my kinsman; a cluster of Cyprus is my brother to me. He rests between my breasts. For in taking a body the Lord Jesus bound himself with the bonds of love, and bound himself not only to our members and our natural sufferings but even to the cross; and therefore, like a cluster, he rests in the faith and the moral grace of the Church.

Nard of Cyprus is my kinsman, in the vineyards of Engedi. If we ask about the place, it belongs to a certain region in which balsam is produced [for there is also a place of that name in Judea]; if we ask about the meaning, Engedi means "temptation" in Latin. In those vineyards, then, there is a tree which, if anyone pierces it, gives off ointment; this is the fruit of the tree. If the tree is not cut, it does not give off such fragrance and scent; but when it has been pierced by the craftsman's hand, it drips a tear. So too Christ, crucified on that tree of temptation, wept over the people to wash away our sins, and poured forth ointment from the depths of his mercy, saying: Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.

Then, on the tree, he was pierced with the lance, and there came out of him blood and water, sweeter than any ointment, a victim acceptable to God, pouring out the fragrance of sanctification over the whole world; and as balsam comes out of a tree, so power came out of his body. Hence he says: I perceive that power has gone out from me. That is why opobalsam is so called, as something pressed out, because when the tree is pierced, the balsam bursts out through the hole of the puncture. So Jesus, when he was pierced, poured out the fragrance of the forgiveness of sins and of redemption. For he was also confined, when, being the Word, he was made man.

And he became poor, though he was rich, so that we might be made rich by his poverty. He was powerful, and he let himself be despised, so that Herod scorned him and mocked him. He shook the earth, and he hung fixed to the tree. He covered the sky with darkness, he crucified the world, and he was crucified. He bowed his head, and the Word went forth. He was emptied, and he filled all things. God descended, man ascended; the Word was made flesh, so that the flesh might claim for itself the throne of the Word at the right hand of God. There was a wound, and ointment flowed; the beetle was heard, and God was recognized.

Christ answers her: Behold, you are good, my neighbour; behold, you are good. Because the Church had come to know the mystery and was preaching the Lord Jesus crucified for the redemption of the whole world, she deserves to hear: "Behold, you are good. You who call me good are good yourself, and because you have seen the beauty of my glory, you yourself are beautiful and comely." And what does it mean for Christ to say "you are good" or "you are comely", if not that saying of the Gospel: Take heart, daughter; your sins are forgiven you?

So whoever has had his sins forgiven by Christ rightly says: Recompense your servant; I shall live and keep your words. He has nothing to despair of in the recompense, because the Lord Jesus came to save the world, not to destroy it; and so he forgets injury and remembers grace, as he himself testifies in the prophetic book, saying: I, I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them.
