But you, remember, and let us go to judgement together; declare your iniquities, that you may be justified. Whoever, then, declares his iniquities to God is justified, and whoever is justified does not fear recompense but asks for it; and whoever does not fear recompense will live.

But why did he say "I shall live" and not "I live"? Because this life, which is set in the place of death, is not the place of reward. The prophet grieves that he has been brought down into the dust of death; the apostle longs to be set free from this body of death. And do we think the prophet is flattering himself about this life? Everything here is full of death. Death comes in through the window; it comes in through your mouth, unless the Lord sets a guard on your mouth;

for sin is born of much talking. Read the commandments of the law and you will find it written that a living person who touches a dead one is defiled. How many dead we touch, among how many dead we move! That is why the author of life says to you: Leave the dead to bury their own dead; that is why it is said to you elsewhere: Wake up, you who sleep, and rise from the dead. How could it be said to you "rise from the dead" unless you were living among the dead? Suppose you are clean of dead works, of the filth of sin: how are you clean, when you are in the body of death, when you live among the tombs of the dead? Peter had to speak to the dead so that they might come out of their tombs.

We need purification, then, because we have touched the dead. The law commands us to be cleansed: who is so great as to be above the law? Even the Nazirite, holy to God, it declares unclean if he touches a dead body. So he shaves his head and lays aside his hair as unholy, and prays again to be heard, since before, because he had touched a dead body, he could not obtain what he prayed for. He counted those days as void of reason, because he had drawn near to what is void of reason. So he lays aside the dead and superfluous growth of his head, that he may be reconciled to Christ. If, then, the Nazirite is purified, we too must be purified.

We have all touched the dead. For who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will dare to say that he is clean of sins? There may perhaps be someone who has not sinned in speech, though such a person is rare, of whom God might say, as he did of holy Job: He did not sin with his lips. Yet even he could not always keep the thoughts of his heart clean; the devil thrusts himself into the human heart.

Suppose someone has fenced in his heart with a guard always ready and wakeful: still he lives in the midst of sinners, and he too needs to be purified. That is why, when Isaiah had said: Woe is me, for I have unclean lips and I live among a people with unclean lips, at once one of the Seraphim came down and touched his lips with a coal, to cleanse his unclean lips.

There is not just one baptism. One is the baptism that the Church confers here through water and the Holy Spirit, with which catechumens must be baptized. There is also another baptism, of which the Lord Jesus says: I have a baptism to be baptized with, which you do not know. And yet he had certainly already been baptized in the Jordan, as the earlier passages make clear;

but let this be the baptism of suffering, by which each person is cleansed even in his own blood. There is also a baptism at the entrance of paradise, which did not exist before. But after the sinner was shut out, there came to be the fiery sword which God set there, which did not exist before, when there was no sin. Guilt began, and this baptism began, to purify those who wished to return to paradise, so that once they had returned they might say: We have passed through fire and water. Here through water, there through fire: through water, that sins may be washed away; through fire, that they may be burned away. But, what is harder, we must endure fire both here and there.

Who is it that baptizes in this fire? Not a presbyter, not a bishop, not John, who says: I baptize you for repentance; not an angel, not an archangel, not dominions, not powers, but he of whom John says: He who comes after me is mightier than I; I am not worthy to carry his sandals. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire. His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor thoroughly and will gather

his wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire. The Lord himself testifies that this was not said of the baptism administered by the priests of the Church, since this baptism will take place after the end of the age, when angels are sent to separate the good from the wicked, when iniquity will be burned away in the furnace of fire, so that in the kingdom of God the righteous may shine like the sun itself in the kingdom of their Father. And even if someone is a saint, like Peter or like John, he is baptized with this fire.

So the great Baptist will come (for so I call him, as Gabriel called him when he said: He will be great). He will see many standing before the entrance of paradise; he will wave the turning sword; he will say to those on the right, who have no grave sins: "Enter, you who are confident, you who do not fear the fire. I had already told you beforehand: Behold, I come like fire; and through Ezekiel I had said: Behold, I will go to Jerusalem and blow on you in the fire of my wrath, so that you may melt away from the lead and the iron."

Let the consuming fire come [?], then, to burn up in us the lead of iniquity and the iron of sin, and make us pure gold. Let it burn my inmost being and my heart, so that I may think what is good and desire what belongs to chastity. But since one who has been purged here must be purified again there, may it purify us there too, when the Lord says: "Enter into my rest", so that each of us, scorched by that flaming sword but not burned up, may enter into that delightful paradise and give thanks to his Lord, saying: You have brought us into refreshment. Whoever, then, has passed through the fire enters into rest; he passes from material and worldly things to things incorruptible and everlasting.

This fire, by which sins are burned away (not deliberate sins but accidental ones), is one thing: the Lord Jesus has prepared it for his servants, to cleanse them from this sojourn of ours, which is mingled with the dead. That fire is another, which he has assigned to the devil and his angels, of which he says: Enter into the eternal fire; in it that rich man was burning who begged that a drop of moisture might fall on him from Lazarus' finger. But Lazarus, reclining in Abraham's bosom, was enjoying eternal life, which the prophet promises himself when he says: I shall live and keep your words. He says "I shall live" as one who is not yet living; for here we live in shadow.

So this life in the body is a shadow and an image of life, not the truth; indeed, man walks about in an image, and we dwell in the land of the shadow of death. But if anyone does not fix the eyes of his mind on earthly things but raises them to spiritual things, so that he can say: The spirit before our face is Christ the Lord, he will be worthy to say: In his shadow we shall live. For Christ is life, and so whoever lives in the shadow of Christ is in the shadow of life; and rightly the Lord's saint says elsewhere: Protect me in the shadow of your wings.

So all, even the saints, are in shadow as long as they are in the body: they do not see perfectly, they do not know perfectly but only in part. Paul himself says: For we know in part. He himself, the chosen vessel, whose eyes Christ restored and enlightened by his grace, saw not face to face but through a mirror. And David asks that his eyes be unveiled,

so that the shadow might be taken away which hindered the full sight of his eyes. And who would doubt that this is the land of the dead, when the saint himself says: I will please the Lord in the land of the living? For no one can please him perfectly here, where, even if it were possible for someone to have no sins of his own, he still, by living in this very land of the dead, needs a purification to free him from the contagion of this land.

Here, then, we live in shadow, and therefore we keep the words of God in shadow. To use an example: we were certainly once under the shadow of the law, when we kept new moons and sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come, as the Jews still do today, who, not seeing the true sabbath, serve a copy and a shadow. We too, now living according to the Gospel, follow a shadow of the words of God.

Nathanael is seen under the fig tree; David says that he hopes in the shadow of the wings of the Lord Jesus; Zacchaeus climbs a sycamore tree to see Christ. For us too Jesus stretched out his hands, to overshadow the whole world. How are we not in shadow, when we are protected by the covering of his cross? How are we not in shadow, when the Crucified defends us from the malice of the world and the heat of the body? Or do we not know that the Word of God, coming into this world, did not come as the Word, such as he was in the beginning, such as he was with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant? He came on a light cloud, and, being the power of the Most High, he overshadowed Mary, so that he might transform the body of our lowliness to be conformed to the body of his glory.

So, just as he changed his form when he was born of the virgin, so too the words of God appear to us transfigured when they are read in the Gospel, when their likeness is seen in the Scriptures as through a mirror, because the whole truth cannot be grasped here. But when what is perfect has come, they will shine no longer by condescension, no longer in likeness, as things transfigured, but in full and manifest truth.

And do not be troubled that he says "I will keep many words", for whoever has come to know the one Word knows many words. In the one there are many, and in the many there is one. We must show, then, how the one Word is many and the many words are one Word. Nor is it hard to show this, since the apostle has said that he is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, in whom all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created through him and in him. There is one Word, then, that works in each thing, and in working in each, he works all things and in all things. This Word,

the only one with the Father, has spread himself out into many, because from his fullness we have all received. And so, if you look at each of all the things that were created in him, you will see in each one the one Word of all things, in whom we share according to our capacity. In me there is a human word, in another a heavenly word, in many the word of angels; there are some who have the word of dominions and powers. There is a word of righteousness, a word of chastity, a word of prudence, a word of piety, and also a word of virtue. Thus the one Word is many, and the many words are one. Nor is this hard to conceive, since we have read that the spirit of wisdom can do all things.

Thus, just as to one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another the gift of healing in the one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another the spirit of understanding, to another the spirit of fuller counsel, to another the spirit of

fortitude, to another the spirit of piety, and in all there is one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills. There is a spirit of the prophets, there is a spirit of the apostles, and there is also a spirit of craftsmen, as in Bezalel and Oholiab, whom the Lord filled with the divine spirit of wisdom and knowledge and of every art, so that they might make the vestment and the tabernacle and the altar according to the understanding God gave them; and he gave it also to the other wise men, to understand and carry out all the works according to everything the Lord commanded. And so they made things they had neither learned nor seen, according to what the Spirit showed them. To many it seems that the spirit of the apostles is one thing and that of the prophets another, different in each; but it is not different. The Spirit is one, distributing different kinds of powers.

So it should not seem doubtful that to some an apostolic word has been given, to others a prophetic word, to others an angelic word, to others a word of craftsmanship, and yet the Word is one, dividing himself among individuals according to our capacity or according to his own free generosity. This Word, then, who is the head of all, I see here through a mirror, and therefore I cannot keep the words of God here. But when I see his glory with unveiled face, then I shall live, and, living by Life, I shall also keep the divine words.

That is why he says in the second verse: Open my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law. Anyone who asks for his eyes to be opened certainly knows that they are weighed down, for no one calls a physician unless he wants a remedy for his sickness. So this man says to the physician who comes from heaven: Open my eyes. If the eye is only irritated, an eye-salve easily soothes all the pain; but if its sight is veiled by a film of fluid spreading over it, stronger remedies are needed. So it is with the eyes of the body,

and so too the eyes of the soul suffer from a similar ailment, which must grow worse unless the good physician removes that veil and the sort of cloud of hardened fluid that is thought to block, or rather to cover, the mind's gaze, so that it does not see what it used to see. The sickness crept in through the old leaven, because when we first came to the church we did not shed the film of either Gentile or Jewish ways. We did not listen to the teaching of the good physician, who says: Strip off the old man with his deeds, and put on the new, which is renewed in knowledge

after the image of the one who created him. So someone has put a new garment on over the old one instead of stripping the old one off. Then a more serious sickness creeps on, and a long-standing veil weighs down the eyes. No one can take it away: not an angel, not virtues, not dominions, not powers. The veil remains. It hinders the reading and clouds the sight, for, as the apostle says, it is not lifted (that is, by anyone else) unless it has been done away with in Christ. But when such a person turns to the Lord, the veil will be taken away.

So now you know how to remove the veil that lies over the eyes of your heart: turn to the Lord, and the veil will fall. Paul turned at Ananias's blessing; something like scales fell from his eyes, and he who had not seen for three days could see. The eye of his body and the eye of his soul were healed together, because that physician from heaven had shown him the remedy. Of this physician it is written: He sent his word and healed them, and delivered them from all their infirmities. This physician, who cures all infirmities and makes whole peoples well, is not from the earth.

Send this physician, then, Father. Let your Word come and open my eyes. Even the apostles' eyes would have stayed closed if Jesus had not opened them. Indeed, when two of them were going to a village called Emmaus, and he explained the Scriptures and blessed them, their eyes, it says, were opened and they recognized him. So if Jesus had not opened our eyes, no one would have seen; if Jesus had not lifted the veil, the grace of the gospel would have shone on no one. Peter had his eyes closed, John had his closed, James had his closed. On the mountain they were heavy with sleep, but roused by the brightness of the divine majesty, they opened the eyes of their hearts. And because, being in the body, they could not see fully, a cloud overshadowed them, so that the brilliance of heavenly glory would not dazzle the eyes of their bodies.

Who, then, is great enough to open his eyes and see the sacred mysteries of the law, unless Christ shows them to him? Not even Moses was so great. At the Lord's command he threw down his rod, and it became a serpent, and he fled from it; he took hold of the serpent's tail, and it became a rod again. Yet still he did not understand the mystery. By it was declared that the Lord Jesus would come down to earth, empty himself, and allow himself to be laid on the cross and thrown into the tomb; and that, rising from it as the oracles of the law foretold, he would return from serpent to the glory of God and to a royal share in the divine throne.

Let us too, then, take hold of the tail of that crucified serpent, so that we may recognize his royal power. The woman who poured ointment on his feet also held him fast. Moses took hold of the serpent's tail, and his mouth was opened. He would not have spoken about him if the Lord himself had not opened his mouth.

Here David asks for his eyes to be opened, and earlier he said: Who will show us good things? He had been raised under the law and knew that the law has a shadow of the good things to come. He longed to see those good things themselves, no longer through a shadow but with open eyes. He knew that those who served according to the law of Moses were serving a copy and shadow of the heavenly mysteries.

He wanted to grasp the very truth of divine worship, and so, to shake the veil from his eyes, he turned to the Lord and prayed: Open my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law. He understood that there is truly a heavenly service, which anyone could come to know from the law, provided the Lord had revealed it to him. For who could climb from earthly things to heavenly ones, from shadow to brightness, from the copy to the inner sanctuary of truth, by human steps without divine guidance?

Who can contemplate that heavenly altar and the true temple, the priests and Levites—not these who serve according to the flesh, but those who serve according to the grace of the Spirit? This was the one grace David desired above all the greatest things when he said: One thing I have asked of the Lord, this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord

all the days of my life, that I may see the delight of the Lord and consider his temple. Who could know what a rich man should offer—a great gift, as much as his hand can afford—so that his sin might be loosed? Who could understand that if a man had nothing to offer, a ram for instance, his sin was not loosed? Who could perceive what those impurities were which are loosed, not by the law as the Jews understand it, but by the spiritual law that Paul recognized? Who could see the true forgiveness of sins, whose copy is in the law and whose reality is in the gospel, when the Lord Jesus says: Your sins are

forgiven you—not through the blood of goats, but through the sacrifice of his own body? That man, then, is the rich man of the law who looses his sin by confessing the fullness of perfect majesty in Christ, and offering it, as it were, with the hands of faith at that heavenly altar. He sees the true priest who sees the high priest; he contemplates the true temple who hears him say: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. Great is the temple from which power went out and healed everyone; wonderful is that altar on which the sacrifice of the one Lamb took away the sins of the world; most excellent is that Levite who came not to demand service but to display to all the service of his passion, whose portion is God, who possessed nothing here and yet possessed all things.

And what shall I say about the Hebrew whom the law commands to serve for only six years and to go out of servitude in the seventh? Who is this Hebrew slave? Who could be understood as the free Hebrew? Who is great enough to keep the eternal years in mind and see the true Hebrew, who does not remain a slave forever, but after serving as a slave for six years obtains the grace of freedom in the seventh?

The patriarch Isaac seems not to have been unaware of the mystery of this slavery and freedom, for he said: You shall serve your brother, and it shall come to pass, when you lay down and loose his yoke from your neck... He meant that a time would come when, even if someone placed here has served his brother, afterward, when the years made up of these days and months we spend here are completed, he will loose the yoke from his neck. This happens in the seventh year, the year of release.

We can see a figure of the true Hebrew in Joseph, who bore the yoke of slavery, yet guilt did not capture him, prison did not shut him in, Egypt did not stain him. We see it in Peter, John and James, who, though born and raised under the yoke of the law, nevertheless loosed their brother's Jewish yoke when the time of lawful rest arrived, when the forgiveness of sins shone upon them.

Yet all this was still done here in shadow, compared with heavenly things. But how great that rest is, which is inferred from the law, is revealed in the gospel, when the Lord Jesus says: I will that where I am, these too may be with me. How blessed is the one who can earn there the fruit of that dwelling, a share in that rest! Then he will understand what it means to have had his eyes opened to see the wonders of God's law.

The gospel reading we have just heard gave us a fitting reminder. In it the leper was healed who said: If you will, you can make me clean, placing the exercise of the Lord's power in his will. And the Lord answered in kind: I will; be clean. The kindness of his will came first, and the authority of his power followed.

Jesus, who does not will that sin should exist, says 'I will' to all. Christ's willing is common to all; being cleansed belongs to the faith of the one who believes in Christ. And he touched him. He touches those by whose faith he is touched. Indeed he says: Someone touched me; I perceive that power has gone out from me. Here you have the working of the spotless body; here you have the pardon of the Godhead.

But to heal him more fully, he opened his eyes, saying: Go, show yourself to the priest. The synagogue had many priests, but the one whose eyes he opens does not see the false priests; he looks upon the true one. Who is the true priest but the one who is a priest forever? That is why the Father said to him: You are a priest forever.

So he opened his eyes, and the man saw and understood what gift he ought to offer for his cleansing. Blessed is the one who hears these things; how much more blessed is the one who sees, who can show himself to the true priest so that he need not fear anything in himself being seen, because he has first looked at himself with unveiled face! For unless he has first seen himself, he will not dare to show himself—like Adam, who wanted to hide because he did not know himself. But now let us also consider what follows.

I am a stranger on the earth; do not hide your commandments from me. This is not just anyone's voice, but the voice of one who has renounced earthly pleasures and stripped himself of every attachment to worldly desire. He is the stranger in this land who can say: But our citizenship is in heaven; who has his portion in the Lord; who can grieve at living on earth too long; who is weary of the length of this life; who is sickened by a long stay in this dwelling, which the saint turns away from, saying: Woe

to those who dwell on the earth; who does not fear to be dissolved and is confident that, if he is dissolved, he will be with Christ. He is truly a pilgrim on earth who is a fellow citizen of the saints and a member of God's household and stores up treasure for himself in heaven. Such a man, having come out of Egypt, certainly does not long to go back to this Egypt that is understood spiritually. He does not dread the approach of old age, now laid aside, or of death. He does not build barns to store his harvests as though he would live on into ages not his own. Rich only in the fruitfulness of the virtues, he gathers what not even death can take from him.

And rightly he says: My soul has longed to desire your judgments at all times. Only someone free from bonds can do this—not only from the bonds of worldly anxiety, but also from the bonds of human affection. There are many bonds in this world: the desire to live is a bond, the enjoyment of pleasures is a bond, honours are bonds, marriage is a bond. Indeed, the good teacher says to you: Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife.

Not that the man who has taken a wife sins; but he ties bonds on his mind, because he is anxious how to please his wife (he would be more blessed if he desired to please God alone), and bonds on his flesh, because he is bound who does not have power over his own body. So, because it is God's commandment, set forth in the oracle of the law and in the apostle's words, that no one should put wife, riches, honour or family ties before God, and whoever does so becomes liable to God's judgments, he first asked God not to hide his commandments from him. For whoever has known and kept the commandments does not shrink from the divine judgments but desires them; and so, as one to whom the commandments have been revealed, he rightly says: 'I have longed to desire your judgments at all times.'

He did not say 'I have longed for your judgments' but 'I have longed to desire them.' Just as to live with true life is more than simply to live—for living is common even to this present life, but living with true life belongs to the blessed—so to long to desire God's judgments is more than to desire his judgments. We long to desire, as if the desire were not in our power but a gift of God's grace. For when the Lord sees us delighting in the longing to desire his judgments, he increases that sober affection; but when we sin, we do not long to desire God's judgments.

A sick man does not want to be cauterized or cut, even to regain his health. The more seriously ill a man is, the more he shrinks from being burned, cut, bound or kept from food; but the one in sound health meets the physician without fear. That is why the Lord did not speak idly when he said: With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you; he not only desired but longed with a doubled desire to grant the forgiveness of sins. Let us too, then, long to desire God's judgments—a good conscience is approved when it is examined—and let us long to desire them at all times, so that no moment of a good conscience passes empty of longing.

The fifth verse follows: You have rebuked the proud; cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments. Since the Lord Jesus redeemed the human race through obedience and restored righteousness, while the serpent brought sin in through disobedience, we can judge from this how much evil there is in pride. Its author is the devil, whom the prophet represents as saying: I will set

my throne above the clouds, and I will be like the Most High. Wicked as he is, in refusing honour to the Lord our God, he has nevertheless trained disciples worse than himself. For he exalted himself only so far as wanting to be equal and like the Most High, but the apostle describes his disciple as one who will scorn to be thought merely equal and like to God. For it is written: When the man of iniquity is revealed, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God.

So the master presumes to be like God, this one to be above him. That is why the Lord said to his disciples: You will do greater things than these, so that to those from whom the serpent had taken more than he himself had lost, Christ granted to do greater things than he himself had done on earth. For in himself he chose to deceive the prince of this world, and in his disciples to triumph over him.

And so, wishing to free the human race from so great a crime, he brought in the Pharisee and the publican praying in the temple, and taught that a proud man, even if he has every other good, gives more offence than a humble man who rests on no endowment of virtues at all. For the devil strives to trip up those intent on good works. How hard that Pharisee worked not to take what belonged to others, not to be unjust, not to commit adultery! How hard he worked not to sin as the publican had sinned! How hard he worked to fast twice a week! How hard he worked to give a tenth of everything he acquired! Which of us does these things?

How many have possessions and brood over their crops alone, storing up harvests for themselves alone! The devil noticed this and covered him with a grievous ulcer, so that, puffed up by a fleshly mind, he did not hold fast to the Head, and in the very thing for which he expected to be praised he was judged more blameworthy. For he gave thanks to God that he was not a robber, an adulterer or unjust. How harmfully the serpent wrestled with him and bound him in heavy coils! He made him higher so as to throw him down from a greater height; he made himself lower so as to bring the loftier man down with a heavier fall. Arrogance is an evil ruin that undermines the one who stands higher; evil is this wrestling of the serpent, in which he twists himself into countless windings.

He wanted to puff up Paul too. Which Paul? That apostle, of course, sent not from men nor through man but through Jesus Christ. And he had nearly deceived him, so that Paul asked for the thorn in his flesh, which kept him humble, to be taken away. But the good Lord, who wanted to make Paul stronger through weaknesses, sent him an angel of Satan, so that the devil would be beaten by his own tricks.

The Pharisee was not lying; on the contrary, what he said was true. But everyone who exalts himself gives offence, even if he speaks the truth. Indeed, the Pharisee went into the temple more commendable than the publican, and yet he came out condemned. How great a crime pride is, that even adultery is ranked above it!

And so the Lord, who gives freely to others, resists the proud. He enters into battle, as it were, with those who exalt themselves and claims this contest for himself; and he who has compassion on others rebukes the arrogant. For nothing is more grievous than to look down on our poor brothers with a proud eye, to repel with intolerable disdain those who share our nature, judging them unworthy of our favour because they are needy, when poverty is more readily acceptable to God than treasure.

Cursed, he says, are those who turn aside from your commandments. Earlier he had said: Do not hide your commandments from me; and so, knowing the commandments as revealed to him, he condemns those who have turned aside from the heavenly commandments. He rightly said 'who turn aside', for the commandment is straight, so let no one swerve from it.

But it is puzzling why he said here: Do not hide your commandments from me. What is hidden becomes dark and secret, yet earlier he had said: The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes. If the commandment is bright, how is it hidden, since no one puts a lamp under a bushel? Unless perhaps the one commandment is bright, but the many commandments are hidden. For he says: Your judgments are a great deep—not 'your judgment is like a deep' but 'your judgments.'

Notice the order. Above he says: Do not drive me away from your commandments; next he says: Do not hide your commandments from me; here he says: Cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments. Truly cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments, who ought to have given thanks, first because they were not driven away, and second because they were granted that the divine commandments were not hidden from them. So a person turns aside from the very thing he prayed for.

Next comes: Take from me reproach and contempt, for I have sought out your testimonies. If contempt is counted as a reproach, how is it written: God has chosen the contemptible things of this world? But notice that he said 'the contemptible things of the world', not 'of God'; for what is contemptible in this world is precious to God. Humility is despised in this world, but it is approved by God's judgment, and if the publican humbles himself, he is exalted.

Hear whom God does (not) count as nothing: whoever is holy, who lives without stain, keeps the truth and has not attacked his neighbour. The wicked man is brought to nothing in his sight; everything that belongs to wickedness he counts as nothing. So heathenism is nothing, but devotion endures forever. Beware, then, of being a reproach to Christ. I do not want anyone to curse me and look down on me as a sinner; how much worse if Christ judges one worthy of reproach! Woe to you, he says, Chorazin and Bethsaida; they are condemned because they did not repent of their sins.

Let us act, then, so that reproach may be taken from us. Who is it that is not worthy of reproach? The one who has sought out the Lord's testimonies. There are indeed many who want to heap reproach on your servants, but they themselves are the more shameful, because it is glorious to suffer reproach for your name.

And so he says: For princes sat and spoke against me. This is the voice of the martyr. Brought before the tribunal of his persecutors, he is pressed to sacrifice to idols and steadfastly refuses; the judges, sitting on their tribunals surrounded by their officials and indignant that their orders are not obeyed, confer about what punishment they think he deserves; and he stands there unafraid, saying:

Princes sat and spoke against me. This is also the Lord's voice. When the elders of the people, the chief priests and the scribes had assembled, and he had been led to the council of the Jews, who said: What further need do we have of witnesses? For we have heard it from his own mouth; and when he stood before the governor and was led to the cross, what finer thing could he say than: Princes sat and spoke against me? That is: 'While I stood, the princes sat, and because they were raised high on their tribunals, they did not see the Lord.'

So they sat, lifted up by the height of their rule, and gave no thought to the Prince of princes. But that is not all. 'They spoke against me,' he says. 'I had come as their redeemer; I had come to cleanse the sins of all, to recover the lost, to restore to paradise the inheritance of holy Jacob—and they spoke against me. So, my imitators, my disciples, do not be ashamed of insult if you stand before princes for my name, since I stood for your salvation.'

Indeed, Peter and the other apostles were put in custody, and the next day, set before the council, Peter spoke boldly: Rulers of the people and elders of Israel, (if we are being examined today about a good deed done to a sick man, by what means this man was made well, let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, by him this man stands before you whole). That is: 'You are the ones who made Christ too stand before you. We count this insult a glory, because we are accused for a sick man's healing. This is the inheritance the Saviour of all left to his humble servants.'

But they conferred among themselves, saying: What shall we do with these men? And they let them go. So Peter and each of the apostles rejoiced that they had been counted worthy to suffer insult for the name of Christ. Each of them could rightly have said then: For princes sat and spoke against me.

The princes sat against Isaiah and debated that he should be sawn in two; but he who said, "Hear, you princes of Sodom," did not fear them. They sat against Jeremiah, that he should be thrown into the pit; they sat against Zechariah, who was killed between the temple and the altar; they sat against Susanna and passed judgment against a chaste woman. But to show that the council of princes was not good, the Lord stirred up the spirit of a boy, and the very woman whom the princes had sentenced to death the prophet acquitted as innocent of every charge.

There are also other princes who speak against us. Of them it is said: "For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world of darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places." These sit and spy out who in this world is righteous, and which Christian serves God attentively and is eager for good works and deeds.

They speak against him, saying: "Let us lie in wait for him, hinder him, and stop him from doing what he desires; let us crush his mind and break his spirit with frequent and sudden misfortunes; and if God approves him for his righteousness, let us ask that we be allowed to tempt him." For they could not have had power to try so great a prophet with the many temptations he underwent

unless the Lord had allowed it in order to prove his soldier and crown him with greater glory. Who, then, stirred up King Saul against him, if not an evil spirit, as we read? That spirit was aggrieved at being shut out whenever David soothed the king's mind and spirit, either with the sound of the harp or with the strings and chords of good counsel and good works. Who stirred up the wickedness of Doeg the Syrian to betray a holy man and bring the priest's kindly hospitality into danger? Who inflamed the passion of Amnon to defile the prophet's house and grieve his father's heart, through one child's incestuous lust and the wrong done to another, so that he who prophesied to others could not foresee the evils in his own house?

Who armed the fury of Absalom to drive his father from his home and hunt him down in a war against his own father? But although the holy man was by now almost the weaker in the strength of his kingdom, he quenched the devil's fiery darts aimed at him by this alone: while the son sought his father's death, the father, out of fatherly love, gave orders that his son's life be spared.

So the princes of the people, such as Ahithophel, and the other leaders of the fighting men sat; the princes of the people plotted with Absalom against the prophet. That is why he says: "For princes sat and spoke against me; but your servant meditated on your justifications." We see here the weapons of the righteous man, with which he drives back every attack of his adversaries.

Elsewhere he says: "They surrounded me and fought against me without cause. Instead of loving me they slandered me, but I prayed." Here he says that he did not devote himself to training young men in the arts of war, or to any cunning of heart to deceive an opponent and conquer the enemy he could see. Instead he fought against those he could not see, and in him piety did battle more than bodily strength. So he trained himself in God's justifications, in order to wound the devil with a counterblow.

The devil tried to draw him away from his commitment to righteousness and his zeal for devotion by keeping him busy with war; but he occupied himself all the more in meditating on God's work and worship. And so the Lord protected him: the Lord in whom he hoped, with whom he spoke, and to whom he clung with all his heart. For the righteous man either speaks to God in prayer or speaks of God's works in praise. He always speaks of the works of God, so that his mouth may not speak of the works of men. The righteous man says nothing earthly and does nothing mortal.

And therefore he says: "For your testimonies are my meditation, and your justification is my counsel." Do you see what he is teaching? The counsels of the righteous ought to be these: to meditate on God's commandments, to occupy oneself with God's praises and oracles, and so always to justify the Lord. Whoever does what God commands, and what he believes pleases God, justifies God. We can understand this from the reading of the Gospel, where the evangelist says that the Pharisees rejected the counsel of God, since they had not been baptized with John's baptism.

That is in one book; in another you find: "They did not justify God, for they refused to be baptized." That is why, when John said, "I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?", the Lord replied: "Let it be so now; for it is fitting for us in this way to fulfil all righteousness." Whoever does God's commandments, then, justifies God, because he does his righteousness. And it is good for human counsels to follow God's counsel, because God's counsel is always certain, while our counsels are mostly uncertain and are tested by how things turn out.
IV. THE LETTER DALETH

Daleth, the fourth letter of the Hebrews, means "fear" in Latin, or, as we find elsewhere, "birth." But both can fit and suit the sense. For birth belongs to the things that are begotten in this world, and by it we understand bodily and material things, which perish; and so it is not far removed from fear, since fear is born of bodily and material things. For what is earthly birth but fear?

Accordingly the verse begins: "My soul has clung to the pavement; give me life according to your word." By "pavement" we understand the earth, and by the earth material things. To the sinner it was said, "Earth you are, and to earth you shall go," because he did not think he should cling to the divine commandments but turned aside to material

and bodily things, and the delight of this worldly life was stamped upon him. Cast out of paradise, then—that is, out of that lofty and heavenly place to which Paul was caught up, not knowing whether in the body or out of the body—cast down from that exalted place to the earth, Adam laments and says: "My soul has clung to the pavement," just as he says elsewhere:

"My soul is brought low in the dust, and my belly has clung to the earth." This is the voice of a penitent, who remembered that while he clung to God he had not known, and could not tell, whether he was in the body or out of the body, a thing Paul too did not decide. So little did he feel the weakness and sluggishness of the body while the Lord's presence clung to him. So the prophetic Spirit, who expressed this grief, or the Lord, who took on Adam's weakness, takes the part of Adam and adopts his feelings.

Let Adam speak, then: "My soul has clung to the pavement." He who once, supremely blessed, breathed the air of heaven and knew nothing of the cares and wearinesses of this life is now bent down by the anxieties of this world, the pursuit of luxury and the greed for money, and thrusts himself like a fox into holes and earthly lairs. Rightly did he cling to the dust, for he could not raise himself up unless Christ raised him on his cross; rightly did he cling to the pavement, for he was hiding from Christ. The one to whom Jesus says "Follow me" does not cling to the pavement. The one who hears and follows the law that says, "You shall walk after the Lord your God and cling to him," does not cling to the pavement.

How each person clings to the pavement, and how to God, hear from the one who says: "He who clings to a harlot is one body with her, but he who clings to the Lord is one spirit with him." This earth that we carry about captures us with a harlot's enticements, as it were, and paints over faces, so to speak, with the cosmetics of bodily pleasures and delights, so that the truth lies hidden beneath them and they deceive those who come near with a showy appearance. But although they may cloud the inner eye of the mind for a time, afterwards, once the dust of such pleasures' charm has been shaken off, as it were, it is easily seen how empty the charm of this world, or of the body, is.

It is good, then, to cling to the Lord and not to have one's neck bent under the yoke of the world. That is why Wisdom says to the Church, or to the strong soul: "Your neck is like the tower of David, built in Thalpioth; a thousand doors hang on it, and all the darts of the mighty." For a neck held up toward God and fitted for the yoke of Christ, not bowed by any bending toward the enticements of the earth,

is like the royal tower of Christ, on which Nebuchadnezzar cannot lay his yoke. For David, that man strong of hand, built that tower and raised it above the heights of the walls, so that it might serve both for defence and for beauty: for defence, because it sees the enemy coming and drives him back; for beauty, because it stands out not only among low things but even among lofty ones. Yet it serves for defence and beauty only if it holds within it the teachings of the Word like ornaments on a harness, and also holds the darts of the mighty prophets, which are hurled by the arms of faith, as it were, against every height that exalts itself.

Do not, then, drag down into the dust of death your soul, to which the Lord has given a natural loftiness and vigour by which to rouse itself and rise up. Hence the verse is also fittingly taken to refer to this union of soul and body: in the natural mystery of our life, the soul, joined to the body, creeps along the ground, as it were, and clings to the pavement, partly because of this earthly dwelling and partly because this body is made of earth. So both the place where we lodge and the very matter of our body bear out this saying. That is why the apostle rightly longs to be set free from the body of this death, for we are shut in a kind of prison, and, lodged in a sort of hovel of luxury, we are wrapped in the darkness of our sins.

Let us walk, then, according to God's will, so that we may be said to cling to God. For whoever lives by the appetites of the body is flesh, and whoever lives by God's precepts is spirit. Let our soul not become flesh, then—that is, let us not be called flesh like those who perished in the flood, of whom it was said, "because they are flesh." Rather, let our flesh, obedient to the soul's guidance, become soul and deserve to be called by that name, as the family of the patriarch Jacob and the holy descendants of his line were called.

For it is written: "These are the sons of Bilhah, whom Laban gave to his daughter Rachel, and she bore these to Jacob: seven souls in all." And elsewhere: "All the souls who entered Egypt, who came from his loins, not counting the women, were sixty-six." And at the beginning of Exodus we read: "All the souls from Jacob who were with Jacob were seventy-five." So those who lived with Joseph and came out of Egypt are also souls.

But consider those who were angels of God—that is, who imitated the grace of the angels by the uprightness of their lives, for those who do not marry and are not given in marriage will be like the angels in heaven. Those who seemed to be angels and yet were captivated by the beauty of women are flesh, as the Lord God said: "My spirit shall not remain in these men for ever, because they are flesh."

Those who are free from lust are rightly compared to angels; they are not flesh, because they are not in the flesh but in the spirit, like those who followed the apostle as their teacher, to whom he said, "But you are not in the flesh but in the spirit." But those who are captured by bodily lust for women are flesh—and would that they were only flesh, and not also neighing horses, for, it says, "they neighed after their neighbour's wife."

So he who feels his soul cast down and bent all the way to the pavement asks to be given life according to the word of God, which draws souls to itself; in its compassion it wishes to raise them up, and so it leads away from the earth whomever it will. The soul that walks in the ways of Christ, dead to sin and living to God, is given life, so that the death of sin can no longer have dominion over it, since, buried with Christ, it has been justified from sin. But whoever desires to be justified must first declare his own ways.

That is why he says in the second verse: "I declared my ways, and you heard me; teach me your justifications." He thinks that, in fitting order, one must come to God's justifications by first confessing one's own sins. For we are taught this elsewhere too: "Tell your iniquities, so that you may be justified." So we ought to know what it means for a man to walk in his own ways and in the ways of God. Whoever does the will of the flesh and lives by the desires of this world walks in his own ways, in which he takes delight and joy. But whoever comes to do the will of his Father who is in heaven, whose food is to fulfil God's commandment, and who seeks not what gives him pleasure but what pleases God, travels the way of the Lord, that Way which says:

"I am the way and the truth and the life." You see, then, that whoever walks the way of Christ lives according to God's word. The Lord God himself also teaches in Deuteronomy how you should walk in his ways, saying: "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, but that you fear the Lord your God, walk in his ways, love him, and serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, keeping his commandments and his ordinances?" It is clear, then, that the ways of the flesh are one thing and the ways of God another, and that whoever wants to walk in the ways of God must first abandon the ways of the flesh, of the body and of worldly wisdom.

So David, leaving these behind, declares them and does not keep silent before God: he confesses his errors and does not deny his falls. He said something similar here: "I will declare my iniquity against myself to the Lord." For if the righteous man accuses himself, he shuts out the voice of the accuser who stands ready, who is accustomed to pile up sins and exaggerate everyone's misdeeds. Whoever has first confessed against himself stops the accuser's mouth, and the shame of the one confessing paves the way for pardon. His own shame excuses the guilty man and accuses the one who led him astray. For whoever has not kept silent about his own sins is seen to have grieved within himself over what he did, and to have exposed in the devil what the devil urged him to do. That is why Scripture says: "The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech."

Whoever accuses himself, even if he is a sinner, begins to be righteous, because he does not spare himself and he acknowledges the righteousness of God, from whom he believes nothing can be hidden. If only Adam had chosen to accuse himself rather than hide! But it is not enough to confess our error; if we wish to be corrected, we must also ask the Lord to teach us his justifications, so that we may not go astray afterwards. So he asks to be taught by the Lord, because, as Christ says, we have one teacher. Nor does he ask this idly, for blessed is not the one whom man teaches, but the one whom you instruct, O Lord.

Everywhere he keeps his own state in mind and does not think it enough for the Lord our God to teach him his justifications, but he added: "Make known to me the way of your justifications, and I will exercise myself in your wonders." See the order. First we must learn the Lord's justifications, and then come to know the steps and the order of those justifications: what ought to come first and what should follow.

For to know what you are to do but not the order in which to do it is not perfect knowledge; things done in the wrong order often give offence. So the man who accuses himself at the beginning of his speech is righteous, but the man who confesses what he had first denied is unrighteous; the one wins the favour due to modesty, the other incurs the stigma of shamelessness. In this way ignorance of order confuses the nature of affairs and the shape of merit. But whoever has learned first the mysteries of God, and then the order of the mysteries, exercises himself in the wonders of God.

The Greek has adoleschēsō, which the Latin renders halucinabor, "I will let my mind wander." In common usage this seems to be an awkward expression, because adoleschēsai is popularly taken to mean either to let the mind wander or to say more than is fitting and seem superfluous, which wearies the listener. It also seems out of place, since keeping things in order can seem tiresome: if you want to recount some case and keep to the order of events, the listener hurries on to the outcome and grows tired of what comes first. But no one can be fully instructed unless he has learned everything in its order;

in this way one grasps not only the deed, but also the weight of the deed and the disposition of the doer. And so David, like a good judge and arbiter of himself, wishes to be taught almost to the point of weariness, and would rather linger for more time than is needed than skip over the necessary order. For adoleschia, or halucinatio, seems to be a kind of long meditation, or a lingering application of the mind, and this is not far from exercise, whether of mind or of body. For just as someone who exercises his limbs in the wrestling school exercises them for a long time in order to strengthen them, so someone who exercises his mind in the divine Scriptures or in counsels ought to exercise it for a long time.

"Isaac went out into the field"—here the Greek said adoleschēsai, the Latin "to walk about" or "to exercise himself." Rebecca was coming, and in her a type of the Church was foreshadowed; a marriage was being prepared in which there would be a great sacrament. Seeing these mysteries, the patriarch went out into the field, letting the keenness of his mind range freely and walking in the innocence of his heart. He was surely exercising his mind with various thoughts and delighting in wonderful mysteries. To become his imitator, the holy prophet longed to be taught God's justifications and to know the way of heavenly righteousness, so that his soul might not sleep the sleep of this world, nor be captured by the enticements of worldly vanity and drift away from its pursuit of truth.

He went on to say how he wishes to be taught: "My soul has dripped away from weariness; strengthen me in your words." Some manuscripts have "has slumbered," because enystaxen and estaxen differ by two letters. The translator or an old copyist could have been mistaken here: enystaxen means "to sleep," estaxen "to drip." The more perfect man, who turns his mind to divine mysteries, does not slumber—indeed he himself says elsewhere, "If I give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids"—but is always awake, and even if the flesh sleeps, the heart keeps watch.

So he was not sleeping who was planning to build a temple to the Lord out of heavenly words, not out of stones. For the word of God drives away weariness; it shuts out the sleep of the soul and the drowsiness of the mind, since sleep creeps in from sorrow and anxiety over worldly things. But whoever clings to God flees from cares and takes his pleasure in eternal knowledge, fearing no change of circumstance there, as one must in worldly things.

Those, then, who prefer easier shortcuts to labour accept "has slumbered"; but Origen, who examined the translations of many with careful inquiry, followed "has dripped," because the soul of the perfect man, being well built and strengthened, does not drip, just as roofs that are well covered and secure do not, whereas badly built ones soon leak. Hence the saying: "Drippings drive a man out of his house on a winter's day"—when we are tried by the harshness of the cold and the frequent changes of the weather. So we are taught to take care that our flight may not be in winter or on the sabbath; for the day of judgment, or of death, ought to find us already proven, so that the departure of death may not find us bereft of the greenness of prosperity and stripped of every flower of good fortune.

Let us take care, then, that none of us is thrown out of the settled state of his mind, his natural dwelling as it were, by having holes in his dwelling through which the dripping water flows, undermining, as though from the foundations, a man who has no firm grounding in wisdom. That is why the prophet says: "My son, do not drip away." Our soul, then, must be strengthened

so that it does not drip, and made solid by an unbroken framework of virtues, so that it can keep the mystery of the eternal King. But whoever is loose with his words is like something full of cracks, leaking this way and that; he empties out what is within him and is flooded by outward passions, not knowing how to cover himself or hold on to the word he has received. He is unlike holy Mary, who kept all these words in her heart, so that nothing should flow out of it.

The Church speaks of herself as fortified with such a dowry of virtues that she may seem worthy to have her Bridegroom accept her invitation and enter her lodging. So she first presumes that she will please him if Christ sees her well covered and keeping faithful silence: "Behold," she says, "you are fair, my kinsman, and truly beautiful; our resting place

is shaded, the beams of our houses are cedar, our panelled ceilings cypress." The Church praises the Bridegroom's beauty, which each of us praises more with silent affection; the faithful interpreter of the mysteries proclaims more by keeping silent, for whoever divulges secrets diminishes the beauty of Christ. So let no one cast his pearls before swine, or he will cause precious ornaments to be trampled underfoot. Christ does not lay down his head, then, in the tent of the talkative and garrulous, since in much speaking sin is committed, but in the tent of a serious man, who is sparing in speech, not intemperate in his words, and avoids the drunkenness of talkativeness by sobriety of speech.

And she rightly calls the resting place shaded, because the power of the Most High overshadows those who are established in the Church. David asked to be protected by this shade, so that the sun might not burn him by day nor the moon by night. Spiritual grace provides this shade to those fleeing the scorching heat and summer blaze of this world. Shaded, then, is the resting place of Christ and the Church, upon whom that eternal rest of God [?] breathes.

In this shade, then, let us rest, worn out by the heat of our sins. If lust has scorched any, let the Lord's cross cool them, the cross on which he reclined to take our sins upon himself; if guilt has wearied any, let Jesus take them into his bosom and cherish them in a gentle embrace. And so I dare to say that the flesh of Christ is the Church's resting place.

"The beams of our houses are cedar." Under the figure of the cedar, the glory of our forefathers who were righteous is declared: "The righteous man will flourish like the palm tree and will grow like the cedar that is in Lebanon." For just as the cedar does not rot, so the glory of our forefathers is not spoiled by any length of time.

"Our rafters are of cypress." This kind of tree never loses its greenness; scorched in winter as in summer, it keeps its foliage and does not change to a different colour. This tree alone the wind never strips of its glory; it alone is never stripped of its old covering or clothed in new blossom. So too the grace of the apostles knows no failing, and flourishes in its own beauty.

So the soul that thrives with its members in flower does not know corruption. With patient greatness of spirit it always holds up the heights of justice and the other virtues, and so it does not drain away or fail, because there is nothing cracked or slack in it. There is nothing unsteady, nothing slippery, nothing that could pour out of it through a fault of speech. That is why the prophet asks to be strengthened in [your] words, so that his feet may not be moved and his steps may not slip away. Whoever is strong with an upright heart does not suffer this; rooted and grounded, he stands unmoved against every flood of the passions.

Strengthened, then, in the words, he says: "Remove from me the way of iniquity, and in your law have mercy on me." He did not say, "Remove me from the way of iniquity," but, "Remove the way of iniquity from me," as though it were in us and seemed to be within us. For as long as we practise anything wicked, the way of iniquity stays within us and does not depart from us. So let us work hard to separate it from ourselves.

But because the inherited glue of iniquity has stuck fast to human minds, we need the help of one who sets us free. You too should pray and say: "Wretched man that I am, who will remove the way of iniquity from me? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord." And he rightly spoke of the way of iniquity, not of iniquity itself, because iniquity is not in us as something natural; rather, the way has been worn down by the footsteps of our forebears running after sin.

And rightly, because the wound is great and old and has long been spreading, he asks for the remedies of a more perfect medicine, begging to be healed by the Lord's mercy according to law. For a wound that has not been healed according to the law of medicine is quickly opened again; indeed, the treatment then makes slower progress. And if the poison creeps inward, it does not feel the medicines applied on the outside.

The method of medicine therefore requires that it be treated by cutting or by burning. For unless the rotten flesh is cut away or the useless fluid is burned off, the physician's hands are applied to the wounds in vain. So the good physician says that a patient of this kind must be treated according to law, so that the medicine can do its work. He has mercy according to law, then, who has mercy with justice and wisdom, so as to forgive what he knows can rightly be forgiven, lest in showing mercy to another he make himself liable to the law. After Agag was granted mercy, he made Saul sin: Saul sinned in that very mercy, and so he sinned after showing mercy.

Let us also take care not to make worse the very person to whom we show mercy unjustly. For often it is a greater severity not to restrain wrongdoers than to punish them. Whoever has committed something shameful is handed over to dishonourable passions and pays no price for the fault. So it was that those who did not believe God took notice of their crimes, and who lived as though without judge and without law: "God handed them over," it says, "to a reprobate mind," because they chose the way of iniquity and refused to choose the way of truth.

But the prophet, who wished to be converted with sincere affection, says: "I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments." No one who errs in doctrine can say this: the Arian cannot say it, nor the Sabellian, nor the Manichee. The greedy man who craves worldly and material things cannot say it, nor can the man who lives for trade; for the eagerness to have and the craving to possess are not the way of truth. How can it be the way of truth, when the rich man in the world could not take his riches with him, and after death began to be poorer than the beggar Lazarus?

Worldly honour and worldly care are not the way of truth. Indeed, he who chose the way of truth says a little later: "Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanities." Temporal things are vanity; eternal things are truth. If, then, we wish to walk the way of truth, let us be strangers to the world rather than to God, and walk by faith. For whoever walks by faith is present with God; whoever walks by sight is at home in the world and is a stranger to the Lord; but such a one is soon put to shame.

Hence David, shrinking [?] from such a man, says: "I have clung to your testimonies, Lord; do not put me to shame." He clings to the Lord's testimonies who does not reject his commandments, does not forget his judgments, and does not indulge his own pleasures. Whoever clings to the Lord's testimonies renounces the world, forgets what lies behind and strains toward what lies ahead, so as to reach the prize, which is the badge of victory. So he is not put to shame whom the allurements of this world have not captured; nor

is he put to shame, even if he has done things to blush at, who asks Christ for pardon of his sins. And so the answer comes to him: "Your sins are forgiven you. Go in peace." But he is not put to shame only if the forgiveness of sins has done its work in him in such a way that it takes away not only the sins but also the inclination to sin. Let justice put away iniquities, fortitude fear, temperance impurities, so that the forgiveness of sins may be not merely temporary but lasting. Let Christ enter your soul, let Jesus dwell in your mind, so that in the tabernacle of virtue there may be no room for sin.

"I have run the way of your commandments," he says, "when you enlarged my heart"; for he could not have run the way if his heart had been cramped and narrow. So to those running the way of the Lord the apostle says: "Be enlarged yourselves too, and do not be yoked with unbelievers"; and of himself he says: "Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged." That is also why it is said of Solomon: "The breadth of his heart was like the sand of the sea." And notice the difference: let the way be narrower and the heart broader, so that it can

hold the dwelling of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, lest the Word of God come and knock, and, seeing the narrowness of one's heart, disdain to dwell there. So wisdom is sung in the going out, and acts with confidence in the broad streets. The streets are broad; so wisdom is sung not in the roads but in the breadth of the heart. It is in this open field of the inner man, then, and not in the narrow places of the mind, that we must run in order to win; for it is written: "Run so that you may all win." Indeed, he won who ran in such a way that he could say: "I have finished the course"; for he ran like a good horse.

For Christ has his horses, of whom the prophet says: "You sent your horses into the sea, troubling many waters," because the apostles by preaching the gospel stirred up the peoples of the nations, who are moved like many waters and roused like the waves of the waters, so that they rose up from the earthly rites of idols and believed in Christ. And earlier he says: "You mounted your horses; your riding is salvation."

O wondrous team of twelve good horses, whose bridles are peace and whose reins are love! Bound together by the bonds of concord and set under the yoke of faith, they carry the mystery of the gospel on four wheels to the ends of the whole world, bearing the good charioteer, the Word of God, by whose whip the allurements of the world have been put to flight and the prince of this world driven out, and the course of the righteous has been completed.

O great contest of rational horses, O wonderful mystery! A wheel ran within a wheel and was not hindered: the New Testament within the Old, running within that by which it was announced. The wheels went in four directions and did not turn back, because the spirit of life was in those who ran to the four quarters of the whole world, and they ran without stumbling, because the good life of the horses was well squared. So the horses ran, because the one who had mounted the horses did not sleep.

Jesus, then, is the charioteer of our souls, and he wants us too to mount our horses, that is, our bodies, but always to stay awake, so that it may not be said of us: "Those who mounted horses have fallen asleep." This sea must be crossed without sluggishness. Even the watchful cross it with difficulty; but anyone who falls asleep will not be able to cross and will be drowned like the Egyptian, whose soul and body both perished: for he threw horse and rider into the sea, those who did not follow the law but persecuted it.
V. THE LETTER HE

Next comes the fifth letter, He, which in Latin means "is" or, as we find elsewhere, "I live." Both interpretations agree, for whoever is, lives, and whoever lives, is. So the heathen are not, and therefore do not live, but are dead. But Jesus is the same yesterday and today and for ever, and he who is, lives; for "I live," says the Lord. How can he who lives not be? And Jesus lives, who even gives life to the dead and calls the things that are not as though they were.

It is no wonder if nature yields to the Lord, so that even the dead are brought to life and things that were not begin to be. And so, since the way is also life, according to him who said, "I am the way, the truth and the life," let us seek the way, so that we may be worthy to have life. Let us listen, then, to one who lives in Christ: and he lives who said, "But we who live bless you, Lord"; for in Christ Jesus even whoever has died lives.

Let us listen, I say, to what he said in order to live: "Set before me as a law, Lord, the way of your statutes, and I will seek it always." A soldier who sets out on a march does not arrange the order of the journey for himself, nor choose his route at his own discretion, nor take pleasant shortcuts, lest he fall away from the standards. Instead, he receives the itinerary from his commander and keeps to it; he advances in the prescribed order, marches with his arms [?], and completes the journey by the right road, so as to find the supplies prepared for the troops.

If he walks by another route, he does not receive his rations and does not find a lodging prepared, because the commander orders all these things to be prepared for those who follow and turn aside neither to the right nor to the left from the prescribed route. And rightly the one who follows his commander does not fail; for he marches at a moderate pace, since the commander considers not what is useful to himself but what is possible for all. That is why he also arranges the halting places:

the army marches for three days and rests on the fourth. Cities are chosen in which three, four or more days are spent, if they have plenty of water and are busy with trade. And so the march is completed without hardship, until they reach the city chosen as a royal one, as it were, where rest is provided for the weary troops.

I would like you to recognize that this law of marching was prescribed for the saints on their journey under the leadership of Christ. For our fathers too set out from the land of Egypt across long stretches of country; all their halting places and stages are recorded, until they came to Kadesh, that is, to the holy land. "These are the stages of the children of Israel," which Moses recorded at the Lord's command. We notice, then, who arranged these stages, and how the children of Israel had to march.

For God went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, to give shade to the travellers, and by night in a pillar of fire, to show the way to those on the march and to drive away the darkness. The pillar of fire and of cloud was the law of their journeys; indeed, he spoke to them in the pillar of cloud. When he wished the army to rest from the toil of the journey, the pillar of fire did not move, nor did the cloud of light pass on; but when he wished the army to move, the pillar of fire went forward by night and the pillar of cloud by day.

That pillar of cloud outwardly went before the children of Israel, but in mystery it signified that the Lord Jesus would come on a light cloud, as Isaiah said, that is, in the Virgin Mary. She was a cloud by her inheritance from Eve, and light by the integrity of her virginity; light, because she sought to please not man but the Lord; light, because she had not conceived in iniquity but gave birth by the overshadowing of the Spirit, and brought forth not in sin but with grace.

This interpretation can also be taken another way. Christ came into Egypt on a light cloud, that is, he came into this world by taking up a body. He came in a cloud, for the mist of the body overshadowed him; but the flesh was light, because no sins of its own weighed it down. For how could he be weighed down by sins of his own, who was taking away the sins of all peoples? "Behold," it says, "the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sin of the world." The day before yesterday it was read that Jesus stood there wearing filthy garments; for he was carrying my sins.

He took our garments in order to clothe us in the splendour of immortality. Christ came on a light cloud, as justice—for iniquity sits on a talent of lead—into the hearts of the righteous, in whom there were no sins. And so it was fittingly read today: "What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?" For us the Word took on the weakness of the flesh; for us he hungered, was beaten, was crucified and died, so that for us, in whom life had before been held ignoble and base, death might begin to be precious.

But let us return to the completion of the journey and the order of the stages. You too should follow this law of marching spiritually, so that you may go out of Egypt; and moving on from there, pitch your tent in Succoth. Let this be your first halting place; Succoth, the first stage, means "tent."

Pitch, then, the tent that is within you, and make the station of your mind firm, so that you may remain rooted and grounded in the faith of Christ. Next comes the stage at Marah, that is, bitterness; not all the stages are alike. From there they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs and seventy palm trees; after bitterness, pleasant and fruitful things had to follow, so that the people would not lose heart. From there to Rephidim, which means "praise of judgment." Next comes Sinai, which held both the testing of the people and the giving of the law.

The merits of the stages vary, because in this world no course of life can enjoy unbroken success. So the good commander in one place supplied manna to the hungry people; in another, with royal providence, he ordered drink to flow from the rock to quench the people's thirst; in another he gave the law; in another he granted triumphs, so that the army, cheered by these benefits, might feel none of the toil of the long journey.

So in that people there was the type, in us the truth. Let us, then, entrust our journey to the leadership of the Lord Jesus, who first brought in the law and earlier, through Joshua, gave the land of promise to his people as a possession. But even when Moses seemed to be the leader, Jesus was with him; yet he was with him not openly or plainly, not acting as leader or ruler of the people, for he was waiting until Moses should complete his time. When that was complete, Jesus took his place.

So if you consider the twenty [?], you will see the mystery of the fullness of the times, and the hundred and twenty years after which Moses came to rest on the mountain and Jesus openly took command of the stages, so that the people might no longer be under the fear of the law, but, raised from the dead, might enjoy the fruit of eternal life. Let us walk, then, according to the teaching of the law; let the law of God be our way.

Walking this way, the Church says: "I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys, like a lily among thorns." For the faith of the believing people has gone out into all the earth, and Christ has set his feet in a broad place; and so she rightly says that she is the flower of the field. Paul too was a flower, who said: "We are the good fragrance

of Christ to God"; and truly a flower, since he could bring out of the treasure of his heart things new and old. The Church is also fittingly called a lily; for as the lily gleams, so the works of the saints shine. Most fittingly of all she is called the lily of the valleys, because grace shines out more among the lowly. But this lily is among thorns: among Jews and heretics, among the cares of this world, which prick the mind and spirit of man. We can also take it another way: just as the lily stands out among thorns, so the Church of God shines above all other gatherings.
It is also worth considering that this lily is surrounded by brightness, while what it has inside is red, and that too has a pleasant fragrance,

because the flesh of Christ, though mortal, was enclosed by the brightness of the Godhead and had the protection of heavenly grace. So later she says: "My kinsman is white and ruddy": white with divine brightness, ruddy with the look of the human colouring that he took on in the sacrament of the incarnation. And rightly even what is red smells sweet, because the flesh of Christ is without sin. The faithless who handled it defiled their hands; the saints who revered it became fragrant with the scent of devotion.

The Lord Jesus caught this scent of his fragrant Church and said: "Behold, my neighbour, you are fair." And the Church says to Christ: "Behold, you are fair, my kinsman. Behold, you are fair like an apple tree among the trees of the wood." The apple has so fragrant a charm that it surpasses the scent of all other fruits. So Christ, fastened to the wood like an apple hanging on a tree, poured out the good fragrance of the world's redemption, because he wiped away the stench of grievous sin and poured out the ointment of the life-giving drink.

"Like an apple tree," she says, "among the trees of the wood, so is my cousin among the sons," because, above the prophets and apostles, he soothed the inmost hearts of men with the sweetness of his words. But the apple has not only fragrance but also sweet food: so Christ is sweet food.

"In his shadow," she says, "I longed to sit, and I sat": for she had received the law, she followed it, she ran this way. So, resting in the law, she was resting in the shadow of Christ. A good shadow, which alone protects us from the heat of iniquity. Who can doubt that the law of God is the shadow of Christ? What is the law of the feast day, of the new moon, of the sabbaths, but a shadow of things to come? What is the day according to the law of Moses, that I may see six days and again a seventh day, and so on to the everlasting ages? What is the month according to the law of Moses, that knowing the month I may know the first new moon of the month and the true holy things to be offered at the new moons?

What is the year according to the law of Moses, made up of those days of which it says, "Six years the Hebrew shall serve, and in the seventh year he shall be set free," so that there are six years in which a man works the land, but in the seventh year he leaves it to the strangers and the poor and the beasts of the earth? What is the seventh year, in which all debts are remitted to the Hebrews? In this shadow the faith of the fathers and the holy devotion of the prophets rested.

So the devout congregation, or the holy soul, says: "In his shadow I longed to sit, and I sat." The year of jubilee is a shadow—for who sees its mysteries so as to know face to face what the law prescribes to be fulfilled in the fiftieth year?—; the feast days according to the law in the first month, from the tenth day of the month to the fourteenth and from there to the twenty-first, are a shadow; that celebration between the first and the seventh month, at that unnamed time, is a shadow; the hallowed freedom of the sabbath is a shadow;

the feast of the new moon of the seventh month and the memorial of trumpets are a shadow, and the tenth day of the seventh month, the day of atonement. You see that the first and the tenth are two feast days; likewise the fifteenth day, the day of tabernacles, lasting eight days. All these are in shadow; in shadow is the first day called holy, and in shadow the eighth day called holy, which are prescribed according to the law at the Feast of Tabernacles.

Picture for me some believers from the circumcision, men learned in the law and of careful observance, now enlightened by the knowledge of the gospel and enriched with spiritual grace.
