In them the Church, which sees Christ, which receives the bridegroom, which is fed with his food, says: "In his shadow I longed to sit, and I sat, and his fruit was sweet in my mouth." What is his sweet fruit but the preaching of the Lord's passion, as he himself says:

"Behold, the inheritance of the Lord is sons, the reward is the fruit of the womb"? For what fruit can be sweeter in our mouth than the forgiveness of sins? And the Church is rightly a flower, since she proclaims the fruit, that is, the Lord Jesus Christ, of whom it was said to Mary: "Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb."

So when she has tasted the fruit of sweetness, she hastens impatiently toward more perfect things, saying: "Bring me into the house of wine, set love in order within me. Strengthen me with ointments, surround me with apples, for I am wounded with love. His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me. I have adjured you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field, that you stir not up nor awaken love until it please."

Rightly does she seek him, rightly [?] does she long for him, because our commander has arranged everything well on this course and journey. First of all he judged that this tent must be made firm on the foundation of faith; then, if any stage is rough, dry and steep for us, this commander nevertheless sets in order what is disturbed, waters what is dry, and makes the desert fruitful. If there is any bitterness, any temptation, any weakness, our leader tempers what is bitter, soothes what is anxious, loosens what is hard and strengthens what is weak.

When an earthly king wants to rest his army somewhere, he does not choose an undistinguished village, one short of provisions, or a stretch of sand where nothing grows. He chooses a city known for its buildings, crowded and well stocked with supplies, or a pleasant field green with pasture, or wooded and level ground suited to a camp. If the kings of the earth know how to provide comforts for those who follow them, how much more does God, who is good, know how to arrange what will benefit those who love him! And first, if an unknown route must be taken, guides are chosen to go ahead of the column.

Such commanders, however, think it beneath them to go ahead themselves. But God went before the Hebrews as they journeyed, and he even spoke to them from a pillar of cloud. And so that you may know that he went before them, Scripture says: "God went before them on their way, by day in a pillar of cloud, showing them the way, and by night in a pillar of fire; and the pillar of cloud did not fail by day."

The Church followed this pillar of cloud as it went before her. It did not fail, and so that she herself would not fail, she was refreshed by its shade. That is why she says: "In his shade I longed to be, and I sat down, and his fruit was sweet in my throat." For she was fed by the Lord, who led her to a place of pasture and to water that refreshes.

"Bring me into the house of wine." Now that supplies have been prepared, she seeks to move on to another stopping place, where she may receive the grace of the mysteries and taste the sweetness of joy. From here, too, she goes on along the true road and says: "Set love in order within me." That is a good camp, where there is the fullness of love. "Strengthen me with ointments," she says, "surround me with apples."

There are other stopping places that the Church gladly comes to next. These are the stopping places of Christ's cross and burial, where the Church was wounded, but with the wound of love. For the wound is the one Christ received, but the ointment is what he poured out, and the apple is what hung on the tree. The Church tasted this apple and said: "And his fruit was sweet in my throat." And so that you may know that the Lord is the apple, you read above:

"Like an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my kinsman." We too acknowledge a wound when we preach Christ crucified, but we are a good fragrance to God, because the cross of Christ is a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks, but to us it is the power and wisdom of God. The Church is wounded with this wound when she preaches the death of her Saviour, but it is a wound of love. The one who does not believe denies it, and the one who loves confesses it: the Manichaean denies it, the Christian confesses it. And so it is written: "Better the wounds of a friend than the willing kisses of an enemy." So the Church rightly says: "For I am wounded by love."

Let us bare our limbs to the good wound. Let us bare them to the chosen arrow. This arrow is Christ, who says: "He has made me like a chosen arrow." It is good, then, to be wounded by this arrow. Reaching this stage is no small advance, and not everyone can say "that they are wounded by love." The apostles said it

when they were stoned for Christ and kept preaching Christ. Paul said it when he was beaten with rods three times and argued day and night that the Gentiles should worship Christ. The martyrs say it, who are wounded for Christ, and they love all the more because they have been found worthy to be wounded for his name.

So the Church comes to this stopping place, to this stage of her advance, where she offers her children for Christ and receives the wounds of love. Finding in these, as it were, the good nourishment of faith, she herself tasted the fruits of devotion and began to urge others on, saying: "Taste and see that the Lord is sweet," like an apple. An apple too has a wound, yet it is sweet.

She went on further to the valley of the cluster and saw a bunch of grapes so huge that two men could hardly carry it, one walking in front and the other following behind. She tasted the mystery. She tasted it in Joshua son of Nun, she tasted it in Caleb, who said to the people: "We have seen a land flowing with honey and milk." Taste and see how sweet the Lord is.

And the Church went on to say: "His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me. I have charged you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field, that you stir up and awaken love until it pleases." These too are stopping places of the Church as she advances along the royal road.

For "there are many dwellings with my Father," the Lord Jesus testifies; "behold, I come and will call you to me." The dwelling place of wisdom is good, and whether it lies at her left hand or at her right, it is a good dwelling, because it is the royal road. That is why the wise messengers say: "We will go by the royal road; we will not turn aside to the right or

to the left until we have passed through your borders." This is what the messengers Moses sent said to the king of Edom, that is, of "the earthly," because all earthly things are bad, whether on the right or on the left. Folly is a bad dwelling, and intemperance is a bad dwelling. And so the Hebrew passes through these dwellings. He does not turn aside to them but passes through, so as to reach the left and right hands of wisdom and stay there, where there are the riches of simplicity, where there is glory, where there is length of life. For length of life is in her right hand, as Solomon says, and in her left are riches and glory.

In the right hand is life, in the left is rest. If only I might rest on his left hand, so that I need not look for pillows! For woe to those who sew pillows, says Ezekiel. These are the dwellings the good guide prepares for his Church, and he directs her journey along the ways of wisdom. And so the Wise Man praises its ways: "Its ways are good ways, and all its paths are in peace."

But wisdom, honour and glory are perfect only if they have love, for love is the fulfilment of the law. So she wants love to be stirred up and awakened again: stirred up in the Old Testament, awakened again in the New.

God is love, as we read, and Christ is love. He is stirred up like a lion and a lion's cub, so that he may rise from the stock of Judah. He is awakened again like one who sleeps, like one lying down, because he was raised from the dead not by human power but by his own majesty and his Father's. That is why Scripture says: "Who will rouse him?" For no angel or other outside power could raise him, since he himself raised others.

So when it says here, "that you stir up or awaken love until it pleases," it speaks of those who can fittingly preach his resurrection and so kindle the ardour of faith and devotion in their hearers. Or else Christ is stirred up in those who are coming to him for the first time, and awakened again in those who fell asleep after they had come. So Christ sleeps in the negligent and is awakened in the saints.

So the Church has a road to travel, and she has lodgings at the stopping places where the saints rest. One of these saints is the one who says: "Set for me a law, O Lord, the way of your judgements." He rightly says "set," so that the law may remain fixed and immovable in his breast, and no whirlwind of this world may tear it from his affection, so that he may be a law to himself, having the work of the law written in his heart.

"And I will seek it," he says, "always." For what we seek is no small thing: the grace of paradise, the kingdom of God, the company of the angels, the home of immortality. So it is not sought for one day, or for two, or for a few months. It is sought always and sought through all things, so that many supporting merits may come together. For διὰ παντός means both "all the time" and "through all things." So when he says "I will seek," he means that it must be sought without end. But seeking is not enough unless you understand what you are seeking.

That is why he says: "Give me understanding, and I will search out your law and keep it with my whole heart." First we must seek. Then we must understand and search out every mystery of the law, and keep it in our heart. But who can keep the law of God unless he has received understanding? And the one who understands and searches is led by his searching onto the path of the commandments.

Here we should notice that the law is justice and the commandment is judgement, as we also read in this letter. There is a way of the law, which is to stand in the ways of the law. There is a way of judgements, according to the first verse. There is also a way of testimonies: "In the way of your testimonies I delighted." And there is a way of commandments: "I ran the way of your commandments." Let us inquire of these ways, then, so that it may be said to us: "Stand in the ways of the law and ask for the eternal

paths, and see which way is better, and walk in it." So when we have walked all the ways, we will come to the end of all the ways, who says: "I am the way." Christ, then, is the end of the ways, for he is the end of the law, bringing righteousness to everyone who believes. From this I dare to say that Christ, who is righteousness, is the end of the judgements, and Christ is the end of the testimonies. Of him it is said: "Be my witnesses, and I am a witness, says the Lord, and so is my servant whom I have chosen."

We see, then, how far we have to walk to come to Christ: we have to walk in the law, because Christ is the end of the law. So no one reaches Christ without the law. This makes it plain that the heretics who do not accept the law of the Old Testament cannot hold the end, even if they say they hold Christ, because they have not held the beginning. Jesus himself is the beginning and the end. So

we must walk according to the spiritual law, so that we may come to the end of the law, the Lord Jesus. We must follow the testimonies, so that we may reach the great testimony, the Lord Jesus. We must also walk in the Lord's precepts, so that we may reach the great precept, of which you have read: "It was said to those of old, You shall not kill; but I say to you," that is, "I say something above every precept." So I would say, not presumptuously but truly, that just as there is a holy of holies, so there is a precept of precepts.

But to be able to keep these things, let us ask the Lord for understanding. Let us understand what circumcision is. Joshua circumcised with knives of stone and took away the reproach of Egypt from the children of Israel. The rock is Christ. Let the word of God and the sword of his mouth circumcise you, and so you will be free of the reproach of Egypt. Circumcision, then, is to be understood as circumcision of the heart, not of the body. If you understand the law, you will keep it in your heart.

The Jew does not keep the law in his heart. He recites the law with his lips and does not know the law. And so Scripture says: "This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." How can one who is far from the law's author hold to the law? Let us consider what the third verse contains.

"Lead me in the path of your commandments, for I have desired it." Who says this but the one who follows Christ? No one else can say it except the one who carries out what is written: "You shall walk after the Lord your God and cling to him, for he leads you." Hear how he leads: "Whoever does not take up his cross and follow after me is not worthy of me."

So Christ goes before us so that we may follow. The Word goes before us. Christ is the beginning, and so Wisdom says: "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways." We notice that Christ is both the beginning and the end of the ways. I am not afraid that someone will say: "So you claim that Christ was created?" I will answer: I say he was created in the same sense in which I read that he was made, that is, "made of a woman, made under the law." In other words, he was created in that he took on flesh, in that he was born of a virgin.

He was created in order to redeem created things. He became man in order to free human beings from everlasting death. He was created in order to show me the eternal ways by which a human being can return to the kingdom of God. So since he is the beginning of God's ways, let us follow this beginning.

He was the first to set out on the way of the New Testament, to pave for us the road of devotion. If we fast, he fasted before us. If we suffer insults for God's name, he suffered them first for our redemption. He gave his back to the scourges and his cheeks to the blows. He went up on the cross to teach us that death is not to be feared. And so, as one going ahead, he said to Peter: "You follow me." That is why Peter finished the race: because he followed Christ.

The fourth verse follows: "Incline my heart to your testimonies and not to avarice." Others have "profit," and I think the wording was changed because profit from a good thing seems something to seek rather than to avoid. But since most people think monetary gain is their profit, if we read

"profit," we must understand that the prophet is turning away not from the soul's profit but from the profit of money. For a saint does not know such gains; he counts all these things as loss, so that he may gain Christ. And rightly so, for what we think is monetary gain is the soul's loss, because it is a loss of virtue. So we too agree with the sense given by those who understood it this way, namely that the prophet prays for his heart to be inclined to the testimonies and not to avarice. And if only we would follow the saint's

prayer, pray what he prayed, and imitate in our disposition what we pray for! What good is it to me if I pray that the Lord turn my heart away from avarice, while I myself am hunting for money day and night? If we pray with our words, let us also feel it in our mind. Jesus hears our thoughts, and when he sees that these two do not agree, our words and our greed, he does not listen to the one speaking. That is why the man who wanted to pray well said: "I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind also; I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind also." So he listens more readily to one who prays if that person scorns avarice.

But we are weak. Often, even when we want to turn our heart away from money, we are captivated by the sight of gold or silver, and we covet another person's field or house when we see it. So the prophet rightly added: "Turn away my eyes so that they do not see vanities; give me life in your way." For one who is on God's way does not look at vanities. Christ is the perfect way.

How then can anyone who is in Christ look at vanities, since Christ in his flesh has crucified all the vanities of this world? Let us turn our eyes away from vanities, then, so that the mind does not covet what the eye has seen. Let us leave the mystical sense aside for now. If only this interpretation could call back those who are hurrying off to the various spectacles of the circus games and the theatre! What you are watching is vanity. You watch a pantomime: that is vanity. You watch wrestlers: that is vanity,

because you see them wrestling to win crowns of green leaves. The true wrestlers are those who wrestle against the enticements of this world and whose eyes are not caught by the gymnastics of the body. You watch horses racing: that is vanity, because they run in vain, since they cannot save the one who rides them. Indeed, the very turn of the racecourse should teach you that they run in vain, for they do not make a straight journey; they forget what lies ahead and strain toward what lies behind.

Christ is before us, and his prize is before us. The one who reached it did not run aimlessly or turn back but pressed on. Direct your eyes to him. Turn them away from shows, turn them away from all the pomp of this world. Whenever you notice the applause of the crowd, turn your eyes away from it. Bend them, lower them, and keep them safe, so that you may lift them up to better things.

Lift them to heaven. At night look at the necklaces of stars and the lovely orb of the moon, or by day look at the sun. Look at the sea, gaze round at the earth, so that all creation, made by God's work, may feed you. What graceful forms there are even in the beasts, what beauty in human beings, what loveliness in the birds! Look at these things, and you will not see iniquity and strife in the city. Look at these things, and death will not come in through the windows of your eyes.

If you look at a woman so as to desire her, death has come in through the window. If you look at the property of an orphan or a widow and desire to seize it, death has come in through the window. If you look at another's

necklaces, gold and silver, and desire to wrest them from him, death has come in through the window. So close this window through which you see the beauty of another man's wife, so that death cannot come in. Let your eyes not look at another man's wife, so that your tongue may not speak perversely. Close your own window, then, so that it is not open to death as it enters. But beware of the other person's window too, for the harlot enters from the window of her house.

She enters from her window. She enters when the wantonness of a lustful eye tempts someone. So shut this window with the door of the word, so that you are not caught by the harlot's eyes and carried off by her eyelids. But there is more than one window through which death usually enters. There is also the window of words, through which the harlot's speech passes. So guard yourself from another man's wife, so that she does not assail you with charming words; for she enters from the window of her house.

Death enters through kisses, so beware that she does not bind you with the snares of her lips. Death enters if a harlot kisses you. Death enters if you quickly agree with her when she speaks. Death enters if you speak, and death enters if you speak a great deal, for much talk brings sin. Death enters even if you do not speak and are afraid to confess Christ, for confession is made with the mouth to salvation. Death enters through the openings of the ears as well, and so the ears must be hedged with thorns, to shut out the enticements of the harlot's talk. So much for the moral sense.

There are also mystical eyes that you should turn away from vanity. For there is also a vanity of the understanding, which the eyes of your soul should not see, because it is seen by those whom the apostle condemns. So let us rather learn from him as our authority what the vanity is and what the eyes are. For it is plain that there are many who are darkened in heart by the vanity of their understanding and alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart. Yet the apostle calls these people Gentiles.

Let that Gentile, then, be ignorant of what he has not learned, ignorant of what he has not believed. But you are not allowed to be ignorant of what you confess. Christ came not in vanity but in power. He did not puff up the human understanding but gave it life. He brought about not blindness of heart but enlightenment of mind. He set your heart on fire, so that you may grasp the meaning of the heavenly commandments, the substance of the soul, the grace of the life to come, and the state we will be in hereafter.

So lift up your mind and use the abilities nature has given you. You were made in the image of God, so that you might look at the things above and not seek the things of earth. Do not bend your neck to be pressed down by the weight of the world. Do not gape after gold and silver, or you will offer yourself to be bound by the chains of this world. That is why the Lord said: "Do not possess gold or silver," so that greedy desire for gold and silver may not possess us. So do not

put your neck into the devil's snares. Avarice strangles the poor man in this world, but the rich man is choked forever by its snares. His understanding is in vanity, and he walks in darkness, labouring over things that cannot profit him. The anxiety of this life is vanity. So we ought to place our delight not in carousing and drunkenness, not in bodily pleasures, but in knowing the heavenly precepts. The one who thinks he is overflowing with worldly successes, which pass away like a shadow, is running in vanity. So turn your eyes away, so that they do not see vanity.

But it is not enough that you turn them away yourself. Perhaps you may want to and not be able, if the devil spreads spectacles of vanity before your eyes and thrusts in incitements to pleasure. Ask the Lord to turn your eyes away. This too is the grace of God, and this

is the gift of the Lord, that he turn the eyes of our soul away from the business of this world. For all blessedness comes from the Lord: "Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not looked upon vanities and false frenzies." The one who does not look at these things is blessed. The one who looks at them is insane and raving. So let each of us come back to our senses from the frenzy of worldly desires, which so disturb the mind and soul that a person cannot be master of himself.

If you are on board a ship tossed by the waves, you turn your eyes away from the bilge so that it does not make you sick. If you are walking in a city and come upon some foul smell, you shrink far away from it and turn aside.

If something you meet makes your eye shudder, the eye shuts or turns away. You are tossed on the sea of this world, and the bilge of vices flows in. In this ship of your body the surge of desires is stirred up. Will you not turn away the eyes of your soul, so that they do not see the bilge of lusts, so that they do not look at the dung of this world, so that the unclean stench does not fill the nostrils of your mind, where the Holy Spirit is accustomed to dwell, so that you can say, "the divine spirit that is in my nostrils"? So let the nostrils of your soul be turned away from the stench of all kinds of crimes, for in them there is, as it were, a distinctive mark of judgement.

That is why it is said to the bride: "Your nostrils are like the tower of Lebanon, looking toward the face of Damascus." For the ointment of the true priest, which ran down from the head onto the beard, that is, the divine fragrance, the fragrance of spiritual grace, which was from the Father in Christ and came down to earth through the sacrament of the incarnation so that all things might be filled with the ointment poured out, stands out with the power of a most lofty judgement and fills the nostrils of the soul. So the soul can tell apart what smells sweet and what stinks: the sweet fragrance of the saints, who can say, "For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God," and the stench of sinners.

These are the nostrils that are like the tower of Lebanon, rising high above the world. That is why it looks toward the face of Damascus, that is, toward the Gentile people, catching the scent of their faith, by whose grace they would wipe away the stench of their sins. The face of Damascus, then, is the faith of the Gentiles, shaded by no mantle, covered by no garment, bare and free, intent on heaven rather than on earth.

The nostrils of the Church watch over this faith and look out toward it, gathering whatever in it is sweet and fragrant with the breath of grace. And her nostrils are rightly like the tower of Lebanon, because the Church's sweet fragrance is in the sacrifices, in which there is a victim of good fragrance, the remission of sins.

So take these nostrils, O man, so that you can tell what is flowery from what smells foul, and then the Lord will give you life. When he notices what you are asking of him, that he turn the eyes of your mind away from vanity, he works together with your soul. If it is captivated by some beauty, or will not bend because of its hardness and weakness, he bends it with the yoke of the word and guides it with his reins, so that by God's will it may be drawn away from vices and catch the scent of eternal life.

For life here is not perfect; this life is lived in shadow. That is why, when the man Christ Jesus was to be born of a virgin, the power of the Most High overshadowed his future mother: he came down into shadow, beginning to work man's salvation from the shadow, and he was to complete it in the brightness of the eternal sun. This life, then, is a shadow. Hurry toward the sun, so that it may protect you from the cold of this shadow and pour summer warmth upon you. And that is why he urges us to pray that our flight may not be in winter or on the sabbath. He is not speaking of a season or a day. He is forbidding us to be cold in merits and to fast from good works.

Learn now how the Lord turns the eyes of the one he pities away from vanity. We can understand this from what follows, for he added: "Establish your word for your servant in your fear." The prophet says that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. And what is the beginning of wisdom but to renounce the world, since to be wise in worldly things is folly?

Indeed, the apostle says that the wisdom of this world is folly with God. But even the fear of the Lord does no good unless it is according to knowledge; in fact it does a great deal of harm. The Jews have a zeal for God, but because it is not according to knowledge, they give the Godhead greater offence through that very zeal and fear. When they circumcise their infants and keep the sabbath, they show fear of God. But because they do not know that the law is spiritual, they circumcise the body and not their heart. They dread lighting a fire on the sabbath, whereas the law forbids the fire of lusts to be kindled on the day of sanctification.

And why should I speak of them? There are also people among us who have the fear of God, but not according to knowledge. They lay down harsher precepts than the human condition can bear. There is fear in this, in that they think they are looking after discipline and demanding the work of virtue. But there is ignorance in it too, in that they show no compassion for nature and do not consider what is possible. So let fear not be irrational.

For true wisdom begins from the fear of God, and there is no spiritual wisdom without the fear of God; in the same way, fear ought not to be without wisdom. Holy fear is a kind of pedestal for the word. A statue is set on a pedestal, and it has greater grace once it has been placed on the pedestal and given a firm place to stand. In the same way the word of God, or God's reason, is better established and more strongly rooted in holy fear, that is, in the breast of one who fears God. Then the word does not slip from a man's heart, and the birds do not come and carry it off, as they do from a careless and neglectful disposition.

But fear itself also seems to be fitted for usefulness and made stable by the word of God, so that it is not foreign to knowledge, just as a pedestal that has received a statue is not foreign to grace. Fear, then, is the place of the word, as it is said, "his place is in peace." Fear is a kind of zeal for the word, and the word is the discipline of fear, for fear full of discipline does not totter toward a fall.

We have called fear the pedestal of the word. In case anyone thinks we have said something foreign to the scriptures, let him take what is read in the word of God in the Song of Songs: "His legs are marble columns set upon bases of gold." This signifies that the columns of the church are the apostles, who are founded on the fear of the saints. Peter, James, John and Barnabas were reckoned pillars of the church, and whoever overcomes this world becomes a pillar of God, which he strengthens who says, "I have made firm its pillars." In the same way the golden base is fear full of discipline, because it is the beginning

of wisdom. So the apostolic preaching is made firm in the fear of the wise, like a column on a golden base. For the eloquence of Christ and the apostolic word, the fear of the righteous is a platform and a golden base full of prudence, while the fine statue, the image of truth as it were, is the speech of the saints. And see how the fear of the saints is like a golden base. Read Isaiah, and see how many things he placed fear beneath, to make fear blameless and good: "The spirit," he says, "of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and

of might, the spirit of knowledge and of godliness, the spirit of holy fear." How many things he placed fear beneath, so that it would have something to follow! It is shaped by wisdom, instructed by understanding, directed by counsel, strengthened by might, governed by knowledge and adorned by godliness. Take away [these from] the fear of the Lord [?], and it becomes an irrational and foolish fear, one of those described in "fighting without, fears within." Paul too would have been overwhelmed by these if he had not had the Lord to comfort him.

Nor is it for nothing that Proverbs says: "Then you will understand the fear of the Lord." What does "then" mean? It means: when you have called upon wisdom and lifted up your voice to prudence, and if you have sought her like money and

searched for her like treasure, then you will understand the fear of the Lord. And so, as if on a good base, he says: "Establish your word for your servant in your fear." This is a prayer full of instruction, teaching us how we ought to pray; every word of it is a lesson in supplication. And since he has taught us to pray, he shows what the effect of this prayer is.

"Take away my reproach, which I have suspected." This seems a little obscure, but the apostle explained what seemed obscure here when he said: "I am not aware of anything against myself, yet I am not justified by this." He knew that he was a man. He took what care he could not to sin after receiving the sacraments of baptism, and so he was not conscious of any offence. But because he was a man, he confessed himself a sinner. He knew that Jesus alone is the true light, who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found, and that he alone is justified, since he alone was truly free from falling.

So it was with the prophet too. Although he wanted to avoid sin, he still wanted God to be, as it were, the one who drove his sin away. He wanted the reproach he suspected to be taken away. Perhaps he had thought of it in his heart without doing it, and although it had been wiped out by penance, he still feared that his reproach might remain. And so he prays God to take it away, since God alone knows what even the one who did it may not know. Indeed elsewhere the prophet himself said: "You know my reproach." Yet that reproach may be the reproach of Christ, which is not truly a reproach but the glory of God, for the cross of Christ is a stumbling block to the Jews and folly to the Greeks.

To them, then, it is a reproach. To me it is power, by which I drive back the adversary and conquer the world. To me it is wisdom, by which I escape the snares of folly. Moses preferred this reproach to the treasures of Egypt: "He considered the reproach of Christ," it says, "greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt." If your reproach is glory, Lord Jesus, how great is your glory!

What then shall we become by sharing in your glory, when we are made glorious by your reproach? "I gave my back to the scourges and my cheeks to blows, and I did not turn my face from the shame of spitting." Behold your reproach, Lord, in which lies the salvation of all,

in which lies the redemption of the world. Through this reproach we who used to blush have begun not to blush, and we who were put to shame are no longer put to shame. Indeed it is written: "Come to him and be enlightened, and your faces will not blush." We do not want this reproach taken away from us, the reproach of the cross of the Lord Jesus, by which our reproaches are taken away. He became a curse to blot out our curses, and became man to relieve man's weaknesses; in the same way he became a reproach to take away the reproaches of all.

He did not take away reproaches at one moment or once only; he takes them away every day. We fall into sin, not one sin but many, and we are covered with reproach and shame. We come to baptism, and every sin is washed away, and the reproach along with the sin. The Lord Jesus took away my reproach by his own reproach, because he was crucified for me, because all of us who

have been baptized into Christ have been baptized into his death. Then I have nothing to ask to be taken away. But if after baptism I have fallen into reproach, I must do penance, so that I can say: "Take away my reproach from me." If I do not do penance, how can I say, "Take away my reproach from me," when the very fact that I do not do penance is the reproach of sin? But if I do penance as I ought, then I rightly say: "Take away my reproach, which I have suspected, for your judgments are sweet."

Why am I afraid to confess? Why am I afraid to speak of my sins? Why am I afraid to mention my reproach before him whose judgments are sweet? What is severe in others is sweet in Christ and gentle in Christ, because he himself is gentle.

Indeed: "Taste and see that the Lord is sweet." His judgments are sweet to one who confesses, because he himself said: "I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them. But you, remember, and let us go to judgment together; tell your iniquities, so that you may be justified." His judgments are sweet to one who repents, because he himself said: "There will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous who need no repentance." If, then, the Lord's judgments are sweet, let us work hard to gather the fruits of that sweetness.

Do you want to know how sweet the Lord's judgments are? "The ungodly do not rise in the judgment." Those who do rise in the judgment have hope of pardon, because they have believed. They are not ungodly. They may be sinners, but they have faith, and even if they have not avoided fault, they believe through faith; and whoever believes in him is not judged. So his judgments are sweet to those who believe.

Those who do not believe are not condemned by the judgment of Christ, for he came not to judge the world but to save and redeem it. They have undergone the judgment of their own ungodliness, since they refused to believe in the forgiveness of sins. They cannot share in the benefit of the one they refused to know. So those who did not believe in him are seen to be unworthy of his judgment. Learn what his judgment is from his own words: "This is the judgment, that the light has come into this world." It is sweet, then, because it is light; sweet is the judgment that mercy goes before. For so it is written: "Of mercy and judgment I will sing to you, Lord."

And because he knew that the judgments are sweet, he says: "Behold, I have longed for your commandments; in your righteousness give me life." He speaks of "good judgments" with authority [?]. See, he who gave liberty loves the liberty of faith; he who came into this world because

he loved this world rejoices to be loved; he who loves all demands to be loved, because he is love. The psalmist longed for God's commandments as a good servant, as a diligent worker. He did not long as a lover longs to lie with a harlot, or as a miser longs for money, or as a profligate longs for indulgence. Of those things the law says, "You shall not covet"; but it commands that the Lord God be loved, and loved with a tender, inward feeling of desire. And since the one who loves is a friend, while the one who fears is a servant, he longed as a friend who has done all that the Lord commanded him: "You are my friends," he says, "if you do what I command you."

"In your righteousness give me life." He dares to say this because true life is the life lived according to God's righteousness, the life the apostles lived, or rather still live. For there are some who are dead while they live, and some who live though they are dead. Indeed some go down alive into hell, while others, though dead in the body, live by their merits. For there are some who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man returning on the day of judgment, when the saints will rise in glory.
VI. THE LETTER VAU
The sixth letter is Vau, which is interpreted to mean "or even thus, not he"; another interpreter says "and it is not."

"Let your mercy come upon me, Lord, your salvation according to your word." Since the meaning of the letter's interpretation is rather obscure, I thought it should be worked out from the sequence of the psalm. When the prophet asks, "Let your mercy come upon me, Lord, let your salvation come," there is no doubt whom he is asking to see: the one in whom the fruit of both mercy and salvation is to come. Indeed he had already asked for the same thing in Psalm 84, where he prophesied the coming of the Lord Jesus more plainly. It is clear enough which earth he asks to be blessed. It is the earth that had contracted sin in Adam, to whom it is said: "Earth you are, and to earth you shall go." But God had cursed not the natural element of the flesh, but the flesh of transgressors. So flesh is blessed in Christ, in order to be released from the former curse. The flesh is blessed that the blessed Son of God took up when he assumed the human condition.

And so he added: "O God, you will turn and give us life, and your people will rejoice in you. Show us your mercy, Lord, and grant us your salvation. I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me, for he will speak peace to his people, and upon his saints, and to those who turn their hearts to him. Surely his salvation is near to those who fear him, that glory may dwell in our land."

This whole passage speaks of the Lord Jesus, who gave life to the dead: to Lazarus before his passion, and to very many at the time of his own passion. He himself is mercy, since he is the forgiveness of sins. That is why the psalmist says "show": he means one he could see in a body. He could not see God in his majesty, because no one has ever seen God. The prophet eagerly longs to see the one he hopes to hold, and once he sees him, he longs to grasp him with his own hands.

So he says: "And grant us your salvation." God's salvation is power; God's salvation is Christ, and that is why this salvation is near to those who fear. Christ was far from us, far from the nations. He came down to earth and drew near, and we began not to fear. For whoever fears Christ is not subject to fear but to devotion; this fear comes from godliness, not from weakness. Indeed, "those who fear him lack nothing."

Hear how he drew near: "that glory," it says, "may dwell in our land." Who is the glory but the Lord Jesus? That is why the apostle Paul says: "The God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory." The Father is rightly well pleased in him, because he is the Father's glory. Whoever separates him from the Father does the Father a greater injury, for he makes [?] the Father to be without glory. Whoever does not consider him equal to the Father judges the Father to be inferior as well. He cannot praise the Father more highly with any other word, because Christ is the height of the praise of glory.

So the prayer is that the salvation of God may come. He is the one to whom the prayer is made, that is, the Lord Jesus, and there is no other, as the interpretation of the letter has it. "Or even thus": the prayer is not made to the Father alone. There is also "he," that is, the Son, to whom the prayer is made, and who in answer came and gave salvation to the world. That is why he is called Soter, that is, "Saviour," and why he is called Jesus, as the angel said: "for he will save his people." So when the prophet called upon him, he was present, to prove the saying: "While we are still speaking, he says: Here I am."

He is present because, when roused by the daughters of Judea, he is as it were roused by the daughters of Jerusalem. The church hears the sound of his voice and says: "The voice of my kinsman! Behold, he comes leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills." The book is made up of companies, so to speak. It has many noble characters, like triumphal companies, and it points to many actions, which we may understand rather than find set out explicitly. For it is as though the bride had heard the bridegroom approaching and talking with some fellow travellers, and she says: "The voice of my kinsman!"

While she is talking with the daughters of Jerusalem and asking them to rouse and awaken the bridegroom, she suddenly catches the sound of a voice that seems to come from far away. She says, "The voice of my kinsman!", announcing the very one she had earlier wanted to have announced to her. She had wanted others to rouse him; now she believes that her own prayer has roused him and that he is coming from the Father, and she joyfully says: "The voice of my kinsman!" She did well to add "my kinsman," so that no other woman, but she alone as his kinswoman, could claim his coming as her own.

"Behold," she says, "here he comes." I am still looking for him, and he is already coming. I am still canvassing for support to bring him, and he is already very close. I long for love to be awakened for me; I think of myself as wounded by love, and love itself hurries all the faster toward me. I said, "Come," and he leaps and bounds over. I ask him to come with grace, and he works an increase of graces. As he comes he brings growth of grace with him, and he gains more by coming, because he too is eager to please his beloved.

He leaps over the heights to climb up to the bride, for the bride's chamber is the throne of Christ. He leaps over Adam, he bounds over the synagogue; he leaps over the gentiles, he bounds over the Jews. Let us watch him leaping. He leaps from heaven into the Virgin, from the womb into the manger, from the manger into the Jordan, from the Jordan onto the cross, from the cross into the tomb, from the tomb into heaven.

Show me, David, the one who leaps; show me the one who runs. For you said: "He rejoiced like a giant to run his course. His going forth is from the height of heaven, and his circuit reaches to its height, and there is no one who can hide from his heat." So even now he leaps and even now he runs, from the Father's heart onto his saints, from the east over the west, from the north over the south. He is the one who ascends over the setting sun; he ascends over the heaven of heavens toward the east. He ascends over the mountains; he ascends over the hills.

If only I, wretched as I am, might say, if only my soul might say: "Behold, here he comes," and comes not over earthly things, not over valleys, but comes leaping over the mountains! For God is a God of the mountains, not of the valleys. Where, then, does he leap? He leaps over the mountains. If you are a mountain, he leaps over you. He leaps over Isaiah, he leaps over Jeremiah, he leaps over Peter, John and James. "Mountains are round about him." If you cannot be a mountain and do not have the strength, be at least a hill, so that Christ may climb over you. And if he bounds over you, may he bound over in such a way that the shadow of his passing protects you.

We have spoken of Christ and the church; let us speak of the soul and the Word. The soul of the righteous is the bride of the Word. If she desires and longs, if she prays, and prays constantly, and prays without any wavering, and is wholly intent on the Word, she suddenly seems to hear the voice of the one she does not see, and with her inmost sense she recognizes the fragrance of his divinity. Those who believe rightly often experience this. The nostrils of the soul are suddenly filled with spiritual grace, and she feels the breath of his presence breathing upon her, the one she is seeking, and she says: "Behold, this is the very one I seek, the one I desire."

Is it not true that when we are pondering something in the scriptures and cannot find its explanation, while we are doubting and searching, the Word suddenly seems to climb up for us, as if over mountains, to the loftiest teachings? Then, appearing to us as if over hills, he enlightens the mind, so as to pour into our understanding what had seemed difficult to find.

So the Word, which seemed absent, becomes present in our hearts. And again, when something is rather obscure to us, the Word is as it were withdrawn, and we long for his coming as for someone absent. Then he appears again and shows himself to us, as though present with us as we come to understand what we are seeking. So he often leaps in the heart of each one of us. He bounds over, goes out and returns, if you follow him, if you seek him, if through the welcome discussion of faithful teachers you ask for the Word who had gone out and passed by to be roused again. So it was with the bride, who sought and found, and who said: "My brother passed by; my soul went out at his word."

So if he leaps over the mountains, follow; if he leaps over the hills, follow. For the Lord's hunters are found on the mountains and on the hills, tracking those who are to be caught for life. For so God spoke through Jeremiah: "Behold, I am sending many fishermen and many hunters, and they will hunt them on every mountain and on every hill." There, then, let the people of God be sought and found, in the teaching of Peter and of Paul, in the grace of discipline, so that they may not be in the valley, where there is weeping, but on the mountains, from which Christ enlightens each one.

When we read Peter, Christ enlightens us, and when we read Paul, Christ enlightens us. Paul healed and Christ enlightened, since the man who was healed by Christ's gift stood up when the name of the Lord Jesus was invoked. Peter raised a dead woman, and Christ enlightened. That is why it says: "You give light wonderfully from the everlasting mountains."

We, then, who cannot be mountains, should stand on the mountains or on the hills. Then, when the Lord sends his fishermen and his hunters to hunt those who are on every mountain or on every hill, that is, those whose whole way of life rests on the precepts of the law and the prophets and on knowledge of the New and Old Testaments, they will find us ready. Like reapers sent at the right time, they will gather us as good ears of grain. If anyone is found outside the mountain or the hill, he cannot be gathered as a good ear of grain by those who, to bring in another comparison, will be sent to separate the wheat from the chaff. The Lord has ministers skilled in many tasks: the same men are fishermen, hunters and reapers as well.

If, at harvest time, when these are directed [?], you wait ripe in merit, you will be able to see him leaping on the mountains, and you will see the Lord Jesus like a roe or a young stag upon the mountains of Bethel. For he leaps upon the Church, which is the house of bread, because he strengthens the hearts of the faithful. Rightly is he like a roe, for the roe feeds on the heights.

The roe is called dorkas from seeing; for the dorkatikon is of keener sight. What could fit Christ better than this, who saw the Father whom no one has seen, or, if anyone has seen him in Christ, it is the Son himself who revealed him? Rightly is he like a young stag; a young stag is like a son, in whom the power of his father's nature has grown, so that hidden things are not concealed from him. Serpents flee from him, their venom does not harm him. Indeed, the serpent that was being driven out of a man, drawn from its lairs, said: “Why have you come before the time to torment us?”

Let us look, then, upon this leaping fawn, so that we cannot fear the serpent. David did not fear; indeed, he spoke of these serpents: “And I will answer a word to those who reproach me, for I have hoped in your words.” Like a good stag that had drunk from the springs of water, he had no fear at all of the coils of human serpents or the venom of slanderers.

The snake was no harm to him but prey. The poison of serpentine speech was food to him, and food of praise. Of this he said: “O God, do not keep silent my praise, for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful has been opened against me.” He grew fat on the words of the venomous; they raised mouths hissing with detraction and surrounded the innocent with words of hatred. The good stag, set among many snakes, had no fear, the stag of friendship and the fawn of graces. They feigned love and poured out detraction; “but I,” he says, “prayed.”

The good stag fed unharmed in the midst of vipers. Their three-forked tongues flickered from their mouths, but holy prayer fed him; more than that, he offered food to his detractors. He answered a word to those who reproached him, for the word is food; indeed, “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.” “They saw me,” he says, “and shook their heads.” They cursed, but I blessed. Those who slandered cursed; I, who preached the word of the Lord, blessed.

How good it is to bear an insult and not return the insult! The one who does not know how to be angry with someone who insults him gains God as his protector. How great, then, is the grace of patience in the one who says: “They will curse, and you will bless!” Blessed is he who does not feel curses, blessed is he whom curses do not disturb: for he cannot be moved by a curse who shuts out the curses of men by the divine gift of blessing. He who has the word cannot feel a curse, and he who always has the word in his mouth cannot return a curse.

But there is also a good serpent, which this stag does not harm: “Be wise as serpents,” and: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.” My serpent was prefigured in the bronze serpent; my serpent was lifted up on that wood, the good serpent. The good serpent, who poured from his mouth not poisons but remedies. He can

have no fear of serpents who knows how to worship this serpent. Of this serpent she who loves says: “Behold, he is behind our wall, looking in through the windows, peering over the nets. My kinsman answers and says to me: Arise, come, my near one, my fair one, my dove, for behold, the winter is past, the rain is gone, it has departed; flowers have appeared on the earth.”

He is truly a serpent, who, when the winter had run its course, wished to strip off the garment of the body, so as to bloom again in lovely beauty. He is, then, both stag and serpent: a stag having the horns of law and grace — his two horns are the two testaments — swift of step, tireless in his going, who easily runs through the whole world in a single moment, to be celebrated everywhere; and a serpent

too, a good one, whose front parts do not bite with the tooth of the law, and whose hind parts do not wound, by the gentleness of the gospel. He guards his head from wounding, he who came not to abolish the law but to protect it from the interpretations of the faithless. He spreads out his tail freely into lashes, wishing rather to scourge his adversaries than to destroy them. The good snake glides easily into the bosom of the beloved and into the innermost fold of her mind, and without any touch, entwining fire in her bones, he feeds on her very heart.

Beautifully was it read today: “Behold, I send you as lambs in the midst of wolves.” For we are celebrating the day of the saints on which the bodies of the holy martyrs were revealed to the people. Like good serpents, they laid aside the cast skin of the flesh, overcame the rigour of wintry temptations, were renewed by the grace of the Holy Spirit, and shone on the world with a summer light, sent truly as lambs in the midst of wolves. For the persecutors are wolves, all the heretics are wolves; they do not know how to teach, they are used to howling.

But let no one be troubled if he is sent into the midst of wolves. By the kindness of Christ even the wolf himself has been changed: Benjamin, the ravening wolf, became the apostle Paul, no longer one who lies in wait for Christ's sheepfolds, but their defender and guardian. It is a pleasure to keep company with this wolf; through this wolf it has come about that we are safe in the midst of wolves. No one fears wolves any longer; we feed with them, as it is written: “Then wolves and lambs shall feed together.”

But now let us consider what the prophet means when he says: “And do not take the word of truth utterly out of my mouth, for I have hoped exceedingly in your judgments.” The Church, or the soul of the just, had seen him leaping like a fawn upon the mountains. Suddenly, seeing her near one behind the wall of her house, looking in through the windows, peering over the nets, she exults and rejoices that she too is loved by the bridegroom. He, as though himself wounded by the beauty of his beloved's love, first came when, in his absence, he was asked for kisses — for he is asked when it is said: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” — and then did not spurn the prayers and endearments of the bride as she praised the breasts so dear to her, and kindly led her into the inner rooms of the house. Then, as though playing in a sportive love, because he wished to test the feelings of the one who loved him, often going out so as to be sought by the bride, often coming back so as to be invited to kisses, he stood behind the wall, looked in through the windows, peering over the nets, so that he should be neither wholly absent nor, as it were, wholly come in, and might himself call the bride to him, so that their exchanges in coming to one another might be the more delightful and they might kindle the strength of their love with words to each other. “Arise,” he says, “come, my near one, my fair one, my dove.”

And you too, if you have a wall well founded — not that middle wall which separates the parts of a single house, but one built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, so that its structure, joined together, grows into a temple and does not divide its interior but fortifies it — if, then, you have in you the building of God, and your windows always stand open to the east, the Word comes, stands behind your wall — for the eyes of the Lord are upon the just — and looks in through your windows.

What are these windows? We read of windows of which Jeremiah says: “Death has come in through the windows,” the windows through which avarice has come in, and lust has come in. Your eye is a window; death has come in through your eye. If you look on a woman to lust after her, death has come in through your eye. If you see the property of a widow or a minor and desire to seize it, thinking that their age or sex is defenceless — but those whom the Lord wishes to be defended are not defenceless — death has come in through the window. If you hear of a woman's beauty or

a minor's treasures and stir up your desires, death has come in through the window. So, just as death comes in through these, so does life: if, looking on the beauty of a consecrated virgin, you venerate the Lord Jesus, because old age, which is a spotless life, has come into her tender years, and you yourself offer your daughter to be consecrated with the holy veil; if you look on a minor's property not as an eager invader, but protect it with devout affection as a careful parent would. Through these windows Christ looks in and calls the bride, peering over the nets.

“Peering over” is well said, because he alone is the one whom the nets of sins did not entangle. All were within the nets — indeed, we are still within the nets — since no one is without sin except Jesus alone, whom the Father, though he knew no sin, made sin for us. For he handed him over to the snares, handed him over to the nets, sending him not in sin, in which all men were, but in the likeness of sinful flesh, so that by sin he might condemn sin in the flesh.

The flesh was sin, in that sense, because it had been condemned by an inherited curse; it was sin as the allurement and servant of sin. The Lord Jesus came, and in flesh subject to sin he waged the warfare of virtue. Our members have become no longer weapons of lust but weapons of virtue; for where there were incitements to lust, there are now dwellings of chastity. So he came to the snares, but willingly; he came to the nets, but secure.

Everything was full of nets, crammed with snares. Hear the one who says: “In the way where I walked they hid a snare for me”; and in the book of the Wisdom of Sirach you are warned to know that you walk in the midst of snares. As many vices, so many nets; as many sins, so many snares; inherited bonds already held you fast. Jesus came to the snares to set Adam free; he came to free what had perished. We were all held by nets; no one could rescue another, since he could not free himself.

Such a one, then, was needed as the bonds of human generation, liable to sin, could not hold, whom avarice had not caught, nor deceit bound. That one was Jesus alone, who, though he had wrapped himself in the bonds of this flesh, was not captured, was not bound, but, bursting and loosening them, called the Church all the more to himself, looking through the snares, peering over the nets, so that she too might learn not to be held by bonds.

Indeed, he came so near to bonds that he even underwent death for us; yet he was not made a slave of death, but was free among the dead: for he was free who had the power to undo death. Let him teach you himself, who says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”

Let us hear, then, what he says: “Arise, come, my near one”; that is: rise from the dead, arise from the bonds that encircled and held you. Arise, for I have risen for you; loose the bond of iniquity, for I have already loosed it for you. Come, for the nets are already loosed.

A virgin has given birth; a child is born of a virgin, owing nothing to the inheritance that comes from woman. He is not held as the son of a woman. See, the middle wall of partition is now taken down, which divided the harmony of the inner affections and stirred up the conflicts of bodily passions against them. Come, then, without fear; I long to see your face and hear your voice. Come, so that you may no longer see me through nets, but, face to face, may enjoy as beloved the countenance of your lover. Let this be our treatment of the moral sense; but let us now look at the mystical sense, if we can, at least in outline.

The bride, devoted to the Lord, was sitting within the house, within the wall of the law and the prophets, founded on a structure of spiritual stones, which enclosed and fortified the royal house, full of delight and gladness. She marvelled at the royal treasures and gazed on them earnestly, longing to take to herself wisdom,

which would show her these riches. She was in a secret place, but she was looking for an interpreter of that very secret. The Lord Jesus came leaping upon the mountains — to us he seemed to come late, but he was hastening — he leapt indeed and leapt over, so as to leap over the bodily and stony doctrines of the Jews. He stood behind the wall of the house that was in the Old Testament, looking in through the window of the law, through the openings of the prophets. The entrances of that house were not yet open,

nor had the keys of knowledge yet unbarred the gates by which the inner parts of the law were shut. Yet, looking out from the upper, that is the spiritual, part, he calls the Church, so that, rising high through the law and the prophets to the summit of the gospel, she might tread with fearless step on the nets and knots of Jewish interpretation. She is called “near one,” therefore, so that she may cling to Christ and not seek worldly things; “fair,” so that she may show forth the beautiful feet of those who preach the gospel; “dove,” so that she may seek spiritual things and leave earthly things behind.

“Behold,” he says, “the winter is past, the rain is gone, it has departed; flowers have appeared on the earth.” Before the coming of Christ it was winter; Christ came and made summer. Then all things were lacking flowers, bare of virtues; Christ suffered, and all things began to be made fruitful with the buds of a new grace. The rain of overflowing luxury is gone, and the clouds that rose from foul crimes are now dispersed by the summer calm of a pure conscience.

That is why those whose flight is in winter do not escape: because they do not follow the Lord's passion, do not take up their cross and follow Christ. Rain hinders flowers, and now flowers are seen on the earth; the apostles are good flowers, who poured forth the fragrance of their various writings and works.

The time of pruning has come, since the ripe grain is being stored in the barns, and he who reaps receives his wage. The voice of the turtledove has been heard, because she has found herself a nest; for the Church is the house of chastity. The fig tree, which was ordered to be cut down for its barrenness, has now begun to bear fruit. The vine brought out of Egypt is no longer ravaged by beasts, its walls torn down, nor is it unsightly with briars; but, now fragrant with blossoms, she who used to produce thorns bends under the fruit of grapes.

Rightly, then, holy David, celebrating the Lord's Pasch and entering with fervent spirit upon the summer season, gathering various fruits in the word of God and turning away from the hardships of winter, says: “And do not take the word of truth utterly out of my mouth, for I have hoped exceedingly in your judgments.” How great is the labour of grasping the word, and how great again the danger if you lose it! And so it is said to you: “Do not neglect the grace that is in you.”

Cultivate your field diligently, like a good farmer, so that your lambs may be fed and your crops may flourish. Let the word not be taken from your mouth, lest perhaps your deeds not match your words, and works of iniquity disfigure the authority of your teaching. The word is taken from the mouth when it is said to the sinner: “Why do you recite my statutes?” And eloquence itself falls silent if the conscience is sick. The birds of the sky come: they too take the word from your mouth, those birds that take the seed of the word from the rock, so that it bears no fruit.

Now let us consider whether the word of truth can also be taken from the heart; for the word that is rooted, pressed down and fixed in our minds can hardly be taken away. Indeed, the Lord said: “Why do you recite my statutes” — he did not say:

“Why do you think on my statutes?” — “and take my covenant in your mouth?” He did not say “in your heart.” The speech of an unworthy mind is restrained, but repentance is not blocked; he forbids insolence, he does not exclude amendment. Yet we must take care that the heart itself is not troubled within and that malice does not spread darkness over it, so that the heart,

blinded by vain thoughts, loses the light of truth and cannot take in the brightness of the word. If, then, David prays that the word not be taken from his mouth, and, if it is taken, not utterly, that is, not entirely, who is so great that he can claim that the gift of discourse lies in his own power, especially if his life refutes what his teaching presumes, and he commits deeds to be condemned by God's judgment? For the one who hopes in God's judgments can keep the word of truth, because, as long as he fears the penalty, he guards the grace.

And therefore he says: “And I have kept your law always, for ever and for ever and ever.” He said two things, when one could have sufficed had he wished to signify only one. But since the law is promised to be kept not only in the present time of this life but also in the future, after the course of this life, I think he therefore pledges himself to live both according to those who serve the copy and shadow of heavenly things, and according to those who, set in the heavenly places, render worship to God according to the true law, so as to keep the law both here and there: here in a copy, in a mirror, in a riddle; there in the very face of the truth.

We can also understand it this way, since diá pantós means not only “always” but also “through all things.” For he keeps the law through all things who, though learned in the law and born under the law, carries the level of his devotion above the law, is freed from the law — for Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the law — and is made not without the law of God but under the law of Christ. Or surely we keep the law through all things if the conduct of our life in no way oversteps the lawful discipline of childhood and adolescence, the manner of life of youth, the maturity of old age, and the path prescribed for each age.

Likewise our soul too seems to have certain ages, through which it runs and passes, so that it can say: “I have finished the course.” Indeed, that is an age of the soul of which it is said: “And old age is a spotless life.” So he keeps the law through all things who has not strayed from the law either in these ages of our body or in those stages of progress of our soul.

The fifth verse is: “And I walked in a broad place, because I sought out your testimonies.” He who, according to the commandments, walks the narrow and strait way walks in a broad place. Hence we read: “In tribulation you have enlarged me,” and elsewhere: “In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he heard me in a broad place.” For the wise man walks in the innocence of his heart, and from its fountain waters overflow onto his

streets — he who does not shut up his mind within bodily and earthly things, but directs it to heavenly things, so that his citizenship is in heaven. Hear one who felt no confinement: “We suffer pressure,” he says, “but we are not hemmed in.” And how could he be hemmed in whose mouth was always open, so that believers should not be cramped? Let him explain what it is to walk in a broad place. For he says that, though the body is confined, our heart is enlarged: “You are not cramped in us, but you are cramped in your own hearts.”

They could not be cramped in Paul, in whom was the height of wisdom and the breadth of faith. How could they be cramped in him who was a vessel of eternal election? But they were cramped in themselves, because the wicked man is cramped within himself and strangled by the snares of his own malice. Picture for me a greedy man, pushing out the boundaries of his estates every day and shutting out his neighbours: does he seem to you enlarged or hemmed in, he whom the earth itself cannot contain? However far he extends the grounds of his house, he is shut in by the narrow limits of his own way of thinking, since what he has is not enough for him. But not such is the one who can say: “And I walked in a broad place.” He added the reason as well: “because,” he says, “I sought out your testimonies.”

“And I spoke of your testimonies in the presence of kings, and I was not put to shame.” This saying fits a martyr well, who, summoned to sacrilege while kings reproached him, did not blush for Jesus crucified, but rather gloried in the cross of Christ and affirmed by heavenly testimonies that it was the salvation of the world.

These Christ calls in the person of the bride, saying in the Song of Songs: “And come, my dove, in the shelter of the rock, beside the outwork,” that is: come close to the gospel. The ramparts of your faith are the deeds of Christ, the supports of your wall are the words of the Lord, the passion of the Lord's body is your strength. “Show me your face and let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet and your face is lovely.” The voice is sweet because with the mouth confession is made unto salvation, and the face is lovely which does not blush for its author and is not ashamed of its redeemer.

She shows her face, then, bearing the sign of the cross before her, and lets her voice be heard, taking up the authority of preaching. For in the shelter of Christ's body, by which she was redeemed from sin, she finds the fortification of spiritual grace, so that she may both think and speak what brings her salvation. Sweet, then, is the voice that spoke in the divine testimonies; lovely is the face that was not put to shame in the presence of kings.

We can also understand those kings to be the ones to whom Peter says: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for adoption.” For they are kings who offer in Jerusalem the gifts of their wisdom, to whom grace has been given to speak the word and, with a kind of royal power, to sway peoples and soothe the souls of the saints. They do not blush in this, because they would say nothing at odds with what is honourable; no one can refute or confute them, as though they were unworthy, since Christ has made them fit ministers of the new covenant; and they do not blush in him, because they had no fear

of being put to shame, defeated by the arguments of those disputing against them. He, then, is a king who does not blush, lest he be reproved in his conduct or refuted in his words, since he ought to be grounded both in his life and in his speech. And so, although the prophet was so perfect that he did not blush in the presence of kings, he nevertheless meditated on God's commandments all the days of his life and lifted up his works, doing nothing that clung to earthly desires.

And so he says: “And I meditated on your commandments, which I loved exceedingly, and I lifted up my hands to your commandments, which I loved exceedingly, and I exercised myself in your justifications.” This is a most beautiful order: first we are to meditate, and meditation on the precepts we love is to become habitual to us;

for through meditation on the heavenly commandments the practice of good works takes root. Just as the end of meditating on words is memory, so that we retain the words we meditate on, so the aim or end of meditating on the heavenly precepts is action, conduct directed to fulfilling the divine precepts. No one can fulfil them unless he loves them, and not merely loves them, but loves them exceedingly.

That is why he first set down: “And I meditated on your precepts, which I loved exceedingly,” and then added: “And I lifted up my hands to your precepts, which I loved exceedingly.” For after meditation it is good to lift up our actions to the precepts of God, and to do this with love and with joy, so that our good is not done out of necessity

nor with grief and sadness, but willingly; for a slave acts unwillingly, a friend willingly. Let us strive, then, that it may be said to us: “I no longer call you servants but friends,” because like friends you have done God’s commandment of your own will. But whoever meditates and loves and lifts up his actions to do what pleases God ought not to neglect the divine commandments or skim over them, but should exercise himself in them and dwell on them at length, turning over God’s justifications again and again with the devotion of an attentive mind.
VII. THE LETTER ZAIN

The letter Zain, according to the Hebrews, means in Latin “lead yourself”; elsewhere it means “hither.” What this interpretation is meant to convey is not quite clear, unless perhaps that each person should govern himself and be his own guide; or, taking “hither,” that he should direct his course to where the words of this section call him. And rightly, in the very first verse, he asks for his rest, since the letter’s own number, seven, is the number of rest. And what greater rest is there than to rest in the word of God and to be soothed by its grace and consolation?

“Remember, O Lord,” he says, “your word to your servant, in which you have given me hope.” The word of God has called us, cast down and oppressed as we were, to heavenly grace, so that we may desire eternity and despise the present, and, unconcerned with temporal things, seek the things to come and the things unseen. So the Word of God calls us to himself, as you have it written: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.” Let us therefore follow the Lord Jesus when he calls, so that we may pass from worldly things to everlasting ones and learn to govern ourselves.

David, then, had often been invited by answers from heaven which gave him hope of a reward for his faith and merits. So you have it written, when God said through Nathan the prophet: “I took you from the sheepfold, from a single flock, to be ruler over my people Israel; and I was with you in all your undertakings, and I destroyed all your enemies before your face”; and further on: “And I will give you rest from all your enemies.” On receiving this answer David said: “Who am I, my Lord, Lord, and what is my house, that you have loved me in these things? Yet these were counted small in your sight, O Lord, and you have spoken of your servant’s house far into the future”; and further on he says: “And now, my Lord, Lord, you are God, and your words are true, and you have spoken these good things of your servant. And now begin to bless the house of your servant, that I may be in your sight for ever; for you, my Lord, Lord, have spoken, and by your blessing the house of your servant shall be blessed for ever.” Called, then, by this answer and by others, David does not cease to hope, and with the authority of prophetic faith he appeals to the Lord to remember his promises, which he never forgets.

For whatever he has pledged to the saints he habitually fulfils, forgetful of our iniquities but not forgetful of his own pledges. Indeed it is written: “I, I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them; but you, remember, and let us be judged.” He wishes to forget whatever he has threatened against sinners, if at some time they turn from their ways; he also wishes to be appealed to, so that anyone who has fought well, since rewards have been set before those who pursue virtue, may expect the fruit of his recompense and even claim it, as you have it written: “I have fought the fight, I have finished the course; there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness.”

For this is not arrogant presumption but faithful confidence, since it confesses that the true God cannot deceive. And so David too reminds the Lord to remember his word, by which he calls us to hope, so that we may renounce earthly things and cleave to heavenly ones.

So David says: “I have fought the fight; I ask for the prize of your word, which you promised me. Remember the promises you pledged to your servant. It was not presumption that made me hope; you yourself made me hope for these things. I am a servant: I expect my sustenance from my master. I am a soldier: I claim my pay from my commander. I have been invited: I ask the one who invited me for what he promised.” Yet he modestly tempered the authority of his faith by calling himself a servant, because the eyes of servants are on the hands of their masters. These words are fittingly spoken in David’s own person.

But if one considers how each person is formed, one may weigh these promises as shared with the Levites, as you have it: “Give to Levi his men, give to Levi his manifest ones.” One may also apply this address to the elect of the believing people, to whom the divine promise passed through the type of Joseph, first to the tribe that bore his name, and then through that tribe to the heirs of the first election, as Moses says: “The firstborn of the bull, his is the glory; his horns are the horns of the unicorn; with them he will toss the nations together to the end of the earth.” For this oracle prophesies that the one Word of God is to be poured out among the nations throughout the whole world. It is this promise, then, made to the Church that was to arise, that David seems to claim, modest on his own account but impatient at the delay of the common advancement.

And he added: “This has comforted me in my humiliation, for your word has given me life.” This is the hope, this hope that came to me through your word, which has comforted me, so that I might endure the bitterness of the present while it makes me trust in what is to come. Hear how it comforts us: “Who,” he says, “shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or peril, or the sword? As it is written: For your sake we are put to death all day long;

we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.” And to show how these things can be patiently endured, he added: “But in all these things we overcome through him who loved us.” So if anyone wishes to overcome adversity, whether persecution or danger or death or grave illness or an attack by robbers or the confiscation of property, or whatever else is thought adversity in this world, these things are easily overcome if there is a hope to comfort us. For even if they befall him, they cannot weigh heavily on one who says: “For I reckon that the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come.” Whoever hopes for better things is never broken by lesser ones.
In the time of our humiliation, then, hope is a comfort, a hope that does not put to shame; and the time of temptations I take to be the time of our soul’s humiliation. For our soul is humbled when

it is handed over to the tempter to be tested by hard labors, so that it may wrestle and contend, experiencing combat with the opposing power. But in these temptations it is given life by the word God speaks to it; for this is the vital substance of our soul, by which it is nourished and fed and governed, and there is nothing else that makes the rational soul live except the word God speaks. Just as the word of God grows in our soul as it is received, understood, and grasped, so too the soul’s life grows; and conversely, as the word of God fails in our soul, so its life too begins to fail.
