Thus, just as this union of our soul and body is animated, nourished, and held together by the vital spirit, so our soul is given life by the word of God and by spiritual grace. Therefore we ought to strive in every way, setting everything else aside, to gather to ourselves the words of God and store them in our ruling faculty, in our thoughts, our cares, our reflections and our actions, so that our deeds may agree with the words of the Scriptures and our conduct may not appear out of harmony with the order of the heavenly precepts. Then we too may be able to say: “for your word has given us life.”

The third verse is: “The proud acted exceedingly unjustly, but I did not turn aside from your law.” The greatest sin in man is pride, since from it flowed the origin of our transgression. With this weapon the devil first wounded us and struck us down. For if man, deceived by the serpent’s persuasion, had not wished to be like God and to know true and false (which in his human frailty he could not fully discern, and for that reason he had been given a command as to what to follow, lest by rash presumption he fall from his seat in paradise), if man, I say, had not been dissatisfied with his own bounds and violated what was forbidden, the inheritance of deadly guilt would never have passed to us. And why speak of man?

The devil himself lost the grace of his nature through pride. Indeed, when he says, “I will set my throne above the clouds, and I will be like the Most High,” he fell from the company of the angels; and, condemned with the just wages of his crime, he sought out man as his partner, into whom he might pour a share in his own offence.

What, then, can be worse than this sin, which began with an injury to God? That is why Scripture also says: “The Lord resists the proud.” As one who repels an insult to himself, he takes up, as it were, a battle of his own against pride, as if he said: “This is my adversary, who provokes me;

this combat is mine to fight.” Hence the apostle too declared pride to be the source of manifold sin, when he said of the heretic that, because he does not assent to the doctrine that accords with godliness, he is proud, knowing nothing, but sick over questions and disputes about words, from which arise envy, strife, blasphemies, evil suspicions, and the wranglings of men corrupt in mind and

estranged from the truth, who think that godliness is a means of gain. How many sins he showed pride to be the cause of! Hence David, wishing to commend his devotion as untouched by any iniquity of the proud, says: “The proud acted exceedingly unjustly.” He declared not only the iniquity of those who act so but also its excess, which is characteristic of the proud. And to show that he was not tempted by any contagion from them, hear him say elsewhere: “With the man of proud eye and insatiable heart I would not eat.”

So, having shown how great a power of evil lies in pride, he had to teach us how it is overcome; and rightly, like a good teacher, he who had made much of the poison shows the remedy. Hear, then, how you may shut out the venom of pride: “I did not turn aside,” he says, “from your law.” The law of God alone, then, can blunt the venom of pride, for it has taught the man devoted to piety with what caution he ought to govern himself.

For many, not only those who are strangers to the faith but even those who seem to have tasted no small part of the precepts of Scripture, are commonly tempted by the prosperity of the proud. They see those who transgress the law, who are the arbiters of impiety, arrogant, scornful of the faithful, exalting themselves against those who humble their hearts according to the fear of God and the heavenly precepts, abounding in this world in riches, renown, honors, and power, and the more grievous their crimes, the more abundant the worldly advantages that favor them; while righteous men, on the other hand, for the most part suffer poverty, the loss of children, and the barrenness of their wives. Shaken and troubled by this, they let their minds incline to the thought that God’s judgment is somehow mistaken in this, for they do not hold fast to the chief point of truth, by which it is most plainly understood that the reward of our merits is laid up not in this world but in the world to come.

But few take note of this. Indeed, even David himself was tempted at first, as you have it written: “Behold, these are sinners, and, prospering in the world, they have obtained riches. And I said: Was it in vain, then, that I justified my heart and washed my hands among the innocent, and have been scourged all day long?” So each of us too, since we are not perfect, says on seeing these things: “Where is God’s providence, where is his justice?

This proud man prospers, that arrogant man grows rich, this impious man is happy and powerful; but that just man, you see how he lies cast down and exhausted, how he lacks even food; he is insulted by this impious man, trampled underfoot and shut out by that insolent one.” This is certainly no small temptation, unless you look ahead to what is to come, unless you are more fully instructed in the heavenly precepts.

Indeed, David too thought before this that he understood, but he did not, and so he labored anxiously with a wavering mind. Hence he says: “And I thought I knew this; it is a labor before me, until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand their last end.” There, by the prophetic spirit, he saw that the proud would be brought lower for having exalted themselves, and he says: “How have they been brought to desolation? Suddenly they have failed and

perished because of their iniquity, like the dream of one who wakes.” He realized, then, that the successes of the wicked in this world are like a dream and not reality; their gains seem real only as long as they sleep. When they have slept off their dream, those who seemed to themselves to be drinking are now thirsty, those who were feast-

ing are hungry, and they bring back nothing solid or complete from that dream. And worldly men do well to be said to sleep a dream, since, though awake to the world, they are asleep to God. Of them holy Job, who had earlier marveled at their abundance, aptly says that they are tossed like chaff by the wind and scattered like dust by a whirlwind; and they die

in bitterness of soul, eating nothing and having nothing good. But the just man, having the confidence of a good conscience, rejoices rather in his last end; he understands that in departing this life he is set free from his labors, and he claims the reward of his good work and deeds, saying: “There is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just judge, will give me on that day; and not to me only, but also to all who love his coming.”

But he who says this is one who could say: “But I did not turn aside from your law,” words in which there shines not only the grace of good works but also the purity of an inner conscience. For the law not only shapes the duty of action; it also cleanses the disposition of the hidden mind. We serve the Lord as soldiers according to the law not only in our works but even in hidden things, for the law says: “Let there be no hidden word of injustice in your heart.” So you are not only to avoid sinning in deed and action when you see the proud boasting, nor slip in your speech, but not even in your inmost heart, while you argue about God’s judgment, are you to incur the offence of iniquity. That offence is the more frequent the more hidden it is thought to be, because each person thinks it safe to entrust arguments of this kind to his conscience, as though fenced in within his own heart, when he himself will be his own accuser on the day of judgment, when the secrets of the heart are revealed and our conscience bears witness to the charges against us.

What the resolve of a holy man should be, then, is set out more clearly in this passage. First, he must be mindful of the heavenly promises, according to which a fixed reward is due to those who live by them. Next, another resolve of the holy man is that, even when he is placed in dangers and adversities, he should console himself with the hope he has drawn from the course of the Scriptures.

The third resolve is that, even if he sees the impious and sacrilegious and the proud who act unjustly abounding in riches in this world, he should not turn aside from the law as though he did not believe, but persevere in its paths and flee the contagion of the proud. For everyone unclean defiles, and the proud man is unclean, of whom it is written: “Unclean before God is every swelling of the heart.”

The fourth resolve of such a man is to be mindful of the heavenly judgments, as David affirms when he says: “I remembered your judgments of old, and I was comforted.” For unless each person, instructed and formed by the examples of the law, believes that God’s judgments are always true, he soon turns aside from the law. But whoever recalls past examples and gathers up the course of ancient history

recognizes that neither does the sinner escape the punishment of his wickedness nor is the just man cheated of the rewards of his justice. For he goes over in his mind how in the beginning Adam was cast out of his dwelling in paradise for transgressing the heavenly command; how Cain, condemned by the authority of the divine sentence, paid the price for murdering his brother; how Enoch, carried up to heaven for his devotion, escaped the poison of earthly wickedness; how Noah, for his righteousness, prevailed over the flood and became the survivor of the human race; how Abraham, for his faith, spread the seed of his posterity over the whole world; how Israel, for his endurance of labors, consecrated the people of believers with the seal of his own name; how David himself, for his meekness, was given royal honor and preferred above his older brothers; how Elijah, for his zeal for God, was borne up into the air in a chariot and, as a new kind of inhabitant, gained a lodging in the heavenly dwelling.

Whoever knows how to go over these things has a source from which to obtain the grace of consolation; whoever does not know them has nothing to console him. Let us therefore keep the judgments of God, because the judgments of God are true, as you have it: “The judgments of God are true, justified in themselves, more to be desired than gold and precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb;

for your servant keeps them.” To one who keeps them, then, the divine judgments are sweet; but to the negligent they are without doubt bitter, because he perceives that the outcome of the divine sentence set before him lies in the shameful disgrace of sinners. But one who has a good conscience is certainly not troubled, and says: “We are heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him.”

But which of us is such that he can console himself with the course of the divine judgments? Even human judgments are terrifying to sinners; how much more are divine ones to be dreaded! To infer the eternal judgments from this example: we see in this world the innocent hurrying gladly to judgment, hating delays, eager for a speedy trial, while the guilty flee and tremble, put it off, avoid it, and are downcast when they hear that the day of judgment has been fixed. Blessed, then, is he who gladly awaits that heavenly judgment; for he knows that the kingdom of heaven, the company of the angels, and the crown of good merits are laid up for him.

Let us now consider what another resolve of the holy man is, and judge it from what follows. “Faintheartedness,” he says, “has seized me because of sinners who forsake your law.” This is not something he shares with many. For most people are grieved if they suffer some injury from someone, if they are hurt, assailed, or disgraced; weaker as we are, we grieve on our own account that some have done us harm.

But one who is stronger does not grieve over an insult to himself but over the sins of others; in his own injury he groans over the other’s fall and laments that he was the occasion of the error that wronged him. Take an example from the apostle. Paul wept over another’s sin, as he himself says: “For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears.” And though he himself was grieved, he did not want those he rebuked to be grieved. Indeed he added:

“not that you should be grieved, but that you may know the love I have more abundantly for you.” He wanted the fallen to be grieved to the point of repentance, not to a deeper despondency, only so that the sorrow of those rebuked might become joy for the one who rebuked them. Hence he says: “For if I

make you sorry, who is there to gladden me but the one who is made sorry by me?” So he rebukes in order to relieve a lasting sorrow, so that repentance might lead to salvation; he condemns in order to absolve, shuts out in order to receive back, withholds pardon in order to set free. That is why Paul was such a man, he who, well versed in the law, had learned the precept of the one who says: “Faintheartedness has seized me because of sinners who forsake your law.”

David grieved, not because he was despised, nor because he himself was attacked, but because the law of God was being forsaken; and he grieved over the loss suffered by those who did this, because they were perishing to God. A good father whose son is in a frenzy, when he is cursed by him, beaten, and subjected to injuries, weeps not for his own trouble but for the sick man’s, and grieves over the insult not because it was inflicted on himself but because the sick man in his madness does not know what he is doing. So too the good man, when he sees a sinner who does not revere or honor even the grey hairs of an elder in whose presence he does something unworthy, and who in a kind of madness of sinning does not recognize how unseemly and shameful are the things he commits, grieves for him as for one about to die, and groans over him as over one the physicians have given up. And like a good physician, he first admonishes; then, even if he suffers grievous things, he bears with him as the physician bears with a sick man, even if he is struck; even if he is cursed, he does not abandon him; he does not withhold whatever remedy he can apply, nor desert him as obstinate, but strives with all zeal to heal him as though he had deserved well of him, exercising not only the skill of his art but also the kindness of his heart.

In the same way, then, the righteous man does not turn away even when a sinner despises him. When he is wronged, he puts it down to madness rather than wickedness. He wants above all to bring healing to the other man's wound; he feels for him and grieves, not on his own account but on account of the one who suffers from a desperate affliction. And he says: “This man, one of the brethren, is so sick and so affected that he does me wrong. If he knew me, he would surely honour me; certainly he would not harm me.”

For what harm has he suffered from anything I have done, that he should have the disposition of one who wounds? Since there is no cause for wounding, the fault cannot lie in his intention. So if I am righteous, I am moved by charity, by love, by the loss to the Church, by the injury to the body. I can grieve over this too: that even though I did not wound the one who wounds me, and am not aware of having provoked him against me by any injuries, I have nonetheless been the occasion of his fall, since he sins by wounding an innocent man, and I have become the material of his sin.

This, then, is what David grieves over, and he grieves because when one member suffers, the other members suffer with it. Perhaps this is why it is also written: “The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech.” For a righteous man may have in himself something to accuse and still be righteous, since no one is without sin except the one God; and a sinner too may be righteous by the very fact that he accuses himself, according to the saying: “Tell your iniquities, that you may be justified.” Yet perhaps some will not think it absurd that this was also said of the man who accuses himself on another's behalf, even if he has nothing in himself to accuse.

Let us consider, then, how well the character of the righteous man fits holy David in all these respects. He accused himself when no one was accusing him; he confessed his own sin when he was struck to the heart for having numbered the people. And he said to the Lord: “I have sinned, O Lord, in doing this thing. And now,

O Lord, take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have sinned greatly.” So although Scripture says that the wrath of God was kindled so that he was angry with Israel, by which the king's fall might seem to be excused, nevertheless, when he saw the angel who was slaughtering the people, he threw himself in the way of the striker's blow, saying: “Behold, it is I who have sinned, and I the shepherd who have done wickedly; and this flock, what has it done?

Let your hand be against me and against my father's house.” Like a righteous man, therefore, he was his own accuser at the very beginning of his speech: he acknowledged his sin, and by confessing his own iniquity he was justified in himself. Elsewhere too, when he was rebuked by the prophet over the death of Uriah, he said: “I have sinned against the Lord”; and he was answered that because of his repentance his sin had been taken away by the Lord.

Again, in another place, when Shimei was cursing him and throwing stones at him while he was surrounded by warriors through whom he could have avenged himself, he bore it patiently and did not return the insult even with a word. Indeed, when Abishai his commander wanted to cut off the head of the man who was cursing, the king said: “What have I to do with you, son of Zeruiah? He curses me because

the Lord has told him to curse David.” First, then, he excused the man's fault and traced the cause back to the Lord's will; second, he turned it back upon his own deserts, to show that it was not the other who had erred but he himself who had deserved it; third, he declared that the man's cursing not only did him no harm but even did him good, as it is written: “And David said to Abishai and to all his servants: Behold, my son, who came forth from my own seed, seeks my life; how much more this son of Benjamin!”

He powerfully checked the avenger's impulse. For how could he avenge a stranger's curse as an injury to the king, while a son's parricide still remained unpunished? Surely a stranger's curse and a son's parricide were not to be weighed in the same balance. And he added: “Let him curse, since the Lord has told him to, so that he may see my humiliation and the Lord may repay me with good for the cursing.”

There is yet another resolve of the righteous man, far more perfect and more powerful than all the rest: to intercede for those who persecute him and to excuse those who sin. We read of this in the Gospel, when the Lord Jesus, crucified by the faithless, said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

It is clear, then, from these lessons of heavenly teaching, that the righteous man would rather accuse himself than disgrace another. Thus of Joseph, to whom Mary the mother of the Lord was betrothed, it is written that when he saw she was with child, being a righteous man, he did not wish to expose her, and this although he had as yet heard no divine message.

So the character of the righteous man is foreign not only to the cruelty of revenge but also to the severity of accusation; he would rather be accused of leniency for not having punished than press another's crime. But you will say: “How then did David himself say: The righteous man will rejoice when he sees the punishment of the ungodly?” It seems to me that he rejoices because he himself has escaped, not because the ungodly are punished. Let us look for another resolve of the righteous man in what follows.

So he says: “Your statutes were songs to me in the place of my sojourning.” Rightly, then, he was not broken by his wanderings; he turned away from the proud and was not disturbed by their prosperity; he consoled himself with the judgments of heaven and was pained by the sins of others, because God's statutes were songs to him. For what we hold firmly we are accustomed to sing,

and what is sung clings better to our minds. Let us not pass lightly over what we read, so that we seem to recall it only while we are reading it. Rather, even when the book is not in our hands, we should be like the animals that are approved and held clean in the Law, which are accustomed to chew the cud even when they are not grazing, bringing up from within themselves the food stored there. So let us too bring forth from the treasury of our

memory, from our inmost parts, spiritual fodder to ruminate on. Let the Lord's statutes be our hymns, our song, our psalms. Let us sing psalms with the spirit, let us sing psalms with the mind as well, lest, if we forget them, it be said to each of us in the time of need: “You have cast my words behind you.”

Therefore, so that forgetfulness might be driven out and banished from his holy house, the true Solomon appointed singers for himself who would devote their whole spirit to seeking knowledge of the Godhead, so that his Church would never lack psalm-singers by whose song the wicked spirit might be put to flight. We are taught this by the example of holy David: when he played and sang, that evil spirit which troubled the heart of King Saul was driven out.

The prophets too, in order to prophesy, would order someone skilled in playing to play, so that, invited by that sweet delight, spiritual grace might be poured in. And in the Gospel we read that music resounded in the house of the father who had recovered his son; the faithful feasting there took delight in it, while the faithless one heard it with impatience. Sweet, then, is the song that does not make the body soft but strengthens the mind and spirit. And so the Lord's testament is called a song, because

in the Scriptures of the Gospel we sing together, with sweet exultation of mind, of the forgiveness of all sins and the righteous deeds of the Lord. The Lord himself did not disdain to say: “We sang to you, and you did not dance.” He sang to us in the Gospel the pardon of sins. The Jews ought to have lifted up their minds, not with an actor's movement of the body but by the Holy Spirit. They did not do so, and therefore they are rebuked.

Yet even dancing with the body is held praiseworthy when done in honour of God. Thus David danced before the ark of the Lord, and Michal the daughter of Saul saw him dancing and striking well-tuned instruments in the sight of the Lord, and after he had returned home she said to him: “How the king of Israel has honoured himself today, uncovering himself in the eyes of his servants' maids, like one of the dancers!”

And David said to Michal in the sight of the Lord: “Blessed be the Lord, who chose me above your father and above all his house to make me ruler over his people Israel. I will play before the Lord, and I will uncover myself still more, and I will be a trifle in your sight; and with the maids before whom you said I uncovered myself I shall be held in honour.”

“And Michal,” it says, “the daughter of Saul, had no child to the day of her death.” It is a clear example: the prophet, who both struck his instruments and danced before the ark of the Lord, was justified, while she who rebuked him was condemned to barrenness.

But it is not enough for someone to find God's statutes songs unless he leaves the slavery of earthly cares. That is why he added: “in the place of my sojourning.” He is consistent with himself, since elsewhere too he says: “I am a stranger in this land.” Hence the Apostle does not want us to be strangers and sojourners in the house of God and in the calling of faith, but fellow citizens of the saints and members of God's household. For whoever belongs to God's household is an exile from the world; whoever has his citizenship in heaven is a sojourner on earth. The Hebrews were sojourners in this world when they did not feel the nature of the fire; God's statutes were songs to them when they sang a hymn to God in praise of his creatures.

Indeed, one who sings is free; he banishes the cares of various thoughts, puts avarice aside, and soothes himself not only with the voice of the body but with the liveliness of the mind. For it was not as one saddened by anxiety over poverty, but as one free from all the emotions and passions of the body, that the same prophet sang: “I will sing psalms to you, O God, on the harp, Holy One of Israel. My lips

will rejoice when I sing to you, and my soul, which you have redeemed.” He sang these things joyfully, as if he were feeding on these better banquets; for his soul was feasting on the food of devout piety. So not only hymns and psalms but also the precepts of the Law are songs to the saints. Thus Moses, who received the Law, sang when, having crossed the sea on foot as leader of the rescued people, he proclaimed the Lord's statutes.

There remains yet another excellent resolve of the righteous man: that at all times he should be intent on the praises of God, not only by day but by night as well. That is why he added: “I remembered your name in the night, O Lord, and I kept your law.” Let us consider whether a man remembers who calls on the Lord with his words but does not keep the divine commandments. Enough has been said of this: not everyone who says “Lord, Lord” is acceptable to Christ, but the one who can prove his faithful devotion by good works. Faith, uprightness and innocence, then, prove a man mindful. And when he says, “I remembered your name,” this is full devotion, for no one says “Lord Jesus” except in the Holy Spirit. Let this name be called upon day and night; let holy devotion allow no time to pass that is empty of prayer.

If, then, those who study worldly learning allow themselves very little sleep, how much more should those who long to know God not be hindered by bodily sleep beyond what nature requires! David washed his bed with tears every night; he even rose at midnight to give thanks to the Lord; and do you think the whole night is to be given over to sleep?

That is when you should pray to the Lord all the more, when you should beg for his protection and guard against sin, when there seems to be secrecy; above all then, when “darkness surrounds me and the walls cover me,” you should consider that God sees all hidden things. So do not say, “I am wrapped in darkness; who sees me, and whom do I fear, shut in and enclosed by walls?” For the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.

Then again, if you do not see a witness, do you not see yourself? Do you not fear the testimony of your own conscience? Do you not know that the gloom of night is not a covering for sin but an incitement to it? When bodies are heated with sleep and food, the vigour of the mind too is slackened by drowsiness and loosened by sleep; then the lust for impure intercourse creeps in, then the heart is disturbed, the filth of uncleanness is not feared, the purity of chastity is not considered, the glory of modesty is not called to mind. It was night when Judas betrayed, when Peter denied.

At that time above all, then, God's statutes should be gone over again in the mind, the commandments that exhort us should be reread, and those precepts about chastity should not be absent, so that the mind, occupied with them, may quench the heat of lust and the burning of the flesh. Hold fast in your mind the words: “Every night I will wash my bed.” For a man given over to debauchery and entangled in shameful deeds does not wash his bed every night.

One who commits deeds worth weeping over does not know how to weep, and though he is himself pitiable, he has no tears for his own punishment. But the one who chastises his body and governs himself with care, groaning and grieving over the offence of an earlier fall, seeks how to wash it away with tears of repentance: he is the one who washes his bed every night. So let us not sleep whole nights through, but devote the greater part of them to reading and prayer.

Hear the voice of the Church seeking Christ even in the nights: “On my bed,” she says, “in the nights I sought him whom my soul loved.” Take it according to the letter. She sought him in the nights by praying, by entreating, even by lamenting with tears. She sought him in the nights because he made darkness his hiding place, so that we might learn to seek him more earnestly. The Church gathered from the Gentiles, then, sought him in the prophets, and therefore she believed. Thus the evangelists and Paul set out testimonies from the prophets to the Lord's coming; hence it is written:

“Night to night proclaims knowledge.” She sought him in the nights: in persecutions and adversities, in tribulations and hard labours. It is night for all who do not have perfect security. Hence the Lord says: “Night is coming, when no one can work. While I am in this world, I am the light of this world.” So let us not work in darkness. For if our works shine, we do not work in darkness but in the light of God; and the one with whom Christ is present is in the light of God.

It is no great thing, then, to give thanks to the Lord when you are in prosperity and good fortune; the great thing is to cling to Christ when a persecutor harasses you, when some storm throws you into turmoil. You have lost a son: in that grief, in that night, in that desolation, remember the Lord your God, lest you be ungrateful as though you had not been heard, and transgress in your distress. You have been driven into exile: remember the Lord your God, lest you prefer love for the homeland now forbidden you to God.

You have been crushed by the power of some rich man, lost your own property, and lack the means to live: remember the Lord your God, lest the night of poverty draw you away from devotion. For this is the commandment of the Law: that you should seek him more in the night, so that when you are more fully heard by the Lord you may say: “In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he heard me and set me in a broad place.”

But a perfunctory search is not enough to obtain grace; you must persevere and apply yourself to the task. Thus that Church, or that soul, which searched on her bed and sought in the nights, did not find him at first, perhaps because she sought him on her bed. But after she rose and went into the city—perhaps into that city to which the Lord sent his disciples when he was about to celebrate the Passover: “Go into the city to a certain man”—after she had sought, as I said, in the marketplace, where the oil is sold that those waiting for the bridegroom are accustomed to buy, where there is justice, where there are laws—

if the Law is spiritual, the marketplace too is surely spiritual, where those learned in the eternal law hold discussion, a marketplace not noisy with lawsuits but glorious with the judgment seats of Christ—when, I say, she had sought in the marketplace and afterwards sought in the streets—from which were gathered those who came to the dinner of the householder in the Gospel, the ones who, when invited, did not think they should excuse themselves from such a feast—after she had sought, I say, in the marketplace and the streets, she came upon those who go about the city, and only then was she able to find what she was seeking, perhaps because, placed in tribulation and fear, she found grace all the more.

Thus later she says: “Those who go about the city found me; they took away my cloak.” So she had a struggle. But why they did not take her cloak earlier, I am at a loss to discover, unless perhaps it is because there she says she asked them: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” She who was speaking of Christ was not stripped of her cloak, and she found him whom she was seeking.

Learn how Christ is sought, at least by those who do not seek him perfunctorily but hold him fast by force, like her who says: “I held him and would not let him go.” She found him by faith and bound him fast by meditation. If we take the watchmen to be good, they are surely angels. Whoever passes beyond the angels, then, finds the Word.

That is why there was no great interval between her passing them and finding Jesus. How is it, then, that later they took away her cloak? Perhaps because the Church, as she advances in active faith, is loved the more by the Lord the more she is stripped, putting off the old man so as to put on the new, whom no garments cover but the secret depths of the mind make glorious. Or perhaps because, as she was about to come to Christ, she laid aside the mantle of worldly wisdom. Noah too was stripped of his cloak after he had begun to be more perfect.

Let us therefore be mindful of the heavenly statutes, so that while we sing them with the secret voice of the mind we may remember the Lord's name in the night and say, as it is written: “This has come to me because I sought out your statutes.” That is: this remembrance has come to me, that I should remember your name even in the night—not dulled by drunkenness, not loosened into sleep by feasting, not so occupied with worldly cares that forgetfulness of your worship should creep over me, but chastising my members by daily meditation and exercising the attention of my mind—so that by constant practice this course may become a settled habit for us, and we may worship the Lord Jesus with all our heart even in the nights. To him be glory, praise and eternity from the ages, now and always, and for all ages of ages.
VIII. THE LETTER HETH

The eighth letter is Heth, which in Latin means “fear.” Fear is characteristic of the saints. Thus fear fell upon Abraham when he was offering a sacrifice full of spiritual mystery. David himself also says: “I said in my fear: every man is a liar.” This signifies the reverence of religion rather than the weakness of fear, although fear itself, when it is according to God, is holy; for the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.

So those who fear God are wise, and those who are wise are blessed; for “blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach from your law.” Those who fear God are also blessed, as the authority of the text bears witness: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord.” So we gather that those who fear God are both wise and blessed. Holy, then, is the fear of the Lord, because fear truly belongs to the saints.

Then, after this letter is set at the head, there immediately follows the voice of the righteous man saying: “You are my portion, O Lord; I have said that I would keep your law.” Many manuscripts place this verse, which is the first of the eighth letter, at the end of the seventh letter. But the Greek book of Psalms, corrected according to the Hebrew, has taught us that this verse is to be joined to the eighth letter. Besides, the very order and number of the verses agree that the eighth letter should begin with it.

“My portion,” he says, “is the Lord.” How rare on earth is the man who can say, “My portion is the Lord”! How far removed from vices, how separated from every stain of sin he must be, who has nothing in common with the world and claims nothing of this world for himself; who is not possessed by bodily desires; whom lust does not inflame, avarice does not goad, wantonness does not make soft, luxury does not tarnish, ambition does not lay low, envy does not waste away, and no care of worldly business troubles—a true minister of the altar, born for God and not for himself!

For Levi, according to its interpretation, means “he himself taken up for me”; it also means “he is mine”; it also means simply “taken up”; and it also means “taken up for me himself.” The same man is a Levite both for me and for God, just as the same man is a priest both for me and for God, both my advocate

and an intercessor with the Lord, offering sacrifice for me and at the same time offering himself to the Lord. Indeed, by another interpretation Levi means “for me.” For if he is called Levi by me, he is for me; if he offers for me, he is for me; if he intercedes for me, he is for me. But if he is called by the Lord, he is said to be “himself for me,” that is, not paying tribute to another, not paying tithes, not making gifts out of his property.

“Himself for me,” that is, as one who suffices in place of all these things. From him I seek no tithes, no produce, no gifts, no offerings. He himself is my offering, he himself is my tribute; he is not generous to me out of his property, but he himself is my property, he himself my produce, he himself my revenue, taken up for me or taken up by me. This cannot happen without divine grace. For just as a property cannot be mine unless I buy it, so a man cannot be a Levite unless he has been taken up by the Lord; for once he has been taken up, he is rightly called “he is mine.”

Thus, when Moses was told to divide the dwelling places among the Jewish people tribe by tribe and to assign a portion to each tribe, God made an exception of the tribe of Levi, saying: “The sons of Levi shall have no portion or lot among their brethren, because the Lord God is their share”; and elsewhere: “I the Lord am their portion.”

These men are denied any share in the dividing of the land, so that, by claiming no worldly portion for themselves, they may become a heavenly possession. Or rather, the only thing they know how to possess is the service of faith and devotion, and this makes them far richer than those who spread the bounds of their estates far and wide. However far such people extend their borders, the land runs out, the sea hems in their insane greed, and they pay taxes greater than their harvests. But this man, who possesses nothing for himself, serves as a soldier of no one but God. His portion is above the earth. The land does not run out on him, and the sea does not shut him in. The one whose portion is God possesses the whole of nature.

In place of fields, then, he is enough for himself, since he has good fruit that can never perish. In place of houses he is enough for himself, for he is the dwelling of the Lord and the temple of God, and nothing can be more precious than that. For what is more precious than God? Or what does that man lack who can say, "Far be it from me to boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world"? The prince of this world cannot claim any fellowship with such a man, because he finds nothing of his own in him.

That is why the Lord, who came to teach that God should become our portion, says, "For the prince of this world is coming, and he finds nothing in me." And since he rightly wished us to imitate him, he says, "Do not possess gold or silver or money." So Peter, showing that his portion was in God and not in the world, says, "Silver and gold I do not have, but what I have I give you: in the name of Jesus of Nazareth, rise and walk." That is: "My portion is Christ; so in the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk." That is:

"In my portion I am rich, in my portion I am powerful. I rightly lay claim to such fruits of this portion that health and life are given. For this is the inheritance of the portion I have chosen for myself." He said this to the lame man, and the man who had been lame from his mother's womb stood up. How then could Peter feel any loss in his own portion, when he was making good the losses of nature?

Tell us, Peter, why you do not have silver and gold. Tell us also what it is that you say you have, since you said that you had left everything you had. For this is what you said to the Lord: "Look, we have left everything and followed you." That is: we have not sought the things of the world, we have not sought a share of possessions, but we have chosen you as our portion. So, Peter, you had already left everything you had. Where, then, did you get what you say you have?

The lame man rises and is lifted up at the sound of your word. You give healing to others, you who yourself needed help for your own salvation. So you left what you had and received what you did not have. Christ is your portion, Christ is your possession. His name is generous to you, his name is fruitful to you, his name pays you rents, and good rents: not of money but of grace. Your portion is not parched by drought, or washed away by rain, or blighted by frost, or battered by storms. "The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night."

Keep the portion you have chosen, for it is a portion that no earthly shares can equal. What can be compared with those of whom God says, "And I will dwell in them"? What is more magnificent than lodging a heavenly guest? What is more blessed than a divine possession? "And I will walk among them," he says.

Others complain that their land is too small. In you God has a spacious possession, in which he says he walks. That is, he who holds the earth in his hand finds broad room to dwell in you. For so it is written: "Who has measured the waters in his hand, and the heavens with his palm, and the whole earth in his closed hand?" For him the world is too narrow, yet you are a spacious house for him. "The Lord," he says, "is my portion." It is a martyr who says this. Let us live, then, for him for whom it is glorious to die.

How well Paul said this in other words, showing that he had no portion in the world! For so it is written: "To this very hour we hunger and thirst, we are naked and beaten, we are homeless, and we toil, working with our own hands. When cursed, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we plead. We have become like the refuse of this world, the scum of all things, even until now."

It may perhaps trouble someone that he said he was refuse, for he is not. But so he seems to worldly people, who think that the highest glory and honor lie in riches. Do these people not regard as refuse all those who fawn on them for their riches and admire

them for their wealth, fear them for their power, and praise them for their nobility? But Paul thought all these things losses rather than gains, and therefore he says, "Whatever was gain to me, I have counted as loss for Christ's sake, because of the surpassing knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord, for whose sake I have suffered the loss

of all things, and am counted as dung, so that I may gain Christ." "I am counted," he says. This is not his own judgment but other people's. For the poor man is often counted as someone to be mocked and loathed because of the filth of his clothes or the scars of his wounds, since he has no portion on earth. And yet his portion is in heaven; his soul has laid up its inheritance there, because it heard Jesus saying, "Do not store up treasure for yourselves on earth, but store up treasure for yourselves in heaven."

But the rich cannot hear this. Their ears are shut and dulled by the clink of bronze; a coin rings louder for them than the words of God. So a certain rich man came to the Lord who did not have the Lord as his portion. He had many possessions, but the Lord is not counted among many things,

for he does not stoop to share fellowship with the world. What portion does righteousness have with wickedness? So this rich man says, "What must I do to possess eternal life?" The Lord answers him, "You know the commandments: You shall not murder, you shall not commit

adultery, you shall not bear false witness." In this he shows that eternal life lies in these commandments. But the man, wishing to justify himself, says, "I have done all these things. What do I still lack?" The Lord wanted the man's portion to be the Lord himself, not money, not possessions, but the true God, and so he says to him, "If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me."

But the man whose portion was gold and silver, which he could not live without and with which the Lord could not be his portion, became sad. That is why the Lord declared that it is impossible for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven, but that what is impossible because of human greed can become possible through divine grace alone.

Elsewhere too he says, "Whoever has given up father or mother, house or brothers or sisters, will receive a hundredfold in this age and will possess eternal life." Perhaps you will say: surely whoever has left his house (and by "house" understand his whole property) and left his relatives, and has followed God, is the Lord's portion, and God is his portion. He also has eternal life. And since he becomes rich in this age by receiving a hundredfold, then a rich man, you say, does enter the kingdom of heaven. And further, if the Lord gives a hundredfold of the very things that usually hinder us from gaining the eternal inheritance even when we have them only once over, then he gives back a hundred estates for one estate and a hundred pounds of gold for one pound.

We do indeed know of many people in this age who gave their goods to the poor and were enriched with more abundant treasure. And it is a very fine passage, since it also spurs people to mercy. But they ought not to demand a worldly reward of this kind from the Lord or hope for the things of the world. They ought rather to look to this: for those who have left everything, God is their portion. He himself is the perfect reward of virtue, and his worth is reckoned not

by counting up a hundredfold but by weighing perfect fullness. "I," he says, "am your God." He did not say "I will be," but "I already am, I already dwell, I already possess." He removes all delay where he finds the confession of a righteous man. Elsewhere, indeed, he says, "Today you will be with me in paradise." He promises something in the future, but he does not allow what is to come to be put off for even the space of a day. He could have said, "You will be with me in paradise," but he added "today," so that delay would not lessen the grace.

But the Lord Jesus does not say to that man alone, "Today you will be with me in paradise." He also says to you, "You will be with me in paradise," if you confess the Lord Jesus, if you ask him to protect you, if you too say, "Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom." But to you he does not say, "Today you will be with me." He says to the martyr,

"Today you will be with me in paradise." He does not say it to you, because you are still living in this feverish body, this body full of desire, this body that still longs for earthly things. But when you can say, "You have broken my chains," that is, "You have brought the course of this life to its end, you have freed me from this body of death," then he will say to you, "Today you will be with me in paradise."

So, O man, among the many things set before you, you have a portion of this kind too. The Lord has set before you possessions as a portion, gold as a portion, silver as a portion, honors as a portion, nobility as a portion. He has also set himself before you as a portion. You have a great many portions; choose the one you think best. Do not let their number confuse you; let grace rouse you instead. Do not let the toil turn you away; let the fruit invite you. In the divine portion there are groans and toils. That is why the holy apostle too, whose portion was God, says, "We are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, provided that we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified with him." You see that where the inheritance of Christ is, there must also be suffering with him. And whoever suffers with him does not do so half-heartedly, but so as to fill up the afflictions of Christ in his own body, as Paul filled them up, and as Jeremiah filled them up, who says under this same letter: "It is by the Lord's mercies that we have not failed, for his compassions have not come to an end. He will renew them like the morning light. Many are my groans, and my heart has failed. 'The Lord is my lot,' I said; 'therefore I will wait for him.'" So whoever has waited for the Lord is the Lord's lot. That is why David too, who says, "I waited for the Lord, and he looked on me," declares in this passage that God is his portion.

How rare is the man who claims this for himself! It is not won by nobility or by riches. That rich king says, "I too am a mortal man like everyone else, descended from the earthly race of the one who was made first. In my mother's womb I was fashioned into flesh over the space of ten months, compacted in blood from the seed of a man and the pleasure that comes with sleep. When I was born I breathed the common air and fell upon the same earth, and my first cry was like everyone's at birth. I was nursed in swaddling clothes and with great care." And he added, "For no king has had a different beginning at birth; for all there is one

way into life and a like way out." And because he saw that the beginning, which he too had uttered weeping [?], was common to all, he strove to be God's portion. He called upon God, and the spirit of wisdom came upon him. But pleasure-lovers choose another share. They say, "Let us fill ourselves with costly wine and perfumes, and let no flower of the season pass us by; let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither"; and further on, "for this is our share and this our lot."

How great a thing it is to despise riches, but how rare! Moses, surely, could have been the king's successor, since he was raised by the king's daughter. So he could have been not only like Pharaoh but Pharaoh himself, and Pharaoh could have been like Moses, for both were men. But all of a man's power lies in his inclination. Moses did not wish to be king, though [?] by birth he could have been, but he judged that the reproach of Christ was to be preferred to the treasures of Egypt.

Yet by fleeing power he became more powerful, for he was made a god to King Pharaoh. Pharaoh was a king, but he was not a god. Moses was made a god to him, that is, someone terrifying to the king himself, whom the king feared and dreaded. This was the power of holiness: "in the assembly of such gods God stands and judges." You too, if you wish to be a god to sinners, a terror to kings, and revered by others, so that they appear subject to you as to God because you act in God's name, then despise the things of the world and strive to prefer the reproach of the Lord's passion to all riches. I call it reproach because it seems a reproach to them, that is, "a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles, but to us the power and wisdom of God."

But Pharaoh thought this a reproach, that is, poverty, low birth and insults, and he preferred to be the devil's portion rather than God's. And so he who refused to be subject to God made himself dependent on the intercession of a man. Therefore, because the holy prophet David was God's portion, he rightly says, "I said that I would keep your law." He certainly means the spiritual law, as Paul also shows. For those who have interpreted the law in a bodily sense do not keep the law; they transgress it.

Let us come to the second verse, which runs: "I sought your face, Lord, with my whole heart; have mercy on me according to your word." We read in the Old Testament that Moses prayed to see the face of God, and was given the answer, "No one shall see my face and live." Let us first understand this in the mystical sense. Moses received the figure of the law.

The law proclaims Christ through hidden mysteries. It did not reveal him face to face, as the gospel did, for in the gospel he spoke face to face, even though in the gospel he appeared as a man born of a virgin, while the Word revealed himself through his works. And perhaps what was made known to Moses was this: that the Jewish people would die because they had seen Christ face to face and had not believed. But if you take it as referring to the law, Christ is also the end of the law, according to the apostle's saying, "For Christ is the end of the law for everyone who believes." The bodily interpretation of the law died when the Lord Christ Jesus revealed its spiritual grace. Or else it means that all of us who have put on Christ and been baptized into Christ have died to sin, because while we were alive we were held by the bonds of the law. But once we died in Christ, we were put to death to the law through the body of Christ, so that we might belong to another, to him who rose from the dead. But this is the mystical sense.

The moral sense of the ancient story about holy Moses should make us remember that he asked God to show himself to him so that he might see him face to face. The Lord's holy prophet certainly knew that he could not see the invisible God face to face. But holy devotion goes beyond measure, and he thought that even this was possible for God:

to let what is incorporeal be grasped by bodily eyes. This was no blameworthy error. It was a pleasing and insatiable longing, for he longed to hold his Lord, as it were, in his hand and to see him with his own eyes. He knew that man had been made in the image and likeness of God. When the Lord chose him to set the people free, he was filled with the spirit of wisdom; he had seen that angel and his face in glory. He was terrified by his shining light, and he saw the bush burning but not burned up. He began to marvel at the sight and its brightness.

Drawn on by longing and by grace, he came closer to look more carefully at that brightness in the bush. When he saw the angel in the flame of fire coming from the bush, he was gripped by such ardor and such longing that, although fear kept him from daring to look, he still wished to look. How much more, then, did he long to see the Lord's face with his bodily eyes, saying to himself: that face full of light, full of glory, full of power, full of divinity! I cannot say or think anything more about God. For when a man has finished, he is only beginning; and when he has come to the end, then he will be at a loss, as it is written, because the eternal majesty of God is beyond comprehension.

His request was indeed not granted, but the servant's longing was commendable. Going beyond his own nature in devotion, he reckoned from the Lord's angels how much more he would long for in the Lord's face, with which he eagerly sought to satisfy his longing. He knew that in man himself there would be another glory after death, another splendor.

For as star differs from star in splendor, so it is with the resurrection of the dead. Although it is sown in corruption, it rises in incorruption; it rises in glory, it rises in power, it rises a spiritual body. So he who could know this was right to venture to long to see the face of God, which he would see once he had passed through the death of the body. He had certainly already received such a form, and the Lord already approved him as such, that this heavenly minister, who carried out God's word, was no different from the angels.

So, since he knew that the angels of the little ones see the face of the Father in heaven every day, he thought that he too ought to see it already, as though he had forgotten the body and laid aside the flesh. He was like the man who was still in the body when he was caught up into paradise, and who said he did not know whether he had been caught up to the third heaven in the body or out of the body.

For the saints, even while they bear a body, are not in the flesh but in the spirit, since those who live in carnal desire and conduct cannot please God. But this saint's way of life was not in the flesh but in heaven, as Paul shows.

And what are we to say about this commendable longing for the divine face? Take human beings: if they hear that someone is noble, or brave, or wise, they long to see him, thinking him above the ordinary human level. When the emperor appears in public, the one to whose royal power a part of the world has been entrusted, everyone runs together, and in so great a crowd they are eager to look at him

alone, and from the splendor of the purple they suppose there is something more in the emperor's face. Are you surprised that God's face is something to long for, when every human heart admires a man of its own kind? From this we can also understand why everyone who is guilty of no crime is eager to go out and meet the emperor. For even if a man's conscience

is guilty of some crime, the hidden places of the heart conceal it, as long as he is not caught up in a public charge and no crime of his has been brought to light. Indeed, when any have been summoned as defendants, they are forbidden to present themselves to the emperor or even to the judges, just as the shameful figures of pimps and prostitutes are kept out of the sight of judge or emperor, so that the sight of the most disgraceful people may not offend the splendor of the royal face. But whoever has a good conscience and is guilty of no crime comes forward openly as an innocent man.

From this, then, let us understand the disposition of holy Moses. As an innocent man he longed to see God's face, as if with a kind of face of conscience, and to open to God the face of his inner mind. Moses longed to be known more fully, and so did holy David himself, who says elsewhere, "Prove me, Lord, and test me." He would not have wished to be proved if

he had recognized any crime in himself, nor to be tested if he had known he was subject to grievous passions. So, being free from sin, he eagerly offered himself to God. But perhaps, since he had not yet been cleansed from vice by more frequent visits from God, he was not perfect at the beginning, being one to whom it had been said shortly before, "Take the sandals off your feet," that is, the sandal he had brought from Egypt, the covering of bodily life. That is why the Lord says to him, "No man shall see my face and live."

Consider when this was said. It had not yet been said to him, "I will make you a god to King Pharaoh." He was still a man, and that is why this is said to him. He was due to advance so as to become a god, and so it was said to him: "I spoke of a man. Stop having the sins of a man, and you will see my face, for whoever sees my face must be without sin." But since a man cannot be without sin, he is admonished so that he may grow into the title of god.

And what shall I say about the title of god? Be an angel, that is, a minister of the divine command; obey the Lord's commandments. When you are an angel, you will see the face of God. It is a great thing to see God's face. The law tells you to present yourself in Jerusalem three times. The Lord Jesus himself says, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God."

Do you notice what is required of you if you are to see God, you to whom the privilege of seeing God has been held out as the reward of your life? Cleanse your heart, then, so that you may be created anew, as it were, with a renewed spirit. Cast every polluted thought out of your heart. Let there be nothing to defile your affections; let there be a simple mind and pure sincerity. To such people the Lord deigns to show himself once they have laid aside the covering of the body.

Now let us speak about the rest of this verse. "Have mercy on me," he says, "according to your word." Mercy is indeed a part of righteousness, so that if you choose to give to the poor, this mercy is righteousness, as the saying goes: "He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever." Moreover, since the poor man is your fellow human being, it is unjust that he should not be helped by his companion, especially since the Lord our God willed this earth to be the common possession of all people and its fruits to serve everyone. But greed parcelled out the rights of ownership. It is just, therefore, that if you claim as your private property something that was given in common to the human race, indeed to all living creatures, you should at least scatter some of it to the poor, so that you do not refuse food to those with whom you owe a share in your right.

Forgiving sin is also a mark of mercy; it is both mercy and justice. Indeed, divine Scripture attributes the pardon of sins to justice, as in the passage read today: "Blessed is the wood through which righteousness comes, but cursed is the wood made by human hands."

The first part refers to the Lord's cross, the second to the error of the gentiles who venerate pieces of wood. And what is the righteousness of the cross, if not that the Lord Jesus Christ, mounting that gibbet, nailed to the cross the bond that recorded our sins and cleansed the sin of the whole world with his blood? In what, then, is God just, if not in this:

that he knew he had formed man from the mud of the earth, and the earth is certainly subject to corruption and to the fault of slippery passion? For this reason the Lord made you in his own image and likeness as regards the soul, that is, rational, just and chaste. For you are in the image of God in this: if you are just, you are an image of justice; if you are chaste, the likeness of the Immaculate One shines forth in you. Yet knowing that in the frailty of his body man lies open to corruption, the Lord, as one who is just, pardoned the offences of a frail and slippery nature.

Perhaps someone will say, "Why then was Adam subjected to a curse and a sentence? Is God unjust?" Certainly not. But because he had told him beforehand what to beware of, as one who was frail and weak (for the weak should not presume but obey commands), he held him guilty of transgression rather than condemning him for a mere slip. Against him,

then, a just sentence of severity went forth, because he wished to know what it did him no good to know. But to us, who are bound by a hereditary chain, who live in this flesh which, worn down and already habituated to sin by the judgment passed on our forebears, could not rise free, he granted pardon as one who is just. For it was just of him to forgive the heir who suffers under the judgment passed on his ancestor.

So there is a just mercy, but there is also an unjust mercy. Indeed, it is written in the Law concerning a certain man, "You shall not pity him," and you read in the Books of Kings that Saul incurred offence precisely because he pitied Agag, king of the enemy, whom the divine sentence had forbidden him to spare. Suppose someone, moved by the pleading of a robber's children and swayed by his wife's tears, thinks he should acquit the robber, though the man still longs to rob. Does he not hand over the innocent to destruction when he sets free a man who plots the destruction of many?

Granted that he holds back the sword and loosens the chains: why does he release him from exile as well? Since he could not wrest the will to rob from him, why does he not take away the opportunity by whatever milder means he can? Again, suppose there are two parties, accuser and accused, contending at equal peril of their lives, the one if he fails to prove his case, the other if the accuser convicts him. Shall the judge not follow what justice requires, but, out of pity for the accused, condemn the man who proves his case, or, out of favour to an accuser who cannot prove it, sentence the innocent? Such mercy cannot be called just.

In the Church itself, where mercy is most fitting, the rule of justice must be most strictly kept. Otherwise someone barred from the fellowship of communion might, by a brief little tear produced for the occasion, or even by more abundant weeping, extort from the priest's leniency a communion he ought to seek over a long period. When the priest indulges one unworthy person, does he not provoke a great many to the contagion of falling? For easy pardon is an incentive to sin.

This has been said so that we may know that mercy is to be dispensed to debtors according to the word of God, according to reason. Suppose a physician finds the scar of a wound spreading inwardly. He ought to cut away the diseased ulcer so that it does not spread further, yet, swayed by the patient's tears, he abandons his plan to cut and cauterize and covers over with ointments what should have been opened with the knife. Is this not useless mercy, if, to spare

the brief pain of cutting or burning, the whole body wastes away and the enjoyment of life is lost? Rightly, then, the priest too, like a good physician, must cut off the wound from the whole body of the Church so that it does not spread further, and must expose the hidden poison of the crime, not nurse it. Otherwise, by thinking that one man need not be excluded, he will make many deserve to be excluded from the Church.

Rightly, therefore, the Apostle exhorts us by the divine example, saying: "See, then, the goodness and the severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but toward you goodness, if you remain in his goodness." He shows that the Jewish people were rightly separated from the body of the Church, so that the poison of their unbelief should not contaminate the Church, while the people

of the gentiles were received by the Lord's goodness and glory in the gift of obedience. Rightly, then, the divine goodness supports them as long as they remain in the divine goodness; but if they too fall away, they will be condemned according to the nature of their crime. This is why the Lord is described as both light and fire:

for one who walks in darkness he shines as a light, so that whoever seeks the brightness of the light may not wander any longer; but for one who has done many works that ought not to last but to burn, the Lord is fire, to consume the hay and stubble of our work and to save us by a profitable loss, just as gold that is refined in the furnace is proved the purer.

Perhaps someone may ask why the prophet wrote, "Have mercy on me according to your word," since the word of God is justice. If he relied on justice, why did he put mercy first? Or if he sought mercy, why did he think it should be asked for according to the measure of justice? For one who acts well and lives well has no need of mercy, since mercy frees from sin.

After all, we do not usually show mercy to the rich, or to the strong and those supported by good fortune, but to the needy, the weak, or those who have fallen from wealth into poverty, captivity or some hardship. So one who needs mercy is a sinner, while one who is not a sinner is surely just and does not need God's mercy.

We must consider, then, in what respect, that is, in what condition, each one needs mercy or possesses justice. An angel needs God's justice in one way, a man in another; an archangel needs mercy in one way, a man in another. The angelic nature is certainly not as subject to corruption as the nature of the human race, and so it needs God's mercy so that it may not go astray and, with God's grace turned away from it, slip into vice. Man, on the other hand, even if he is now of firmer resolve, still seeks mercy because of the long series of sins he has committed.

So although both need mercy, mercy is owed to an angel in one way and to a man in another. A slight fault in an angel is judged more severely, while in a man the sin of youth is bound by a milder sentence than the sin of old age, and is more quickly released.

In this verse, then, the prophet distinguishes the grounds: he asks for mercy as a man, since no one is free from the stain of sin, and he demands justice as a prophet. Or else, though he sinned as a man and as a sinner needs mercy, he has nevertheless corrected his error, done penance, and abstained from the drunkenness of sinning through the sobriety of virtue. So he asks for justice according to the word of God, for it is the sentence of God's word that pardon be granted to those who turn back, provided the conversion is genuine.

"I thought on my ways and turned my feet to your testimonies." The sense is twofold. Either it means: I thought on my former ways, full of lapses and sin, and so, in order to be able to merit the remission of sins by a change of conduct and the pursuit of virtue, I turned my feet to your testimonies, so as to walk no longer in my own steps, in which I had fallen before, but on the paths

of your testimonies, where the paths of your commandments would not let me stray or turn my step aside into byways and crooked tracks. For those who do not know the way often reach the place they want to reach, and avoid the detours of going astray, if they follow the paved roads. But if they presume to know what they do not know and think they should take some shortcut, leaving the course of the public highway, they often run into labyrinths of error, so that they regret having turned off the road, and therefore, after much wasted labour, they strive to return to the road they had left.

This, then, is one sense. The other is as follows: "I thought on my ways," not my former ways but those to come, so that I might anticipate my actions with reflection and not, by proceeding rashly, run into some stumbling block in the very attempt. So if I want to do something, I should think first whether what I desire ought to be done, and in what way. Likewise, if I am to speak to someone, I should consider whether I ought to speak to him, and then whether in public or in private, with others present or with none. This is like the rule that if you wish to correct a brother, you should first correct him alone, second in the presence of two or three witnesses, and third, if he does not listen, before the Church. So if you skip this order and choose to rebuke before the Church a brother whom you ought first to have admonished, you yourself recognize the mistake. Do everything, then, with reflection, so that you will not regret what you have done.

When you have set out on a journey and come to a crossroads (as the meeting of several roads is called), if you do not know which road to take, you stop and think to yourself whether to choose the first, the second, the third, the fourth, or even the fifth road, if there is one, and you do not think you should start along it before you have settled it in your mind and decided with fuller attention. You stand there, then, thinking which road leads to the city you believe you must go to. How much more, then, ought you to stop in heart and mind, you who are making for the heavenly kingdom, and think it over with yourself, since not every road leads there, not every road takes you to that Jerusalem which is in heaven!

There are roads with evil endings, worn by the devil's temptations, and therefore their endings are endings of death. These are surely the roads you have read of in Proverbs: there are ways that seem right to a man, but their end looks down into the depths of hell. But the road that leads to the kingdom of God is narrower. So when you wish to enter the road that leads to God, will you not look around, will you not weigh it within yourself, will you not consider, lest you be easily caught by desire and, drawn on by the breadth of the road, set out on the way that leads down to hell? Think first, then, and weigh what you are doing.

"Whoever looks at a woman to desire her," he says, "has already committed adultery with her in his heart." This man certainly thought about it, so as to look at the woman, to look at her with desire; but let such an evil thought abandon its ways. Another did not think about it, but suddenly looked and was captivated: he saw and desired, and so he fell. Yet if he had considered his own frail feelings and had beforehand

feared that on seeing the woman he might be captured in mind and heart, he would surely not have looked at the woman, so as not to desire her. So when he saw the woman he did not direct his foot to the testimonies of the Lord, though if he had been able to think before his fall he might perhaps have done so. Let each one, then, think first how he looks at a woman, so as not to look at her to desire her, so as not to fix his attention on her. But if, having seen her suddenly, he is grounded in good thoughts and directs his foot to the Lord's testimonies so as not to remain captive, then reflection has surely helped him.

Finally, let one who loves, cherishes and desires a woman consider Christ, his judgment, and his testimonies about the rewards of chastity; let him abandon the ways of desire and follow the ways of Christ, and he will find praise in them, if, contemplating the Lord Jesus, he scorns the heat of the flesh, quenches the flame of lust as if from a spring, and dashes his tender and weak desires against the rock of Christ.
Let him think first, then, to repeat what I have said, how he looks and how he speaks. He thought well who said, "Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth," lest perhaps, while the mind kindles

its passion, the tongue should slip in speech, or through careless talkativeness fall, by mere ease of speaking, into saying even what the mind had not intended. Let him think how he directs his foot and lays his hand on anything, lest, driven by a surge of indignation when he ought only to ward off an injury, he himself deal another a blow that leaves a conspicuous wound. We must think, then, about what we do, for where thought goes first, maturity is brought to the action. So this foot is the footstep of faith, which, after weighing the matter in meditation, he turned from bodily impulses to the divine testimonies.

What good it is to think beforehand about what you are going to do afterward is taught by the verse that follows: "I was ready and was not troubled, so that I might keep your commandments." When someone anticipates by reflection what he is going to do, he is always ready to act, always steady and strong, so that he cannot be troubled by any sudden setback that befalls him. No gusts of overweening ambition, full of hidden rocks, can dislodge him; no storm or tempest of unjust attack can toss him about; the eye of a wanton harlot does not ensnare him, for the harlot's eye is the lover's snare.

The wretch is taken captive in another's possession who, overtaken by an unexpected fire, has lost possession of his own mind. If persecution comes upon such a man, it finds him already prepared, so that where there might be anxiety over his uncertain safety, the hoped-for crown of the sacred contest comforts him through his foresighted meditation on what is to come. If he is often gnawed at by slanderous detractors, let him consider that the disciple is not above the teacher, nor the servant above the master. If the unspeakable insults of revilers fell upon the Son of God, how can a servant hope to be exempt from them?

So he must prepare his mind, so that when these things happen they cannot trouble him. Let him prepare his spirit and compose it by meditation, so that he may be able to say, if indeed he can: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or famine?" and the rest. And he added why he would not be separated: "But in all these things we overcome," he says, "and conquer, because of him who loved us." And with good reason, strengthened, he says: "For I am confident that neither death nor life, nor angels nor powers, nor things present nor things to come, will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus."

The Apostle named many things against which we must struggle; but some are easy, or at any rate not suited to this time or place, for us to examine them all and determine which could separate us from the love of God unless we resist with great care. But we will not pass over the point that seems more obscure, when he says, "neither height nor depth," which are grave temptations. Indeed, you find it written in Isaiah to King Ahaz: "Ask a sign of the Lord, in the depth or in the height."

He replied, "I will not ask, nor will I tempt the Lord." A mystery was set before him, but he did not understand it, and he was afraid that he would appear to be tempting the Lord if he asked for a sign in the height or in the depth. But the Lord, wishing to overthrow grave temptations with a divine remedy, said: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb." This is the great sign that destroyed the temptations of height and depth. For the Lord Jesus did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, nor did he seek

his own, but took the form of a servant and humbled himself even unto death. So he was neither exalted by power nor troubled by any degradation of death. This sign, then, was set before the king so that he might ask for a remedy for himself, through which he would neither be lifted up by the arrogance of royal power nor be troubled by the onset of some hardship, as he was then troubled in heart when he saw war being brought against him by the Syrians. We wanted, then, to show by the example of a divine oracle what these grave temptations were, for which Christ alone could provide a remedy.

Yet it is easy, from prophetic words as well, to show something of the weight of these temptations. For holy Solomon declared these two greatest temptations in his own prayer and asked to be able to shut them out, saying: "Give me neither riches nor poverty, but appoint for me what is needful and sufficient, lest, being filled, I become a liar and say, 'Who sees me?' or, being poor, I steal and swear falsely by the name of God."

Can you, then, make light of these temptations, which Solomon feared, he who asked for wisdom and received it? He was rich, and feared being lifted up; he dreaded becoming poor, lest under the pressure of poverty he fail to keep the grace of restraint. How many who seemed to be holy have fallen from the height of their heart! How many, though strengthened by the practice of virtue, have been cast down by some hardship and could not bear the injury with contentment! Rare is the Job found on earth, who lost both his wealth and his children, and though his body was furrowed with welts and worms swarmed over all his flesh, still could not be separated from the love of Christ.

Let us prepare our hearts, then, so that no sudden force may trouble us unprepared. Indeed, the Lord, knowing that we are quickly broken, said even to the apostles: "Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it be afraid." If greed and craving tempt you, read the Gospel, and let Jesus say to you, "Let not your heart be troubled." If some terror comes upon you, let Christ say to you, "Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it be afraid." If a persecutor inflicts tortures, read the Gospel, and let Jesus say to you, "Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it be afraid."

Read the Apostle, who says: "The sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come." If, as you sail the sea, a heavy wave rises and a black storm rages, let Jesus say to you, "It is I; do not be troubled." So when you enter some great and grave contest, say first: "I was ready and was not troubled, so that I might keep your commandments."

And what shall I say of worldly matters? Be ready not only against the things you see but also against those you do not see. "Fightings without," he says, "fears within"; you have a war within yourself. It is good for your mind to be in tranquillity and a kind of calm;

but the better pilot is the one who steers the ship in a storm. Steer yourself, then, when your spirit is troubled and your mind is tossed about. Should I praise the skill of a pilot who has met no gales and has steered the ship's course without being tossed by any storm?
