No, I would praise the one who struggles against the winds and rises up against the waves,

and is not afraid, whether the ship is lifted up by the waves or plunged to the bottom of the deep. So too he is to be praised who is pilot of himself, who conquers adversity by patience and overcomes it by virtue, who is not lifted up by prosperity nor broken by adversity. You are also at war against spiritual wickedness. Notice how many you must fight against, and so meditate and resolve in your mind, so that as you go out to battle you may say: "I was ready and was not troubled, so that I might keep your commandments."

The fifth verse follows: "The cords of sinners have encircled me, and I have not forgotten your law." That is: sinners have surrounded me with cords to entangle my steps, so that I cannot escape their attacks by quickly foreseeing them. These, then, are not the cords of which it is written, "The cords have fallen for me in excellent places." Those are the cords used by people who measure the boundaries of fields, mark out their limits, and fix the extent of properties.

Those cords are stretched out to mark the extent of each person's property: thus Israel became the measuring cord of his inheritance. Those cords, then, are good; but these are the cords with which sins are dragged along, as with a long rope, and iniquities as with the strap of a heifer's yoke. For an untamed heifer tosses and shakes herself all the more when she is held, and neither submits to command nor is restrained by the bond, but grows more furious when she is pulled back by the strap. So she does not submit even when forced, and yet she is not free of her bonds.

Just as the heifer drags the strap of the yoke, and though she is not held close at hand, she is held nonetheless and does not untangle and free herself, so every sinner of untamed habits drags his iniquities along. He thinks himself free because he is not under the yoke or subject to judgment, and does not know that he is not loosed, but rather, like that heifer, entangles himself in the knots of his own sins. These, then, are the cords of our offences, by which we are wrapped round and bound, just as there are also the chains of offences.

And so the Saviour, who has the power to forgive sin, says to those who are in chains, "Come out." Would that he might say to me too: "Come out of your chains, come out of the knots of your sins, loose the cords of your error with which you are surrounded and bound!" For even if I am the most wicked of all and the most detestable of sinners, I am set free at the command of him who in a single moment snatched from punishment a robber condemned for his crimes and placed him in his kingdom.

There are, then, chains by which we are bound, even if we seem to ourselves to be free. Blessed is he who loosens these chains for himself. And so David says: "Let us burst their chains and cast their yoke from us." He certainly does not mean that visible chains are to be broken by hand, but that the invisible knots of crimes are to be loosed by a change

of conduct and the profession of faith; or else by hand, that is, by the work of your hand: give to the poor, lift up the weak, ransom captives, and you have loosed your chains, for almsgiving delivers from death. "Rescue the one who is being led to death": that is, rescue him by intercession; you, priest, rescue him by your favour; or you, emperor, rescue him by signing a pardon, and you have loosed your sins and freed yourself from your chains.

For each of us is bound fast by the chains of his own sins, as you yourself have read; the allurement of the flesh binds us with chains. Avarice is our chain, drunkenness is our chain, lust is our chain, pride is our chain. There are also the devil's chains. Indeed it is written:

But this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound for eighteen years. The devil also binds us with the knot of crimes. He binds us with the chain of fornication, the chain of adultery, the chain of faithlessness by which Christ is denied, the chain of envy by which even a brother is often attacked, and the chain of cruelty by which sometimes a companion, one of our own nature, is killed. These are the chains that bend down everyone who is bound by them, so that he cannot lift up his soul or raise the gaze of his mind to heaven, unless the Lord says to him, You are released from your infirmity, and raises him up by the gift of his blessing.

These are the chains of the wicked that bind sinners harshly: that is, the devil and his ministers, or else Nimrod, which means 'bitterness', or else Esau, which means 'earthly and cunning'. For these were hunters, who were used to catching wild beasts in snares and binding dumb animals with chains. Useless hunters, who capture beasts to put on a show for the popular spectacle, a service to cruelty! Indeed, in the whole course of the divine Scriptures we find no hunter who was righteous.

But there are other chains, as I said, those of the Lord Jesus, whom they follow, it says, bound in chains: that is, held fast by the chains of charity and love, bound with the chains of faith. It could also be understood in this way: bound in chains they follow Christ, that is, the one who forgives sins and crimes, the fount of pardon, the author of redemption. Let us therefore follow the chains of Christ and flee the chains of the hunters, so that the foot of our mind does not run into their snares while we walk along unawares, and so that we do not thrust the neck of our soul into their nooses.

For they lie in wait like the worst of hunters. When we relax our minds because things are going well, when we slacken in good fortune and do not keep the watches of caution alert, then they cast their snares all the more, or hide them in the road where we walk, so that once our footsteps are tangled in their snares they may drag us off, to trip up the traveler who is off his guard, or to strangle passers-by caught by the neck.

So do not walk with your neck held high like the daughters of Judah, for a noose is quickly knotted around necks held high. Do not fix your mind and heart on worldly things. Instead, look around carefully with the eyes of the soul, because the Lord rains snares upon sinners, so that the snares do not catch you as they fall. You will be able to avoid them if you do not forget the law of the Lord.

For even one who is bound, if he is conscious [?] of his own [?], does not give up [?] his freedom. Sometimes he pleads his case from his chains, defends it by what the laws prescribe, and is often acquitted by the court. So you too, if you have sinned, remember the law; if you have sinned, remember Christ, who sets you free, saying: I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them. Hold him fast day and night; confess your sins to him.

The prophet teaches you how to hold the Lord Jesus fast: At midnight, he says, I rose to confess to you for the judgments of your righteousness. The day is not enough for prayer; one must rise at night too, and at midnight. The Lord himself spent the night in prayer, to invite you to prayer by his own example.

And indeed he was asking pardon for your sins. He asked it of the Father, and he brought it about by his own will. The prophet does not tell you only to rise at midnight, but to rise at night, and especially at midnight. For he had first set out that one must rise at night, saying: I remembered your name in the night, O Lord. Anyone can remember and not rise; anyone can also rise and then, once he has risen, ask for whatever his own judgment has settled on. So he added:

I rose at midnight, teaching that one must rise at midnight. Nor is it idle that he added: to confess to you. That is, at that time above all we ought to pray to God and weep for our own sins, and not only ask pardon for past sins but also turn away from present ones and guard against future ones; for many temptations creep out at that time.

That is when the allurement of the flesh burns hot, when the tempter plays his tricks. The food is being digested and the drink absorbed; the stomach is heavy, the mind drowsy, the spirit preoccupied. So in one who is resting the heat of sleep grows stronger, while in one who is awake full vigor has not yet returned to guard against the attacks of error. That is when the tempter stands by, when he casts the nets with which he can throw the unwary mind into confusion.

That is when the spiritual forces of wickedness pour out darkness, when they strive to urge every wicked deed, since there can be no judge of the fault, no accomplice to the crime, no witness of the error. That is when they pour various arguments into the breast of the drowsy, so as first to dislodge the one who resists from his steadiness of mind. The example is put before him of certain people regarded as saints, who once fell into sin but afterward obtained pardon and covered their former sins.

For although the enemy hates any amendment of ours, yet for the moment, in order to overthrow a man of sober mind, he holds out future pardon to win him over to present sins. And when he has driven someone to consent to error, if he sees that the man is now being called back from the fault not by love of virtue but by the thought of punishment, he slips in various arguments, so that the man says to himself: 'Who sees me? Darkness surrounds me, and walls. Whom do I fear? The Most High does not see; our sins do not reach him; he does not deign to look at what is shameful.' We certainly know these things from experience and example, for no one can be free of temptation.

Therefore, just as this time is suited to temptations, so it is also a time of punishment, as we can learn from the divine reading. For it was not without reason that the Lord our God, though he could have destroyed the firstborn of the Egyptians at any moment, nevertheless judged this time more fitting for the sinner's grief and mourning. For it is written that at midnight the firstborn children of the Egyptians were slain by the destroyer.

And so the holy prophet Moses, to forestall this hour and so that it might pass without harm to the Hebrews, sacrificed the lamb beforehand, that is, in the evening. In this way those who ate it and celebrated the Lord's Passover would not be caught by the destroyer's ambush, and the night-time darts of the dark enemy would not overwhelm them while they were unarmed and empty of spiritual nourishment.

Attend to these things carefully, understand them wisely, search into them anxiously. These things are not said casually; divine mysteries are being made plain to you. You too must forestall the tempter's ambushes: first set out the heavenly banquet.

A fast has been proclaimed: take care not to neglect it. And if hunger drives you to your daily midday meal, or lack of self-control makes you turn aside from the fast, keep yourself all the more for the heavenly banquet. Do not let a meal set before you force you to go without the heavenly sacrament. Put it off a little; the end of the day is not far off. Indeed, there are many days of this kind, when one must come to church right at midday, hymns must be sung, and the offering must be celebrated. Then above all stand by ready, so that you may receive protection, so that you may eat the body of the Lord Jesus, in which there is forgiveness

of sins, a plea for divine reconciliation and for eternal protection. Receive the Lord Jesus first as a guest into the dwelling of your mind: where his body is, there Christ is. When the adversary sees your dwelling occupied by the radiance of the heavenly presence, he will understand that Christ has shut that place

off from his temptations. He will flee and withdraw, and you will pass through midnight without stumbling. The evening sacrifice also reminds you never to forget Christ. When you go up to your bed, you cannot forget the Lord to whom you poured out prayer at the close of day, who filled you when you were hungry with the banquet of his body. For what you have thought about in the evening you will quickly go over again when you wake. The Lord Jesus himself will rouse you; he will remind you to rise and take up the weapons of prayer at the hour when the tempter usually attacks.

49. Hence it was not without reason that the apostle Paul and Silas, thrown into prison with their feet in the stocks, nevertheless rose at midnight with the step of the mind [?], prayed earnestly to the Lord, and offered the sacrifice of praise. And so, where the duty of devotion was not lacking, the remedy of release was also at hand. For suddenly at midnight there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; the doors were opened, and everyone's chains were loosed.

Do you hear how, if you are bound, you can free yourself, and with what hands, with what works; and how you need not fear the guards? Rise, then, to pray. That is the hour when the tempter usually does harm and wickedness usually rushes in; that is the hour when the heavenly remedy usually comes against grievous temptations. You must keep watch so that you are not overcome by some trick; you must take care that, at the time when you can conquer, you do not lose your time for conquering.

Since we have said that prayer must be undertaken at midnight, it seems we should speak no less of the corresponding hour of the day. For night is the opposite of day (what does light have in common with darkness?), and therefore the same hour of night and of day are opposed to each other. For just as the tempter killed the firstborn of the Egyptians at midnight, and from this we know that the adversary is most at work at that hour, so, conversely, we know that the power of the divine light is at work at midday.

That is why Abraham too kept sober watch around midday and looked for some good outcome, lifting up his eyes and surveying the land nearby, because at that time he was seeking the grace that was coming to him. It was then that the divine guest came to him with two holy angels; it was then that he received Christ as his guest; it was then that the mysteries you read of and understand were celebrated. For when should the divine presence have shone upon a faithful man, if not when the light of day was shining at its fullest?

And it was fitting that holy Joseph too, after receiving his brothers and sending for the youngest, whom he loved most, set out a banquet at midday. For it was midday in holy Joseph's heart when he served his brothers the joyful feast of shining grace and shared out the food of his most gracious words. While they feared punishment for the brother they had attacked and sold into slavery, he told them it had been arranged by divine judgment that he should be brought into Egypt, so that he would not deny food to those suffering from famine.

We have, then, a midday within us. It is midday for the one on whom the Sun of righteousness shines, the one whose good work, or blameless thoughts and pure and sincere mind, give Christ food. Learn, then, how to make midday for yourself: Reveal your way to the Lord, it says, and hope in him, and he will act; and he will bring forth your righteousness like the light, and your judgment like the noonday. For where there is true faith, there is the grace of the true light; where there is a lasting guard over innocence and progress in the virtues

through long meditation, where the splendor of a good conscience long endures, there is the spiritual midday. There you too will set before Christ the feast of your mind and will yourself be fed on his riches, so that the true light does not set too early, and no dark evening falls quickly on your efforts and comes between you and your good works to hinder them. But if the night of temptations comes, then it is right to rise at midnight, to pray long, and to draw out the hours with psalms until the day comes and Christ dawns upon you.

See, then, that midnight does not come upon you even in the daytime, when the dark and squalid prince of the world may pour the full force of temptation over you. Rise, then, and rouse your mind. He who keeps you does not slumber, provided he does not find you asleep. Rather, he will rise, if he too is roused by the vigils of your soul, and he will command the wind, and there will be calm in your heart, which was tossing in the whirlwind of many storms. So we must rise. The bridegroom usually comes at midnight: take care that he does not find you asleep, take care that you are not too drowsy to light your torch.

We must rise, I say, and confess to the Lord, so as to give thanks. We must also acknowledge his eternal judgments, so that we attribute to his justice whatever good befalls us. Whether we are rich or in good health, let us credit it to the Lord's justice, for he is just in protecting and preserving his own work: those whom he cast naked into this weakness of the body, by a lot of nature that gave them no dowry, he deigns to clothe, poor as they are, with vigor of soul and the dowry of his mercy. Clearly this must be done with all our strength, so that neither by day nor by night nor at any time do we cease giving thanks.

The seventh verse follows: I am a partaker with all who fear you and keep your commandments. Christ too has his partakers and companions. Indeed David proves it, saying: God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions. He has partakers of his flesh, because he took on flesh. He has partakers of prophecy, for The Lord your God, it says, will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You shall listen to him in everything he says to you. And every soul that does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from among the people.

He is the true prophet, who knows the future without receiving it as anyone's gift, who spoke through the prophets the things that were to come. Or is he not a prophet who makes others prophesy? He is the one who is listened to as the law is, because the law too is his. Indeed it says: If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if someone goes to them from the dead. And so the Jewish people, because they did not listen

to this prophet, were destroyed from among the people, so that those who were formerly called the people of God ceased to be the people of God. He has companions in baptism, because he was baptized for us. He has companions in righteousness, because he himself is righteousness and gave us of his own so that we might share in it. He has companions in truth, because he himself is the truth and willed that we should hold to the truth. He has companions in resurrection, because he himself is the resurrection. He has companions in a spotless life, because he himself is spotless; and whoever walks in newness of life, whoever keeps to the path of righteousness,

is a partaker of Christ. He also has partakers in his tribulation; and so the one who longed to be his partaker says: Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and in my flesh I fill up what is lacking in the tribulations of Christ for the sake of his body, which is the church. We are also partakers of his burial, for whoever has been buried with him through baptism into death is his partaker. And so the same apostle, affirming the grace the Lord Jesus has given us, says: For we have become partakers of Christ.

But he too is a partaker of Christ who comforts the mourner with sorrowing affection, who does not cheat a prisoner of the service due to him, who sits by the bed of the sick, not to lay a trap for an inheritance but to ease the force of the illness with anxious care and soothe the weary patient with attentive conversation; who clothes the naked and refreshes the hungry. For Christ is often in these, as he himself says: I was in prison and you did not come to me; I was naked and you did not clothe me; for what you did not do for one of these, you did not do for me either.

If I hate falsehood, I am a partaker of Christ, because Christ is truth. If I flee iniquity, I am a partaker of Christ, because Christ is righteousness. Blessed is he who can say this. For just as we say that a limb is a partaker of the whole body, so too whoever is joined to all who fear God, and does not say to another, 'You are not of my body', is a partaker of the body of Christ, which is the church. That is, the rich must not say to the poor, nor the noble to the lowborn, nor the healthy to the sick, nor the strong to the weak, nor the wise to the unlearned, 'I have no need of you.'

But whoever knows that those in the church who seem weak, poor, foolish, and even sinners need more abundant honor and must be supported with greater protection, whoever understands this, can himself say: I am a partaker with all who fear you. He is one who feels compassion for such people rather than disdaining them, who has compassion on the weak, knowing that we are all one body and limbs joined to limbs, so that one cannot exist without another, and when one suffers, the other suffers with it. Such a person, then, can rightly claim the authority of these words.

Notice how modestly the prophet said: I am a partaker with those who fear you. He did not say 'who imitate' but 'who fear', for the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. In humility he placed himself among the beginners, though in devotion he surpassed the veterans. Yet fear too is a mark of virtue, for it is written: Fear the Lord, you his saints.

But in case this fear should seem to some not to be holy, since there are people who are terrified with cowardly dread and tremble with dull fear, he added: and who keep your commandments, to show that he shares in holy fear. Or take it this way: someone can indeed fear, devout in heart but sluggish in deed, religious in feeling but idle in action;

yet one who keeps the Lord's commandments cannot be sluggish. So whoever fears keeps them; therefore it is the one who fears who keeps them. A holy man, then, says this; but I cannot claim it for myself. For how many there are who fear God, and I feel no compassion for them! They seek help, and I am unwilling to give it; they need mercy, and I do not help them with my means! But whoever does these things can say that he is a companion of those who fear Christ.

The earth, O Lord, is full of your mercy; teach me your statutes. How is the earth full of the Lord's mercy except through the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, which the prophet foresaw as still to come and yet celebrates as though it had already happened? For the prophets, who foresee what is to come, are accustomed to speak of things belonging to a later age as though they were already past.

The earth, then, is full of the Lord's mercy, because forgiveness of sins has been given to all, and the sun is commanded to rise upon all. This sun of ours indeed rises upon all every day, but that mystical Sun of righteousness has risen for all: he came for all, suffered for all, and rose again for all. And he suffered in order to take away the sin of the world. But if someone does not believe in Christ, he cheats himself of the benefit meant for everyone. It is like someone who shuts his windows and keeps out the sun's rays: the sun has still risen for all, even though he has cheated himself of its warmth. The sun keeps its own prerogative; what belongs to the foolish man

is that he shuts himself off from the grace of light that is common to all. The rain falls on all, and this is credited to the divine mercy, because he rains on the just and the unjust. Or else it may be interpreted this way: the earth is full of the divine mercy because the earth is the Lord's, and all its fullness. He founded it upon the seas and established it upon the rivers. For through the church the Lord's mercy has been spread among all nations, and faith has been spread among all nations.

Perhaps you will ask: 'Why was it not said, The heaven is full of the Lord's mercy? Is it because there are also spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places?' But those forces, for whom eternal fire is reserved, have no part in the common right to God's pardon and the forgiveness of sins. And the beings that belong to the heavenly powers or ministries, though they are upheld by the Lord's help, do not need his mercy as much as the lower and earthly beings do, for they are not clothed in the wrapping of flesh, which carries the allurement of frequent error.

That is why the same prophet says in an earlier place that God gave the heaven of heaven to the Lord, but the earth to the children of men. So that heaven is purer and more refined, free of every stain of sin, and far removed from the heaven of which it is written: like the birds of the heaven. For this latter heaven is said to be a kind of airy region midway, as it were, between heaven and earth, where the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places are also found.

For in that heaven which is heaven not in name only but in truth, I nevertheless think that no temptations of wickedness are at work, even if we have read [?] that the devil was not absent from the council of the angels in God's sight. Indeed it is written that the angels loved the daughters of men, because the prince of this world and his ministers are held captive by earthly allurements. In them spiritual wickedness has been steeped in the poisons, so to speak, of this flesh and infected with human crimes.

And so the Lord says [?] in his gospel: Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth. The same wickedness is not found there: driving a neighbor off his land from the adjoining estate, cheating a widow of the profits of her inheritance, pushing younger heirs out of their right to a share, and finally shutting up in wood, or in any metal, silver, gold or bronze, what is supposed to be an image of heavenly power. These things are full of the greatest sacrilege; they are absent in the heavens but common on earth. For it was the heavens that were made firm by the word of the Lord, not the earth.

And so he wants to be taught the justifications of God by the Lord himself, because it is hard to find on earth a teacher of this kind, one who can teach what he has not himself seen. So the prophet strives with his inmost affection toward that teacher who alone is the true master. For how can a man teach as true what he does not know, since he himself is a liar? And rightly

did the Lord say that no one on earth should call anyone his master, because there is one master of all. And how could David look for another teacher, when he himself said of God: "He who teaches man knowledge"? God teaches, and he enlightens the minds of each person and pours in the brightness of understanding, if you open the doors of your heart and receive the brightness of heavenly grace. When you are in doubt, inquire diligently; for he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it is opened.

There is much obscurity in the prophetic scriptures. But if you knock at the door of the scriptures with the hand, as it were, of your mind, and diligently examine what is hidden, little by little you will begin to grasp the reasoning of what is said, and it will be opened to you, not by another but by the Word of God. Of him you have read in the Apocalypse that the Lamb opened the sealed book which no one before could open, because the Lord Jesus alone revealed in his gospel the riddles of the prophets and the mysteries of the law; he alone brought down the key of knowledge and gave it to us to open.

The Jews say that they have the key of knowledge, but they do not; for if they had it, they would enter in themselves, they would recognize the inner chambers of the scriptures. But as it is: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who have taken away the key of knowledge; you did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering!" For how can you have the key of knowledge when you deny the author of knowledge?

And so David turns to him and says: "Teach me your justifications," because you are true justice; teach me what has been wisely spoken, because you are wisdom; open my heart, you who opened the book; open that door which is in heaven, because you yourself are the door. If anyone enters through you, he will possess that eternal kingdom; if anyone goes in through you, he will not be deceived, because whoever has entered the dwelling of truth cannot be led astray.
IX. THE LETTER TETH.

Here begins the letter Teth, which is interpreted as "exclusion." What is "exclusion"? Is it that, just as someone is shut out of a house and thrown out of a lodging, so one who is shut out of God's kingdom is cheated of his goods—as those virgins were shut out who did not take oil with them, whose torches went out when the bridegroom came, and who, busy buying oil and lighting their torches, were delayed, and, wishing to go in after the bridegroom had already entered, are read to have been shut out? I do not think so. For how could the good and holy prophet, if he had been cast down and shut out of God's kingdom, say: "You have dealt pleasantly with your servant"?

Neither the prophet's merit nor the sequence of the verses that follow seems to allow such an understanding. You hear him saying: "You are sweet, O Lord, and in your pleasantness teach me your justifications"; you hear him saying: "The law of your mouth is good to me above thousands of gold and silver": and can you say that one is shut out of the kingdom who is not shut out of the law? What then shall we understand? The interpretation is stuck; it seems to cast darkness over the sense of its own word.

The prophet's merits call on us, his grace calls on us, the sequence of the verses calls on us to dig out some deeper understanding. And it occurs to us, in good time, that we sometimes exclude in a good sense.

For it is written: "Perfect love casts out fear." And in general, indeed, love excludes fear: so a soldier who loves his emperor does not fear the wars he undertakes for his emperor; so a servant who loves his master, though he be sent through trackless and precipitous places, nevertheless despises every danger out of love for his master, and if anyone attacks his master, he does not hesitate to offer himself; so one who longs to see his children settled across the sea does not fear shipwreck—out of love for his children he goes out on the waves of the sea and submits to the uncertainties of the voyage, but his longing for his children lightens his fear of danger. How finely this is said also of the martyrs, who truly serve as soldiers of Christ, who, fearing neither persecutions, nor hooks, nor swords, nor fires, offered themselves to hostile kings! For the fear of punishment they might have had they excluded by love of martyrdom.

That this is the sense of this interpretation we can also confirm from the Lamentations of Jeremiah. For there too it is written under this letter: "The Lord is good to those who wait for him, to the soul that seeks him; it is good to wait and to hope for the salvation of God. It is good for a man when he has borne a heavy yoke from his youth; he will sit alone and keep silence, because he has borne a heavy yoke." What else do these words establish but that this interpretation is to be seen as a good exclusion? For who waits for the Lord except out of the zeal of love? Who is it that hopes, except one who desires and loves what he hopes for? For what we hope for, we wait for with patience.

So he who hopes waits, and he who waits certainly excludes the feeling of impatience. Who is it that bears a heavy yoke from his youth except one who renounces delights and flees from luxury? Who is it that sits alone except one who, having renounced worldly pleasures, excludes the tumult of all troubles? He, then, will be able to fear nothing who has swallowed up the force of fear by the grace of love.

There is also another who is excluded in a good sense, like the man who by apostolic authority was removed from the midst of the people because he had done an evil deed, handed over for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit might be saved. From this we understand that the one who is ordered to do penance is excluded in a good sense, so that he may be humbled and pierced in heart; for these are usually the supports of reconciliation.

Indeed, what is written under this letter in Jeremiah also seems to mean this; for so we read of that earthly Jerusalem: "Her uncleanness was before her feet; she did not remember her last end, and she fell mightily: there is none to comfort her. See, O Lord, her humiliation, for the enemy is magnified." And because Jerusalem was humbled, rightly is it said to her afterward: "Your iniquity has come to an end, daughter of Zion." And to everyone who has done penance and wept for his sins with his own tears it is well said: "Your iniquity has come to an end."

Elsewhere too, under this letter, Jeremiah says: "Better off were those wounded by the sword than those wounded by hunger; they went away pierced, from the produce of the fields." We are pierced, then, when we do penance for our sins; we are pierced also by remembering what was said. Hence the prophet David says: "What you say

in your hearts, be pierced with sorrow for it on your beds." And whoever is pierced certainly excludes the delight of error, and whoever does penance excludes shame and sets aside his embarrassment at confessing a disgraceful deed, so that he may find hope of recovering salvation. And rightly David himself, when he recognized his error, said: "I have sinned against the Lord." So great a king, so great a prophet, did not blush to confess his own sin, and therefore it was said to him: "And the Lord has taken away your sin."

So, his sin having been taken away, he says: "You have dealt pleasantly with your servant, O Lord, according to your word." Many things in this world seem pleasant which are not, many seem sweet, a great many seem good. Luxury seems pleasant, but when one's inheritance is used up it becomes bitter; lust is sweet while it burns, but the same thing is hideous and detestable when it is exposed;

banquets are sweet when they are eaten, but foul when they are digested. Many things are reckoned good in this world while we live, because they are of use to us, such as money, honor, gold, silver, possessions; but these same things can be of no profit to the dead. Here all is left behind; indeed, a man dies with greater pain when he groans at being robbed of these riches. So there is no true pleasantness except that which is according to the word of God, when someone rejoices that he is fortified with the support of good merits and virtues.

David rejoices in this pleasantness, or goodness, of God, because he bore a heavy yoke from his youth and waited patiently and looked for the Lord's grace toward him and did not snatch at it beforehand. Though he was often given the opportunity of killing King Saul, he nevertheless preferred to wait for the Lord to bestow on him the time of rule rather than to seize it beforehand by killing the king. God is always good, and so Paul too says: "See, then, the goodness and the severity of God"; for his goodness is toward all, his severity toward few.

Then the same apostle adds: "toward those who have fallen, severity; but toward you, goodness." For if they had not fallen, they too would surely enjoy the goodness of God. For he is good to you precisely because you continue; but if you do not continue in his goodness, you too will be cut off. God, then, will not cease to be good because you have fallen and are in need of severity, since even God's severity returns to goodness, so that each one, having been chastened, may draw his foot back from sins and return to the path of the virtues and to a good way of life.

Indeed, the apostle teaches about those who have fallen that if they do not continue in unbelief they will be grafted in; for God is able to graft them in again, so that, just as cut shoots are grafted, so men too, grafted as it were onto certain stocks of virtue, may be able to bear the fruits of good merits. Otherwise you would have to accuse a physician of cruelty because he thought the rotting tissue of wounds should be cut away with the knife, because he cauterized harmful and spreading sores with fire so that the poison would not creep further, or a teacher because he beat a careless pupil so that fear of the rod might make him diligent. For to chastise belongs to one who loves, not to one who curses, and so it belongs to goodness, not to cruelty. Rightly, then, the Lord is good everywhere, both when he forgives disgraceful deeds and when he chastises sins; for the Lord chastises the one he loves.

David too was chastised; indeed he says: "And I was scourged all the day." But as a wise man who understood that the Lord's chastisement had benefited him, he says: "You have dealt kindly with your servant, O Lord, according to your word." That is: although that chastisement seemed bitter to me for a time—to me according to the flesh, to me according to the sorrow of the body—yet according to your word that chastisement brought forth the fruit of goodness. I understand that this chastisement benefited me, that by this chastisement I was called back from vices, that by this chastisement shameful deeds were not

allowed any power over me for long, that through this chastisement of the Lord nothing was allowed to the adversary against me, nothing to death. Indeed, the prophet himself recalled: "The Lord has chastened me sorely, and he has not given me over to death"; for the one who is received is chastised, but those who are not received are not scourged; for "they are not in the labors of men, and they will not be scourged with men." And so he said above: "How good is God to Israel, to the upright in heart!" He is good, then, to all, because he wants all to be upright of heart. But whoever turns his heart aside turns the grace of divine goodness away from himself.

There follows: "Teach me pleasantness and discipline and knowledge, for I have believed in your commandments." According to the apostle we understand chrēston as "good," because he said: "See, then, the goodness of the Lord"; according to the gospel we take chrēston as "sweet"; for he said: "Take up my yoke,

for it is light, and my burden, for it is sweet"; for he said: τὸ φορτίον μου χρηστόν, "my burden is chrēston." So rightly he asks to be taught the goodness of God by God himself, lest perhaps someone, taking it superficially that God is good, should persist in his errors, thinking that through God's mercy impunity can be granted to his sins; whereas, even if the Lord forgives, it is still a foul way of life to cling forever to crimes. This goodness, then, is not the common sort, but one that always looks for progress in discipline.

And so whoever understands that the goodness of God is profound desires to be taught discipline as well. For many turn away from the pursuit of discipline because they think it severe and gloomy; but one of keener perception understands that discipline, though it may be gloomy for a time, becomes pleasant in later times. But there is a more severe discipline or correction, and there is also a more moderate one. The more moderate is the one of which the Lord says: "I will correct them by hearing of their tribulation." The more severe is correction in wrath and fury.

So, shrinking from that correction, David says: "O Lord, do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor correct me in your fury," and Jeremiah: "Correct us, O Lord, in judgment and not in fury." Every discipline, then, even though for a time it brings bitterness and brings disturbance, is nevertheless accustomed afterward to produce peaceful fruits.

But whoever asks to be taught goodness and discipline ought also to ask to be taught knowledge. For unless he has knowledge, discipline is burdensome, correction is burdensome. What knowledge is, let Solomon teach you, who says of the Lord our God: "For he himself has given me true knowledge of the things that are." And elsewhere this same prophet says: "He who teaches man knowledge." And whoever asks for knowledge believes in the commandments of God.

Now it is one thing to believe in the commandments of God, another to believe the commandments. For whoever believes in the commandments of God quickly brings it about that he is in the commandments of God and lives his life in them. Through faith, then, knowledge is gained, and through knowledge discipline; for in what we know can be pleasing, our very way of life delights us. Indeed it is written: "But our way of life is in heaven." Knowledge came first; the way of life followed. We have spoken of "believing the commandments of God"; "in the commandments of God" means this: to be in them and to believe that the commandments are true. But unless you believe the commandments of God, you will certainly not be able to have knowledge of the things we are taught through God's commandments.

The third verse follows: "Before I was humbled I went astray; therefore I have kept your word." Another version has: "Before I was humbled I did not know." From this some think that the soul of man is saying: "Before I was humbled so as to enter this clay of the body, I did not know your commandments, which I had not read." But since the Church rather follows the renderings of the Seventy, and this sense is plainer and admits nothing offensive that might raise a scruple in anyone,

let us therefore take it so that "I was humbled" is said because he seems to have been humbled by sin. For temptations are often born on account of sin; indeed Adam and Eve were certainly cast down after their fault. Sin, then, is the cause of our humility, or of our humiliation; for I do not shrink from that word. For humility can very often be understood of adversities, as in: "It is good for me that you have humbled me, that I may learn your justifications," and: "Unless your law had been my meditation, I might then have perished in my humiliation," and: "I have been greatly humbled."

Here, then, he shows that humiliation arose from guilt. And because guilt came first, he therefore shows that he was humbled, that is, worn down by temptations and adversities and handed over to anxieties, just as the man who was handed over by Paul for the destruction of the flesh was certainly humbled, so that afterward he might be able to merit reconciliation.

But although this humility—that is, a kind of casting down—belongs to distress rather than to virtue, it nevertheless often produces virtue, and becomes not a punishment but a remedy for the sinner. For if you attribute to your sins the fact that you have been humbled, you turn back upon yourself whatever has befallen you, and from being guilty you begin to be just, since you condemn yourself; for "the just man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech."

Nor can you judge yourself unworthy of humiliation when you recognize your own errors, in which, through blushing, you are certainly not puffed up but humbled. You see, then, that you were humbled because you went astray and did not keep the words of God. So keep them more carefully, so that you do not sin, so that you are not again swallowed up by sadness because you have been cast down, and so that your casting down, which ought to be an occasion for correction, does not become for you an increase of iniquity.

For in temptations a man is tested like gold in the furnace. You see what the prophet says: "Before I was humbled," he says, "I went astray." Rightly, then, he was handed over to temptations, since he was going astray; and he was going astray because he did not hold fast to the word of God. But he found the way of amendment from the very place from which his fault had proceeded: he began to be subject to the divine word, and his fault ceased.

The fourth verse follows: "You are good, O Lord, and in your goodness teach me your justifications." Even the practice of secular training has adopted the custom that each person praises his judge. Hence the apostle, following the order of the divine scriptures, when he pleaded his case, began thus: "Concerning all the things of which I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa, I consider myself fortunate to be making my defense before you," and further on: "King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets?

I know that you believe." So if men are praised, in whom for the most part qualities not their own are praised, how much more ought each person to win for himself the favor of God, so that he says: "You are good, O Lord!" For if he says this to a man, so that the man is reminded to be what perhaps he is not, even that man grows gentle at the proclamation of his goodness and lays aside the terror of a harsh disposition; how much more should his due praise be offered to God, for unless he were good, who could stand upon the earth?

Now it is proper to God that he is good. Indeed you have it in the gospel that a good tree bears good fruit. His fruits are the angels, his fruits are men—that is, rational beings—who are holy if they keep the Lord's precepts; his fruits are those who are born on earth, his fruits are the virtues of men. Rightly, then, the good tree bears good fruit. Let the root therefore be praised first, so that the fruit can be approved. But elsewhere too the same Lord Jesus says: "And your Father who is good will give good gifts to those who ask him."

But although God is good, whose very bitter things do more good—for they are not inflicted to harm but to correct—he is nevertheless asked to teach us his justices in his goodness. Consider a physician applying useful medicines to wounds, yet medicines that bite into the poison of the sore, or indeed cutting away the rotten flesh with the knife.

Although in this very thing he is a good physician, because he works for the benefit of the sick man and does what he knows will help, nevertheless, because the sick man either does not want to or cannot bear the pain on account of the weakness of his condition, he asks the physician to cure him with a certain goodness and gentleness of his own, not to apply harsh medicines, not to cut into the tissue of the wounds with the knife, or, if it cannot be otherwise, to do it with moderation and to soften the force of the pain with a certain delicacy.

And so the justifications of God are better taught in the goodness of the gospel than in the severity of the law. Now justification is the work of justice. Hence it is written that the Pharisees refused to justify themselves, not being baptized with the baptism of John. In this they did not perform justification, because they refused to do penance for their sins—the penance which the prophet wishes to do in goodness, so that remission of sins may be granted him without the harshness of condemnation, with the grace of forgiveness.

The fifth verse follows: "The iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me, but I will search out your commandments with my whole heart." The more someone desires to serve God, the more he stirs up adversaries against himself, and like a strong athlete who wants to carry off the crown of justice, he provokes and challenges many who envy our progress. He shows this clearly in later verses as well:

"With those who hated peace," he says, "I was peaceable." Yet his calm did nothing to settle by its tranquility those who hated peace and to check their zeal; "when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause"—that is, though they had no reasons for attacking, they still did not lay aside their eagerness to attack.

In this way, then, either spiritual wickednesses or men are multiplied, and their iniquity is multiplied against the just man. For example, if a just man loses a son, as often happens in the course of this world, if he loses his inheritance or is afflicted with various misfortunes in his affairs or with bodily infirmities, then the proud say: "Where is his justice, where is his mercy?

Look how he has been punished; look how his innocence does him no good!" And so, to draw an illustration from this life, those three who were friends to the holy man in appearance, but unjust in their disparagement and envious of his uprightness and justice, heaped grievous reproaches on him, and those who had come to console him began to insult him.

But the just man is not moved by these things, and so Job was not broken. Indeed, at the loss of his children or of his inheritance he said: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord." So let us too, when we are set in adversity, say: "You have dealt kindly with your servant." For the Lord can change what has happened for the better, as we have the example of holy Job, and he who even begot better children for Job after he lost his children can restore what has been lost.

Is it hard for God to give better things? Even if he gives nothing, he can still have provided for the just man by that very fact, if perhaps those were taken away who would have become wicked, so that malice might not change their hearts. Likewise with an inheritance: as if we did not see that very many have been led into peril of their salvation on account of the wealth of their inheritance, and that for very many a cause of sinning has arisen from an abundance of riches. For whoever has nothing to give cannot be blamed for not having given; but whoever has something to give and does not give it certainly begins to be liable to sin.

The sixth verse follows: “Their heart is curdled like milk, but I have meditated on your law.” The heart of the saints is fine and flowing, but the heart of the proud is curdled. Milk is by nature pure, lovely and unmixed, but when it spoils it turns sour. In the same way the nature of the human mind and heart is pure, unmixed and clear, until it is soured by the admixture of vices. For when milk curdles it becomes a kind of lump that has neither the same sweetness nor the same charm.

So it is with people who once, by their kindness, grace and sweetness of speech, showed the look of milk unspoiled by any envy. If they begin to envy, their heart curdles into vice, and the sweetness of friendship turns into the bitterness of ill will and a kind of harsh roughness of envy. So the heart is curdled by pride and by envy, which have spoiled the gentleness of nature and its flowing goodwill by the curdling of malice. The heart of the wicked, then, is curdled, but the righteous man, who has humility for his teacher, is humbled by meditating on the precepts of the law.

The seventh verse follows: “It is good for me that you have humbled me, that I may learn your statutes.” The apostle followed this when he said: “I am content in weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in distresses.” For when someone is content in weaknesses and is not broken in spirit and does not give way under insult, he has both earned and fulfilled the learning of God’s statutes. So here he says, “You have humbled me,” that is, “You have exercised me with various trials and hardships.” Symmachus made this clear when he wrote: “It profited me that I was afflicted, that I might learn your righteous decrees.”

So let the one who is humbled not let his spirit sink or break; rather, let him make progress by being humbled, so that by his humility he may soften the proud, by the gravity of his conduct put the insolent to shame, by his patience break the insulting, and sometimes even, by bearing loss with an even temper, turn the greedy away from their bent on quarrelling. For so you have read that “wisdom is justified by her children,” when Christ offers himself to punishment, gives himself up to insults, does not withdraw from reproaches, and does not turn his face away from the shame of spitting; and therefore he has taught all by his patience and healed them by his bruises.

The eighth verse follows: “The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver.” Not just anyone says this; indeed, it is rare for anyone to say it—that is, one who prefers the law of God to gold and silver, who is able to leave everything for the sake of the law of God.

But even Christ found no such person except among those whom he himself deigned to teach. Peter said this and proved it in deed, since he valued the law more than gold. And so he says: “Silver and gold I do not have.” The miser does not say this, who broods over his buried gold; the moneyed man does not say it, who searches out his daily profits with anxious longing, who heaps up wealth every day, who goes hunting for inheritances, who keeps tireless watch by the bedside of the sick.

Here some take “the law of God’s mouth” as the law of God’s Word, just as you might say “the law of God’s right hand.” This too, then, fits Peter well when he says: “You have the words of eternal life, and we will not leave you”—that is to say: “The law of your mouth is above thousands of gold and silver; and could we abandon so great a good and grasp at the profits of this world?” But Moses too can be called the law of God’s mouth, since through him the Lord spoke and gave the law.
X. THE LETTER YODH

Here begins the tenth letter among the Hebrews, “Yodh,” which in Latin means “confession,” or else “desolation.” The two interpretations do not seem to clash or disagree, since those who are desolate are quicker to confess. For the mind tends to be lifted up more in prosperity, but when it is pressed by adversity, then it begs for divine help. We know this is the custom even in human affairs: someone for whom things go well is more elated in spirit, but someone who faces the hostility of this world and the opposition of some power then takes refuge, then seeks help, either to soften the power of a superior by entreaty or to arm himself with allied forces, so as not to be crushed, being the weaker, by stronger forces.

So Jeremiah says under this letter: “The one who afflicts her has stretched out his hands over all her desirable things; for she has seen the nations entering her sanctuary, those whom you commanded not to enter his assembly.” The prophet is certainly speaking of Jerusalem, whose distress he laments, and whose desolation and abandonment came first so that confession might follow afterward; for “the Lord chastises every son whom he receives.” Being about to receive Jerusalem, then, he first scourged her with the miseries of captivity.

For she had grown too insolent and had boasted with a swollen heart, so that she could not hold to the Head, the Lord Jesus—that is, humility, grace, justice and wisdom—which means she did not hold to the teaching of the true faith. And therefore the Lord, who as ruler of all knows how to chastise each one, chastised her. For just as a physician usually treats more serious wounds with harsher remedies and lighter ones with gentler, so our God chastises graver sins with greater severity; yet the chastisement itself serves for salvation, for the Lord said: “I will strike, and I will heal.”

Then the prophet Jeremiah began to hold out hope for Jerusalem; for later, under this letter, he says: “He will give his cheek to the one who strikes him and will be filled with reproaches. He will give his mouth to burial, if indeed there is a hope of patience.” In the Gospel the Lord Jesus, teaching the virtue and distinction of patience, says: “Whoever strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other as well”;

for he wants his disciples to be patient under insults and not quick to strike back, much less to strike first; for patience is a sign of humility. And therefore, since Jerusalem was desolate and abandoned, he says: “He will give his cheek to the one who strikes him,” so that he does not withdraw from insult or avoid the pain of a blow, but offers his cheek to the one who strikes. This can be understood either way, whether of one who is beginning to strike or of one who has already struck, so that the Gospel saying may be fulfilled:

“Whoever strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other.” And this was set down prophetically, to teach Jerusalem—that is, the assembly of the Jewish people—that she could be saved in no other way than through the discipline of the Gospel, so that when she begins to keep the precepts of the Gospel and to fulfil the command of the Lord Jesus in her works, she may then lay down the yoke of captivity from the neck of her soul, when she has submitted herself to the yoke of Christ.

“And he will be filled,” he says, “with reproaches.” He did not say, “He will undergo reproach”; for it is easy to bear one or two insults. He added, “He will be filled with reproaches,” so that, pitiable in the disfigurement of many reproaches, he might the more easily move the Lord’s mercy.

You can certainly understand this from the book of Kingdoms. When Shimei son of Gera was railing at holy David, calling him a man of blood, and cursing him as he fled from his son Absalom, avoiding for the time a war against his own son, the king kept silent and displayed the highest mark of patience. For he understood that this was the time of his testing, when a war of parricide was being stirred up against him, and he preferred to appear humble, so as to appease the Lord’s displeasure, rather than provoke His judgment in the midst of his trial by perhaps going to avenge his own injuries.

So he said to Abishai, the commander of the people, who wanted to take vengeance: “What have I to do with you, son of Zeruiah? He curses me because the Lord has told him to curse. See, my son, who came forth from my own body, seeks my life. If now a stranger curses me, let him alone, let him curse, because the Lord has told him to, so that he may see my humility, and the Lord may repay me with good for this curse.” He said this by the prophetic Spirit and proved it by the outcome;

for when humility has reached its fullness, sin is loosed. So you have in the book of Isaiah that the Lord says: “Priests, speak to the heart of Jerusalem, comfort her, for her humiliation is fulfilled; her sin is loosed, for she has received from the hand of the Lord double for her sins.” You see, then, that where there is desolation, there is humility; for in due order humility follows desolation, patience follows humility, proof follows patience, and consolation follows proof. You have this written in the apostle too: “Tribulation produces patience, and patience proof, and proof hope; and hope does not put to shame, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit,” who is indeed the comforter of our feelings.

When he says, “He will give his mouth to burial,” he shows a silence that goes beyond the ordinary measure of patience, so that one buries one’s own mouth, as it were, so as not to speak, and blocks it up with a kind of rampart of virtues so as not to let out a cry of pain. He ascribes such weight to a patience nourished by hope that it buries and shuts up the voice itself as if in a tomb and a grave, a voice that no insult can wring out or even rouse. We have explained the meaning of this letter too as well as we could; let us come to the psalm.

So the first verse is: “Your hands have made me and prepared me; give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments.” He uses a weighty opening to commend himself, saying that he is God’s work, so that the Maker’s favour might more easily incline toward the grace of his own work. For even in human affairs it is a great privilege that someone should favour his own works and benefits

and not look at another’s merit, but attend to the gift of his own grace, so as not to seem to revoke what he himself has given. And so, even though the substance of our body is from clay, we are clothed with flesh, and the body is woven together with bones and sinews, yet no one will doubt that we are the most precious work of God. Indeed, if anyone cares to consider the very structure of the human body, he will be able to judge nothing on earth more precious. For man is upright in stance, handsome in face, graceful in his head of hair, not bent toward his belly like the other animals, but raised up by the very law of nature, so that he looks up to heaven with a free gaze, not pressed down to the earth by the servitude of a captive neck, but as one aware of his own freedom and an ample witness to his Maker.

Yet let the shape of their limbs be praised in the other animals, in which nothing else is sought beyond the beauty of the body. Man is more beautiful in what is not seen, not in the body that is seen, since he has within himself the grace of eternity as well as the loveliness of things present—for “the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal.” In this earthly lodging he is clothed with a heavenly dwelling, and it belongs to him both to be seen on earth and to be joined to God.

A great gift indeed, if he knows himself, and a kind of pattern of justice, to be born for the world more than for himself. So Solomon says: “A man is a great and precious thing, a merciful man; but a faithful man is hard to find.” And truly great is he who is both an interpreter of God’s work and an imitator of God. For it is a man who could say: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.” He tills the earth, he uses the sea as his possession, he gazes in wonder at the ornaments of heaven as their grateful champion. The natural world would have come to nothing had not divine providence added one to make use of it.

So after God had made heaven and earth and the seas, after all the creeping things, the birds and the animals, he then made man, to set him above the living animals; and concerning him the heavenly decree rang out, not without reason: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.”

The other things he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. For man to be made, a special exhortation of God is added, so that the working of God, as if labouring at this gift of creation, might be signified. God is indeed free from labour; but what else do the words of Scripture show but his zealous working on you? So if God created you with a kind of greater zeal, why should you yourself abandon zeal for yourself? If God, who knows no labour, laboured over you, why should you be one who runs from labour?

“Your hands,” he says, “have made me and prepared me.” The prophet cries to God: “Do not desert your work, Lord, do not forsake it. I appeal to you as my Maker, I hold fast to you as my Creator; I do not seek help from others. Gird yourself to help, you who were girded to create.” Tell us yourself, David, what you meant, why you said: “Your hands have made me.” But you said further on: “Lord, you will repay on my behalf; Lord, your mercy

endures forever; do not neglect the works of your hands.” That is to say: “Your hands did not make the beasts; rather you said: ‘Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls,’ and the earth brought forth according to their kind four-footed creatures and creeping things and beasts of the earth. But me,” he says, “you made; me you shaped with your hands.” That is: “You did not shape the beasts with your hands, nor the creeping things, nor the birds; but your hands made me and prepared me.”

It is no ordinary work that has been prepared, since each thing is arranged and prepared with wisdom. So Wisdom says: “When he prepared the heavens, I was with him.” And the same prophet says of men: “The voice of the Lord preparing the stags.” What is the voice of the Lord but “Let us make man”?

Who are these stags but the enemies of serpents, who walk upon asps and do not feel their venom? I do not think, then, that what God prepared is something cheap or merely bodily. Know yourself, O man; to your soul it is said in the Song of Songs: “Unless you know yourself, fairest among women.” Know yourself, O soul, that you are not from earth, not from clay, for God breathed into you and made you a living soul. You are a magnificent work, inspired by God’s begetting. “Attend to yourself,” as the law says; that is, “to yourself,” meaning to your soul. Let worldly and earthly things not hold you, let earthly things not delay you. Hasten with all your intent to him by whose breath you exist.

“A man,” he says, “is a great and precious thing, a merciful man; but a faithful man is hard to find.” Learn, O man, where you are great and precious. The earth shows you to be lowly, but virtue makes you glorious, faith makes you rare, the image makes you precious. Is anything as precious as the image of God, which ought first to pour faith into you, so that a likeness of your Maker may shine in your heart, lest whoever questions your mind should fail to recognize your Maker?

Is anything as precious as humility, so that, looking into the nature of body and soul, by the one you humble yourself and by the other you recognize yourself? The allurement of the flesh, prone to vice, urges mercy, because what you bestow on another you pay to yourself; whatever goes out from you returns to you, and whatever you do you pay to yourself, and whatever good you do profits yourself.

Let the vigour of the living soul, its sense capable of reason, understanding and judgment—that it may appear a house worthy of so great an indweller—not lose the prerogative of its nature, lest it lose the name of man. For Scripture calls him a man who is in the image and likeness of God, but the sinner it usually calls not a man but a serpent, or a horse neighing after women, or a little fox, or a beast of burden.

“Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding; with bit and bridle bind the jaws of those who do not come near to you.” And: “Tell that fox,” he says of Herod; and the people are called “brood of vipers” by John. You are a great work of God, then, O man; great is what God has given you. Take care that you do not lose what God has granted, that great gift of being in the image of God, and that this be punished in you all the more. For God does not punish

his own likeness, but punishes the one who, made to the likeness of God, could not keep what he had received. What is punished, then, is that which has ceased to be in the likeness of God—that is, your sin. For God does not condemn his own image or cast it into that eternal fire; rather, he vindicates his image against the one who did injury to that image, so that through wickedness you ceased to be what you were and turned from a man into a mule. The image, then, is vindicated, not condemned; it is vindicated as one driven out, not condemned as guilty.

For after you sinned, you began to be something else, and ceased to be what you were. How then can there be punished in you what is not found in you? For if the image and likeness of God were found in you, you would begin to deserve not punishment but reward. So that image, by which you were made in the image and likeness of God, is not condemned but crowned. But you are condemned in that you yourself have been changed, so that from a man you became a serpent, a mule, a horse, a little fox. For Scripture has already condemned us with these names, because, stripped of the adornment of the heavenly image, we also lose the name of man, since we do not keep the grace of man.

In some manuscripts, however, we find: “Your hands have made me and formed me.” Nor is this out of place, since Job too said: “Your hands formed me and made me.” And so it is said here too, that God may remember that we are dust, and may pour in the gift of a richer grace, and not desert a frail work. A helmsman spends more labour when the ship is tossing than when it glides over the waves with favourable oarage and runs ahead with the breath of the winds filling the topsail.

“Your hands,” he says, “have formed me.” He says “hands” in the plural, not “hand.” Yet elsewhere he says: “With my hand I made firm the heaven,” and: “My hand made these things.” In the making of man, what was ample for the making of the whole world seems not to have been enough. One hand made the heaven firm, as it is written, and both hands of God shaped man, as we read. The heaven was not made to the likeness, man was made to the likeness; for the angels were made for service, man to the image.

Granted that the angels too are to the image; still, it is of man that Scripture has said that he is to the image. For we have something that the angels perhaps do not have: “Where sin abounded, grace has abounded all the more.” For us Christ was born of a virgin; for we read: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us.”

For us he took on flesh—or rather, he took us up in that flesh, since he set the Son of Man on the seat of God. I do not read of angels on God’s seat except standing, except rendering service; I read not of angels but of men buried together with Christ and raised up in Christ. So the apostle says that “he made us alive together in Christ—by whose grace you are saved—and raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.”

So it is the Son of Man who is at the right hand of God, not an angel, not an archangel, nor the Cherubim and Seraphim. They praise; the Son of Man sits. The Son of Man is praised by the mouth of angels because he conquered the evil angels, because he triumphed over the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, because he made men like the angels, men in whom formerly there was the contagion of the dead.

“By the word of the Lord,” he says, “the heavens were made firm, and all their host by the breath of his mouth.” Man too received from the Spirit of the Lord the perfection of life and the fulfilment of virtue. God breathed into him the breath of life, and man became a living soul. Our life, then, began from the divine breath; but this life

is dissolved by the separation of soul and body, whereas the divine breath is not dissolved. And therefore understand that what was shaped is one thing, and what was made or prepared is another; and so with good reason you have it written of man in two ways. For first it is written: “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” and: “They shall have dominion,” he says, or “they shall hold rule,” and: “God made man in the image of God.”

But in the second place it is written thus: that God took dust from the earth and formed man. Where there is dust, there is forming; but where there is no dust, there is no earth, no matter, but something incorporeal, something wonderful; there it is not matter but the immaterial. For what is according to the image is not in the body or in matter, but in the rational soul. There man is at work, there he is shown to be in the likeness and image of God, where justice, where wisdom, where every form of virtue is taken up.

If you understand the image, you will see what is “to the image”; for man is not the image of God, but was made to the likeness. Another is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, through whom all things were made. He is not to the image, but the image; you are not the image, but to the image.

So you have in your substance something of the image and likeness of God, something like the divine image. That is why the image comes to the one who is to the image, and the image seeks the one who is to its likeness, to seal him again, to conform him again, because you lost what you received. For God had breathed into you, so that by the gift of his breath you might have the grace that your own fault had taken from you. You had been made a living soul; hear what he says: not into flesh, but into a living soul.

But because the sinner could not keep the seal, and, placed [?] in guilt, did not mind the things of God but those of men, our Lord Jesus Christ came for that reason, as you have read in the Gospel; and rising from the dead, when he found the disciples shut in, he entered while the doors remained closed and said: “Peace be with you; as the Father has sent me, so I send you.” When he had said this, he breathed on them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit.”

So do you see which hands made man, and which man they made? Surely the one whom we have put on according to Christ, stripping off the old man with his deeds and putting on the new, who is being renewed in knowledge after the image of the one who created him, where there is neither slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all.

So we have put on Christ, as it is said elsewhere too: "You have put on Christ." We have received the Holy Spirit, who not only forgives our sins but also makes us his priests, to forgive the sins of others. That is why the prophet says: "You formed me and laid your hand upon me." He formed me from clay; he laid his hand on me by spiritual grace, although many take this psalm as spoken in the person of the Saviour. Hear how the Spirit, too, is called the hand of the Lord. Job cries out: "The divine Spirit, who made me."

These, then, are the hands that made man: Christ and the Spirit. So the Lord Jesus is the author of our body as well. He first made man in his image, and afterwards formed him from clay, and he willed to preserve what he had made and to save what he had fashioned, so as to make the whole man well, as he himself said in the Gospel:

"Are you angry with me because I made a whole man well on the sabbath?" This is what the Church especially teaches: that not only our soul but our flesh too is saved, the soul through the knowledge of God, the flesh through the resurrection. The first he taught by the authority of his divine word, the second by the example of his own resurrection.

Thus man is of a twofold substance: the substance of what was made is one thing, the substance of what was formed is another; the one comes from the Spirit of God, the other from the clay. That is why Job says: "He will raise up my skin," because what is from the clay is raised up, for earth returns to earth. But you understand that what was made in order to have dominion over the other living creatures is the more excellent part. For you understand that even the beasts share a common fellowship with us. And so a special prerogative was given to man, namely the soul, by which he rules over the other living creatures;

but in order to be able to rule, he must be subject to God. So he is taught to serve, that he may be found worthy to attain the kingdom; for whoever serves Christ pleases God. Whoever serves Christ certainly pleases the truth and ought to know nothing of falsehood; whoever serves justice ought to reject iniquity; whoever serves the Immaculate One ought to keep the discipline of chastity; whoever serves the light ought to hate the darkness of sins. So, since the body is weak, let us ask for the Lord's visitation; hence the prophet says: "What is man that you are mindful of him, or the son of man that you visit him?" [?]

And now in the remaining part of the verse he says: "Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments." Knowing himself, then, to be spiritual, the prophet asks for the grace of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, you have learned from the reading of the Apostle that understanding is given by the Lord and is placed first among the gifts of grace, because "to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good"; and in the prophet, too, the spiritual grace of wisdom and understanding is asked for first. So it is asked for as a gift of God. Next, notice the order: "Give me understanding," he says, "that I may learn your commandments."

Understanding is put first, so that knowledge may follow; for unless one has understood, one cannot be learned. It is understanding, then, that makes learning, not memory; for it is no use to have read a great deal unless you yourself understand what you have read. And in the Apostle you have read that the word of knowledge is placed after the manifestation of the Spirit, so that you may know that understanding is to be preferred to memory, and that a person can have knowledge only when understanding has first shone upon him.

Consider at the same time his humility. If the prophet asks for understanding to be given to him, who is so arrogant as to claim that intelligence lies in his own power? He asks for understanding so that he may know himself and be able to know the principle of his own nature. But those who argue about the nature of things search the regions of the sky; though they cannot know themselves, they think intelligence can be granted without the gift of God.

Hence we too ought to take on humility, so as not to be puffed up if perhaps we have grasped some single parable of the Scriptures, or—since we sometimes read plain passages according to the letter—if perhaps we have understood something according to the letter, and so lay claim to the knowledge of learning.

That prophet, who received the Holy Spirit, who after being anointed to kingship was anointed to be a prophet, when writing the hundred and eighteenth psalm asks that understanding be given him so that he may understand the commandments of God; and he knows that unless he receives grace from the Lord he cannot understand his commandments. In the Gospel, too, I read that the Lord Jesus would set forth parables and the apostles did not understand them; and so they would ask for an explanation of the parable he had set forth.

The Lord Jesus himself, when he said, as you have read in the book of the Gospel written according to Matthew, "Blessed are the poor in spirit," added further on: "Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man." So it is not the one who merely hears who will be like him, but the one who does what he has heard. Therefore neither doing without hearing nor hearing without doing can belong to the wise man, but he is wise who both hears and does. Let us hear, then, so that we may understand; let us do, so that we may prove that we have understood what we have heard.

The second verse follows: "Those who fear you will see me and rejoice, because I have hoped exceedingly in your words." Perhaps to some this may seem contradictory, that the righteous man says, "Those who fear you will see me and rejoice"; for to many the righteous man is burdensome to behold. Indeed in the Gospel many could not bear to see the Lord Jesus: the Gerasenes asked him to depart from their region, and others refused him passage, though in fact he did not wish to pass through their country.

So I think that, just as there the pattern of Jewish impiety is expressed, so here the grace of the Church is revealed. For he prophesies that the whole world is to be filled with the fear of God, and so he says that those who fear God, as it were, rejoice in knowing the saints; for whoever sees a righteous man and is glad wants to be righteous himself. It is a beautiful thing to take delight in others in what one wishes, if possible, to keep in oneself.

For it is ingrained in good people that the modest man loves the chaste, the wise man the prudent, the merciful man the generous, with devoted affection, and that they love their own virtues in others. For many, the sight of a righteous man is a prompting to amend; for the more perfect, it is a joy. How beautiful, then, to be seen and to do good by it! A righteous man, then, is a good thing.

That, in fact, is why the apostle Paul went up to Jerusalem, to see the righteous, and stayed with Peter fifteen days, so as to gain something from living with him. That is why Paul himself and Barnabas, when they came into Jerusalem, were received splendidly by the church, by the apostles and the elders.
