And when they wished to leave, they were begged not to go, and, as we read later of Paul, he was escorted on his way with tears. For if there is such power in natural things that a certain animal, when seen, helps those with jaundice—so much so that even the horn of that animal when dead is said to help, if it is shown to those who have fallen into this kind of ailment—can we doubt that the sight of a righteous man heals?

So a worthless, irrational animal has such power that it can heal a man in the brief moment it is seen; and does a righteous man confer nothing, provided he is looked upon with faith by one who longs to receive benefit from him? Do not the very rays of his eyes seem to pour a certain power into those who faithfully long to see him?

But just as the righteous man gladdens the heart of the innocent when he is seen, so the wicked are tormented by knowing the righteous, because they are rebuked even by the silent conduct of the saints. Chastity torments incontinence, generosity avarice, faith impiety. On this point too let us take a like example from a lowly creature.

For just as we said that a dumb animal does good when it is seen, so we learn that the wolf does harm if it sees someone first; for those whom a wolf has seen first are said to lose their voice. The basilisk too, a deadly serpent, is said to kill any animal it sees first, and it is claimed that whoever is seen first by such a serpent dies at once.

The serpent itself is also said to die if a man's glance reaches it first. So if there is such power either in the eyes of a serpent or in the eyes of a man that whichever sees the other first can kill, is there no power in the eyes of a righteous man who is filled with the grace of virtue—especially since faith works so mightily that the woman who touched the fringe of the Lord's garment was healed, and the man on whom the Lord Jesus fixed his gaze at once drew the grace of healing from his eyes?

But whoever sees a righteous man ought to know what he is seeing. He does not see him in his body, nor in his clothing, nor in his possessions, nor in his face; he sees within. He does not, I say, see him unless he has seen his mind, unless he has attended to his words, unless he has been able to grasp his thoughts and take in wisdom from his discourse.

Then, therefore, he will rejoice, when he has looked into these things, when he has come to know them. So we too, wherever we hear of a righteous man, should hasten to see him, like that woman who heard that the Lord Jesus was reclining at table in the Pharisee's house, and went in and poured ointment on his feet. Let us be her imitators; for who would doubt that the Church was prefigured in that woman? So wherever a righteous man sits, wherever he reclines, let us hasten to see him.

It is a precious thing to see a righteous man, so that you see him according to the image of God. What is outside is of no use; what is within heals. Yet in the one who is outside we often behold the one who is within, so that, if we see a poor man, we honour in the poor man the one in whose likeness he was made, of whom he says: "You gave me to eat," because "what you gave to one of these, you gave to me."

For whoever crowns the emperor's image certainly honours the one whose image he has crowned, and whoever shows contempt for the emperor's statue is considered to have done injury to the emperor himself, whose statue he has spat upon. The pagans worship wood because they think it is the image of God; but the image of the invisible God is not in what is seen, but surely in what is not seen.

You see, then, that we walk among many images of Christ. Let us beware lest we be seen to snatch from an image the crown that Christ has placed on each one. Let us beware lest we take anything away from those to whom we ought to add. But what is worse, we not only fail to honour the poor, we even dishonour them, ruin them, persecute them, and we do not realize that we are heaping these injuries on the image of God when we think that those made in God's image may be harmed; for whoever mocks the poor provokes the one who made him.

But he will be there to say: "I was hungry and you did not give me to eat; I was thirsty and you did not give me to drink; I was sick and you did not visit me." And how much lighter these words are than if he were to say: "You did me injury, you stripped me, you beat me!" And if anyone asks him, "When did we do you injury, when did we rob you, when did we even beat you?", he will say: "As long as you did it to one of these least ones, you did it to me." Therefore let us take all the more care not to inflict insult on anyone, even the least, lest we be found to have insulted the Lord himself in those least ones.

Why he said, "Those who fear you will see me and rejoice," he himself explained, saying: "because I have hoped exceedingly in your words." That is to say: they saw me within, they touched me within, they beheld me within, where I took hope from your words, where I received your words. Blessed, then, are those who see a righteous man and rejoice, because they hope in the words of God. But how many there are who hate the righteous because those who are righteous search into the words of God; and when the ungodly hear learned men, they are accustomed to avoid them on account of their teaching!

The third verse follows: "I have known, O Lord, that your judgments are justice, and in your truth you have humbled me." Whoever can understand the things of divine providence uses the language that the holy prophet David used: that all things happen by the judgment of God—that someone has a sick body or a healthy one, that he is rich or poor, that he dies young or old. If anyone pays attention to the divine Scriptures, he understands that these things happen by the judgment of God;

for nothing lies outside God's knowledge. Do we want an example? It is not hidden: Job would never have lost his possessions had he not been handed over to the adversary's power. For the Lord gave the devil power over his possessions so that he might be tested as to what disposition he would have once his estate was lost; he gave him power over his children, he gave him power over his body, so that it might be proved that his soul would not fall away from steadfastness of mind through grief for his dead children or torment of body. The Lord

knew indeed that he was strong, but in him he wished to teach and examine us, whether we could be his imitators. So too he tested Abraham, when he asked that the old man's only son be sacrificed to him. He certainly knew Abraham's mind, but the Lord tests while knowing, as you have read in the Gospel: when the Lord Jesus asked the disciples how many loaves they had, and they replied that they had only five loaves, he said: "What shall we do," he says, "among so many people?" He said this to test them, for he knew what he was going to do. So the righteous man believes in the testing of his righteousness, because the judgments of God are just, or, according to the Greek, because the judgments of God are justice itself.

But it was the prayer that went before that brought him to recognize this, since he asked that understanding be given him so that he might learn God's commandments. So he received the grace of understanding and knowledge, and he recognized that God's judgments are just. Now to recognize belongs to the perfect. Indeed, believing is one thing, recognizing another: faith belongs to the one who fears, recognition to the wise. For the one who fears does not seek the reason, but the wise man investigates the knowledge of whatever he desires to grasp. "I believed," he says, "therefore I have spoken"; but having understood, he knew what he had spoken.

In what way, then, are the judgments of God just? Because it is through labours and tribulations and afflictions that we reach the heavenly reward. For just as the crown is awarded to athletes who compete by the just judgment of men, so the palm is decreed by divine judgment to Christians who compete lawfully. "To him who conquers," he says, "I will grant to sit with me on my throne." Our life, then, is tested by fire like the brightness of silver, so that virtue may be proved by contests. "We passed," he says, "through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment." By these things, then, I have known that your judgments are true.

For I was humbled so that I might see these things, because those who are lifted up in heart cannot open their eyes to the truth; but when we are humbled we recognize our sins, and by that very humility we cleanse our faults. "I was humbled," he says, "and he saved me." So the one who was humbled unto salvation was humbled in truth, and the one who pursued the salvation of truth did not endure suffering in vain.

There is a difference, then, between knowing and fearing, to return to that point. The reading from the Gospel ought to teach us this; for the Lord says to those of the Jews who believed in him: "If you remain in my word, you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free." "If you remain," he says, "you will know."

You see that whoever heard his word fearing God could not know it from the beginning. And not only are fear and knowledge not the same, but faith and knowledge are not the same either, since the Apostle too taught that the gifts of grace are diverse. "For to one," he says, "is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit." If, then, faith is given to one and knowledge to another, you see that where there is faith there is not at once knowledge; but where there is knowledge there is also faith and prudence, nor can we separate diligence from it.

Holy David, then, as a perfect prophet, had knowledge, since he knew so perfectly that he was humbled in the very truth. Either, placed in adversity, he recognized that hard and adverse things must be endured for the sake of proving, but that God's judgment is just, and that therefore those who fight well are never deserted or abandoned and that a crown can be awarded them after their labours; or, placed in good and prosperous circumstances, he recognized that wealth and various successes are also wont to be supplied for the sake of testing, so that the one who enjoys them may be tested by prosperity. In this, then, the prophet David is to be praised: that when he recognized these things he humbled himself, so that by his humility he might either shut out the temptations of prosperity or undergo the endurance of adversity with steadfast equanimity.

The prophet would not, then, be greatly praiseworthy if he praised God's judgments while enjoying an abundance of good things. For what great thing do we do if we praise God when we are in good fortune, when we are rich, when we are troubled by no injuries? What is splendid is to praise God's judgment when subjected to insults, to proclaim God's judgments when afflicted by sickness, to let no poverty hold you back from praising God's justice. So the judgments of God are always to be praised, as it is written: "The daughters of Judah rejoiced because of your judgments." Who are the daughters of Judah but devout souls, the souls of the Church that confess Jesus Christ as Lord, which, seeing the reason of your judgments, always rejoice? For whoever puts on gladness not from some favourable turn of fortune but from knowing the reason of things is established in nothing but everlasting rejoicing.

The fourth verse follows: "Let your mercy now come to exhort me, according to your word to your servant." Some have in this place: "to console me." But in the Apostle too we read exhortation used for consolation and consolation for exhortation. Great, then, is the mercy of God, which not only grants forgiveness of sins but also applies the spurs of exhortation to those who are contending, so that they do not abandon in cowardly fear the sufferings of the contest they have taken up. So he does not implore mercy as one who yields in defeat, nor as a sinner begging pardon, but so that, girded by God's compassion and supported by so great a gift, he may accomplish things beyond his strength. Observe the outstanding and singular virtue of the prophet.

For another man, humbled by hardships, would ask that the temptations around him cease and that the Lord would deign to calm his adversities, so that the storm of tribulations might not rage against him. But this man, like a strong and patient athlete who knew that his soul was trained and anointed by tribulations, does not desire to remove sorrows or to avoid what assails him; he does not beg that everything bringing weariness and toil should cease. Rather he begs that, in the time of his greater toil, a word of consolation be given him against the storms of temptation, so that he may bear with a strong mind what bears down on him and not be worn out by any disturbance of sorrow. In this, then, he entreats God's mercy: that he may not, deprived of help, abandon the warfare he has begun to carry through.

Indeed, clear testimony shows that divine exhortation is a matter of mercy. For God says to Moses: "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion." So it does not depend on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy. Perhaps you will say: "Then ought we not to will, to run?" Yet God is accustomed to abandon the negligent.

That, then, is not what he is saying; let us consider what he does say. Perseverance does not belong to the man who wills or runs; it is not in man's power, but it is of God who has mercy that you are able to complete what you have begun. Again he says to Moses: "For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you." We conclude, then, that exhortation is to be ascribed to divine mercy. Hence it follows: "So he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills." The one he pities he exhorts; the other, whom he has cursed, he does not call back. And truly, the warfare of our sufferings is God's mercy, through which our sins are diminished. Thus the poor man Lazarus, because he endured very many evils in this life, found the rest of consolation in Abraham's bosom, while that rich man, who had his consolation in this world, lost the fruit of rest after the course of this life was run; had God pitied him, he would rather have chastened him in this world, so that he would not be scourged afterwards. And so Job, though grievously scourged, and indeed with many scourges—poverty, the loss of his children, pains of the body, the reproaches of his friends—nevertheless enjoys eternal consolation.

So the greater the tribulations, the richer the consolation held in store. And yet, so that you do not fall and give way, the greater the temptations you see, the more you should ask the word of God to bring you encouragement, as Paul also asked when he said: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who encourages us in every distress, so that we ourselves may be able to console those who are in any tribulation through the encouragement with which we ourselves are comforted by God. For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds.

With all the force of an apostle's petition he asks to receive consolation from the Lord in every tribulation, so that he may not only put on endurance himself but also console others, so that they too may bear the distresses of their own minds. If, then, you yourself have been proved fit in every tribulation, only then will you be worthy to receive consolation in every tribulation. And yet not every suffering is worthy of consolation; it is suffering for Christ's sake that deserves Christ's consolation.

He did well to add: according to your word to your servant. For the Lord himself promises help to those who fight for his name, saying: When they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you are to speak; what you are to speak will be given you in that day; for it is not you who speak, but my Father who speaks in you. So, that we may not be unequal to the contest, let us always pray for divine help, that he may grant us encouragement; for if we have someone to encourage us, we do not readily give way.

Many copies, however, have: who may console us, and this is not far from the truth. For when someone urges another on, his encouragement has a certain gentleness. It fires the contender with eagerness for praise and soothes him as with a kind of consolation, so that the harshness of his labours does not call him back.

Verse five follows: Let your compassions come to me and I shall live, for your law is my meditation. Whoever has the law of God for his meditation has mercies at hand, so that he may live for ever. For how can anyone be blessed without divine compassion? But blessed is he who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night. Now whoever meditates

on the law is instructed in the law, and whoever has been instructed by the law has been instructed by the Lord, who spoke the law. That is why it is written: Blessed is the one whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach out of your law. Let us too, then, learn to meditate on the law. Let us not be drawn away by worldly enticements or taken up with hindrances, but let us always attend to the law. For it is written: The mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom, and his tongue will speak judgment. That is in the Old Testament; hear him say it in the New as well: The word is near, in your mouth and in your heart.

And he shows that this meditation is especially necessary for priests when he writes to Titus that a bishop must hold fast to the faithful word that accords with the teaching, so that he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict it. This certainly calls for careful and intent meditation, not perfunctory reading. And writing to Timothy he says: Attend to reading, to exhortation, to teaching. For reading that is frequent and never broken off accomplishes the task of teaching.

As for his asking that he may live, we have often shown that the life of this body does not have the grace of true life, and that the true life will be the one whose good things each of the saints believes he will see in the land of the living. What we believe we shall see is certainly not present but future.

Verse six follows: Let the proud be confounded, for they have unjustly done iniquity against me; but I will be exercised in your precepts. Earlier the same prophet says: If I have repaid with evil those who repaid me. Is he cursing those who have done wrong against him? Certainly not; for he saw that love must be shown even to one's bitterest enemies, now that the preacher of the gospel had come. So I think that, like a physician, he wishes to heal the very people who have injured him, so that, brought face to face with their own iniquity, they may blush at their own crimes. In this way

they begin not only to put the prophet's patience to the test but also to amend their own insolence. For shame is often what corrects us, and when we begin to be ashamed of what we have done, we are prompted to abandon what is shameful, so as not to be ashamed any longer. So the prophet is not cursing; like a good physician he wants them to recognize what they have done, so that when they take into their conscience how great is the filth

of their sins, they may begin to blush, and by blushing be able to renounce their former sins. Consider now, I ask you, certain people who commit fornication, who ride roughshod over widows and orphans, who seize what belongs to others, and who are accustomed not only not to blush at these things but even to boast of them, as though displaying them as badges of their beauty or their power. The apostle rightly said of them that their glory is in their

shame. They are all the more detestable than their very crimes, because they commit such things and are not confounded. But if any of them later comes into the church, believes in the Lord Jesus, hears the gospel and is pierced to the heart, then at last he will begin to recognize how atrocious and grave his sins have been, and to blush at what he has recognized.

What it means to be exercised in the precepts of our Lord, since he said: But I will be exercised in your precepts, you have learned in the law. It is this: if your adversary's ox or beast of burden has fallen, you should judge that it must not be abandoned but rather raised up. And as for his saying: they have unjustly done iniquity, consider against whom this is said, if not against someone who perhaps does iniquity justly. That is, if someone who has been injured wishes to avenge himself through the law, according to the precepts of Moses, he seems to do iniquity justly, but not according to the precepts of the gospel. And so he says: I came not to call the righteous but sinners, because the Jews use the authority of the law to avenge themselves.

You have this in the apostle too: Be sober, and righteously so. He plainly taught that we ought to be not only sober but righteously sober. Someone can be sober and yet not righteously sober: sober as regards wine, but not sober in equity and justice, for there is a drunkenness of iniquity. Again, someone who is always given to drunkenness and luxury may yet, while trying to plunder what belongs to others and absorbed in that pursuit, be sober as regards wine but not sober as regards robbery; and he is not righteously sober either.

So the apostle urges that there be a righteous sobriety in us. Then he added: and do not sin. For whoever sins, even if he is sober, still cannot be called righteously sober. Do not, he says, be led astray, that is, do not let the drunkenness of someone else's error make you intoxicated; bad conversations corrupt good morals, because from the mouth and lips of unbelievers a kind of drunkenness is poured into the morals of the hearer. And rightly he added:

be righteously sober and do not sin. For some have no knowledge of God. So the sober man is the one who is not ignorant of God and does not stagger with the drunkenness of unbelief, while the righteously sober man is the one in whom the grace of good works shines out together with the sobriety of faith.

Verse seven follows: Let those who fear you turn to me, and those who know your testimonies. Another version, keeping very close to the Greek, has: Let them be turned unto me. If we read 'to me', let those who fear God be turned. Let them blush at their own misdeeds, or at least pay the penalty for their sins, but let them turn to God's humble servant and to the prophet's teaching, so that they may unlearn shameful deeds, put off their old ways through the correction of so great a teacher, and, with the stain of their sins wiped away, put on the discipline of the virtues.

But if we read: Let them be turned unto me, the meaning is: since I will be exercised in your precepts, let them be turned unto me, now that I no longer sin, no longer go astray. Let them be turned, he says, who in fear of you have renounced their own sins, so that the prophet may be carried further forward by the fellowship of the righteous, and may himself bestow much on his hearers from the grace that is in him. Let the righteous, then, be turned to the righteous, now that I no longer sin. As for the testimonies, I think there is no need to repeat what has already been said.

Verse eight follows: Let my heart be made spotless in your justifications, so that I may not be confounded. The more exalted the prophet is, whether by the gift of prophecy or the grace of kingship, the more he pursues humility and teaches us what we ought to imitate, since so great a prophet asks that a spotless heart be made in him. Earlier he asked: Create a clean heart in me, O God.

He did not say 'make' but 'create', so that God might restore and cleanse his heart entirely anew. This expression has a wider scope. For great is the heart created by the Lord that can receive the word from the heavenly virtues and powers; great is the heart that can receive the Lord himself, who says: I will dwell in them and walk among them. So, that his heart may receive these things, he prays that its creator may be not an angel but the Lord himself, who created heaven and earth.

And he does well to say 'spotless', because the human heart is stained, as it were, by the filth of unseemly thoughts. If thought itself pollutes, how much more do deeds defile! Do not defile your inner chambers with outlandish thoughts [contrary to nature], or you will pollute with grave defilement what you suppose you keep clean. You wash your hands, as though you could wash away guilt, when you cannot wash your mind, which is defiled by unclean thoughts. Pilate too washed his hands, but he could not wash his heart; he remained polluted with crime, although he had poured water over his hands and washed them.

Hear that thought also defiles: It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a man, but what comes out of the mouth. For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies. These are what defile a man. If, then, you are defiled within, first cleanse what is within.

If you have cleansed what is within, you have cleansed the outside too. Just as, if the water flows [?], you would think it useless to clean the pool while the spring flows out muddy, for scouring the reservoirs will do no good when the fault lies in the spring. You must first be purified yourself, so that everything that flows from you is pure. Your heart is the wellspring of your thoughts. From that spring either the turbid water of impurity gushes out or the clear stream of piety bursts forth.

You have learned that the heart must be cleansed; now learn how to cleanse it. This spring is cleansed by lawful justification, that is, by the confession of sins. Indeed, the tax collector who confessed his own sins went out of the temple justified rather than the Pharisee, because the Pharisee paraded his fasts, his gifts and his innocence. Cleanse your water, then, that water of which it was said: Counsel in a man's heart is deep water.

Nature has given you good water, unless you pollute it with your own mire. It washes you clean if it is pure, if it is simple, if it is also natural, if it has nothing sordid or earthly in it. What an evil it is when the water that ought to cleanse pollutes instead! But it is not your own water that pollutes you; that water is foreign. Indeed, you have been told: Keep yourself from foreign water. Foreign water lies and deceives and flows contrary to nature. That is why he says: Foreign sons have lied to me;

for had they not been foreign, they surely would not have deceived. So let no one boast that he has a chaste heart, as Solomon said; rather, let whoever boasts boast in the Lord, who has deigned to create a clean heart for his saints and to make it spotless by his justifications. What the justifications are, you have heard him say: Declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified. So whoever declares his iniquities is justified, and whoever is justified is not confounded, because he has forestalled the shame of his sins by timely confession.
XI. THE LETTER KAPH.

Here begins the eleventh letter, 'Kaph', which in Latin translation means 'they were bowed down'. The very sound of the translation teaches us what it is to be bowed down; for whoever bends toward the ground is seen to be bowed. Hence the prophet says under this letter: They almost made an end of me on the earth. Whoever does penance is bowed down, for he bows his neck as he humbles himself before the Lord, and even more his inner neck, that is, the neck of mind and heart. For it was of this neck that it was said: Not even if you bend your neck like a ring; for whoever does not bend his heart will have bent his neck in vain.

The prophet Jeremiah also teaches that this meaning signifies humility; for he says under this letter in Lamentations: For the Lord will not cast off for ever; for when he has humbled, he will have mercy according to the abundance of his mercy; for he has not humbled with his whole heart, nor cast off the sons of men. It is good, then, to be bowed down, so that we may be humbled before the Lord and the Lord may have mercy.

Indeed, earlier under this letter too, the same prophet Jeremiah, describing the groaning and humility of the people, says: All her people groan, seeking bread; they have given their desirable things for food, to revive the soul. See, O Lord, and behold, for she has been left without honour. So whoever seeks refreshment for his soul should be bowed down in humility, so that he may the more quickly attain the Lord's mercy.

And so, as one bowed down far more in soul and mind than in body, David began by saying: My soul has fainted for your salvation, and in your word I hope. We must not let ordinary usage mislead us into thinking that this fainting is like the failing that comes from bodily weariness. For he did not say only: my soul has fainted, but: has fainted for your salvation.

So, to take an example from ordinary usage, if we say, for instance, 'he is fainting for her', the expression seems to convey that he has passed over wholly, in his longing, into desire for the woman. And whatever we crave intensely, unless we obtain it fairly soon, seems to wear us out through long straining after it.

Impatient love, knocking day and night at a harlot's doors, faints in its very expectation while it hopes, if the fulfilment of its desire is put off too long; and in this there is certainly no end of love, but an increase of it. And whenever something desirable does not come to the one who desires it, he faints for it and as it were lays down

his very soul. If, however, hope draws nearer, the nearness of hope gives strength; but if the beloved is absent, the lover suffers a fainting of soul by the very fact that he desires someone absent. So the farther off the thing desired, the more the one who desires it faints. This, then, is what it means to faint: for each person

to pass over with all his energies into what he loves. He thinks of it, clings to it, speaks constantly of what he has taken to love, and is poured into it through a kind of fainting of the soul, as when a mother waits for her son to come home. So Tobias's wife waited for her son who was travelling abroad, fainting with longing, in great distress and as though drained of strength. For what else do her words signify but a kind of fainting? But the more the heart's affection is wearied, the more love grows, and the longer the one desired is away, the more the desires of the one waiting are kindled with a greater force of love. The flesh faints, but longing is fed and increased.

From this, then, we can gather what is meant by: My soul has fainted for your salvation. For the soul that cleaves to the spirit faints away from what it is as soul and becomes one spirit, since whoever cleaves to the Lord is one spirit. And so the holy man

who fears the Lord knows nothing to desire except the salvation of God, which is Christ Jesus. Him he longs for, him he desires, toward him he strains with all his strength, him he cherishes in the bosom of his mind; to him he opens himself and pours himself out, and does only this. He fears that he may lose him. And so the greater the desire with which the soul is exercised in its longing to cleave to its salvation, the more it faints.

So this fainting brings about a lessening of frailty, but an increase of strength. Indeed, he himself, after saying elsewhere: My soul has thirsted for you, added below: My soul has clung close behind you, your right hand has upheld me. For whoever is thirsty desires always to cling to the spring, and seems to seek and touch nothing but water, so as to be nourished by his very longing. So [your] right hand, taking up my soul and imparting to me something of its own power, makes it what it was not, so that he may say: I live, yet it is no longer I, but Christ lives in me.

Learn also from an example that this fainting comes from intense longing: My soul longs, he says, and faints for the courts of the Lord. First it longs, he says, and pours itself out wholly, as it were, in longing; then, held long in suspense, it dissolves in fainting. Jeremiah, too, teaches how the soul faints for the salvation of God: And there was in my heart, he says, something like a burning fire, flaming in my bones, and I was dissolved on every side and cannot bear it. Inflamed with this desire, then, David says: My soul has fainted for your salvation, and in your word I have hoped.

He rightly said 'I have hoped in the word'; for hope comes first, and fainting follows. He hoped in the word that had been proclaimed as one who was to come, which can be understood of God the Word. Or at least whoever believed the heavenly word hoped in the word, the word by which the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ is announced or his glory declared.

So the prophet, reflecting on what he had read and perceiving that, while he was present in the body, bound as it were by the chains of this life, he was absent from the salvation of God, longed, desired, fainted, and was dissolved in all his affection, so as to become wholly that which he desired. As he himself also says later: I pour out my prayer before him, I declare my trouble before him, when my spirit faints within me. For his spirit faints; or rather, the spirit of the one who denies himself in order to cling to Christ faints away from him. That is why his paths are known by the Lord, because they are not the paths of the flesh but the paths of Christ.

For Christ is the way of those who seek God. Let us too, then, long for that eternal thing, that salvation of God. Let us not long for money, which the most avaricious long for; let us not long for the beauty of another man's wife; let us not be driven by ambition's desire; let us not aim at worldly glory; let us not busy ourselves with the schemes of deceitful fraud; let us not wish to cheat our neighbour through iniquity; and finally, let us not become a portion for foxes, sunk into the depths

of earthly pleasure, like exiles from eternal things, cast down from our confident expectation of heavenly hope. Let our soul, then, failing in its own strength, be lifted up so that it may cling to the salvation of God, which is Christ the Lord Jesus, a name that means 'salvation of the Lord'. For he is salvation, truth, power and wisdom. So whoever fails to himself in order to cling to power loses what is his own and receives what is eternal.

Verse two follows: My eyes have fainted for your word, saying: When will you comfort me? Above was the practical, here the contemplative. There the soul fainted for salvation, because it longs for the one by whose passion it was saved; here the prophet's eyes fainted for the word of God. And let us see whether, just as there the soul cleaving to Christ faints into one spirit and becomes one spirit, so too the eyes may faint so as to become one mind. For these are the eyes of the mind, that is, the eyes of the inner man, not the eyes that perform the service of sight.

For there is an eye and a mind of the flesh, but that eye is blind which does not see divine things and is vainly puffed up by the mind of the flesh. There is also another eye, the mind of Christ, by which the church sees Christ, as he himself says to the bride: You have captured our heart with one of your eyes. It is fitting that Christ should be seen with one eye, because he is not seen with the eye of the flesh. Or else it is because the church, which has two eyes, the moral and the mystical, sees Christ more with the eye of faith; for the mystical eye is sharper, the moral eye sweeter.

And perhaps these are the eyes with which Paul saw eternal things, once he began not to see bodily things. Indeed, he who did not see Christ before he lost his eyes saw him after he had lost the sight of his eyes. For he saw, he who said: Who are you, Lord? He certainly saw Christ, whom he even acknowledged as Lord. And further on he says: Lord, what do you want me to do? Did he not, then, see the one whose command he was awaiting? With what eyes, then, did Paul begin to see more, if not with those he himself pointed out to us when he said: I will pray with the spirit, I will pray with the mind also?

Indeed, so that you may know that he saw by praying, he says: It happened, when I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, that I was seized with fear, and I saw him saying to me: Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, for they will not accept your testimony about me. These, then, are the eyes that faint for the word of God and say: When will you comfort me? It was because of these eyes that the prophets were called 'seers', because through revelation they perceived with the mind things that were hidden.

What does it mean for the eyes to fail? Let us speak of bodily things so that we may understand spiritual ones. When we long for someone and hope he will soon arrive, do we not turn our eyes toward the place from which we hope he will come? And so, after watching intently for a long time in daily expectation, we grow faint. So Anna, looking all around along the road, kept anxious watch for her son's return. So the prophet David, an anxious father, was eager to question the runner coming from the battle, after posting lookouts in the tower, about the safety of his son.

So a young wife on a lookout above the shore waits with tireless expectation for her husband's return, so that whatever ship she sees, she thinks her husband is sailing in it, and she fears that someone else may steal from her the joy of seeing her beloved and that she herself may not be the first to say, 'I see you, my husband,' just as Anna said to her son: I see you, my son; from now on

I will die gladly, for the sweetness of the sight she had longed for would keep her from feeling the pain of death. So, just as a woman who wants to go out to meet her husband on his return lays aside all her household tasks and studies the paths of the traveller and the prints of his feet, so the prophet, stripped of worldly cares, kept the gaze of his inner eyes fixed on the word of God, an ever-wakeful watchman, until he himself failed, bringing his body

into subjection and training his soul to the patience of humility, wasting away like a spider. For he longed as the deer longs for springs of water, and he thirsted for the Lord his God, desiring to see his presence and to appear before the face of God; and, fainting with excessive longing and

vehement desire, he trusted that by prophetic grace he was then better fitted to obtain what he asked of the Lord. Let us too, then, apply our hearts, so that we may understand the sequence of the Scriptures, and let us ask that the word may come to us from the Lord and that understanding may be given us. If someone sees the word of God from afar with the gaze of the mind, while it is not yet plain and distinct, he perceives, as it were with certain inner eyes, the ship of the word drawing near to his soul. And the more clearly he begins to see it, the more he hastens to approach, as it were, the harbor of truth, so as to be close at hand to be carried aboard.

So the prophet's eyes failed for the word of God, saying: When will you comfort me? If the eyes meant here were those with which we look and see, they ought to have said, 'When will you comfort us?' — that is, in the plural, not the singular. But because the eye of the mind and the eye of the flesh become one eye, and a man is upheld by comfort when flesh and mind do not desire different things but long for one thing and seek one thing, therefore these eyes too, intent on him who said, I and the Father are one, confess that they are one, since they perform one and the same desire and office.

The prophet, then, was failing for the word. We, however, consider ourselves idle if we are seen to devote ourselves only to the word, and we value those who work more highly than those who pursue the study of knowing divine things. For many say, 'Look at the man and his works!' as though one who studies the word does not work, when in fact this work is greater than all others. For if justice is a work, if temperance is a work, if fortitude is a work, then surely wisdom too is a work; for these are held to be the four principal virtues.

For if Christ works insofar as he is justice, surely he works insofar as he is the Word [?], and he was working when he was in the beginning with the Father. Indeed, all things were made through him, so you may know that Christ Jesus is the worker of all things and is our work. For insofar as he is the Word, the Word

is to those who seek him [?]: the Word is a great work. Hence when Martha was busy about serving, while Mary was listening to the word of the Lord, the one who listened deserved to be preferred to the one who served. For when Martha said, Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me, the Lord answered and said: Martha, Martha, Mary has chosen the good part, which shall not be taken from her. Thus by the authority of a divine judgment it is established that knowing the word is a greater work than serving.

But perhaps someone will say that the Apostle said that the kingdom of God is not in word but in power. I do not deny that it is written; but learn what kind of word is meant. It is, of course, the word that a puffed-up man pours out, a word that cannot benefit its hearers, a word without the demonstration of the Spirit and of power: this is the word Paul does not deign to acknowledge;

for he wishes rather to recognize the power of the word. Indeed, the Apostle did not want his own word to be of that kind, he who came in weakness so as to make others stronger, in fear and trembling, so that those who feared might fear nothing but the Lord Jesus, and those who trembled might keep his peace and calm. Hear, then, what kind of word the Apostle had: My word, he says, and my preaching were not in the persuasiveness of wise words, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power — because faith is established not by the wisdom of courtroom speech but by the power of God.

So in the speech of the saints there is power, but in this courtroom and philosophical speech there is the vanity of the world. And that there is power in the speech of the saints this prophet too may teach you, when he says: The Lord will give the word to those who preach the gospel with great power — that is, so that they may be able to preach the gospel with great power. It is proved, then, that there is power in the preaching of the gospel; and the preaching of the gospel is the speech of the saints. Thus no doubt remains that there is power in holy speech.

The third verse follows: For I have become like a wineskin in the frost; I have not forgotten your statutes. This is the voice of a righteous man who has put his body to death. For the righteous man is rightly called a wineskin, since though stripped he is not found naked; for a wineskin is made from the hide of a dead animal. Let us too, then, die to sin, so that we may live to God.

Filled with the delight of the Spirit and the sweetness of joy, we shall be spiritual hides, free from bodily weakness, and in the unbroken fold of the mind preserving the grace of the divine mysteries poured into us. Of these wineskins it is said that those who wish to preserve both — both the body and the grace — put new wine into new wineskins.

So let this wineskin of yours not leak, let it not be full of cracks, let it not grow old with earthly mold, lest the new wine burst the old skins, the skins be torn, and the grace be spilled. Nor again let them dry out in the sun of iniquity and the excessive force of heat; rather, let the various desires of the burning inner parts be tempered by a kind of snowy cold.

Let the heat of lust grow cold, and, held in check by a kind of frost of continence and fasting, let it be cooled by the breath of morning prayer, when the words of God come down upon our earth like dew, like rain upon the grass and like snow upon the hay. This snow does not know how to harm a good wineskin, this snow that shines with the splendor of divine speech. This snow cools; it does not scorch; it makes the crops fruitful; it does not kill them. This snow is the precept of continence, which makes bodily heat grow cold and quenches all the fire of our inner nature.

And perhaps this is why, when Jesus showed the glory of his resurrection, his garments were white as snow: so that not only would he himself be seen to be free from the contagion of sin, but also whoever is raised would be seen to rise cold, with the desires of marriage frozen; for in the resurrection they neither marry nor take wives, but will be like the angels in heaven. Good wineskins, then, are cold — that is, bound fast by hoarfrost in the frost, not softened by the heat of lust.

That this body may be called a wineskin is clear from many passages, but understand it also from this: when Adam and Eve laid aside the image of the heavenly man which they had formerly borne, and put on the image of the earthly man, they are said to have been clothed with garments of skin; for the sin they committed had made them bodily instead of spiritual. Nor is it absurd to understand David's saying that he had become like a wineskin in the frost to mean that, though placed in icy harshness, he nevertheless put his body to death,

so as not to feel the harshness of that winter which the Savior says will be grievous for those who flee. For just as a wineskin does not feel the ice, because it is the skin of a dead animal, so the prophet, being dead to sin, could not feel the cold of sin; or else it means that the flesh is not broken by necessities and does not resist the mind, but, made more pliant, bends to the commands of the soul under its guidance and does not

dry up in this frost of the world; or else it means that we are a body of affliction and must always carry about the death of the Lord Jesus in our body. This is the wineskin that chastises its body, not like that fattened and gross people who sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play. This is the wineskin that makes one drunk not with wine but with the Spirit, in which there is no cluster of bitterness, no rage of dragons, no rage of asps, but the cup that inebriates, how excellent it is! In this, then, David glories: that he has become like a wineskin in the frost, not feeling the working of sin.

And sin is rightly compared to frost. For just as frost is useful for nothing, for no work, so sin is of no use, of no service to any work, and therefore it must be shunned like frost, lest it harm and scorch. It is good for me, then, to become like a wineskin in the frost, so that I may not forget the statutes of the Lord, and so that, steeped in their liquid, all the fever of inner desire may be cooled.

This wineskin, then, should not be empty but full — full of the Spirit, full of statutes — so that I may confess my sins myself and may curb the wantonness of my flesh; for we must die to the world so that we may live to God. But if we live to the flesh, then the wisdom of the flesh is certainly death; we cannot live to God, because this carnal wisdom and worldly life are hostile to God.

The fourth verse follows: How many are the days of your servant? When will you execute judgment for me on those who persecute me? It can be taken this way: How many are the days of your servant? as if he were saying, 'How many are the days of man, how much time, how much space? Why is so short a life begrudged us, so that we may not enjoy a peaceful course through this world? Why in so short a space are so many snares of our persecutors laid? Let the judgment come now, in which the faithless are punished, in which persecutors are paid the due wages of their impiety.'

Or this way: 'How long will they be able to insult us, how long to ride roughshod over us, who seek to afflict us in various ways?' The end will not be late; for the prophet, as it were, reckons the swiftness with which this life runs its course not by an estimate of years but of days, saying: How many are the days of your servant? And he did well to say 'days,' so that not only might he pass over the delays of years in prophetic vision, but also show that the course of this life was bright for him with the light of the virtues.

And rightly he says with confidence: When will you execute judgment for me on those who persecute me? 'You will execute judgment for me,' he says, 'on my persecutors; you will not pass judgment on me at the instance of my persecutors,' since the ungodly do not rise in the judgment. 'But grant judgment to me,' he says, 'so that when you reward innocence, advance faith, and crown mercy, the ungodly persecutors may be judged by the rewards of the merits promised by the prophet's mouth.'

Nor is it absurd to take it this way: that since the days of this life are short and few, the Lord should not further delay his grace toward his prophet, but should execute judgment for him on his persecutors. For here too there is judgment on persecutors, since whoever does not believe in Christ is already judged. And this is the judgment that the Lord Jesus gave to his servants when he said: You will have power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy. And it is a true judgment, in which the enemy is tormented, as he himself confessed when he said: Why have you come before the time to seek [?] us?

This, then, is what the prophet, grounded in the steadfastness of the virtues, asks: that there be made subject to him not a man, but the one who has claimed a place for himself in man. Hence the Apostle too thought that it is rather he who should be condemned in man's sin, he who should be made subject, of whom he says:

May God soon crush Satan under your feet. It is on this persecutor, then, that he longs to have judgment executed for him, so that the adversary may be crushed beneath the footsteps of the prophet's faith, and the prophet may grind him beneath his feet like dust; and, stationed in this warfare of his body, though the days of life are short, may yet win a triumph over the adversary, so that the adversary may groan at the freedom, and feel the power, of the man restored to his former grace — the man whom he had before held bound in the chains of his sins and wearied with the heat of burning lust.

So the adversary has been made subject, according to the Lord's sentence. For the Lord Jesus, coming into this world through the Virgin's childbearing, made all hostile powers subject to our soul, so that they may be crushed by your faith, your word, your way of life, and your works. If, then, you do not crush the adversary, the fault is yours, for not using the power granted you. It rests with us, then, whether the adversary is made subject or springs back.

For if our conduct is displeasing, the adversary begins to grow proud; but if we hold fast to good works and practice the pursuits of chastity, justice, and continence, we tread upon the serpent and the scorpion. For we tread on him with the feet of chastity; we crush the scorpion so that he cannot strike; we tread on him with the footsteps of continence and the steps of modesty and justice. So even in this short life we can have a lasting triumph over our adversaries.

The fifth verse follows: The unjust have told me idle tales, but not like your law, O Lord. He rightly wishes judgment to be executed for him on his persecutors, who tried to hinder not only the works of the righteous man but also his faith with superfluous storytelling. For he says that what was told him were, as it were, the trifles of some fable — adoleschiai, that is, superfluous chatter. For superfluous talkers, like swallows, spoil the pleasantness of a discussion by the incessant flow of their innate chatter, as Aristotle puts it.

So the heretic speaks superfluous things, for he does not speak the truth and does not speak according to the law. But one who is grounded in the law knows how to distinguish false from true, and by the learning of spiritual doctrine to separate heretical teachings from those of the gospel. And therefore, lest many be deceived, the sinner is commanded by the Lord to be silent; for to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous decrees?

Let faithlessness, then, fall silent, which does not know the path of truth and does not keep God's commandments. For why do sinners take the gospel of truth into their mouths, when there is no truth in their mouths? But all God's commandments are truth, and Christ is truth. Christ, then, is not in the disputations of the faithless, he who says to the faithless man: Your mouth has abounded in wickedness, and your tongue has framed deceit;

for a tongue that wants to build up a lie surely weaves deceit into its assertions. But such a man is a thief and runs with the thief. For there are many thieves who steal and snatch the word of God not for their own benefit but for fraud, and who twist a sort of inheritance of the heavenly

Scriptures to their own thefts, gathering for themselves counterfeit gains acquired by deceit rather than by truth. But these are the ones who mix water with wine like the worst of tavern-keepers, adulterating the word of God and producing as insincere whatever they have brought out of their faithless and, as it were, drunken mouths; and therefore they speak things foreign to the law. Hence the prophet rightly flees and rebukes them, knowing what he has received by the prescription of the law.

Rightly, then, does he say in the following verse: All your commandments are truth; they have persecuted me unjustly; help me. Like a good soldier he does not flee from wars, nor does he, a seasoned warrior, dread the clash of battles, however heavy; but, faithful and prudent, he prays that aid may breathe upon him from God, and asks for the faithful help of devout piety.

And therefore he does not ask that persecutions cease, but asks to be helped in persecutions. For he knew that all who want to live godly lives in Christ Jesus suffer persecution. He prefers, then, to suffer persecutions so that he may be able to live godly in Christ. And he did well to speak not of one persecution but of many, and not to name his persecutors, because there are many persecutors, not only those we see but also those we do not see. The spiritual forces of wickedness persecute; the heretic, the Jew, the pagan persecute. All who want to live godly lives, then, are under persecutors, because where there are many persecutors, no time is free from persecution for one eager to live godly.

And perhaps when we do not suffer persecution we are regarded as condemned, as though we had no wish at all to live godly in Christ. For since the sentence is fixed that all who want to live godly lives in Christ Jesus suffer persecution, the one who does not suffer persecution seems to be disowned, as not having a godly intention in Christ; for battles pursue the devotion of faith. If struggles are lacking, I fear that the one who has ceased to struggle may seem to be lacking.

All your commandments, he says, are truth. What commandments, if not these: If they have persecuted me, they will persecute you too? These commandments David, though he came before the mystery of the incarnation, was already hearing in the Spirit, and as a disciple of Christ he did not withdraw from sufferings but offered himself to the struggles.

He knew that this was fruitful for his glory and safe for the keeping of his salvation: that the righteous man's piety should be strengthened by frequent exercise. For untrained faith quickly grows languid, and idle faith is tempted by frequent troubles. The cunning ambusher breaks in when the watch is relaxed, but the fraud of the enemy only trains the man accustomed to war and advances him to the palm of a glorious victory. Peace, then, is for the faithful an occasion of corruption.

How beautifully the times of persecution went for us! The inmost affection of the mind toward God was intent, like a physician [?]. It clung to him, and the soul of one praying felt no thoughts clamoring against it. Prayer poured out from the whole heart, and a kind of conversation was carried on with the Lord.

Daily meditation already held danger in contempt and had acquired the habit of trampling death underfoot. Now that we have lost that exercise, leisure tempts those whom wars had not broken. So the leisure of peace is dangerous too; in peace more persecutions have begun. In the time of persecution there was no flatterer to tempt the mind with cunning flattery.

The soul had no time to be weakened by bodily pleasure or to admit such passions as prosperity usually arouses. Therefore the apostles, when they were beaten and imprisoned, rejoiced, because by those injuries they were gaining the merit of eternal grace, they who had been found worthy to suffer injuries for the name of Christ. They had no concern for property, no eagerness for powers and honors, none for precedence — which tends to trouble even the righteous — but each thought himself preferred who had been scourged with more blows.

Rightly, then, does David seek occasions of triumph and does not fear an abundance of struggle for the training of his devotion, since he knew that the persecutions of the wicked serve to increase virtue. For he did not say, 'Because I suffer persecutions, help me,' but:

They have persecuted me unjustly, he says; help me. For a person can suffer persecutions, but not unjustly, since there is also just persecution: if we hate the obscene, if we are hostile to the unjust, if we want to restrain the wicked so that they do not harm more people, if we strip the greedy man of the gains of his fraud, if we abhor the insolence of the proud. But one who suffers persecution for faith, for justice, for chastity rightly says: They have persecuted me unjustly; help me.

The seventh verse follows: They almost finished me off on the earth, but I did not forsake your commandments. Not needlessly did he seek divine help, for he knew that his struggle was against strong foes and that many battles were prepared for him, as he was to fight now against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, now against the heat of the blood and the countless allurements of this body; wearied by their varied entanglements and by long wrestling, he would have fallen in a shameful contest, had he not held fast by the root of faith.

Let us learn to beware of what we carry about. This is our enemy within the household; this is the grievous foe of our own body. It is inflamed by wine, burns with lust, is kindled by the beauty of a woman it meets, is fed by hope, scorched by despair, burned up by allurements; it is not cooled by fulfillment; it is troubled by fear, broken by dread, softened by luxury, undone by wantonness, afflicted by toil, wearied by anxiety, worn down by suffering.

Do you wonder if, amid so many hostile turns of the passions, even the righteous man can scarcely hold his ground, when we are unequal to the struggle with even a single passion? Whom does lust alone not claim? Whom does avarice not subdue, whom does fear not shake, whom does luxury not drain, whom does wantonness not soften, whom does drunkenness not trip up?

So, as one aware of the weakness of the flesh and with experience of hostile persecution, he says: "They almost made an end of me on earth." On this earth, surely, where Adam first fell and, thrown down by a shameful lapse, bent the course of all his posterity to come; on this earth, where Cain, grieved that his brother's gifts were preferred to his own, was laid low by the ruin of envy; and then the voice of a brother's blood cried out from the earth.

On this earth holy Noah, whom the floods that covered the whole world proved watchful amid such great storms and waves, nevertheless, once he relaxed his cares and let his body rest at leisure, fell into the sleep of drunkenness and suffered an affront to the reverence due to a father. He teaches us that leisure is dangerous to a virtue that feels secure.

On this earth Lot, who followed the example of his revered kinsman, whom the impurity of the debauched people of Sodom did not stain and whom the flame of burning Sodom did not engulf, nevertheless did not escape the incest of a shameful union, though his ignorance made it pardonable. He who was not burned by the flame of sulphur was burned by the flames of women.

On this earth David too said that he had almost been made an end of, since he felt that his feet had almost been moved and his steps had all but slipped, because he thought that the riches of the world and success in bodily prosperity abounded to sinners in place of blessedness.

For this reason he was also scourged; but to the just man scourges are remedies for salvation, for "the Lord chastens the one whom he receives." So David, having turned to the love of the Lord and been instructed in his precepts, and knowing that perishable things come to perishable people by a kind of chance, and that the merits of a commendable life are weighed not by an abundance of riches but by the grace of virtues, loved God's commandments rather than forsaking them. By these alone could he overcome the spiritual wickedness that assailed him and the appetites of this body that rose up against him in the weakness of so fragile a nature. Great, then, is the virtue which, set amid such persecutions and almost overwhelmed, nevertheless did not forget its protection and did not forsake God's commandments.

And so, because he knew that God alone had helped him, he directs his prayers to the Lord and says in the next verse: "According to your mercy give me life, and I will keep the testimonies of your mouth." What giving of life he asks for himself we explained above: he prayed not for what he had, but for what he desired, that is, to live for ever, understanding that the blessedness of life cannot be found in this

wavering and untrustworthy body of ours, whose weakness abandons the purpose of the soul. We need God's mercy, then, so that there may be a continual and unending giving of life in this body, so that every day the just man may live to God and die to sin. For if guilt dies in us, there will be a life that lives to God and a persevering keeping of the heavenly precepts, which is surely kept by the one who is given life by the Lord.

So he first asks the Lord to give him life, and afterwards promises to keep the heavenly testimonies; for it is not this common life that keeps the heavenly commandment, but the life that is upheld by an eternal gift through the working of spiritual grace. We can also understand it this way: since the prophet already knew what belonged to the law, he longs for the mercy of the Lord's coming, so that he may receive the precepts by which the law is fulfilled, and know not only that adultery must be avoided but also that the desire for adultery must be shunned.

For the Lord Jesus, the mouth of the Father, said in the gospel that whoever looks at a woman so as to desire her has committed adultery with her in his heart. How much the pursuit of chastity has advanced through the gospel, which removes the disgrace not only of the shameful deed but also of the base desire!

And who are those of whom he says that they almost made an end of him on earth, if not persecutors? Of one of these the Lord Jesus says: "Go and tell that fox," meaning Herod. And elsewhere, when he noticed that he was being questioned deceitfully, he said: "Foxes have holes and the birds of the air have nests where they may rest," because such people deceitfully linger in certain hiding places of earthly passions.

That is also why Samson tied foxes together in pairs, fastened torches to their tails and let them loose through the crops of the Philistines. By this figure he signified that wicked and deceitful people, and above all heretics, have a free tongue for barking, but their outcomes are hampered, or their beginnings are contentious, while the end of their deceit is consigned to burning.

And so he let loose three hundred foxes, because the faithless do wish to commend themselves by preaching the cross, but cannot hold fast its mystery; with this contrived, false and feigned preaching they try rather to burn up the fruits

of others, whereas the true cross of the Lord does not burn up the merits of others but makes them fruitful. And rightly is it written in the Song of Songs: "Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, so that our vineyards may flower." This shows that either the Lord Jesus or the Church commands that the tricks of the deceitful be driven out of their vineyards, so that they may not harm the very young vines, since they cannot harm vines that are already grown. For a heretic can tempt someone who is imperfect, but cannot trip up someone who is perfect.
XII. THE LETTER LAMED.

The twelfth letter, Lamed, begins here. Its meaning is "heart" or, according to another interpretation, "I keep." So it seems to remind us either to understand these precepts wisely or to keep them carefully. Indeed, the very first verse reminds us of this at once. For that a clean heart be created in him

is what this prophet asked earlier, as we read, and his son Solomon prayed to the Lord that he be given a prudent heart. Whoever, then, has a clean heart, whoever has a prudent heart, understands the sequence and the force of the verses that follow. Hence we also find elsewhere "a single heart," meaning either one that is unique or one that no allurement of this world hinders and no wisdom of the flesh can disturb. And whoever has a heart keeps God's commandments, as you have read of Mary, who kept in her heart all the words and deeds of the Lord and Saviour.

Let us then circumcise our heart; let us seek nothing bodily, nothing base, and everything earthly is base. So let us place nothing earthly, nothing worldly, nothing bodily, nothing light and changeable in the heavenly words (for the words of the Lord are pure words), so that the spotless and chaste purity of the heavenly mysteries may shine out in them through spiritual interpretation. Let us not, by some adulterated opinion, mix earthly things with divine ones, nor violate the inviolable sacrament of prophetic vision or of the everlasting oracle by judging it according to our own nature.

This is why he added: "Silver tried in the fire, purified of earth, refined sevenfold," so that, like good money-changers, we may test by the Spirit the silver of the prophetic word, setting apart the Lord's money and cleansing it of every earthly stain by pouring over it the saving spring, and so be seen to think worthily of Christ, who says: "Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy, but store up treasures for yourselves in heaven."

Your treasure is faith, piety, mercy; your treasure is Christ. Do not think of him as being from the earth, that is, from among creatures, for he is the Lord of all creation. "Cursed," it says, "is the man who puts his hope in man"; and yet salvation came to me through a man. But see what the old scripture said: "He is a man, and who will know him?" That man, then, forgave me all my sins not by human power but by divine power: the Lord Jesus, God in a body, reconciling to himself the world which he was redeeming from guilt.

Our precious treasure is understanding. If our understanding is earthly, if it is frail, the moth of heresy and the rust of impiety will consume it. Let us, then, lift up and raise our minds, and let us not judge it impossible for this weakness of the human body to be carried up to knowledge of the heavenly mysteries, since the Lord Jesus, in whom the treasures of knowledge and wisdom were hidden, has now come down to us in his divine compassion, to unlock what was closed, open what was hidden and reveal what was secret. Come, then, Lord Jesus, open to us the door of this prophetic word as well; for it is closed to many, even if at first sight it seems open.

"For ever, O Lord," he says, "your word abides in heaven." You see that what abides and endures in heaven ought to abide in you as well. Keep, then, the word of God; keep it in your heart, and keep it so that you do not forget it. Keep the law of the Lord and meditate on it, so that the Lord's ordinances may not slip from your heart. The meaning of the letter teaches you to keep it diligently; the prophet teaches you in the verses that follow, saying: "Had your law not been my meditation, I would perhaps have perished in my humiliation;

I will never forget your ordinances." Meditation on the law, then, enables us to endure and bear times of tribulation, times when we are humbled by some adversity, so that we are not broken by a spirit too much humbled or too much cast down. Indeed, the Lord wants us to be humbled not to the point of despair, but to the point of correction.

Hence the prophet Jeremiah too says under this letter in Lamentations: "To crush underfoot all the prisoners of the earth, to turn aside a man's right before the face of the Most High, to condemn a man when he is judged: the Lord did not command it"; and further on: "Evil things will not come forth from the mouth of the Most High." The humbling that comes from the Lord, then, is full of justice and full of fairness, because evil things do not come forth from the Lord's mouth. Indeed, the one who was humbled by the Lord said: "I was humbled, and he saved me."

Therefore, just as we must consider wisely when humbling from the Lord is a means of testing, and when the pressure of humbling is inflicted by a human being (which, however, is usually borne with patience and magnanimity), so too we must consider wisely what it means that the word of the Lord abides in heaven "for ever," or, as some manuscripts have it, "for the age." For the Greek has eis ton aiōna, which translators have rendered differently, some as "for ever," others as "for the age."

So then: "Your word, O Lord, abides in heaven for the age." And how is it that you yourself said: "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away"? The word abides for the age, not beyond the age and the ages, for ages belong to time. So heaven and earth, that is, the works of this world, will pass away, and the times will remain. Another, who is spiritual and judges the words of the law, says: "For ever, O Lord, your word abides in heaven"; for the eternity of a word that abides excludes any notion of a word that passes away.

But how does the word abide in heaven if heaven itself passes away? How can the roof stand if the foundations give way, or how can the inhabitant remain in his dwelling unless the dwelling also endures? But perhaps this objection may come to mind, because it is written: "There will be a new heaven." Yet even so the difficulty is not resolved, because what passes away cannot abide in it, nor can what has had a beginning be said to have abided. The moth will gnaw your understanding if you think that the word, like heaven, either begins or passes away.

So if we wish to learn the force of the prophet's meaning, let us first consider the moral sense in things that are visible and perceptible, so that from it we may make clear the things that are intelligible. If the word of God abides in heaven, let us imitate heaven, where the word abides, where the solemn order of the heavenly ordinances abides, and where the frequent turns of the Lord's benefits continue with their regular gifts.

For from above, by rains or heat or the warmth of this air, abundant fertility is poured into the earth and nourished. Through heaven the year glides on through days and months and seasons, ordered into autumn and winter, spring and clear summer. Take from heaven an image of your own life: even when you are not producing fruit, still sow seed for fruit.

There are seeds that come from heaven and are sown on earth. There is also a heavenly vintage, which is why the prophet says: "Sow for yourselves for righteousness, gather the vintage for fruit." And when your works are not in flower, still tend your seeds, so that they do not run wild in wantonness. What runs wild in the flowering of the seed is thin and dull in the fruit. Ripen the fruits themselves until they are mature.

Let us also imitate the heavenly element itself. It does not always blaze with burning sun; often it bristles with clouds [?], with heavy rains, and covers the earth with falling snow. So let there be no lasting wantonness in you either; let sober times of aged cares follow, and let a grey-haired ripeness, as it were, restrain this field of your body.

Sadness is often more useful, since it usually has seriousness as its companion. Is there any transgression in the sun itself? Does it not keep its daily courses? Does the moon know continual waning, and does it abandon the duty of the service entrusted to it? The year returns with the same changes, the seasons are restored in the same order and renewed with the same services. The sun

lights up the day, keeping its appointed times; the moon shines with nightly splendour, and its light gleams in the darkness. The sphere of shining stars glows red, and they carry out their regular station, revolution and change. One law governs these diverse things: to keep the turns of the courses once established and not to cross the boundaries prescribed. The change itself remains unchangeable, and the revolution does not know how to overturn its order. All share one obedience: with distinct duties, to keep the undivided harmony of the prescribed ordinance.

So the word abides in heaven, because Satan fell from heaven. He had no place in heaven; that is why he fell. Where did he fall, if not to earth? That is why adulteries, murders and drunkenness began to abound here. Shut out from there, he came to us more savage, and in his rage he wields temptations harsher than before.

The word abides in heaven, then, because the devil was cast down from there; it does not abide on earth, because he has come here entirely. And consider whether the word can abide in us here, where the devil has scattered so many snares, when even while he was in heaven the word could not abide there. Indeed, it was because he himself did not hold fast to the word that he fell from heaven.

So the word abides in heaven, which is ruled and governed according to the ordering of the Word. But because heaven itself also passes away, he did not say that it abides "for the ages" but "for the age," although it passes away precisely so that there may be a new heaven, a new earth, a new testament, and so that we may be able to see the glory of the Lord face to face.

Yet because there was a place for vices even in heaven (for the adversary would certainly not have fallen from there had he not been caught in crimes; and "the fool changes like the moon," and heaven itself is overcast with darkness), it seems that this was said not of the element but of the heavenly virtues and powers. For there are holy powers in heaven in which there is nothing unstable or earthly.

There are also heavens on earth which declare the glory of God. Hear who these heavens are from the one who says: "As we have borne the image of the earthly one, let us also bear the image of the heavenly one." These, then, are heavens who, though placed on earth, dare to say: "But our citizenship is in heaven."

These are the heavens in which there is faith, seriousness, self-control, teaching, a heavenly life. For just as the one who fell from heavenly grace through that transgression, was cast down into these earthly vices and bound himself with the chains of his transgression, was called earth, so on the contrary the one who lives the life of the angels by guarding his integrity, and governs his body with self-controlled sobriety,

who also composes his mind in gentle tranquillity and distributes his money to the poor with merciful generosity, is called heaven. So there is a heaven on earth too, in which heavenly virtues can exist. "Heaven is my throne": I understand this as the disposition of the just man rather than the element. I consider that one to be heaven to whose soul Christ comes and knocks at the door, and if you open, he enters. Nor does he enter alone, but with the Father, as he himself says: "I and the Father will come and make our dwelling with him."

You see, then, that God the Word both stirs up the idle and wakes the sleeping. For he who comes and knocks at the door always wishes to enter. But it is due to us that he does not always enter and does not always remain. Let your door be open to him when he comes; open your door, spread wide the bosom of your mind, so that he may see riches of simplicity, treasures of peace, the sweetness of grace. Enlarge your heart, go out to meet the sun of the eternal light which enlightens every human being. And indeed that true light shines on all;

but if anyone closes his windows, he will cheat himself of the eternal light. So Christ too is shut out if you close the door of your mind. Although he could enter, he does not wish to burst in uninvited; he does not wish to force the unwilling. Born of a virgin, he came forth from the womb shining upon the whole world, so as to give light to all. Those who long for the brightness of everlasting radiance, which no night interrupts, receive it. For this sun that we see every day is followed by dark night, but the Sun of righteousness never sets, because wickedness does not follow upon wisdom.

Blessed, then, is the one at whose door Christ knocks. Our door is faith, which, if it is strong, fortifies the whole house. Through this door Christ enters; this is why the Church also says in the Song: "The voice of my brother; he knocks at the door." Hear him knocking, hear him longing to come in: "Open to me, my sister, my bride, my dove, my perfect one, for my head is filled with dew and my locks with the drops of the night."

Consider when God the Word knocks at your door most of all: when his head is filled with the dew of night. For he deigns to visit those who are in tribulation and temptation, so that no one may perhaps give way, overcome by hardships. His head, then, is filled with dew or drops when his body is in distress. That is the time to keep watch, so that when the bridegroom comes he does not go away shut out.

For if you are asleep and your heart is not awake, he departs before he knocks; if your heart is awake, he knocks and asks that the door be opened to him. We have, then, a door to our soul; we also have gates, of which it was said: "Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory will come in." So there is heaven also in those in whom there are eternal gates.

If you are willing to lift up these gates of your faith, the King of glory will come in to you, bearing the triumph of his own passion. Righteousness too has gates. For we read that these also are written of, when the Lord Jesus says through his prophet: "Open to me the gates of righteousness"; and further on the prophet David says: "Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem; praise your God, O Zion, for he has strengthened the bars of your gates."
