There is, then, a soul that has a door, and there is one that has gates. Christ comes to this door and knocks; he knocks at the gates too. Open to him, then; he wishes to come in, he wishes to find his bride awake. Do not keep the good lover waiting; he quickly withdraws, and you will be seen to have shut out the one who knocks through the sleep of your sluggishness. For you shut him out when you are idle, when you are lazy, when you are drowsy; by these bolts Christ is shut out. Even if you are chaste, even if you are sober, beware of being careless; the one who repels him when he comes does Christ a greater wrong.
Sometimes, too, if you delay, he puts his hand through the window, as the bride says: "My brother put his hand through the opening, and my belly was stirred for him. I rose to open to my brother;

my hands dripped with myrrh, my fingers were full of myrrh." First, then, he puts his hand through the opening, as it were, when he is judged to be God by his works; hence he says: "If you do not believe me, at least believe the works." Then love grows and, conceived in the inmost parts, takes root. Then, once his seeds have been poured into the intelligible womb in which the Word is received, our soul longs to draw in his fullness dwelling there bodily. For the womb of women is not stirred unless they are heavy with child.

So the soul rises to open to the Word of God. But while it spreads itself out and opens, so as to put to death the works of this world by receiving the Word (like the one who says: "We carry about in our body the dying of the Lord Jesus"), while it is opening, the bridegroom has passed on. For he wishes always to be sought and to be found more often,

and if he finds the door closed, he knocks, and if he is shut out by delay, he withdraws. But he quickly returns and knocks again, so that at least afterwards he may find the bride ready. It can also be understood in this way: "My brother passed through," as we read, because he pierced to the inmost marrow of his beloved, just as it was said to Mary: "And a sword will pass through your own soul, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed." And then the bride added that her soul went out at his word, which happens when the soul is away from the body and present with God.

We have explained, then, as well as we could, what is meant by: Forever, O Lord, your word abides in heaven. Yet we can also understand it this way: that it abides forever in heaven above all, where there are angels and archangels, Cherubim and Seraphim, because human beings, however holy they may be, still often change in their feelings. One moment we rejoice, the next we grieve, grow angry, groan.

Even in penitence itself the apostle does not want us to be overly saddened, lest we be swallowed up by sorrow. So where there is anger, where there is heavy sorrow, the word does not abide. Indeed, it was said by John of the Lord Jesus alone that he saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove and remaining upon him.

For the prophets too did not always prophesy, but only when the Spirit poured into them the grace of prophesying. Indeed, not even David knew beforehand what Nathan, sent by the Lord, would announce; and certainly Nathan, the lesser prophet, knew what David, the greater, did not know. And another prophet said: The Lord has hidden it from me.

Hence many also take it that the word of God abides in heaven, that is, in the heavenly powers, in whom there are no fluctuations of feeling. Some, however, take it of the Trinity itself, which alone is unchangeable. And so the word abides in heaven, that is, in the Father, because the Word said: I am in the Father and the Father is in me.

Your truth is from generation to generation. There are many who are called gods, but they are not. So among the gentiles there is falsehood, in the church there is truth. Yet the synagogue had this truth first, since it had the oracles of God; for there is truth in the Old Testament as well, truth which was formerly among the Jewish people; for God is known in Judah. And God is truth; therefore truth was in Judah. So truth was in the fathers, in Moses and Joshua son of Nun, in

Samuel, in David, Elijah, Elisha, and in those seven thousand men who did not bend the knee to Baal. But because the later offspring of the Jews strayed from the ways of their fathers, truth withdrew from them and came to the church. For it withdrew from them when they said of the Lord Jesus: Away with him, away with him, crucify him! For they handed over the truth and chose iniquity. All other generations, then, have no share in the truth; the generations of all the heretics do not hold the truth.

The church alone possesses the truth with devout affection, because the generation of the Jews, which possessed it before her, lost it. The Jewish people, then, was the first generation of faith, and therefore more childish and weaker, and it could not keep its footing on the slippery ground of youth. But the Christian people is the second generation of faith, and therefore sturdier and riper with venerable age. That was the generation of the law, this is the generation of grace. Hence elsewhere too he says: From generation to generation he will proclaim your truth.

There follows the third verse: You established the earth, and it abides. By your ordinance the day abides. How God established the earth, Scripture has taught us, where the prophet says: God by wisdom founded the earth, and by understanding he prepared the heavens. The earth, then, is like a foundation on which we stand, although the learning of outsiders proclaims that it lies within the hemisphere of the sky, and Scripture too seems to indicate this when Job says: hanging the earth upon nothing. It is therefore enclosed by the sphere of the heavens, and that is why the sun is not seen at night: in its circuit it is in the lower part of the heavenly sphere. But the saints have no interest in describing the axis of the heavens and the extents and numbers of the elements in the manner of the philosophers—for what does this contribute to salvation?—because the saints always attend to spiritual things and are eager to learn or to teach whatever will profit eternal life.

Indeed, Ecclesiastes has beautifully shown us that this passage is spiritual, not material, when he says: What abundance does a man have in all the labor at which he labors under the sun? A generation goes and a generation comes, and the earth stands forever. That is: what abundance does the spiritual man have who labors under the sun of righteousness? And he added: A generation goes and a generation comes. A generation goes, because the rich have been in want and gone hungry.

Those who once abounded in grace later began to be in want because of their faithlessness. But the peoples of the nations, who were poor, are now filled and abound through faith in Christ, as it is written: The poor shall eat and be satisfied. For they have heard someone saying: abounding in every good thing—not, of course, in money, not in gold and silver, but in every word, he says, and in knowledge; and elsewhere he says: in the riches of simplicity.

These riches bring health, for worldly wealth cannot bring salvation. But whoever has spiritual abundance, his fruitful earth stands forever, well founded on the root of the virtues—whether it be the soul bearing good fruit, or the flesh, [?] though its desires make it prone to slip and fall.

This earth the sun of saving righteousness circles, of which it is written: The sun rises and the sun sets, and draws to its place; rising, it goes there toward the south and turns round toward the north; circling, circling goes the spirit, and the spirit returns upon its circuits.

The sun rises for the just but sets for the unjust; it rises for the calm of a devout mind, it sets for anger. Hence he says: Do not let the sun go down upon your anger. From this we can gather that it rises and sets for the same people, burying their vices and illuminating their grace. For he died to sin, that he might live to God; that is, in him we died to sin, that we might live to God forever. See the very mystery foretold: The

sun, he says, rises and sets, and draws to its place. This is what the Lord said: When I am lifted up, I will draw all things to myself. For he drew to himself the strivings of all, either to crucify our sins or to call good natures to righteousness. Notice how he draws to himself: Father, I desire that where I am, these also may be with me; and to the thief he says: Today you will be with me in paradise. Notice how he draws all things: he was lifted up on the cross, and the whole world believed.

The Dawn itself, he says, goes toward the south and turns toward the north—he, surely, is the Dawn who said: Dawn is my name; who always dawns for the devout and never sets. This Dawn went to the Hebrew people toward the south, to a softer people, more liable to the slippery ways of a body burning with luxury than hardened by the savagery of impiety—or at any rate to a nobler people, which was a chosen race claiming for itself the lineage of the patriarchs. But because it persisted in its vices and did not correct its error, the sun of righteousness turned toward the gentiles, who, formerly cheated of the heavenly oracles, were regarded as savage and ignoble;

for the north wind is heavy, like the people of the nations. But those who were formerly heavy with faithlessness have now been made lighter than eagles by faith and devotion, since he came who would say: Bring them from the north; and in the gospel: They will come from the east and the west and from the north and the south, and will recline at table in the kingdom of God. And behold, those are last who were first, and those are first who were last. Indeed, the psalmist himself says: Mount Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great king; that is: those who were the side of the north have become the people of the eternal King, who alone is the great Lord.

But perhaps you will say: 'How then is it said in the Song of Songs: Arise, north wind, and come, south wind?' For many take it as though the north wind is driven off and the south wind invited. If they take it this way, the icy harshness of faithlessness is driven out of the church, so that our flight may not be in winter or on a sabbath, and the mild spring warmth of the south is invited in.

Or else Arise, north wind means: Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead; people of the nations, you who have long been asleep, wake up at last, and Christ will shine upon you. In short, all are invited to the church, both the people of the synagogue and the people of the gentiles, but the synagogue first, because the apostles, being Jews, believed first, and through them the peoples of the nations were afterwards gathered in.

See, then, our sun coming to the south and afterwards turning to the north. Jerusalem, Jerusalem—he certainly came to her whom he even deigned to call by name; but this is the earthly Jerusalem, which kills the prophets, that is, the synagogue of the Jews—how often, he says, I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks, and you would not! Behold, your house will be left to you desolate.

So he turned toward the gentiles; and circling, the Spirit of God circled, and returned upon its circuits, so that God might be all in all. That is why the holy man is called heaven: the brightness of the sun, being nearer to him, always illumines him; he has his own splendor at home, so that he does not feel the darkness of night. That is why the church is called both heaven and world, because it has

saints comparable to angels and archangels, and also has many earthly people. It is also called the world, which is founded upon the seas and established upon the rivers. Indeed, it is as the world that the church says: Do not look at me, for I am dark, because the sun has not looked upon me; for the sun of righteousness long judged the congregation of the gentiles, bound as if by winter frosts and the ice of pagan error,

unworthy to be illumined by the serene light of his face. Did it not seem to you like the stiffness of wintertime, when God was known only in Judah? But now the fullness of summer light shines, when Christ is all and in all. Is not the earth the Lord's, and its fullness? And truly the whole world is in the church, in which there is not only Jew or Greek, not barbarian or Scythian, not slave or free, but we are all one in Christ. The sun shines for all; the day gives light to all.

And so he says: By your ordinance the day abides. For unless you understand it this way, how does the day abide, when after the brief span of daylight comes sunset and night follows in turn? But there are some for whom it is always day, namely those with whom Christ is present, who says: Walk while you have the light. You have him whom Abraham saw, the day of the forgiveness of sins, of which you read: This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it. There are, then, saints for whom the sun never sets, because the Lord is their light, as it is written: And the Lord will be an everlasting light for them.

And he stated the reason why the day abides, adding: By your ordinance, he says, the day abides, for all things serve you. So he seems to point to that future time when there will be no more night, and there will be no need of lamp or of sunlight, because the Lord will give them light.

Who they are he says above: And his servants will serve him, that is, they will do the Lord's will. For now not all of us serve; but when he has handed over the kingdom to God the Father, then all things will be subject to him who subjected all things to himself, winning the faith of all through the passion of the Only-begotten. It is the subjection of minds, then, that makes service diligent.

So when all have believed in the Lord Jesus, then all things will serve God, so that God may be all in all. But now not all are servants of God, because many are servants of sin; for whoever commits sin is a slave of sin. And the Lord does not wish to share his dominion with others. So 'the day abides' is said in the present tense. He could have said 'will abide', but to the prophets future things appear as present in the Spirit.

There follows the fourth verse: Unless your law had been my meditation, I might perhaps have perished in my lowliness. The prophet, whose meditation was the law, shone like the day; for he received the oil for his light from the law. Indeed, so that the light of day might not be extinguished by the body of death, he walked in the law, and so he walked in the light. Otherwise, he says, I would have perished in my lowliness.

Lowliness is not always a matter of virtue; it can also be a matter of affliction—that is, it is not always voluntary, but is sometimes undergone out of necessity, when we are tried by some affliction. Otherwise no one perishes in lowliness, which tends rather to preserve. So when we are in a time of affliction and are shaken by adversities, let our meditation be in the law, so that the storm of temptation may not strike us unprepared.

An athlete does not dare to enter a contest unless he has first been hardened by training in the wrestling school. Let us, then, anoint the muscles of our mind with the oil of our reading. Let us practice all day and night in a kind of wrestling school of the heavenly Scriptures, and let the wholesome food of spiritual dishes strengthen the limbs of our souls, so that when the adversary begins to stand against us and sprinkles us with the dust

of his temptation, we may stand undaunted, and strive not as one who runs uncertainly, nor as one beating the air. We strike better when we are struck, if we offer the other cheek to the one who strikes us, if we do not seek revenge but leave the whole matter of vengeance to him who said: Vengeance is mine, I will repay. We strike the powers of the air if we know how to discipline ourselves. Paul disciplined his own flesh

so as to beat his adversaries, and brought his body into subjection so as to master his enemies. Let us train, then, by tireless practice of meditation; let us train before the contest, so that we may always be ready for it; and when the adversary's blows fall thick and fast—now poverty, now robbery, now bereavement, now bodily sickness, now grief of mind, now fear of death and the bitterness of torments—let each of us who has been able to endure and bear them say: Unless your law had been my meditation, I might perhaps have perished in my lowliness.

How many things were heaped up all at once to make holy Job perish in that affliction! But because he had been shaped by the ways of the patriarchs and formed by instruction in the heavenly oracles and in the natural law, he could not perish in such great temptations. Indeed, when he had suddenly lost such great possessions and his dearest children, he said, as one whose daily meditation was in the divine law: Naked I came out of my mother's womb, naked I shall return there. The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done; blessed be the name of the Lord. And when, covered with sores over his whole body, he was tempted by his wife's words, he remembered that Adam had been brought down in just this way by trusting his own wife, and he replied: You have spoken like one of the foolish women. Had he been willing to listen to her as if she were wise, he himself would not have been wise. Tempted also by the various speeches of his friends, when he had earned from the Lord the rewards of steadfast faith and unshaken patience, did he not say: Unless your law had been my meditation, I might perhaps have perished in my lowliness?

How gratefully does one say this today who in martyrdom has endured many scourgings and been tested by the rack and the hooks, by lead, by red-hot plates, by the sword! For he could have perished, had he not, by meditating on the law, believed that the punishments to come are heavier than those of the present.

How much holy Joseph endured, how bitter, how hard! First his brothers' hatred, the hardships of degrading slavery; robbed of his parents, banished into exile, the house-slave of merchants and the cheap chattel of an ignoble Egyptian. What temptation could be heavier for a boy of noble lineage than to be cast down from such splendor of family and to be a slave among the Egyptians?

Slavery can be borne with some comfort if one serves at least just masters; the injury of slavery is lightened by the fairness of the master. So, cast down from so great a lineage, he was content enough if his service won the approval of a royal officer. Not even this was enough for the bitterness of his temptation. The adversary returned to his arts and set his well-known strength in motion with every kind of deceit, to tie snares for an innocent conscience by means of a woman.

With the goads of lust he inflamed against him his master's wife, who demanded adulterous intercourse from the young slave, so that if he consented he would commit the crime, and if he refused he would incur her displeasure and not escape the net of slander. And so he was thrust into prison and, though innocent, counted among the guilty, and he began to be pressed harder by the very man to whom he had kept faith at his own peril. But because insults could not break the man, the temptation was changed—far harsher under the guise of prosperity;

for prosperity has tripped up very many whom bitter torments had not broken. He is brought out of prison at the king's command, interprets a dream, and is chosen to be preeminent in honor over all the Egyptians, so that, second only to the king, he might distribute food to the starving peoples. His brothers are put in his way, who without any brotherly love had sold him into the injury of slavery, so that, tempted by the pain both of the insult

and of the attempt on his life, he might cast off his brotherly affection. But the just man forgot the insult and heaped up kindness; he wished to show himself all the more a brother the less he had found them to be brothers. Indeed, by this favor he both got his father back and, by a devout ruse, sought out his brother. What better, then, could holy Joseph say to the Lord than this: Unless your law had been my meditation, I might perhaps have perished in my lowliness?

It is told of a certain prophet—and many say it was Isaiah, when he was put in prison—that when he was weighed down by the threat of impending death, the devil said to him: 'Say that what you said you did not speak from the Lord, and I will change the minds and feelings of all toward you, so that those who resent the offense will grant you release.' But he judged punishment for the truth more welcome than a favor bought by flattery. This he surely would not have done, had he not been trained by meditation on the law.

Let daily reading, then, be our exercise, so that we meditate on imitating what we read. Let us sweat in this wrestling school of the virtues, so that when temptations break out with a crash, the time of temptation may not find us untrained, deprived of spiritual food and wasted by a fast from reading. But if it finds our soul fed on an athlete's fare, if the sap of the gospel is in us, if apostolic food has made firm the maturity of our mind and the robust muscles of our soul [?], if a memory made retentive of the heavenly precepts by frequent meditation brings out examples ready for the occasion, then no onset of temptations will be able to throw us into disorder.

There follows the fifth verse: I will never forget your justifications, for in them you have given me life. The law, according to the apostle, is the tutor of little children, until we come to the riper age, as it were, of perfect faith. In the law there are commandments, justifications, testimonies, judgments, precepts; we are therefore given life in the law, which is why the apostle says: The law is not of faith, but whoever does it shall live by it.

But because the same apostle said just before: since no one is justified by the law, you certainly understand that the justification of the law is an appearance and an image, not the truth. According to truth and perfection, then, no one is justified by the law; according to appearance, one is justified. So the holy prophet, who was still living in the justification of the law but saw the radiance of the gospel, kept his gratitude toward the law as toward a useful tutor, as one mindful of his old schooling. Think of someone who has left boyhood behind and is established in wealth and honors, yet keeps showing respect to his old tutor, knowing that it was by his care that he was formed so as to be able to govern his riper years.

Indeed, the law itself admonishes us that we must by no means be ungrateful to those who have once done us good. For, as we have it in the Old Testament, the Passover was celebrated within the borders of Egypt while our fathers, still under King Pharaoh, were lamenting the injury of wretched slavery; and afterwards, once freed, they celebrated the Passover again in the land of promise—the first time as a warning, the second as

a remembrance. If, then, someone asks a Hebrew why it was celebrated in Egypt, he will answer: 'Because we were still held bound to King Pharaoh by the chain of slavery; that lamb freed the people of our fathers, that lamb called us to freedom, that lamb made the depths of the sea solid so that we could cross out of Egypt. So whenever we celebrate the Passover, we must remember the old slavery and the new freedom, what we were and what we have received.' For no one can fully understand what he has received unless he remembers what he was before.
Let us not forget, then, that the Lord Jesus, the Lamb of God, the sacrifice for the world, has freed us from the chains of grievous sins, in which that

most foul Pharaoh, prince not of Egypt alone but of this world, held us bound fast by the chain of heavy slavery. Let us never forget, so that when we come into that truly promised land, where the land of the living is, we may remember how much the cruel Pharaoh inflicted on us here, how much we have suffered in this world, from what evils we have at last been rescued; and let us give thanks to the Lord Jesus, who rescues us, who made the troubler of all a captive.

The sixth verse follows: I am yours; save me, Lord, for I have sought out your statutes. It seems an easy and common thing to say, but few can say it. For rare indeed is the one who can say to God, "I am yours." He says it who clings to God with all his senses and does not know how to think of anything else. He uses these words who can say:

Show us the Father, and it is enough for us. Does a man greedy for money, honour or power use these words? For many it is not enough to know God, indeed for most. So many peoples, so many nations, so many rich men think it poverty to serve the Lord. He who is above all things is small and cramped to them, and the Son of God, in whom all things are, is not enough for them.

Take that rich man in the Gospel to whom it was said: If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have and give to the poor. He judged that God was not enough for him. Indeed he was even saddened, as though he were being ordered to give up what was more and choose what was less. So the one who says "I am yours" is the one who can say: See, we have left everything and followed you.

These, then, are the words of the apostles, yet not of all the apostles. For Judas too was an apostle and reclined among the apostles at Christ's supper. He too used to say "I am yours," but with his voice, not with his heart. Satan came and entered into him and began to say: "He is not yours, Jesus, but mine. Indeed he thinks about what is mine; he turns over in his breast the things that are mine. He feasts with you and grazes with me; he receives bread from you and money from me; he drinks with you and sells me your blood. He is your apostle and my hireling."

The worldly man cannot say "I am yours," for he has many masters. Lust comes and says: "You are mine, because you covet the things of the body. In your love for that young girl you sold yourself to me; when you lay with that harlot I counted out the price for you." Avarice comes and says: "The silver and gold you have is the price of your slavery. The estate you hold was the purchase of your rights, the sale of your freedom." Luxury comes and says: "You are mine.

One day's banquet is the price of your life. That outlay on feasting was the auction of your person, the full sum of your contract; and, what is worse, you were bought for the price of meat and are cheaper than your own food. Your table for one day is worth more than your life for all time. Among the cups I bought you; among the feasts I acquired you." Ambition comes and says to you: "You are plainly mine.

Do you not know that I made you command others precisely so that you yourself might serve me? Do you not know that I conferred power on you precisely so that I might subject you to my power? Or are you unaware that the prince of this world said to the saving Lord himself, when he had shown him all the kingdoms of the world: All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me? So whoever wants to have others subject to him is himself subjected first." All the vices come, and each one says: "You are mine." How cheap a slave is the one whom so many claim!

How then can you, being such a man, say to Christ, "I am yours"? He will answer you: Not everyone who says to me "Lord, Lord" will enter the kingdom of heaven; not everyone who says to me "I am yours" is mine. You are certainly mine if your conscience does not refute your words, if your mind or your works do not contradict what you say. I do not deny that he is mine who does not deny himself to me, or rather who denies himself for my sake. I do not want a slave who serves many masters. For how is he mine

if he says to me in words "I am yours," yet denies it in his works, and by his deeds assigns and binds himself to the devil? He is not mine whom lust inflames, for chastity is mine. He is not mine whom the urge to plunder the weaker harries, for integrity is mine. He is not mine whom fickle anger disturbs, for tranquillity is mine. He is not mine who is drunk with a surfeit of wine until daybreak, drunk with ambition for worldly glory to the point of danger, and cannot keep to the path of sober moderation. I am peace; I do not know how to quarrel. What have I to do with one of whom the devil comes and says: "He is mine, for he has bowed his neck to me. I find more of what is mine in him; he claims your name but does my service"?

So no one belongs to Christ unless he is free from sin; no one belongs to Christ unless he can always show himself Christ's servant. For if someone is changeable, as I am changed now by grief, now by indignation, anger comes and says: "He is mine. An hour ago he was mine, and I hope he will become mine again."

Sadness comes and says: "He is mine. An hour ago he was in my possession and under my authority. He could not lift up his spirit for grief or raise his eyes, and if anything sad befalls him he will come straight back to me." Who then belongs to God except one who can say: I am conscious of nothing against myself? That is why Paul was called an apostle of Jesus Christ, because he was held bound to no one else. But I belong now to my God, now to sadness, now to anger, now to idle words. And so one who has many masters cannot say to one: "Lord Jesus, I am yours."

Hence I think Paul was speaking also of the lords of this world when he said: For although there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him, and one Lord Jesus, through whom are all things and we through him. So the apostle Paul belonged wholly to the Word. That is why he said: Since you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me.

He, then, would say, "I am Christ's," and the Lord would answer him, "You are mine." The one who truly says "I am yours" hears from the Lord: "You are mine." Indeed, when the Lord sent Ananias to heal Paul, he said of him: Go, for he is a chosen vessel to me. And because he persevered in belonging to Christ, he was found worthy, once the contest was finished, to obtain the crown of righteousness.

Rightly, then, did the prophet David, who always remained in the Lord, say: I am yours. And to show on what ground he said "I am yours," he added: I have sought out your statutes. That is: I have sought nothing belonging to others, but have desired only what is yours. Others seek pre-

cious necklaces; I seek only your statutes, as garlands of righteousness. Others join house to house and estate to estate, as though they alone could dwell in this land, and they want to seize the element that is common to all; others want to claim possession of the very air. For me, my whole inheritance lies in your statutes. I know how to possess nothing except what belongs to you by right. In your words my concern is for spiritual silver, and it has shone out for me. God is my portion. I am yours, because my share of the inheritance is not in gold, not in silver, but in Christ Jesus.

The seventh verse follows: Sinners lay in wait for me to destroy me; I have understood your testimonies. These words can suit martyrdom. The saint, having now come out from the persecutor's tribunal, may say: Sinners lay in wait for me to destroy me. That is: they applied every kind of torture and every art of persuasion, but they could not draw me away from my purpose;

faith overcame the allurements of this life and the torment of the body. Sinners waited to triumph over me; but thanks be to Christ, who has granted me to triumph over my persecutors. Go back defeated, you who hoped to be the victors; go back cast down, you who came in pride. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting? The victory has begun to be no longer yours but

ours, because we conquer in you, death, in whom we were once conquered. Well, then, does the martyr say: Sinners lay in wait for me to destroy me. A moment later, indeed while still in the body, he sees the choirs of those who escort him and the joy of the angels (for if they rejoice over the conversion of one sinner, how much more over the suffering of the just!). He sees the glory and says: The just have waited for me to escort me. He sees the Lord Jesus and says: Christ has waited for me to crown me.

Whoever wishes may understand it another way: Many, he says, tried to persuade me to sin and to wrest the faith from my breast, one urging adultery, another murder, another the oppression of a widow or an orphan, another something else, and they thought I could be caught in their nets. They waited for me in order to destroy me by the contagion of sin. But I did not let the allurements of sin turn my mind from the pursuit of divine knowledge, nor did I turn my purpose, Lord, from the course of your commandments; rather, I understood your testimonies. For had I not understood them, those sinners would surely have destroyed me.

What I understood with my mind I also followed in my works. For this is not bare understanding, but understanding to which deeds also bear witness. Indeed: Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor. He truly understands concerning the poor who gives to the poor; for what use is it to pity the needy unless you give him food?

The eighth verse follows: I have seen the end of all consummation; your commandment is exceedingly broad. We cannot express the force of the Greek language in every case; the Greek generally has greater force and splendour of expression. The Greek says telos [?] for what we in Latin call both "end" and "consummation"; but peras [?] is the end of consummation itself, just as Christ is the end of the law

for righteousness to everyone who believes. You have it written: Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age. So the consummation of the age is the end of the age; but the end of all things is Christ. Consummations, however, are many. There is a consummation when there is also resurrection to salvation. A finished work is also called a consummated, that is, a perfect work. Malice is called consummated, that is, complete, when it lacks nothing in zeal and skill for doing harm. There is a consummation of man, and many consummations, until he comes to perfection.

We read, then, both of the consummation of the age and of the end. We gave an example above of the consummation of the age, which the resurrection follows: For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive. After the resurrection comes the consummation, but each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ's, who believed in his coming, then the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, when he has done away with every principality and power. So according to the apostle the end follows the consummation of the age; from which we gather that the end follows every consummation.

The world lies in the power of the evil one, as John said. So the age too lies in the evil one; the world is full of sin. The world had consummated its malice, just as Saul had consummated his. His son Jonathan, seeing that his malice against the prophet David was consummated, told David so, that he might turn aside and flee. So the consummation of malice is the consummation of sins. There came the Lamb

of God who takes away the sin of the world, who is Christ Jesus, the end of the law, the beginning and the end, and the forgiveness of sins. The prophet saw in the spirit this end of consummation, who would abolish the consummated error of the age; he saw the various sins of all people cleansed by his blood. Well, then, did he say: I have seen the end of all consummation. That is: I have seen the one who forgives consummated adultery; I have seen him who through his cross pardons the offences of consummated luxury and wantonness, of consummated cruelty and savagery, in short of every outrage.

There is also consummated virtue, consummated wisdom and consummated righteousness, but it has an end. The end of all virtues is Christ, who is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. You see that he is the end of faith. Well, then, does he say: I have seen the end of all consummation.

Now that we have recognized the end of consummation, let us recognize what is meant by: Your commandment is exceedingly broad. We read that narrow is the gate through which those enter who obtain the fruit of eternal life. For virtue is rare and the endurance of suffering is hard. More numerous are those who follow the spacious ways of this world, who say: The way that leads to God is narrow and confined for us; we are crushed in it; let us abandon it.

How, then, does the prophet call God's commandment broad, and exceedingly broad? Because a narrow way needs a broad commandment. Indeed this same prophet says: In tribulation you have enlarged me; and again: In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he heard me and set me in a broad place.

This breadth of the heavenly commandments enlarges the prophet's heart; it enlarged the apostle's heart too. Indeed he himself said: Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. For by dispensing the heavenly commandments he had enlarged

his heart, and what the faithlessness of his persecuting days had once constricted, the grace of Christ had expanded. And the commandment is broad for this reason [?]: so that we might not be hemmed in by narrow commandments. Hence he says: You are not constrained in us. If Paul did this, how much more Christ, who opened what was shut! So he says: I do not want my people to be constricted in me. On the narrow path of the virtues, the breadth of my precept ought to be a comfort to travellers, so that no one may faint or be crushed.

Let us walk, then, in God's commandment, for it is broad enough. For it is the commandment of wisdom, which is sung in the ways out and acts with confidence in the broad places; for plateia is the Greek word for what in Latin is called breadth. Let us enlarge our heart, then, to take in the force of the apostle's saying, when he says:

Make room for us. Let us receive his words into our heart; let us put on a heart of mercy, kindness, humility and patience. O man, how broad you are, if you spread the bosom of your mind to the breadth of the heavenly precepts! How broad is the commandment of love! Love your enemies, he says. He surely included everyone in the embrace of love who did not exclude enemies;

for who can seem left out when even an enemy is taken in? Hence the apostle says: If it is possible, be at peace with all men. This cannot be said to Jews or to Gentiles, that they should be at peace with all. They scarcely love their own; the Christian is not permitted not to love even his enemies. When I say "Christian," I mean perfect; for in Christ, whose name you claim, is the fullness of the Godhead.

You who bear the name, why do you shrink from what the name means and from its perfection? Hear a broad commandment: Bless those who persecute you, and do not curse. He who says the commandment is broad proved it above, when he said: They slandered me, but I prayed. What do you pray, David? Tell us yourself. But you have told us, for I read your words: They will curse, and you will bless.
XIII. THE LETTER MEM

Here begins the thirteenth letter, called Mem, which in Latin means "from the innermost parts," or, according to others, "fire from the farthest depths"; and neither meaning is at odds with the text. For the very first verse expresses a love that comes from the inmost heart, which surely proceeds from the deepest marrow and is bound into the bones by a kind of tie of heat.

Indeed, in the Lamentations of Jeremiah the text under this letter contains these words: From on high he has sent fire into my bones. Good, then, is God, who sends into us the means by which, loving him, we may find merit in his sight. What fire he sends, let him teach us himself: I came to cast fire on the earth, and what do I wish but that it be kindled already?

Good is the fire which the Saviour of all desires to be kindled, especially since we have read that God himself is fire. He consumes our sins, pours into our inmost breasts a longing for the knowledge of God, and lights up our heart within us when we read the sequence of the divine Scriptures,

in case by spiritual understanding we grasp something that may open the hidden meanings of the prophetic reading. Cleopas said that his heart burned with this fire when Christ opened the Scriptures to him and his companion. Of this fire the Lord said in the book of Ezekiel: Behold, I will go to Jerusalem and blow upon you in the fire of my wrath, so that you may be melted free of lead and iron and the other base materials.

We see profound mysteries in ordinary words; all of this is spiritual. By what prayers may I earn that the word of God should come and enter the Church and become a consuming fire, to burn up the hay and stubble and consume whatever is worldly; that the heavy lead of iniquity which is in so many may be melted by the divine fire, and the iron rigidity of sin be softened by the heavenly blaze; that the vessels of gold and silver may be refined, so that every mind of the wise and every word of the prudent,

once the heat of burning passions has been purged away, may begin to be more precious? Good is the fire of love, by which the whole body of the Church grows into mutual grace; good is the fire of charity, by which each saint is kindled to reverence for his Maker. But whoever loves God does not love him half-heartedly: he loves his law, keeps his precepts, and justifies his heart not by resounding proclamation of words but by earnest imitation in deeds. Let God, then, teach us how he is loved by his saints.

Speaking thus, the prophet adds: How I have loved your commandment, Lord! It is my meditation all the day. These are the words of one whose love is set on coming to know the law, the law that forms man's perfection, which this whole psalm sets out. And since he knew that the greatest commandment in the law is that we love the Lord our God with all our heart and with all our soul, he wants us too, whom he is eager to instruct, to become perfect by imitating him, saying: How I have loved your commandment, Lord!

Love grows through this very affection, in that it calls as witness the very one on whom the gift of love is spent, and by such an appeal it bears witness not to the appearance of love but to its fullness. Peter used this appeal: You know, Lord, he says, that I love you. But whoever loves the Lord loves his law, just as Mary, loving her Son, pondered all his words in her heart with a mother's affection. Loving you, I have done your will, as it is written.

That is why Christ entrusted Peter with feeding his flock and doing the Lord's will: because he recognized his love. For whoever loves does what he is commanded willingly; whoever fears does it out of necessity. So the Lord approves the voluntary works of his servants rather than forced ones. That is why he makes free men out of slaves, so that we may offer the gifts of our will rather than the services of necessity.

The Marcionite cannot say: How I have loved your law!, for he does not accept the law. The Jew cannot say it, for he does not know the spiritual law, and meditates on the bare letter of the law, not on its sense and meaning. Only the Christian says it, who has already made great progress in knowledge of the law; who does not dread the law's penalty with a fearful heart, but searches with fearless affection into the divine mysteries of the true Hebrew, the true sabbath, the true remission. So he truly loves who keeps the precepts without sadness and without fear, with willing rather than forced zeal.

In another verse he soon showed the fruit of his long meditation, when he understood the Lord's commandment above his enemies. But what enemies does the prophet have, when he ought both to embrace the men of his own people with the love the law requires and to invite foreigners to God's grace by preaching the gospel?

Wild beasts are said to love those who share their nature; how could the prophet have refused love to one like himself? So there must be some just cause for which those he means are rightly regarded as enemies. We can find out what it is if we remember that he himself said elsewhere: And I pined away over your enemies; I hated them with a just hatred.

So, on the authority of the Gospel, he calls those his enemies who are enemies of God. For if one who does not leave his parents for God's name is not worthy of God, how much less can one who loves God's enemies be acceptable to him? Whom, then, does he have as enemies? If the Gentiles, how did he foresee by the prophetic spirit that they would believe? Indeed, in earlier verses he urged them too to bless the Lord. And what great praise is it to have understanding above those who, by worshipping metals and stones, have taken on a stupor as rigid as theirs?

Who, then, are his enemies, if not the heretics? For they are the assailants of the faith, the enemies of the truth. Who, if not the Jews? For they are the more bitter enemies, since from friends they have become enemies. He understands above them who understands that the law is spiritual. What use is the law, then, if you do not know the end of the law, if you are ignorant of the mystery, if you do not recognize the sacraments? For the Jews a lamb from the flock is slain to celebrate the Passover; for us the only-begotten of God, the Virgin's child, is sacrificed for the redemption of the world. What do the Jews gain by smearing their houses and doorposts with the blood of a lamb? Nothing at all, since wood and stones can be of no benefit to them.

For us the whole mystery is of benefit, since we believe it foreign to spiritual grace to stain our dwellings with the blood of a beast or to dye our mouths with gore. Rather, we consecrate our bodies with the sacrament of the Lord's cross, and we sanctify the words of our mouths by confessing the death of our Lord Jesus Christ; for with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.

What good is it that the Hebrews pierce a slave's ear with an awl and circumcise the foreskin of their body? They have no real understanding of what the divine law sets apart. These things are signs, not the truth. But he understands who purifies his heart by spiritual circumcision, so as to cleanse away all the filth of bodily stain. He understands who by the vigour of his mind passes beyond the awl and the ear, and raises up to the reward of everlasting freedom that soul which the sword pierced to reveal the secrets of the heart; or who, serving with care in the testing of words, sanctifies by a spiritual mystery whatever words he has received with the ear of his virtue.

The Jew is accustomed to make unleavened bread for himself every year, and he does not know that he is himself the leaven of malice. But one who understands what it means to purge out the old leaven, lest it corrupt the whole lump, purges out the old man with his deeds, so that there may be a new lump of truth. These things were said to the Jew, and the Christian heard them; for the Jew, while piercing his ear with that awl, could not hear, since he bore a wounded ear.

It was not with the awl of the law but with the awl of his own folly that he bloodied his ear. He pierced with iron the ear meant for hearing what is revealed spiritually; for he preferred to believe in iron rather than in the Word. That is why he is a slave, why he has not deserved to be free, why the grace of the completed time does not avail him: because he did not receive the fullness of time, in which the Son of God was sent for salvation and came for redemption, made under the law, born of a virgin, conqueror of death, giver of resurrection.

So the wound remains for the one for whom Christ has not risen. O wound that cannot be mended, unless perhaps he leaves the awl and takes up a sword, one he would not refuse for the name of Christ, or by which he might distinguish bodily things from spiritual, the shadow from the truth! Let him take up the word of God, the two-edged sword, and let him be taught from that divine mouth to recognize in the commandment of the Lord and the precept of the law that it does not consist in the observance of a temporal festival, but pours in saving and everlasting remedies with the sap of spiritual grace!

Meditate on the law, then, all the day long; you must not just skim through it. If you wanted to buy a field or purchase a house, you would call in someone more experienced and examine carefully what the legal position is, and you would not trust yourself, for fear you might be deceived in some point. But now it is you yourself who are to be bought for yourself. Consider your own price; consider what you are, what name you bear, what you are acquiring for yourself: not a field, not money, not necklaces of jewels,

but Christ Jesus, with whom no price, no ornament can be compared. Take as your counsellors Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Peter, Paul, John, and the great Counsellor himself, Jesus the Son of God, so that you may gain the Father. With them you must deliberate, with them you must confer about everything, on this you must meditate all day long, as David meditated, and this was his sole meditation.

His mind was not drawn away by worldly allurements; it did not burn with greed for money to heap up an estate; no anxious tide of cares about extending his boundaries and shutting out his neighbour turned aside his heart from its intent pursuit of meditation. Whatever time the day could hold, meditation on the law alone claimed all of it for itself.

But even this is too little for the diligent man who wishes to attain the grace of blessedness; for the blessed man meditates on the law day and night. The day is too short for meditation on doctrine; the day is not as long in time as meditation on the law is great.

So consider whether it may rather signify this: that for one who meditates on the law it is always day, and a light without failing, which no darkness of night interrupts. Otherwise, how could the prophet declare less diligent in the course of his work the man whom he wished to be more diligent at the very beginning of his work? The preacher of the law and the gospel, then, meditates in the day.

And perhaps those who do not accept the New Testament read by night, and that is why they did not know or understand. So the Saviour, so that we too should not read in darkness, warns us, saying that we must walk in the day, because one who walks in the day does not stumble; for he sees the grace of the light. But one who walks in darkness runs against a rock of stumbling.

The third verse follows: I have understood more than all my teachers, because your testimonies are my meditation. The scribes of the Jews profess to teach, because they were privileged to possess the law and the prophets first. But they profess to teach, yet they do not teach. It is fitting for the people drawn from the gentiles to say: I have understood more than all my teachers, because those did not understand. The Jew replies: 'Where did you get your understanding? It is written: Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will declare it to you.

I am your father; ask me.' But even if I ask you, you will not answer me, said Jesus; and from that time they cannot answer, and from that time I understand more than those who did not understand, because I have learned testimonies which he does not know. I have learned: Whoever follows me, let him take up his cross; I have learned: Love your enemies. And that is why Paul wishes to be accursed for his brothers by race, who are his enemies by faith.

Such a claim might seem unbecoming to a prophet's modesty, in that he presumed to say that he had understood more than all his teachers, when Moses received the law from the Lord and handed down its ordinances to his people, Aaron taught the priestly discipline by going through the rite of all the sacrifices, Joshua son of Nun showed how circumcision could be repeated, and Samuel

displayed the sacraments of prophetic and royal anointing alike. It would seem presumption, I say, had he not first set down what went before, by which he could prove, not without reason, that he had understood more than his teachers. He who was taught by the Lord had a right to take on this confidence; both the commandment he was taught was the Lord's, and the one who taught him was the Lord himself. Rightly did he understand more than all, since Wisdom herself taught him. Hence elsewhere too he says: Blessed is the one whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach out of your law.

He shows, then, that what is divine men cannot teach, and so those who presume to teach do not know it, but the disciple who is taught by God comes to know it. Here, besides the gift of knowledge which he had obtained from the Holy Spirit, there is also a pleasing moral point: that there are many [?] who teach, who claim to teach what they do not understand, and there are a great many disciples who by their own zeal and industry attain what they did not learn from their masters. Indeed, one writer before us said that there is a difference between teachers and doctors, perhaps thinking that doctors are those chosen for this office by the judgment of others, while teachers are those who have taken this office on themselves by their own usurpation. But even doctors must yield to the one whom the teaching of God, the Teacher, has filled through meditation on the heavenly testimonies.

I have understood more than the elders, because I have sought your precepts. Nor is it hard for one whom the Lord has taught to understand more than the elders, since by the grace of God he advances to the learning and maturity of old age. For since a spotless life is old age, the teaching of a spotless life surely confers the age of an elder. Thus when Jeremiah excused himself on the ground that he was young, the answer was: Do not say, 'I am a youth,' because by divine reckoning one was not counted a youth who had grey-haired prudence, shining with the grace of heavenly sanctification.

Yet the prophet does not seem to me to be praising himself and setting himself above the elders, since you read: Do not let the discourse of the elders pass you by; for they too learned from their fathers. And elsewhere the Wisdom of Sirach says: Where there are old men, do not speak much. But he knows which elders he sets himself above: those, of course, grown old in sin and doting in the lethargy of impiety and the senility of unbelief. These are the elders of the people who

handed over the Lord Jesus to Pilate the governor. For the priests and scribes and elders assembled, as Mark says; and again: The priests took counsel with the elders to hand him over. And that the elders of Israel assembled against the apostles, holy Peter and Luke the evangelist bear witness in their Acts. So he did not disparage old age, but, speaking in the voice of the younger people, he prophesied that that aged people of the Jews, grown old in days,

would be unteachable by God, a people who could not find in old age what it had not acquired in its youth. For the people that from the beginning provoked the Lord with repeated offences, whose grace it could not earn when it was young, did not deserve in its old age to recognize his coming, and could not hold on to his gift. The judgment of grey-haired old age is indeed fair in understanding, and the knowledge of seasoned counsel is preferred for maturity of intellect, not for length of life.

Let us therefore seek out the commandments of God, so that we may understand more than the elders; let us flee the slippery way of sins, so that we may keep the heavenly precepts; for this is what the following verses declare. Jacob, the younger brother, understood more than his elder, because when the elder, Esau, claimed for himself the prerogative of the

blessing by the privilege of his age, he left behind the gentler dishes while he went after wild game. When he had gone off to hunt, the younger brother, following his mother's counsel, took his garments and handed them on to me, the people of the nations. That robe of wisdom, then, which the people of the Jews once had, Rebecca put on me; her robe is a good one: the law and the prophets. Of this robe that people has been stripped, and we have been clothed; that mother, the Jerusalem which is above in heaven, has clothed us. So we approach the Father.

We offer him gentler dishes: the food of patience, the mildness of mercy, the sweetness of understanding. I receive the blessing; I snatch the spiritual grace from my elder brother. He comes, he is angry, he finds nothing to receive; our mother comes to meet us and instructs us with loving encouragement. That robe, woven with good commandments, remains with me.

I have kept my feet from every evil way, that I may keep your words. Truly worthy is he to have understood more than the elders, since he was honoured with the divine Spirit so as to teach the elders not only the truth of understanding but also flight from sin and caution against guilt. And so, since human frailty is prone to be carried downward by its affections and to run headlong into vice, he teaches how the slipperiness of this road and the twists of this journey cannot entangle the traveller.

I have kept my feet, he says, from the evil way, that is, from the vanity of this world, because the world lies in the evil one. Whatever is doubtful and uncertain in its outcome is 'malign'; just as an uncertain light is called a 'mean' light, so whatever mixes the darkness of malice with the truth is malign. Draw back, then, the feet of your soul and the steps of your mind from the slipperiness of this world. Restrain them, I say; resist desires, oppose the impulses that seem to rush in like beasts and cattle to graze down the tender fruits and new crops of this field of ours.

I have kept my feet, he says. He certainly did not restrain the feet of the body, which for the most part obey the will of a devout mind. For they are not to be restrained when they go to the temple of God, when they hasten to bring help to a widow, to forestall the wicked, to trip up some deceiver. There is, then, another foot which is rightly restrained. What it is, let the prophet himself teach us:

Let not the foot of pride come against me, he says. There is also the foot of iniquity, which quickly slips and cannot stand, like the foot of the faithless, of whom it is written: There the workers of iniquity have fallen; they were driven out and could not stand. Keep your feet, then, so that you do not fall; for there are feet not only of crimes but also of weakness,

and you must see that you do not fall. Perhaps you think you are standing firm, but Paul says to you: And you who stand, take heed lest you fall. Watch your way carefully, so that you may hear: But you, stand here with me. For standing with God you will have no need to fear a fall; standing with God you will be able to say: He has delivered my feet from slipping. But the Lord

delivers your feet from every slip only if he knows that you are keeping your feet from slipping. David deserved to have God deliver his feet from slipping because he himself kept his feet from sliding along the headlong and careless track of sins; and so he was also able to keep the divine words. For no one can keep them unless he has first been able to stand. But when he keeps them, the word of God itself begins to keep guard over him. He rightly says that he has kept his feet from the evil way who knows that Christ is the Way.

I have not turned aside from your judgments, because you have laid down a law for me. He has explained what it means to keep one's foot from the evil way: namely, not to turn aside from the divine judgments, and to keep a firm and unmoving footing of persevering innocence; not to deviate in one's step nor turn aside from the course of discipline, but to walk in the paths not only of the old law given on Sinai but also of the new law, according to the brightness of the gospel.

There is also the law of the gospel, of which this prophet speaks earlier: Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver over them; let the nations know that they are men. We understand that this prophesies the coming of the Lord and the calling of the gentiles, who before seemed stuck fast in the mire, as it were, of this body, clinging to the pleasure of their own corruption as to dregs and to lust, because they did not know the Lord.

And so, in anger, he says: Let sinners be turned into hell, so that they should not see the soul of the Lord Jesus descending and ascending and be converted to the Lord, they who refused to be converted while they were alive. But he is speaking of those nations that forget the Lord.

They knew, then, and they forgot. Yet with prophetic kindness he prays that the Lord may arise and that man may not prevail, so that earthly thoughts and all the seething impulses of this body may be stilled. Let the nations be judged, for the Lord is recognized when the hearts of those who fear are turned by the heavy terror of judgment; and let the nations learn that they are men, [?] dissoluble by corruption and formed of hardened clay, something which those who had not received the law did not know before.

Hence the prophet, as though he too were troubled by contemplating earthly frailty, says: Why, O Lord, have you gone far away? He does well to fear who knows that he is a man; but because he fears more for us, the sinners from among the gentiles, he prays that the Lord may not be far from his nations, so that we who were far off may begin to be nearer and may know that we are men, made, that is,

in the image and likeness of God, to whom Christ too was made conformable through the Virgin's womb. Rightly, then, the words Let the nations know that they are men are taken both of weakness and of grace: the one through a certain common, fleshly fellowship with the beasts, the other through the image of God and the sacrament of the Lord's flesh. What seemed lowliness has begun to be dignity.

Rightly, then, the people of the nations did not turn aside from God's judgments, since it can say: because you have laid down a law for me. Not through Moses, not through the prophets, but you yourself, Jesus, have laid down a law for me, that is, the gospel. That is why I have not turned aside: because I looked and came to know your paths, and by following you I came to know the true Way.

And so, hearing the preaching of the gospel which the prophetic Spirit foretold in song, he says: How sweet are your words to my throat, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth! And rightly 'sweet', for in them are proclaimed the forgiveness of sins, everlasting life, and even the resurrection of the dead, which have tempered the bitterness of perpetual and cruel death. Through these we have begun not to fear death, we who have begun to say: O death, where is your victory? And rightly 'sweet to the throat', because spiritual grace is poured into our inmost being.

More than honey and the honeycomb, he says, sweet to my mouth. And so, because your words have become sweet to us, you say to the Church: Your lips drip honeycomb, my bride. Teach us, Solomon, what that honeycomb is; for you said: Good words are honeycombs. And truly good is the honeycomb which the Church eats, fragrant with the honey gathered by many prophets, like bees, out of their spiritual abundance. This is the honey of which he says: I have eaten my bread with my honey, I have drunk my wine with my milk.

The mystical discourse of the heavenly Scriptures is like bread, which strengthens the heart of man as the stronger food of the word; but persuasive moral discourse is sweet and softer, because moral preaching soothes the inner parts of the mind, and hearts made bitter by fevers, that is, by penitence for sins, grow sweet through gentle speech. The lips of the preacher drip honey when the limbs of a soul bruised by hard falls or ruined by a lapse are revived.

There is also a more fervent force of the word, like wine, and there is a clearer discourse in the form of milk. Eat, my neighbours, he says, and drink and be inebriated. Good is the inebriation which produces a kind of ecstasy of mind toward better and joyful things, so that our soul, forgetful of its cares, is gladdened by the wine of joy.

Good is the inebriation of the spiritual table; indeed, how splendid is the inebriating cup! And elsewhere you have: Inebriate its streams, multiply its offspring, because the inebriation of the earth, when it has been drenched with heavenly rain, usually awakens the seeds and multiplies the fruits.

So the word of God, which comes down from heaven like rain, when it has inebriated the veins of our earth, that is, of our soul and mind, with divine preaching, has stirred up zeal for the various virtues and made the fruits of faith and chaste devotion grow. And rightly it is said to him: You have visited the earth and inebriated it. For by taking a body he visited it, to heal the sick; he inebriated it with spiritual grace, to soothe the anxious with joy.

Rightly, then, it is said to the bride: Your lips drip honeycomb, my bride; honey and milk are under your tongue. For the mouth of the just distils wisdom; from the mouth of the just come forth the honeys of sweetness and mercy; in the mouth of the just there is no guile, no deceit, no

bitterness of sin. The Church hears the words of the just man, the people of God hear the precepts of the wise man; they delight in the sweetness of his speech, they are soothed by the pleasantness of his moral discourse, saying: How sweet are your words to my throat, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth! For the honey of bees delights for an hour, but its taste soon vanishes,

and often it harms a diseased stomach; but the honey of moral words, even if it stings, does no harm. Yet consider to whom these things are to be entrusted, for it is written: Say nothing in the ear of a fool, lest he mock your wise words. For the fool, who cannot perceive its sweetness, will vomit up and reject your word.

The eighth verse follows: From your commandments I have gained understanding; therefore I have hated every way of iniquity. In keeping with this verse is: If you desire wisdom, keep the commandments; but no one can keep them except one who understands. Indeed, all the words of the law are recited daily by

certain elders of the Jews, and none of them can keep the commandment. For I would not say that a tree keeps the fruitfulness of its nature if it runs riot in leaves and comes to nothing in fruit; nor would I say that land keeps its fruits which, because it feeds the bracken hateful to farmers, does not usually yield grain; nor does a shepherd seem to keep his flock if he does not know how to choose wholesome pasture, to beware of wolves, to fence his folds with dogs, and if he does not know how to provide water when it is needed.

For merely to lead out dumb cattle without any care is just the same as the Jewish people's reading of the Scriptures. Where the pastures of the spiritual sacrament lie, where the letter kills, where the wolves of the mind attack, where the rest of refreshment is, where the hope of resurrection is, which are the dogs that can bark to guard the flock: of all this the people, more dumb than the flock itself, are ignorant.

So if he says, 'I keep the commandments,' the answer to him is: But you have hated discipline and cast my words behind you. If you saw a thief, you ran along with him, and you threw in your lot with adulterers. Your mouth abounded in wickedness and your tongue framed deceits; you sat and spoke against your brother. This is not keeping the commandments but transgressing them; to do the opposite of what is laid down is not understanding but ignorance.

How can the words of God be sweet in your throat, when the bitterness of wickedness is there? How can honey and milk be under your tongue, when you frame deceit with your tongue, conceiving one thing in your heart and putting forward another in public speech so as to deceive the unwary? For the apostle Peter tells you to lay aside all malice and cast off the disguise of pretence, saying: Like newborn infants, long for the rational milk that is without guile.

For he shows us what it is to have honey and milk under the tongue: that we should know not to curse those who curse us but to return a blessing, and that we should know how to hate nothing but the way of iniquity, so that with resisting affection we guard against doing what we abhor. That is why Paul guarded against the evil in his flesh, because he hated it; that is why John warns in his epistle that we should not love the world, because everything in the world is the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes and the pride of life.

It lies with us, then, both to hate something rightly and to love something rightly. For just as we can rightly love the servants of God and rightly love our enemies, according to the word of the Lord, so we can rightly hate the enemies of God: hate iniquity, hate faithlessness, hate shameful deeds, hate the vanities of this world. Therefore the things of the world ought to be

hated, so that the allurement of pleasure, that coaxing go-between, may not creep into careless and idle affections. The beauty of a wanton harlot easily captures the eyes, unless a just hatred restrains them and an affection indignant at impurity turns them away. Boasting of noble birth and an abundance of worldly goods often puff people up and tip them backwards in swollen disdain, unless you are ashamed to be praised for what belongs to others rather than for what is your own. Christ, though he was rich, became poor; it was in a poor man, not a rich one, that he redeemed you. He ordered those who confessed him as the Son of God to be silent, so that God might be recognized by works rather than by words;

and do you call yourself noble, you who were made from earth? King David says: Remember, Lord, that we are dust; and do you glory in this perishable and muddy stock, and think yourself rich, when tomorrow you may be a beggar, since your life lies not in your abundance but in the mercy of God? To him be honour, glory, praise and everlastingness from ages past, and now and always, and for all ages of ages. Amen.
XIV. THE LETTER NUN

Nun is the fourteenth Hebrew letter; it is interpreted 'only one', or in another interpretation 'their pasture'. See how the very letters of the Hebrews testify that the Lord Jesus is the only Son of the Father, the Word of God. Indeed, right in the first verse David speaks of the only Son of God: Your word, Lord, is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths. From this we understand that this psalm was arranged according to the Hebrew letters so that our inner man, formed like a little child from infancy by the elements of letters to which childhood is accustomed, might grow up to the maturity of virtue. Each letter is like a title of the verses written under it, declaring their sequence and content; so here the letter signifies 'only one', and this portion of the psalm prophesies about the only-begotten Son of God and the brightness of his eternal light.

Nor indeed is the other interpretation of this letter, found in another manuscript, at odds with this one. For what are our pastures, that is, the pastures of the faithful, but Christ? The prophet rejoiced to be placed in his pastures, saying: In a place of pasture, there he has placed me; for he feeds us and refreshes us. The divine sacraments are good pastures.

There you pluck the new flower which gave forth the sweet fragrance of the resurrection; you pluck the lily, that is, the splendour of eternity; you pluck the rose, that is, the blood of the Lord's body. Good pastures too are the words of the heavenly Scriptures, on which we feed in daily reading, by which we are restored and refreshed when we taste what is written, or when, having sipped it with the tip of the mouth, we chew it over again and again. On these pastures the Lord's flock is fattened.

Good too are the pastures of Christ, who feeds among the lilies, in the splendour of the saints; good pastures also are the mountains of the valleys, for Christ feeds on these too, like a roe or a young hart. The mountains of the valleys are like the lights of this world, shining with diligent humility, who excel on the summit of various virtues and

rise above the world by their merits. These are the ones of whom it is said: They are not of this world, just as I am not of this world; for those who follow Christ are above the world. The valley, however, is the world, and so he set ascents in the valley of weeping, because in this world there is weeping and there are tears. And the Lord in his providence set his covenant in this world, so that we might weep for our sins here rather than keep them to be wept over later.

These little verses which we are to treat today are also our pastures, in which David says: I was feeding my father's sheep—showing the true lamp, learning humility. In such pastures the true David, truly humble and strong of hand, who did not consider it robbery to be equal with God but emptied himself and, born as man through the virgin's childbearing, humbled himself even to death, fed his Father's sheep with divine preaching, when he proved his coming from the Scriptures, when he filled many thousands of people with five loaves and two fish.

These, then, are our pastures, the pastures of those who can say: How sweet are your words to my throat! These are the pastures of those who say: Your word, Lord, is a lamp to my feet. For our mouth is fed by the word when we speak the commandments of God the Word. Our inner eye too is fed by the light of the spiritual lamp which shines before us in the night of this world,

so that we do not stumble with uncertain steps like those walking in darkness, unable to find the true way. The steps of the feet, then, are to be understood spiritually, and so is the lamp, because the word of God is a lamp. But was not this Word in the beginning with God? How then is it a lamp? Was not this the true light which enlightens every man coming into this world? How then is it called a lamp? Isaiah cries: The people who sat in darkness have seen a great light; how is it that he says 'lamp' here?

But let us see whether perhaps the same Word of God is a great light to some and a lamp to others. To me it is a lamp, to the angels it is light. It was light to Peter when the angel stood beside him in prison and a light shone upon him. It was light to Paul when, as he was going to persecute the Christian people, a light from heaven shone around him and he heard someone saying to him: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? And a great light it was; indeed, the light of Paul's own lamp vanished when the splendour of the divine light flashed out.

And truly Christ is a lamp to me when he is spoken of by this mouth of ours. That treasure which we have in earthen vessels shines in mud, gleams in a vessel of clay. Pour in oil, so that it does not run short for you, for oil is the light of a lamp—not earthly oil, but that oil of heavenly mercy and grace with which the prophets were anointed.

Your oil is humility, by which the hardness of our necks is softened. Your oil is your mercy, by which even bodies dashed against the rocks of sin are soothed. This is the oil that the Samaritan in the gospel poured on the man wounded by robbers as he went down from Jerusalem: seeing him, he was moved with mercy and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. This oil heals the sick—for mercy frees from sin; this oil shines in the darkness if our works shine before

men; this oil shines at the solemn feasts of the Church. Indeed, those who did not lack oil did not lack the light of faith either, but were found worthy to enter the wedding hall with their lamps; but those who did not carry oil in their vessels, that is, did not have faith, nor

prudence, nor mercy while their soul dwelt in this body, were rightly shut out for their faithlessness. So you too should always keep a lamp burning or a torch shining. For if neither your lamp nor your torch shines, you will be called a foolish virgin and will not enter the bridal chamber of your Bridegroom on high, but will remain in the darkness of blindness, like one who hates the light so that his shameful works may not be exposed; for everyone who does evil hates the light. Have faith, have prudence, so that you may always have in your vessels the oil of mercy, the grace of

devotion; for the wise took oil in their vessels together with their lamps. Anoint your lamps, O men; when you fast, anoint your head. Let us pour oil into our minds, so that our body may be full of light. Let the word of God always shine for you as a lamp, and let your eye, the lamp of your body, shine too. Your conscience, shining well in this body, is the light of the lamp; it is your eye.

Let your eye be pure. If your conscience is clean, your flesh is clean; but if your conscience within you is dark, your body too is darkened by the night of your conscience. We too, then, are lamps, covered over by the whole body, having scarcely some small opening through which we can shine.

John too was a lamp, as the Lord said of him: He was a burning and shining lamp. A good lamp, which received light from Christ so that it could shine in this world: rightly burning, rightly shining, because he was the herald of Christ, enlightening the hearts of each one by the preaching of faith. But he also granted to those lamps that they should be the light of the world, saying to the apostles: You are the light of the world. So if the glory of the saints shone in this world now like a lamp, now like the light of the world, what shall we say of the Word of God, which is also a lamp to my feet?

And perhaps where there is no darkness, the Word of God is not a lamp but something more than a lamp, because it is light. There is no darkness for those who see the light; and then the just will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. And perhaps according to the law the Word of God is a lamp, according to the gospel a great light.

To the Jews it is a lamp, and a lamp under a bushel. The law shines, but it is not seen, because their teaching is covered over both by the contagion of vices and by the blindness of unbelief; but to the people from the nations it is light. Indeed, for the people who sat in the region of the shadow of death a light has risen. Open your windows, then, so that the splendour of the great light may come in to you. Make your lampstand ready and secure, so that your light is not covered by the covering of your body and the measure of this earthly frailty, but that you may shine forth by the strength of your soul above the measure of bodily weakness.

Or if you are held to a measure, see that the measures themselves do not overflow [?]—that they do not overflow, but are content with good seeds. Let your speech not be idle; let your word not take holiday and stand empty, lest it become a lamp under a bushel.
