God is able to set your lamp upon a lampstand, so that it gives light to all who are in the house, and those who come in may see the light. Our lampstand is our ruling faculty.

Place your speech in your ruling faculty, and it gives light to all who come into the church. Take another lampstand as well. Consider your mouth, and consider your speech too. Is not your mouth a lampstand, and your word a lamp, when it is brought forth from your mouth? May this lamp always shine for you, that is, may your word shine and never be put out.

Do you ask me to teach you how it may never be put out? It is written: The light of the just is always unquenchable, but the light of the wicked will be put out. This light was the lamp that shone in the tabernacle of testimony, and the lamp that shines today in the Church is the wise man. He is the eye of the Church, which does not say to the hands, that is, to those who work but are not sharp in understanding:

I have no need of you. So he was shining on the lampstand who said: But our citizenship is in heaven. For David too was already dwelling in heaven with his whole mind, and yet he still said: Your word is a lamp to my feet. Or perhaps, like a good teacher, he wished to go before me, so that I might learn to follow the light and walk in his footsteps.

[?] So he shows me, set as I am in the darkness of this ignorance, of this bodily covering, how to learn to follow the lamp, so that in following Christ I may not run against any stone of stumbling. Peter was wandering in the darkness of ignorance; he denied that Christ was to die, because he did not yet see that he was to die and rise again for us. Turning to

him, the Lord said: Get behind me. He showed him the lamp he ought to follow when he said 'behind me'. He was strengthened according to the word of God; afterwards he began to cling to Christ, fearing that he might again slip into some error. Did not he too, like the one who said: Your word is a lamp to my feet, hasten towards this lamp when he said on the sea: Lord, bid me come to you over the water? But because he was not following the lamp, he was shaken and staggered, thrown into confusion by the mass of a more violent nature.

Let us then follow this lamp as a lamp, and let us walk towards the light as though in the night. Many pits, many rocks go unseen in the gloom of this world. Hold before you the lamp which the prophet pointed out; see where you ought to move your step; look where to set the foot of your inner mind.

Take care over every single step; entrust your advance to nothing except the light of this lamp going before you. Where you think something shines, there is a whirlpool: it seems to shine, but it defiles; and where you think the ground is solid or dry, there it is slippery, if the lamp is too far from you. Let faith go before you on your journey; let divine Scripture be your road; the guidance of the heavenly word is good. From this lamp light your own lamp too, so that your inner eye, which is the lamp of your body, may shine.

You have many lamps; light them all, for it has been said to you: Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning. Because the darkness is great, many lamps are needed, so that the light of our merits may shine out in such great darkness. These are the lamps which the law signified ought always to shine in the tabernacle of testimony—not those which the Jews light every day. Those shine in shadow and go out every day, because they do not see what they do and do not understand what they read, taking according to the letter what is commanded according to the spirit.

For the tabernacle of testimony is this body of ours, into which Christ came through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, as it is written, in order to enter the holy place through his own blood and cleanse our conscience from every dead work and every stain, so that in our bodies—which by the testimony and character of their deeds bear witness to the hidden and secret things of our thoughts—the clear light of our virtues may shine like

lamps. These are the burning lamps which shine day and night in the temple of God. If you keep the temple of God in your body, if your members are members of Christ, your virtues shine, and no one puts them out unless your own sin puts them out. With this light of a chaste mind and pious devotion let the feasts of our solemnity shine.

Let your lamp, then, always shine. Christ rebukes even those who use a lamp, if they do not use it always, saying: Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning. Let us not rejoice in the light only for an hour. He rejoices for an hour who hears the word

in church and is glad, but on going out forgets what he heard or neglects it. This is the one who walks about his house without a lamp and so walks in darkness, who does the works of darkness in revelling and drunkenness, in debauchery and licentiousness, in strife and jealousy, clothed in the garments of the devil, not in Christ. These things happen when the lamp of the word does not shine. Let us never neglect, then,

the word of the Lord, from which comes for us the origin of all virtues and a kind of progression of all our works. If the members of our body cannot work rightly without light—for the feet stagger and the hands go astray without light—how much more must the steps of our soul, the movements of the mind, be directed by the light of the word! The soul too has hands that touch well, as Thomas touched the signs of the Lord's resurrection, if the light of the present word shines for us. Let this lamp be lit in every word and every work; let our step, outward and inward, move by this lamp.

But let us go on to the rest, and let the word of God become a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths. For the feet a lamp is enough for walking; for the paths it is not enough to light them up. Yet the same Word is both a lamp to the feet and a light to the paths, because the same only-begotten Son of God is both advocate for those who sin and rewarder of the strong, forgiver of sins and bestower of prizes.

So for one to whom the word of God has been a lamp, the paths shine wherever he goes, as they shone for holy David; and therefore, as one walking in the light, he says: I have sworn and set myself firm to keep the judgments of your justice. [I have been humbled exceedingly.] It is the voice of one walking in the light to say with authority: I have sworn and set myself firm.

For one who has set himself firm is not moved and does not fear falling, because to set oneself firm is more than to stand. David therefore stands, grounded in the steadfastness of his mind, and does not fear that he might go astray in the darkness of this world. For if he were afraid, he would not swear; if he were anxious whether he could keep the divine judgments, he would not make it fast by the solemn bond of an oath. No one swears well except one who can know what he is swearing.

To swear, then, is a sign of knowledge, a testimony of conscience. And he swears well who directs his feet by the lamp of the word, who sees the light on his paths. Let the light go before, if you intend to swear; that is, let knowledge of the truth come first, so that the bond of the oath cannot harm you. Where religion is holier, there the faithfulness of truth is fuller.

That is why the Lord, who came to teach the little ones, to instruct the new and to strengthen the perfect, says in the gospel: Do not swear at all; for he was speaking to the weak. Indeed, he was not speaking to the apostles alone but to the crowds—for he wished you not to swear, so that you would not swear falsely—and he added: not to swear either by heaven or by earth or by Jerusalem or by your head, that is, by these things which are not subject to your power.

The Lord has sworn and will not repent. Let him swear, then, who cannot come to regret his oath. And what did God swear? That Christ is a priest forever. Was what God swore uncertain? Was it impossible? Could it be changeable? So do not appropriate the example of an oath if you do not have the power to fulfil the oath.

What, then, did David swear? To keep the judgments of the Lord's justice. Clearly the judgments of divine justice no longer troubled in any respect one who was already perfect, already instructed. How many are troubled when they see some just man bereaved of his children and brought by repeated losses to the extremity of utter want, so that he cannot have even the support

of food, broken by grave illness and afflicted with lasting infirmity, so that he cannot perform the ordinary functions of nature! But the one who is firm is not troubled, and he understands all the more that God's justice must be proclaimed, because the Lord chastens whom he loves. Is not a son chastened more often than a slave? Is a father's affection, then, more unjust than a master's severity? A father trains his son with harsher things than a master his house-slave, but the hard lashes a father deals out are not held against him, because he wants his son to be better than the slave. Discipline, then, is full of justice.

Holy Job was bereaved of his children, over whom the Lord gave the devil power. Is God unjust? Far from it; on the contrary, he is just, for he meant to prove his just man by exercises of this kind; and in them, by proving his patience, he made him more worthy for having been proved. For the more glorious the merit of the one crowned, the richer the justice of the one who crowns. He was stripped of his possessions,

though he had been rich, and he underwent these losses too with God's permission. These were no longer losses of money but of life, since with everything taken from him he lacked food. Who would accuse God's justice, when, had Job not lost all his money, he would not have found such great grace? God wished to anoint his athlete, stripped bare, with the oil of patience, so as both to make him stronger for the contest by enduring it and more worthy of the prize by earning it.

Pierced over his whole body with a grievous ulcer, he sat on the dung heap, scraping off the pus that flowed from the cruel weals of his wounds; and this the devil had inflicted on the just man by the Lord's permission. The devil would have seemed to have won for himself, had he not himself been overcome after receiving the power he had demanded. What, then, was that temptation, the loss of his property, the loss of his children, the endurance of his wounds, but an exercise of faith, a mark of patience, a glorious schooling in virtue, a confession full of victory, so that he who before had the devil as his adversary should afterwards have him no longer?

Let no one, then, think that what is just is hard. These things did not seem hard to him who could say: Naked I was born, naked I shall depart; the Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord. For the just man blesses the Lord when he is in hardship, the sinner when he lives in luxury.

Is it not, then, because of our weakness that the commandments of righteousness have seemed hard, since we think hard whatever we cannot bear through feebleness of spirit? Take away persecutions, and there are no martyrs. But God also allowed persecutors, that is, the powers of this world, to rise up, so that there would be no lack of those who would conquer for Christ. Who in his weakness did not say at that time: 'Lord, why have you given your people into the power of their persecutors?' But who today would deny that those who suffered are more blessed than those whom no tortures of the persecutors afflicted?

So the righteous man desires to be tested. He is not afraid of being tried, for one who has resolved to keep the judgments of God is not afraid of temptations. Where has he resolved this, if not in the heart? For that is where we ought to be rooted and grounded, not tossed about or carried here and there by every wind of doctrine. Let us then resolve inwardly, in our heart, in our breast, in our mind, so that the prophetic saying may come true for us:

'The thoughts of the righteous are paths.' In these paths the righteous man [?] walks; that is why he says: 'Prove me, O Lord, and try me.' Accordingly, in this passage, answering to his own pledge (for he had sworn and resolved to keep the judgments of God's righteousness), he says that he wished to be proved, since he believed that humiliation must be undergone for Christ.

And so he says: 'I am humbled exceedingly.' He rejoices that he has been humbled, and not only humbled but exceedingly humbled. Blessed is he who glories in humility rather than in power. Power deceives; humility does not forsake. Humility is good, for even in Christ it found the praise due to virtue. This I revere in him more than creation, because we were created for toil but redeemed for rest.

Indeed, when he calls the peoples to his mercy, he himself glories in his own humility, saying: 'I was made manifest to those who did not seek me; I appeared to those who did not ask for me'; and elsewhere: 'I gave my back to the scourges and my cheeks to blows, and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting.' Rightly, then, did David wish to humble himself, so that he might fill up in himself what was lacking of the afflictions of Christ.

Christ himself, too, speaking in his own person through the mouth of David, may have said 'I am humbled exceedingly', he who said in the Gospel: 'Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and

lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.' Let us learn, then, from him who wished to teach us what would profit us for salvation, and who says to us: 'Learn from me.' It is no small thing that he says 'learn', and adds 'learn from me'. One who is puffed up cannot easily teach humility, even though the mind of the flesh may exalt human wisdom. The man who is content with poverty is not content with injury; the man who can bear the pain of blows is stirred up by insulting words; the man who can despise public office grieves that someone has been preferred to him in honor. It is a great thing to keep the measure of humility in all things.

It was pride that first cast man down. While we want more, we usually lose even the less we have. Humility is good: by seeking nothing, it gains all that it despises. The Lord Jesus himself humbled himself in order to raise us up, and humbled himself even to the cross. 'Therefore God has exalted

him,' it says, 'that at his name every knee should bow.' I dare to say: how great were the things the Lord did, and yet I did not bow the knee to him? But I bowed to him after he humbled himself; for in this way, that is, through humility, through the cross, he gathered the Church to himself.

David was a king, and he testifies that the uncertain and hidden things of wisdom were revealed to him; yet for that very reason he humbled himself all the more. Hezekiah, on the other hand, fell from the loftiness of his heart. That praiseworthy king, who was delivered from siege and from sickness by the Lord's kindnesses and wonders, fell through pride and diminished the grace of his earlier merit. What would Joseph have been had he not been humble? He knew that being preferred to his brothers had done him harm; even a father's loving affection had brought on the misery of preference.

Preference armed his brothers; humility won over strangers. Preference stirred up his own kin; humility made a king subject to him. So we may think that what David himself said above, 'I was humbled, and he saved me', was truly spoken as if in the person of Joseph; and yet, if we consider what David endured, we shall find that he said it in his own person.

When Goliath had been overcome, young women came out to meet him singing: 'Saul among thousands, David among ten thousands.' The king's bile was stirred, and he sought to kill him. And David humbled himself before Jonathan, the king's son, and won his affection, so that the one who might have regarded him with suspicion as a rival for succession to his father's kingdom protected him against his father's designs, saying to his father: 'Why do you sin against innocent blood?'

and wrung from his unwilling father the admission that David did not deserve to be killed. Rightly, then, he says: 'I was humbled, and he saved me.' And again, when the prophet had come to him and announced the Lord's indignation in the matter of Bathsheba, he humbled himself and said: 'I have sinned against the Lord.' And Nathan said to him: 'Because you have repented, the Lord has taken away your sin; you shall not die.' Humility, then, is good. In short, he was humbled and was

saved. And in another place, when the Lord was offended because the people had been numbered and had sent the prophet Gad to say to King David, 'Choose what you wish to happen: three years of famine upon the land, or three months of fleeing before your enemies while they pursue you, or three days of death in the land,' David answered: 'These three put me in a strait; but let me rather fall into the hand of the Lord, for very great is his

mercy, than fall into the hands of men.' And when the Lord had sent death upon Israel from morning until the hour of the midday meal, and seventy thousand men had died, David looked to the Lord, and when he saw the angel striking the people, he said: 'Behold, it is I who have sinned, and I the shepherd who have done wrong; and these in the flock, what have they done? Let your hand be upon me and upon my father's house.' And the Lord was appeased when a sacrifice of reconciliation had been offered to him. Humility, then, is good: it saved both king and people. So when the Lord had been reconciled, David says: 'It is good for me that I have been humbled.'

Humility, then, is good, especially if willing devotion is joined to it. And so he asks to be given life according to the word, that he may live according to the word and do all things with reason, not according to the will of the flesh. Hence that mystical passage can also be taken in a moral sense: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.' And you, be an imitator of God.

How an imitator? Can you make heaven or earth or sea? Certainly not. But you can do all things through the word and nothing without the word, all things with reason and nothing without reason, because you are not irrational, O man, but rational.

The fourth verse follows: 'Approve the freewill offerings of my mouth, O Lord, and teach me your judgments.' He who humbles himself is given life according to God's promise, and he who is given life by the Spirit of God is a willing minister. For it makes a great difference whether you do what pleases God willingly or out of necessity. Indeed, the willing minister has a reward, while the one who is compelled merely discharges a duty, as we have learned from the Apostle's teaching.

For he wrote: 'Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel. For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me.' See here a willing executor of the heavenly will. He was free from all, and became the servant of all (by his will, of course, not by necessity) that he might win as many as possible. To those too who were held by the bond of the law he showed himself as if

under the law, though he was not under the law, that he might save those who lived under the law. To the weak he became weak, that by taking weakness upon himself he might support the weak; he became all things to all, not by the necessity of law but by the obedience of his will. He has revealed to me the depth of this design in the letter he wrote to Philemon, because he wanted another to be what he himself was, so that Philemon might be seen to have made his offering to the Lord by will rather than by necessity.

So, interceding for Onesimus, he says: 'Receive him as my own heart. I wanted to keep him with me, so that he might serve me on your behalf in my chains for the gospel; but I wished to do nothing without your consent, so that your good deed might not be as if from necessity, but voluntary.' What a careful persuader! Though he was a vessel of divine election, he did not

disdain to share his counsel with another, so as not to cheat the other of the fruit of his own will! Rightly, then, David says as a prophet: 'Approve the freewill offerings of my mouth, O Lord', offering to the Lord the voluntary sacrifice of his mouth, because, like that prophetic bee, he was accustomed to gather good flowers with his mouth, to shape honeycombs with his mouth, to make honey with his mouth, and to gather offspring from sweet herbs with his mouth: the bee which, as Scripture says, though weak in strength, prolongs the span of its life by proclaiming wisdom. Recognize what this voluntary sacrifice of the mouth is: 'Offer to God a sacrifice of praise.'

The Lord waits for willing ministers. Indeed, in the book of Isaiah the Lord says: 'Whom shall I send?' He could certainly have commanded his servant, whom he had found worthy to be sent, but he wished not to cheat him of the reward of a spontaneous offering, and he waited for him to offer himself.

And though he knew his disposition, he still waited for his voice, so as to heap up grace. So Isaiah, offering himself, says: 'Here I am; send me', and so afterward he was sent to the people. That is why it was said of him: 'Isaiah dares and says.' For Christ filled him, as a willing instrument, with a richer grace of his Spirit.

Nor do I think it was set down idly that he desires the freewill offerings of his mouth to please the Lord. There are many prophets, but not in all of them do the freewill offerings of the mouth please. Jeremiah excused himself, saying: 'You who are Lord and Master, behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am too young'; and the Lord said to him: 'Wherever I send you, you shall go, and according to all that I command you, you shall speak.'

Out of modesty the prophet pleaded the age of his body, for fear that his youth would prove unequal to carrying out the heavenly commands. But God, who judged that age should be reckoned by character rather than by years, and who foresaw in his servant's youthful body the maturity of robust wisdom, said: 'Do not say, I am too young'; that is, he forbade him to weigh his strength by regard to his youth, since faith would supply him with the gray hairs of wisdom.

And again, later on, when the same prophet had said, 'You deceived me, O Lord, and I was deceived; and I said, I will not name his name, nor speak any more in his name,' he added: 'and it became in my heart like a burning fire flaming in my bones, and I was undone on every side and cannot bear it.' We observe, then, that even with those who thought they should excuse themselves or decline their office for some definite reason, our Lord nevertheless either persuades them by reason or inspires in them a longing for prophetic revelation, so that they may take up their office willingly rather than yield to it out of necessity, and so the reward of wholehearted devotion may come to them more fully. Caiaphas also prophesied 'that it is expedient for one man to die for the people'; but this was not a voluntary ministry of the mouth, because he spoke unwillingly. In fact, he did not know what he was saying.

What freewill offerings of his mouth, then, does David desire to be pleasing to the Lord? 'I have chosen to be cast down in the house of the Lord rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.' 'I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me.' 'I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter propositions from the beginning of the world.' 'I have prepared a lamp for my anointed.' His own body, which was formerly muddy and clogged with the filth

of inherited defilement, so that it could not receive spiritual oil, he prepared for Christ, that it might shine. He shines for Christ whose works shine in the light of Christ. Peter shone for Christ when he said: 'In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise and walk.' He shone for Christ who said: 'The Lord Jesus heals you.' The lamp of the martyrs, who underwent martyrdom for Christ, shone for Christ. David shone for Christ, since he could say: 'My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God.'

He had prepared his mind for Christ when he said of the man who had often sought his death: 'The Lord forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, and lay my hand on the Lord's anointed.' Though he had the stronger case for protecting his own life by killing his persecutor, he even restrained others, who urged him not to spare the enemy whom the Lord, according to his promise, had delivered into his hands, from their eagerness to kill him. The prophet shone for Christ when, concerning the one

who had stained his father's house with shameful incest and who sought his father's life in parricidal battles, he nevertheless said, as a loving father, to those setting out for battle: 'Spare my son Absalom.' He kept silent about the crime of wickedness and put forward instead the bond of affection and the name of kinship, so that those about to fight, thinking of him not as the king's adversary but as his son, might hold back their resentment at the wrong done to a father's love.

And after his death he covered his face and cried out with a loud voice, saying: 'My son Absalom, my son!' The parricide did not deserve this cry, but it prophesied the grace of Christ. The prophet had learned from Christ to be a good father, since he was serving the good of the Son.

That is why he said: 'And teach me your judgments', because the judgments of God are like a great deep, and unsearchable, as the Apostle says. So he could not come to know them unless Christ taught him, because Christ is the one teacher of all. And these are the judgments of Christ: that we should understand that we must not repay injury in kind to those who have plotted against us, but should rather return kindness for injury.

Indeed, when he was cursed he did not curse back, and when he was struck he did not strike back; still more, when he was crucified, he offered his persecutors the help of loving intercession with the Father, saying: 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.' Whoever, then, carries out these judgments of the law is rewarded by Christ.

But who can be taught the judgments of God except one who has always directed his soul toward the Lord, who can say: 'My soul is in your hands always, and I have not forgotten your law'? Some have: 'My soul is in my hands always', that is, 'in my actions', that is, 'in my works'.

For although he is beset by dangers, the righteous man says to the Lord: 'For your sake I die daily, daily I am in danger. I am in danger from the one who lies in wait, in danger from the slanderer, in danger from those whom I rebuke and refute; I am in danger for the sake of truth and righteousness. Yet I have not been frightened by dangers into forgetting your law. Therefore my soul is in my hands.' But since most have 'My soul is in your hands always', I think this should be explained at greater length.

The prophet knows, he knows where to place the protection of his soul and where to hope for help. He wishes to set his soul in the hands of God, because the heart of the king is in the hand of God. Whoever has subdued his own body and, as ruler of himself, has with fitting vigor not allowed his soul to be disturbed by its passions, restrains himself well with a kind of royal power and is called a king, because he knows how to rule himself and is master of his own affairs, so that he is not dragged captive into guilt nor carried headlong into vice. His soul does not perish forever, nor does anyone snatch it from the hand of the almighty Father or of the Son. For the hands of God, which made the heavens firm, do not lose those whom they have held.

Let us consider, then, what these hands are. In the Song of Songs you have: 'His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.' The bride says this of Christ, the soul of the Word of God; and Christ is himself the Word and the Wisdom of God. Blessed, then, is the soul that Wisdom embraces. Great is the hand of Wisdom, great the right hand that embraces the whole soul. For the soul betrothed to the Word of God is fortified on every side; for the fullness of wisdom is to fear God. So the soul that fears God fortifies itself with full protection. Wisdom puts her left hand under its neck and her right hand around it in an embrace. Both her arms are indeed stretched out for useful ends; yet each hand of Wisdom has its own properties: 'In her right hand is length of life, in her left riches and glory.' Both hands are surely endowed with good gifts, yet their gifts differ in this, that they embrace present and future times: the left rewards in the present, the right in the future.

We can learn this also from the prophecy of the holy patriarch Israel. For when he had placed his right hand on Ephraim and his left on Manasseh, and Joseph, considering their ages, wanted to switch them so as to place his father's right hand on the head of Manasseh, the elder son, he refused and said: 'I know, my son; this one too shall become a people, and this one shall be exalted; but his younger brother shall be greater than he.' Greater in what? Surely in this, that he was preferred in the blessing, as their descendants, that is, Ephraim's, say: 'May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.'

Or else because his seed is the multitude of the Gentiles, which has chosen toil in this world, believing in the Lord Jesus, so as to have the consolation of the things to come. The seed of Manasseh, on the other hand, is the people of forgetfulness, which, having forgotten its own Author, is exalted for a time in this world but will hereafter pay heavy penalties because it denied its God and Lord.

We have said this to prove that the things to come are better. Indeed, Wisdom's left hand is under the bride's head, but her right hand is above, embracing the whole bride. So the left is like a support for present rest, on which the soul leans and rests. It has a place to lay its head, because Wisdom's left hand is riches and glory.

These soothe us for a time and give partial comfort. And that is why the Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head: though he was rich, he became poor and sought no glory of this world, since he had come to help not a portion but the whole human race, saying: 'Are you angry with me because I made a whole man well on the Sabbath?' 'Whole', that is, not by enriching him with a gift of possessions, nor by heaping upon him the insignia of honors or an increase of worldly glory (for these do not have the fullness of blessedness and grace), but 'whole', that is, so that he might take hold of the length of eternal life. For the life in Wisdom's right hand is not like ordinary life; it is length of life, so that whoever receives life from Wisdom gains not a meager span of life but perpetuity and the length of eternity.

Eternity of life is a good garment. This is the cloak, the one of which the first man had been stripped, that the watchmen of the walls tried to take away from the bride; but the soul devoted to God, by holding fast the beloved she had long sought and not letting him go, clothed herself in the precious wrap of divine love. Blessed, then, are those who are clothed with such a cloak and have earned a garment of this kind by keeping the law,

because they have not forgotten the law but have done what the law requires; for whoever acts outside the law has forgotten the law. And therefore this soul ascends white from the earth, because it shines clothed in the garment of wisdom, and those powers who guard the gates of heaven say of it: 'Who is this who comes up white, leaning upon her brother?' For she has laid her head on Wisdom's left hand: she has opened her hands to the poor and has used riches that she acquired or that were left to her, not seized or plundered, to help the needy; desirous of glory, she has gained it by good works and has not canvassed for worldly honors with empty boasting. For this is to set one's head, and what is, as it were,

the ruling center of the senses, upon the hand of Wisdom. That soul, I say, ascends with shining merits from this desert of the present life (as most texts have it) to that ever-flowering place of eternal delight. These are the powers who also say in the book of Isaiah: 'Who is this who comes from Edom, the redness of his garments from Bozrah, so beautiful in his robe?' These, I say, are the ones who marvel that any soul could ascend from this rough and rocky desert without the stain of great vices, and therefore they rejoice to find one that has not polluted the garments of natural innocence with the black ink of worldly folly, but has made them clean with the brightness of spiritual grace.

So that soul, now secure, now glad, says: 'Sinners have laid a snare for me, yet I have not strayed from your commandments.' These are words fit for one leaving this world, since it has escaped the nets of persecutors and the snares of those lying in wait. They are words fit for martyrs, to whom many tortures were held out and many rewards also offered,

so that they might be called back from their zeal for martyrdom, either by terror of punishment and horror of a cruel death or by the lure of rewards. Heavy is the snare of proscription, which often breaks with the ugliness of want saints whom the fear of death had not broken; another snare is fire, another is prison and prolonged torture. A great snare it is when riches are promised, or honors, or the friendship of tyrants. So whoever has escaped these and has been able to attain martyrdom rightly says: 'Sinners have laid a snare for me, but I have not turned aside from the paths of your commandments.' To him, since he despises the present and seeks the future, the heavenly kingdom has been opened by the promise of your divinity.

Who are these sinners who have laid snares? The apostle has revealed to you the author of all sins and pointed him out, saying: "Those who want to become rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil." Do you notice that riches are the devil's snare, the snare he set even for the Saviour? But he, who had nothing that the prince of this world could come and call his own, broke the bonds of his snares.

And lest you think this a minor snare, it was this snare that strangled the apostle Judas. When the wretch had been snared into betraying the Lord and realised how great a crime he had committed, he hanged himself with a noose. But that too was a snare of the devil, that he should not repent but strangle himself with a noose. For God is merciful even to traitors, so that they may be called to repentance and

turn back from their shameful purpose and come to their senses, escaping the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive to do his will. To have fallen in is then no longer a misfortune but a crime, because they have not only given themselves up to be caught, but are held bound to the devil's will, though they could say: "Let us break their bonds asunder." For divine Scripture has granted you not only to beware of the devil's snare but also to break his bonds through repentance.

What have you to do, O man, with delights and pleasures? The snare does not catch you unless the bait has caught you first; while you go after the prey, you tie yourself up in the snare. The bait of the snare is avarice, the bait of the devil is luxury, with which he wants to lure us, not to feed us. That is why the apostle cried out: "Do not handle, do not taste, things which all lead to corruption by their very use."

So do not handle luxury, and it will not be able to defile you; do not taste the corruption of avarice, and you will be free from the snare. In short, what have you to do with earthly things, you who have risen with Christ? "Seek the things that are above, where Christ is; set your minds on the things that are above, not on things that are on the earth."

We have died to earthly things; we have hidden our life with Christ in our God; it is no longer we who live, but Christ lives in us. Why do we go back again to earthly things? "Lo, I have fled far away," says the holy man; "I have seen snares of iniquity and contradiction in the city"; for there are snares where there is usury and deceit. He fled far from earthly disgrace, and so he attained heavenly rewards.

Why, I ask, do you bend back toward the earth, if in Enoch you were caught up to heaven, in Elijah you were lifted up in a chariot, in Paul you were caught up into paradise and have your citizenship in heaven, in David your prayer was heard that you might take the wings of a dove and fly, in Christ you were exalted and made a bird in the Spirit? When he descended like a dove, he gave you those wings so that you might learn to fly away from the earth.

Nor should you think you must hesitate over how you are to fly, or with what oarage of wings. David did indeed say: "Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly away and be at rest?" And he seemed, as it were, to have been in doubt from whom he could

receive wings, although this is the usual way of declaring divine grace, which cannot be found on earth. Yet he himself later showed clearly what these wings are, saying: "If you sleep among the lots, the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her hinder parts with the sheen of gold." Even if you sleep, your wings still rise up. For there are those who keep watch while they sleep, as she kept watch who said: "I sleep, but my heart is awake." Even if it is night, the spirit keeps watch, of which it is written: "In the night my spirit keeps watch for you." Then your wings will be spread

and your flight will rise from spiritual words and the precious gold of wisdom. Where then could you fear snares, when you have spiritual oarage at hand? If sincerity of soul, if purity of mind shines out, you are a dove. That is why it was said to you: "Be simple as doves." If the greater oars are lacking, do not despise even the lesser. Be at least a sparrow, so that you may foresee the snares with keen tracking, and, though almost caught by the allurements of sins, yet at last be called back and able to say: "Our soul has escaped like a sparrow from the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken and we are set free." Since we thought that this should be treated elsewhere, it seems that we must now pass on to something else.

It is enough for you to know that you are a bird, taken up into a nature made for flying, as the Lord says through the prophet: "Free yourselves from the snare of the hunters and from the word of disturbance; for not unjustly are nets spread for birds." You are a bird, O man, you who like a bird have been renewed to a youth like the eagle's, and therefore not unjustly are nets spread for birds.

For why do you cast yourself down to the earth, you who were already making for heaven? Not unjustly are nets spread for one who has been renewed, because you have now begun to belong to Christ and have ceased to belong to the hunters. Before, the hunter caught you with a snare; before, the devil took you by his own right as his prey. But now why does a stranger assail what was bought by the Lord's cross? Yet you can avoid even these snares, so that you need not say, "The hunters have caught me like a sparrow," if you escape the snare of the heart which the devil put into the heart of Judas, and so armed him for the crime of betrayal.

May the Lord turn away from us these snares which he rains upon sinners. And so the prophet says: "You will give them, O Lord, the snare of their heart which you have prepared for them." But to us, Lord, give help, that we may follow after you bound by your bonds. For no bonds are stronger, none more welcome, than the bonds of love. Whoever is bound to you is set free from the world.

"I have inherited your testimonies for ever, for they are the rejoicing of my heart." This too is the voice of the martyrs, who say that they have received the inheritance of the heavenly testimonies. So the prophet says: "I am the heir of your commandments; I have entered upon your succession [?] by right of faith and piety." No one can say this except one who keeps the commandments, which were secured with heaven and earth as witnesses. For the Lord said: "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth."

The Lord calls the elements to witness in order to refute those who refuse to keep the divine precepts, so as to block every refuge of excuse. He also calls men to witness, saying: "Be my witnesses, and I am a witness, says the Lord." The commandments of the Lord, then, are full of testimonies and are themselves testimonies, and of them God, who does not lie, is a fully reliable witness; before him your own conscience too is a witness, your thoughts accusing or else defending you,

a witness faithful enough even in a faithless breast, since nothing that has been committed can be hidden from the judge of all. For if in an earthly court even someone who has come suborned to lie usually reveals the truth when he has been refuted by another's testimony, how much more in the heavenly court, before the Lord Jesus, must he confess what is true, knowing that the Lord knows what was done!

And he says well: "I have acquired your testimonies as an inheritance," for just as before we were heirs of the sinner, so now we are heirs of Christ. That was an inheritance of crimes, this is an inheritance of virtue; that bound us, this sets us free; that, when we were in debt through the interest

on our sins, handed us over to the enemy; this, when we had been redeemed by the title of the Lord's passion, acquired us for Christ. Eve's evil succession was devouring the whole man; Christ's glorious inheritance has set the whole man free. Jesus did not write his testament for one, nor for a few, but for all. We are all written in as heirs, not for a portion but for the whole.

The testament is common, the right belongs to all; the inheritance is everyone's, yet each receives it entire. The new testament is entered upon by each and possessed by all, and nothing is lessened for an heir by whatever his co-heirs claim. The benefit remains whole, and grows the more for each the more people it has been acquired for. The condition of a human inheritance is different.

If it is divided, the benefits are diminished, and the naming of a co-heir is the heir's loss. The kingdom of Christ is undivided, the inheritance is undivided. How could the inheritance be divided, when its fruit, which is the kingdom of heaven, is undivided? Gold, silver, an estate left by a man to several people are distributed and cut up; the gifts of Christ come entire to each; all have them and no one is cheated.

Let us hear, then, the benefits of the inheritance. The forgiveness of sins is Christ's inheritance. Certainly it is entire for each and profitable for all in common; for whoever it is conferred upon, it is taken from no one and added to all. Whatever is remitted to each individual is gained for the body. For if the angels rejoice over one sinner who repents, because they count the redemption of a man as their own gain, how much more is it the gain of our own race, which is the gain of our nature!

The resurrection is Christ's inheritance. Would anyone call this his loss, which in one man found the name of a common grace? For Christ in rising rose for all, since "through a man came the resurrection of the dead." How then can that be a loss to individuals which is the renewal of the whole body and of the human race?

So let the testament be read aloud, and let us consider its provisions. The Holy Spirit too bears witness to us, for he has said: "This is the testament that I will make with them, says the Lord: I will put my laws in their hearts, and in their minds I will write them, and their sins and their iniquities I will remember no more."

O truly eternal testator, who fixes his laws in our hearts and writes them in our minds, so that we can think of nothing but the divine precepts and ought to feel nothing but the oracles of God! He has given grace, he has renewed nature; he who is accustomed to forget nothing has taken from himself the memory of my sins and given me the memory of his precepts.

Do not, then, remove God's law from your heart and fix there the law of sin; do not write the enticements of the devil in your mind and erase the commandments of God. "Behold, I have painted your walls," says the Lord to Jerusalem, that is, to the soul eager for tranquillity and peace, which he made in his own image.

Do not, I say, take away the heavenly image and put on the image of death. You have refused the inheritance of the world; keep the testimonies of Christ, since in them there is rejoicing and gladness, for every tear will be wiped away, and there will be no more death, nor mourning, nor weeping, nor crying. Christ's passion was a heavenly image of the kingdom. No one heard his voice in the streets, because

by the silence of his passion he was abolishing for the future every cry of an impious voice. He did not want to be wept for, he who said to the daughters of Jerusalem: "Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves." For since he was going to take away all tears by the benefit of his cross, in his own passion he displayed a likeness of the blessedness to come, so that no one should weep except one who did not hold fast to the benefits of Christ.

Rightly, then, does the man of the Gospel say: "I have acquired your testimonies as an inheritance for ever, for they are the rejoicing of my heart." Who would not rejoice, since he has acquired as his inheritance heaven and earth, the two elements that God also called to witness when he gave the law; since he has acquired God, of whom the holy man says, "The Lord is my portion"; he has acquired the Lord Jesus, he has acquired the Holy Spirit, and after these he has acquired the angels and lives with them, not only today and tomorrow but for ever, and is not saddened by any injuries suffered for the name of the Lord? Indeed, the apostles rejoiced when they were flogged, when they were thrust into prison.

Rejoicing, then, in the testimonies of the Lord, he rightly said: "I have inclined my heart to perform your righteous deeds for ever, for the sake of the reward." Whoever hopes for the reward of good works from God and hastens toward him inclines his heart to perform the righteous deeds of Christ. What is Christ's righteousness? "Let us," he says, "fulfil all righteousness"—the righteousness by which sin is lessened and guilt is forgiven.

And he says well, "I have inclined," so that it may not be steep and hard for you when you turn your mind, as it were, toward low and level ground. Or certainly, since the wisdom of the flesh is not subject to the law of God, he seems to incline his heart who makes the bodily sense that exalts itself subject to the law and bends it down by regard for religion. And the man who once exalted himself in vain and was puffed up by the mind of his flesh inclines when he humbles himself.

For Christ himself also humbled himself in order to establish the new testament. When I read the Gospel and hear that the Son of God took flesh from Mary, I seem to myself to be descending with Christ. For I read of him who, though he was in the form of God, emptied himself—and he emptied himself to take the form of a servant—and being found in appearance as a man, humbled himself even unto death. I read him saying: "Whoever exalts himself will be humbled." I read him saying: "Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart."

He did not say, "Learn from me, for I am mighty"; he did not say, "Learn from me, for I am glorious"; but, "Learn from me, for I am humble"—which you are able to imitate. Do not exalt yourselves, do not lift up your hearts. He has taught me, then, to be humbled and to incline my heart to perform righteous deeds—to incline it not toward iniquity but toward equity, for the sake of the reward. The reward is the kingdom of heaven and a dwelling in paradise.
XV. THE LETTER SAMECH.

The fifteenth letter, Samech, begins, and it is interpreted as "hear." It also has another interpretation, which is "firmament." What does "hear" mean? It is not idly said, though hearing is common to all and available to everyone by the very law of nature. And so it is not idle that you are urged to hear, even though we usually hear a sound or a voice even against our will and while doing something else. But since hearing is not only that which is supplied by the function of nature, but also that which is greater—that you should hear not so much with the use of the body as with the understanding of the mind—therefore consider more carefully the interpretation of this letter and the series of verses that follow.

And so that you may know that hearing is a mystical thing, so that you should hear and understand the mysteries, it is written of the Jews that they heard the mysteries of the law but did not understand them. Hence the Lord says: "Hear, my people, and I will speak." The law is certainly spiritual; hear, then, spiritually. Finally, one who knew how to hear says: "I will hear what God speaks in me," that is:

"I will come to know what God has spoken in me." And so elsewhere he says: "How great the things we have heard and known," to make clear that he had not only heard but also understood; for no one comes to know unless he has first understood. Hear, then, lest Peter, seeing you negligent, should come, seize his sword and cut off your ear, since you have the ear of the body to no purpose if you do not know how to hear and weigh what you hear. And perhaps those who cannot hear with the depth with which Scripture was written have had cut off that power of the soul by which whatever is heard is weighed.

And rightly others have interpreted this letter as "firmament," which agrees with the former interpretation; for unless each one hears what he ought to follow, no one is made firm. In the duty of hearing, then, lies the firm foundation of all things.

So in Lamentations the prophet Jeremiah says to you by this letter: "Hear." And so that you may know that what you must hear is mystical, he placed after this letter a passage of this kind: "The Lord has taken away all my mighty men from my midst; he has summoned a time against me to crush my chosen ones; the Lord has trodden a pit for the virgin daughter of Judah."

The Lord did not take away all the mighty men of Judea at the time when the Jewish people were led captive to the land of Babylon, but when Christ came and the captive did not see the freedom of her soul, not knowing how to raise the neck of her mind, bowed down by grievous sins, and lift up, as it were, the neck of faith to the light of knowledge. That is why the Saviour's passion became a pit for the Jews, while it showed the Gentiles a harbour of salvation, because the Lord's cross is a precipice to unbelievers but life to believers. For this reason he put "hear" first, so that you might understand things to come.

In another place too he placed these words after this letter: "All who pass along the way have clapped their hands at you; they have hissed and wagged their heads at the daughter of Jerusalem: 'Is this the city,' they will say, 'the crown of glory and the joy of the whole earth?'" Prophesying the Saviour's passion, Jeremiah left behind a lament for

the destruction of the Jews. This can be understood from other passages and especially from the one where he says later: "The breath before our face, Christ the Lord, was taken in our destruction, under whose shadow we said: We shall live among the Gentiles." What could be clearer than this, when the name itself is stated, his seizure at the hands of faithless persecutors is declared, and the life-giving shadow and the grace to be bestowed on the Gentiles are described?

But the very words also point to what we read in the Gospel about the Lord's passion, since in this passage his death was announced by the prophet. For Matthew wrote thus: "And those who passed by blasphemed him, wagging their heads and saying: 'Aha, you who would destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days! Save yourself, if you are the Son of God.'" When the common crowd mocks someone, it usually hisses.

At the same time, because those who denied the Word had no voice, they hissed like irrational animals, and so they passed along the way, they who ought to have stood in the way. So they did not stand as steadfast men but passed by as fickle ones. But the feet of the righteous stood in the courts of Jerusalem, where the faithless could not stand, and therefore they passed by, as Mark indicated. A shadow passes, not the truth. The days of one who forgets, who forsakes, pass like a shadow. But we also read that unbelievers pass by, as in this passage:

"And all who pass along the way strip its vintage." For who but a faithless man plunders the vineyard of Christ? And it is also written elsewhere: "And those who passed along the way did not say: The blessing of the Lord be upon you"; for it is to those who stand that it is said: "Behold, now bless the Lord." Yet we also read of passing in a good sense, as in Moses' words: "I will pass over and see this great sight"; and he who saw the wicked exalted above the cedars of Lebanon said, "I passed by, and behold, he was not"; and "No one says to his servant: Pass on, sit down at table."

Let us consider, then, what the distinction may be—unless perhaps it is this: where passing is taken in a good sense, it is said absolutely; he did not say "passing this" or "passing that," but only "passing"; whereas in the bad sense he says, "those who pass along the way." For the way is good that is frequented by travellers and not easily attacked by robbers, who are accustomed to lie in wait on the byways; the king's highway is well protected.

Moses, however, did not pass the way by, but stood in the way, for it was said to him: "But you stand here with me." He stood with him who said: "I am the way, the truth and the life." Whoever passes this way by falls. But Moses did not fall; rather he passed through from worldly things to spiritual, from temporal to eternal. And he who saw the wicked man and did not stay but passed on escaped, because he did not cling to the wicked, lest he become one body with him, but separated himself from him.

And the one to whom it is said, "Pass on, sit down at table," certainly escapes the toilsome servitude of the present in order to have the glorious rest of the things to come. And it is said to the bride: "Come hither from Lebanon, my bride, come hither from Lebanon; you will pass and pass through from the beginning of faith." She who hastens to the bridegroom passes and passes through: she passes through the world, she passes over to Christ.

Now let us examine what it means to wag the head. Who is the head of the people but Christ? For "the head of the woman is the man, and the head of the man is Christ." But the law too is the head of the woman understood spiritually; indeed, the woman was under the law as under a husband. But once the Jewish rite, which followed the letter of the law, had been put to death, the woman married him who rose

from the dead. Hence some, interpreting mystically, held that once the Jewish rite had been put to death, that spiritually understood woman, in accordance with the law, married the Gospel, as the brother of the deceased old rite, because the law preceded the Gospel with a kind of brotherly proclamation. So the head of the synagogue has

died, that is, its head, the law, has died—namely the observance of the law; the letter of the law has been made void, and its spiritual understanding is established. David mentions this moving in the forty-third psalm, saying: "You have made us a byword among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples," because a moving took place from the law to the Gospel, a kind of passing over. And in the twenty-first psalm, in which the whole course of the passion is prophesied, it says: "All who saw me scorned me; they spoke with their lips and wagged their heads: 'He hoped in the Lord, let him rescue him; let him save him, since he delights in him.'" So they moved the law, which seemed immovable, and Christ, the end of the law, entered in.

Those who had wagged their heads were the Pharisees, that is, those separated from the truth, and that is why they did not believe in the truth. But it can also be taken this way: they moved their head, Christ, who had come to his own; they moved him, because his own did not receive him. And they moved him by saying, "Away with him, away with him, crucify him." And they moved their head, they who refused to move their own burdens, though they bound heavy burdens and laid them

on others, but "they themselves," he says, "are unwilling to move them with a finger." This has a mystical meaning, because they never wanted to change the observance of the bodily rite and bring in the spiritual understanding. We read of the finger as standing for the Spirit, as the law was written by the finger of God, and therefore the law is spiritual. So they refused to move their own burdens, which are heavy, and to take up the light yoke of Christ and his sweet burden.

But since the Savior's passion redeemed everyone, it is not absurd to understand that these men moved their heads in the same way that that ruler of the synagogue prophesied: "It is expedient that one man should die for the people." He meant to say one thing, but he signified another. These men too moved their heads with one intent, as if mocking, but announced something else: that he was the one who came to stir that sluggish and earthly ruling part of human beings, so that, once observance of the letter had been done away with, we might seek the mystery in the words.

Hence he says: "You have made us a parable among the Gentiles, a shaking of the head among the peoples." This is certainly to be taken in a good sense, since he said before: "and you have scattered us among the nations." For the Jews were scattered so that their remnant might be saved according to the election of grace. They were made a parable so that from their end we might learn that what was spoken in parables has been revealed, or so that we might be warned by their example to beware of faithlessness.

For Jeremiah knew all the better that Judea was to be mourned, and so he prophesied that Jerusalem was captured at the time when she did not receive her own Redeemer. So it is she who is mocked, she of whom, he says, they will say: "This is the city [?] of the whole earth." For where once there was the joy of faith, there is now the bitterness of faithlessness. Or else, by moving her head and passing from bodily things to spiritual ones, she may deserve to hear, once she has believed in Christ, that she is a crown of glory.

And what is the crown of glory but the Church, which crowns her head, Christ? What is the joy of the whole earth but the house of the Christian people, the hall of the saints, of whom it is written: "Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world"? So, because the Church is the crown of glory, it is said in the Song of Songs: "Go forth and see King Solomon in the crown with which his mother crowned

him on the day of his espousals and on the day of the gladness of his heart." This is said to souls: they should come out of the hovels and prisons of the body, go out beyond the body's thoughts, and depart from desires and cares and the other affections and slippery passions of this flesh. They should rise above the world,

go out of this world, run to meet Christ, and be present and ready, shining with burning torches. It is as though Christ's angels were saying: "You cannot see his brightness and his glory unless you go out of the body of human frailty, daughters of Jerusalem", as if to say: "Why do you seek the living

among the dead?" Christ is not sought within this world, for he wished his disciples to be above the world. What is the crown with which Christ is crowned but the crown of glory? Joseph had the crown of chastity, Paul the crown of righteousness, Peter the crown of faith. These are the crowns of individual virtues. Christ alone has the crown of glory, with which the Church has crowned him. All crowns are in this crown, because glory is not the share of one crown but the reward of all crowns.

In a third reading, they moved their head, that is, Christ, who is the head of his people: "His head is gold of cephaz." Aquila therefore said "rock gold" and Symmachus "golden stone", which signifies a stable and eminent wisdom. The Church is the body of Christ. Its "head of gold" is the precious wisdom of the saints, that is, of just and prudent men. "His locks are fir trees, black as a raven", and elsewhere he says of this: "Your hair is like a flock of shorn ewes." He speaks of hair because the strength of all the senses is in the head, for "the wise man's eyes are in his head."

The locks, therefore, are the deep prudence of teachers, which can reveal what is obscure and open up the heights of meaning. Expounders of this kind are the locks of the Church. They are like the young ravens to which the Lord gives food, as he gave it to holy Jacob from his youth and fed him. The Lord feeds these men, lofty and deep in the richness of their doctrine, with heavenly sacraments.

"His eyes too are like doves." The eyes are men adorned with spiritual senses, sharp to see mysteries and ready to penetrate the secrets of divine Scripture. They shine with rational milk, and in them there is no stained confusion of deceit, only the pure and spotless sincerity of a simple heart. That is why he spoke of these doves as washed in milk beside abundant waters.

We understand the rest, the teeth and the cheeks and the bride's lips like a scarlet cord, to be the virtues of the soul and the different kinds of teachers. Some supply spiritual nourishment to the mind by diligent stewardship. Some bind the hearer by preaching the Lord's cross, as if with a thread of the word. Others are modest and reserved and most pleasing in the flower of youth, and even if shyness holds them back from expounding, the fragrance of Christ still breathes from them, and, as ointment runs down onto the cheeks as if from the priestly [?], the beauty of doctrine shines out.

The synagogue moved this head too, and therefore the Lord took away "the wonderful counselor and the wise master builder and the wise hearer", "head", he says, "and tail", since those who had not held on to the head cannot have the last things. But now let us consider what follows.

"I have hated the wicked, and I have loved your law." In this little verse the holy prophet David declared how great an affection draws him toward the Lord. He never persecuted his own enemies. He did not think that the life even of King Saul should be sought, though he could scarcely guard against the danger Saul's plots posed to his safety, and he judged that Saul's death ought to be avenged. He lamented the death of his parricidal son, and when he was assailed by the crimes of many persecutors he forgave them, so that, as he himself

says, he did not repay injury to those who harmed him. Yet he shudders with loathing at those who transgress the divine law. Here are revealed the clemency of his character, the gentleness of his piety and the vehement intensity of his devotion, in keeping with the discipline of the gospel precept, which he foresaw by the prophetic spirit. For the Lord Jesus commanded that we should strive to love our own enemies, but that we should pursue God's enemies with hatred, even if they are joined to us by the bond of parents or children, of marriage or of brotherhood. For it is written: "If anyone comes to me and does not hate father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, and even his own life besides, he is not worthy of me."

If someone heard this with idle ears, he might perhaps say: "Lord Jesus, you gave the law, saying: 'Love the Lord your God, love your neighbor', and you came to fulfill this law. Through the law you said: 'Honor your father and mother', and in the gospel do you order me to hate my parents? How do these commands agree with each other? Is this how you came, meek and lowly of heart? I cannot hate my father without violating the duty of piety, for I owe it to him that I was created. Nor can I hate my mother, who carried the burden of a loving pregnancy through the long weariness of ten months, for whom the delivery held more danger and the delay more weariness.

"What have my dearest children done to deserve being shut out of their father's love, when it is impious to be unwilling to die for one's children? What has my beloved wife done, a sort of co-heir of my life and common partner in nature? What have my brothers done, who grew in the same womb, were formed in the same lodging of nature and were sent out into this light? Am I, then, to hate the pledges of love? Do you so bend the rigor of the very harsh law by the gentleness of the gospel that, by your gospel, you condemn love toward those whom the law forbids us to injure?"

I see that I cannot answer an assertion of this kind. But you answer it, Lord; you have no need to be excused, for you had no need of anything in order to conquer. He will answer, then: "Do I condemn piety, I who hate iniquity? Do I teach that parents are not to be loved, I who urge that enemies be loved? But have you not read: 'A time to love and a time to hate, a time for war and a time for peace'? What is Ecclesiastes speaking of here?

"Is it not that, depending on the time, we can piously both love and hate certain people, so that it is right to hate those you once loved and to love those you once hated? I did not pour hatred of parents into the hearts of children, nor did I persuade husbands to scorn their wives.

"Ask nature what I demanded. She certainly bears witness to the will of her Author by the innate affection that belongs to each relationship. It is the law of nature that fathers love their children. It is divine law that husbands love their wives, and this law turns the love of marriage into nature, so that they become one flesh and one spirit. It is a privilege of nature that brothers love brothers, for nature has accustomed those long nurtured in the same home to the grace of love.

"So I did not command civil wars within families. Rather, I held allurement to be suspect. And was it not rightly suspect? For when that crafty and cunning serpent was devising the arts of his wickedness to undermine the affection of Adam, the first-formed, which was founded on the gift of an uncorrupted and innocent nature, he entrusted the task to a woman's allurements rather than to his own poisons.

"And so the woman, with the soft and winning affection of a devoted wife, led astray the man whom the serpent had not dared to tempt, swaying him by the food of her mouth and the force of love. And Eve did not yet have children,

"whose charm, as sweet in winning love as it is easy in causing a fall, has often called many back from completing their martyrdom. Indeed, we have often learned of a man whom the fearsome parade of executioners did not terrify, whom the furrow cut in his side did not break, and whom the burning plates could not draw away from the firmness of triumphant courage; and yet, when he already stood among the sacred rewards, his wife deceived him by holding out their tender child and by the pity of a single wretched tear. Samson was captured through his wife: are you stronger? Solomon was captured in his wife: are you wiser? He whose wisdom is celebrated through all the ages became foolish because he loved his wife too much.

"What shall I say of brothers? The prophet's own house learned from its children that brotherly kisses are more detestable than brotherly hatreds. So the father wept indeed over the fratricide, but he was more indignant at the incest. In fact, though the son was a fratricide, the father still called back the one who had slain the incestuous brother."

"A time to love and a time to hate", then, means the time of martyrdom, when divine things must be put before all love of family. "A time for war" is when we wage war for the name of Christ even against faithless loved ones. "A time for peace" is because "his place is in peace." Indeed, he himself plainly explained in the gospel why we ought to hate our own, saying: "Whoever loves father and mother more than me is not worthy of me."

He did not say that whoever loves his parents is unworthy. He said that those are unworthy who love their parents more than Christ. For if we give our love to our parents because they brought us into being, how much more ought we to love Christ, who brought the parents themselves into being! They gave what lay not in their power but in their service. Christ, who preserves the benefits that parents give, grants salvation.

He spoke beautifully, then, when he said: "I have hated the wicked, but I have loved your law." For if we love the law, we ought to hate the law's adversaries, who attack its commands by their deeds. The Greek named them better and more precisely, saying: παρανόμους ἐμίσησα. A παράνομος is a lawless man, one who is outside the law. Whoever is in the law of Christ hates such people, because they do not keep the commands of the law.

For it is not only the one who does not know the law who has no share in it, but also the one who does not act according to it, since "it is not the hearers of the law but the doers of the law who will be justified." David himself refutes me if I understand it otherwise. How could he have hated wicked men, when he commended his parricidal son to his fighting men so that no one would kill him, and when he even avenged King Saul's death on the man who reported that he had killed him?

So he hated not wicked men but wicked words. Indeed, he said: "I have hated the wicked"; he did not add "men." Moreover, Jesus says in the gospel: "Love your enemies", and the apostle says: "Bless those who persecute you, and do not curse." How, then, could this man, who lived according to the discipline of the gospel, be excused if he hated wicked men? Only if you understand that he hated wickedness, not the people who,

though they worked wickedness, could still be converted by the preaching of the gospel. Or, if we do not take it this way, let us take it like this. Whoever does not honor his father is wicked; yet the same person is even held worthy of praise if he hates his father in the sense of what is written: "Whoever does not hate father or mother or brothers or sisters or his own life cannot be my disciple." In the same way, this man hated the wicked as one would hate a father who transgresses, or one's own life: he put the grace of Christ before the sweetness of this life.

The second verse follows: "You are my helper and the one who takes me up, and in your word I have hoped." He is our helper through the law and takes us up through the gospel. Those he helped through the law, he took up in the flesh, since it is written: "He bears our sins", and that is why I hope in his word. The Greek, however, has ἐπήλπισα, that is, "I have hoped beyond." This is said of someone who keeps adding to his hope: when he has hoped for something, he hopes again and advances in hope, always stretching out toward higher things and forgetting what lies behind.

He says beautifully: "In your word I have hoped." That is: I have not hoped in the prophets, nor in the law; I have hoped in your Word, that is, in your coming, that you may come and take up sinners, forgive their offenses, and, as the good shepherd, lay the weary sheep on your shoulders on the cross. Whoever hopes in Christ must separate himself from the company of the faithless.

And so he says: "Depart from me, you evildoers, and I will search out the commandments of my God." The testimony of this verse shows that where there is malice, the heavenly commandments cannot be kept, for "wisdom does not enter a malicious soul", and elsewhere: "The wicked will seek me and will not find me." Christ loves a simple mind and a pure, cleansed spirit, and spotless virtue can have no fellowship with stained vices.

He who says "Learn from me, for I am meek" hates, flees and spurns their contagion. He drives away the malicious and calls those who labor. To the first Jesus says: "Depart from me, all you who work iniquity"; to the second he says: "Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened." They are burdened not, of course, by malice of mind but by weakness of the flesh; burdened, I say, by the inheritance of another's sin. "I help those who labor; I must not benefit the deceitful, lest they harm more people. Let punishment restrain the one group, and let grace amend the other."

For malice is the source of sin, while a lapse is a fault of weakness. I ought to help the one who labors, and even to hate the one who deceives. So he drives away evil works. Unless you take it this way, he seems to be saying: "Depart from me, because I am clean, because I am pure." The Pharisee said this, and Christ rebuked him. So the prophet does not say "I am clean", but: "Create a clean heart in me, O God."

And so, having banished the company of the malicious, as one who could not be taken up by the Lord while he was still mingled with them, he says: "Take me up according to your word, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my expectation." If someone who is in the bosom of the patriarch Abraham lives, like the poor man Lazarus, how much more does someone live whom Christ takes up! For how can he fail to live forever whom everlasting life has taken up, whom Christ has wholly

taken to himself, who belongs wholly to the Word, whose life is hidden in Christ Jesus? But he too who sits in Abraham's bosom has been taken up by Christ. Yet it would seem intolerable presumption to say to God "Take me up" if he did not add God's promise, as if to say: "You yourself made us bold. We appeal to you by your own bond, you who took away our bond. We wrote the bond of death; you wrote the bond of life."

So do not put your little servant to shame in his expectation, because I hope in you, and hope does not put us to shame. If we are afflicted, give us patience so that we can bear it. Because I wait for you, let me not be overwhelmed by weaknesses, not give in to temptations, not be crushed by the storms in which patience must be tested, so that proven character may follow, which confirms and strengthens hope, the hope that does not put us to shame. That is: we are often broken by our labors and grow weary;

if hope is lacking, we are put to shame and troubled in our whole mind. Granted, some people are hardy in labor and steadfast in bearing injuries; but take away hope, and patience cannot last. Patience itself is not proven if faith is lacking, and the root of faith is hope. For what proof can there be unless you endure hardships or every kind of danger for the name of Christ? So hope alone does not let our hearts be put to shame. Where there is hope, that saying of the apostle, "fighting without, fears within", can do no harm.

Another translation has: "Do not make me blush." Whoever hopes in Christ will not blush. So whoever hopes rightly says: "In you I trust; let me not blush." And he rightly says "I trust", for confidence is the strength of our hope and gives a certain assurance to the one who hopes. Hope always, then, and no one will put you to shame in your expectation. Our expectation is eternal life; our expectation is the kingdom of God, the company of the angels and spiritual blessings. Hope every day. This is a thing that has no end and knows no truce.

Hope even when you are in adversity. Perhaps you have been struck by the loss of someone close to you, and someone says to you: "What good is your righteousness to you?" Hope all the same; do not let your faith fail. If someone says to you: "What good have your daily fasts done you, or your chastity of body and modesty of mind? Look, you have been wounded just like the unjust and the impious", do not let your faith fail. For even if you are weak, you are still faithful, and Christ is concerned for you. He says to the disciples: "You give them something to eat, so that they do not faint on the way."

You have the apostolic food; eat it, and you will not faint. Eat that first, so that afterward you may come to the food of Christ, the food of the Lord's body, the banquet of the sacrament, that cup by which the hearts of the faithful are made drunk, so that they put on gladness at the forgiveness of sin and lay aside the cares of this world, the fear of death and their anxieties. With this drunkenness the body does not stagger but rises again, and the mind is not confounded but consecrated.

"Help me", he says, "and I shall be saved, and I will meditate on your justifications always." Whoever hopes is confident that he will be helped, and where God's help is, there is sure aid for salvation. Above he said: "You are my helper and the one who takes me up"; here he asks again to be helped, as if to say: "Help me without ceasing. What I asked for is not enough for me; I ask again that I may be saved. Here salvation is not great, not true. I shall be saved when I am in paradise, when I begin to live among your chosen angels, when I have escaped the snares of this earth."

But having been helped in our needs, we might grow careless afterward when we prosper. So he teaches us that we must never forget heavenly benefits, but must meditate on the Lord's justifications, so that even when we have done some good work we may still always confess our sins to him; for this is the justification of the Lord. Indeed, the Pharisees, who refused to be baptized with the baptism of repentance, did not justify God.

So whoever repents of his offenses justifies God, for whoever repents confesses, as in that saying: "Against you alone have I sinned and done evil in your sight, so that you may be justified in your words." That is why the tax collector went out of the temple more justified: the Pharisee justified himself by proclaiming his own righteous deeds, while the tax collector justified God by confessing his own iniquities. So whoever meditates on the Lord's justifications is always humbled. He is not

humbled today and exalted tomorrow, but is always humble of heart and gentle in spirit. "Always" is more than "day and night" or "all day long", for it is above time. So even when you are numbered among the angels, you must always speak of God's justifications. You must not claim for your own merits the glory you have attained, but always ascribe it to the divine mercy, so that it is not said to you: "What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?" For every creature has received whatever good it has from Christ, who is the author of all creation.

"You have spurned," he says, "all who depart from your statutes, because their thought is wicked."
