Every proud man is unclean in the sight of the Lord, because one who heaps up error with an arrogant spirit cannot cleanse his sins through pride. So he is spurned and despised, because he holds the divine commandments in contempt.

The prerogative of heavenly mercy is rightly preserved, for it drives no one away; rather, whoever will not confess their own sins depart of their own accord from the Lord our God. That man indeed departed who went off to a far country and squandered the whole inheritance of faith and grace he had received from his father. And because he repented of having departed, he afterwards returned to the father he had left when he was unwilling to confess his own sin.

So God is not left behind by distance of place, but by depravity of character and ugliness of deeds. He departs from the Lord who puts himself far from him, as Adam, when he heard the presence of God, wanted to hide. But in departing from the Lord he could not have salvation, since it is written: "Behold, those who put themselves far from you shall perish." Each one, then, either joins himself to God or separates himself from him by his own pursuits.

That distance of place does not separate many people, nor do nearness and neighbourhood join them, is shown by this: many who are placed in the body are absent from the body and present with God, like the one who, when God said, "Whom shall I send?", answered, "Here I am, send me." Paul too dares to be present with God, because he saw nothing bodily in himself except the matter of his flesh. And Cain went out from the face of God after he had murdered his brother and did not think he ought to do penance for his sins.

Rightly he says: "You have brought the transgressors to nothing." He did not say "sinners" but "transgressors"; for what hope would we have, since we are all under sin? This too is well said: "You have brought all the transgressors to nothing." Whether a man is rich, his riches profit him nothing; whether honoured, his rank profits him nothing; whether powerful, his power profits him nothing. But it is one thing to be a transgressor who departs from the statutes of God, and another to be a transgressor of the earth; the first is graver, the second lighter.

So that what follows may not trouble you, see what he added to these words: "I have counted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors; therefore I have loved your testimonies always." Rightly one who departs from the Lord is called a transgressor; indeed in Greek he is called an apostate, from the word for departing. Hence the saying: "Wine and women make men fall away."

We must therefore beware of the incitements and allurements of sin, lest they slide into crime. In Latin the one called praevaricator is also called transgressor, because he crosses over from the law of the Lord to error and transgresses the heavenly commandments — he who was told to cleave to the Lord his God. Cleave to him, then, always, with undivided affection, so that no force can tear you away from him. If the adversary sees anything slack, anything left off, he at once thrusts himself

into your breast and your heart, so as to hold you in the snare of his deceit, and you, bound in the chain of a hostile power, are drawn back from devotion. Yet not only is he a transgressor who sets the church aside and crosses over to the worship of idols, but also whoever does not keep the commandments of the law. Every sinner, then, is a transgressor; hence the saying: "Every transgression receives a just recompense." The name is common to all, but the deserts of the offences differ, and so the price paid for faults differs too.

What does he mean by "sinners of the earth"? There are, then, sinners of heaven as well, like the one who says: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you." Some say that whoever does not keep the heavenly oracles is a transgressor of heaven. But it may be this, or it may be because he diminishes the grace he received from heaven, which the Holy Spirit poured in, or because, having become a bird of heaven, you ought not to come back down from heaven to the earth. You sin against heaven, then, if, being a dweller in heaven, you leave heaven. There is therefore a difference among them: some are sinners of heaven, others sinners of the earth.

"In the mornings," he says, "I put to death all the sinners of the earth." How could one man put to death all the sinners of the earth? But if you consider the righteous man, for whom the night is far spent and the day has drawn near, you can see how, as the Sun of righteousness rises for you and you keep watch from first light, you may put to death all that kindles sin.

Would that this grace might breathe upon me, that with the spiritual sword, which is the word of God, I might abolish from the Lord's church every incitement to vice and take away earthly sins, by which we are hurled into a kind of pit of slippery error, so that the worker of iniquity may be driven out of the city of God! The city of God is the church; the church is the body of Christ. He sins against heaven who defiles the laws of the heavenly city and violates the holiness of the spotless body with the filth of his vices.

And consider whether there may perhaps be some who are sinners both of heaven and of earth. For Adam certainly, while he was in paradise, was heavenly; but after the fall he became earthly and was driven out and cast forth from paradise. Hence the apostle says: "The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly." Let us cast away from us the image of the earthly and take up the image of the heavenly — an image not expressed in paint, not in wax, not sketched in colours, but in conduct, in which Christ may recognize himself.

"Pierce my flesh with nails from fear of you; for I have been afraid of your judgments." He who loves the Lord's testimonies pierces his flesh with nails, knowing that his old self, nailed to the cross with Christ, destroys the wantonness of the flesh, so that its desires may not run riot with untamed

heat, and the root of avarice may not spread out with creeping roots. Pierce it with nails, then, and destroy the kindling of sin; let every enticement to sin die in your flesh; let the craving for pleasures, fastened to the cross, have no freedom to roam. There is a kind of spiritual nail that fastens this flesh to the gibbet of the Lord's cross. And perhaps the soul has a certain flesh, just as it has a body. The flesh of the soul is carnal thoughts;

let the fear of the Lord and of his judgments nail down this flesh and bring it into subjection. But if this flesh rejects the nails of divine fear, then beyond doubt it is said: "My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh." Unless, therefore, this flesh is fastened to the cross and pierced with nails from the fear of our God, the Spirit of God will not remain in them.

Just as there are goads of fear by which we are pricked, so there are nails of fear by which we are pierced. He who is pricked is roused; he who is pierced is put to death, so that he may die to sin and live to God. And so that we may know the nails are spiritual, there are also spiritual goads, of which it is written:

"It is hard for you to kick against the goad." Goaded by this goad, Paul rose from the ground and lifted himself up, so as to live as a citizen of heaven. The apostle Thomas was pierced with nails, so that he said: "Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails and put my finger into the place of the nails." They were nails of good desire; they were nails of a faith that, though not yet perfect, was nevertheless seeking to grow.

With these nails is he pierced who dies with Christ for Christ's sake, so that he may rise with Christ; with these nails is he pierced who carries the dying of the Lord Jesus in his body; with these nails is he pierced who is found worthy to hear Jesus say: "Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death, jealousy is hard as hell."

Fix, then, the seal of the Crucified upon your breast and upon your heart; fix it also upon your arm, so that your works may be dead to sin. Let no crime come back to life in them, no error rise again. Perhaps not only the nails of fear but also those of love fasten this image, because love is strong as death, jealousy hard as hell. So do not let the hardness of the nails offend you, for it is the hardness of love; nor their unyielding strength, for love too is strong as death.

For love slays guilt and puts all sins to death; love kills like the stroke of death. Indeed we die to crimes and to sin when we love the Lord's commandments. God is love; love is the word of God, which is strong and sharper than the sharpest sword, piercing even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and the inmost marrow. Hard, then, is the jealousy of love, which does not yield to hell, since for the sake of zeal for God each one does not spare even his own.

Let our soul and our flesh be pierced with these nails of love, so that the soul too may say: "For I am wounded with love." Love, then, has its own nail, it has its own sword by which the soul is wounded. Blessed is he who is found worthy to be wounded by this sword. These are the wounds that are preferred to kisses: "Better are the wounds of a friend than the willing kisses of an enemy."

Let us offer ourselves to these wounds; whoever dies of them cannot taste death. Such is the death of those who followed the Lord, of whom it was said: "There are some of those standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom." Rightly Peter did not fear this death; for he did not fear,

he who said that even if he had to die for Christ, he would not leave him or deny him. Let us take up, then, the cross of the Lord, to nail down our flesh and destroy sin. There is a fear that nails the flesh: "Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me." For he is worthy who has the fear of Christ, so as to crucify carnal sin. Love follows this fear — love which, buried with Christ, is not torn away from Christ, but dies in Christ, is entombed with Christ, so that it may rise with Christ.
XVI. THE LETTER AYIN

Here begins the sixteenth letter, Ayin, which means "eye" or "spring." The eye performs the office of seeing; but we often see things that please us and often things that displease us, and the eye is neither to blame nor to be praised according to the quality of what it has seen, for the eye's duty is to report what it has seen. There is indeed offence or delight, according as it is delighted by pleasant things or offended by unpleasant ones. That is why we often hear of the eye of punishments, the eye of temptation, the eye of the kid, the eye of the heifer, the eye of generation or the spring of generation.

We read in the gospel that John was baptizing in Aenon. Aenon has been interpreted as "eye of punishments." For no one comes to baptism except one who desires his own sins to be forgiven, and whose punishments he dreads with a foreseeing heart. So although it is called the eye of punishments, it belongs to one who foresees punishments, not one who suffers them — although the baptism of repentance does involve some endurance in accepting punishment. It is the eye's part to perform the office of looking; it is yours to beware of what you see.

It is also called the eye of temptation, because we are often tempted through the eye. The eye of a harlot is a snare to her lover. But the eye commits no fault, and so the Saviour's sentence is full of justice when he says: "Whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart." He did not say "whoever looks at a woman," but "whoever looks to lust." He acquitted the eye; he bound the mind. Nor did he say "has committed adultery with her in his eye," but "in his heart." In the eye is the seeing; in the heart, the sin.

The eye of the kid is the one on the left, because the sinner cannot see the things that are on the right. But the saint says: "I foresaw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand, that I may not be moved." And to the holy apostle Peter, when he had caught nothing all night, as we read in the gospel, the Saviour said: "Cast the nets on the right side of the boat." So, relying on the heavenly command, he cast the nets and gathered a great many fish. On the left was night; on the right shone the daylight brightness of the divine word.

There is also the eye of the heifer, which likewise refers to sinners, because like heifers with the strap of the yoke they draw iniquities along, not bursting or cutting away what is their own, but dragging their sin with a long rope. For an untamed heifer is tamed late; she drags the straps rather than accepting them, because she cannot bear to be held; and the longer she drags them, the more she is entangled.

It is also called the eye of generation or the spring of generation, because from what the eye sees things either good or bad are generated. You saw the beauty of a woman and praised the work of the Craftsman, the loveliness of nature: that is a generation of faith, a birth of devotion. You were content with the comeliness

of her form and took her as your wife, not out of ambition for wealth; she bore you children of nobler grace: your eye was for you the generation of good things. You looked upon a consecrated virgin; reverence for strict chastity lowered your eyes, and you proclaimed the Lord Jesus, who had given the gravity of old age to a young girl's years, and had poured into human affections a spotless life amid the weak

enticements of this so slippery flesh: your eye became for you a spring of good things. You looked upon the property of orphans not to seize it but to protect it, and you groaned with a father's heart if you noticed that anything of the minor's interests had been

neglected; you drove off the one who sought [?] to encroach on his boundaries; you judged in the orphan's favour: your eye was for you a spring and source of justice. You judged in the widow's favour — for as a bad drachma is no drachma, so a bad judgment is certainly no judgment — you judged, then, as a just and good judge; you saw the shameless usurper who thought that a woman bereft of her husband's help was his prey; you did not tolerate the injustice; you brought help to the defenceless, so that, aided by this protection, she practised the works of chastity unharmed and was not forced to seek a husband's help. The Lord says to you: "Come, let us reason together, for you have done justice to the widow":

your eye has become for you a spring of grace. You saw the naked body of a dead pauper lying there; you did not pass by like the priest and the Levite described in the gospel, but at once, moved with pity, you gave it the comfort of burial: your eye generated for you the means of redemption.

On the other hand, if you looked at an orphan's field planted with vines, rich in crops, pleasant with shady groves or running streams or bubbling springs or grassy banks, and, kindled by the torches of avarice, you moved the boundaries set by the fathers and shamelessly broke into the undefended property, your eye has generated for you the bitter fruits of everlasting death.

You violated the rights of the widow next door; you forced her, who ought to have nursed her grief or her modesty shut away within private walls, to rush out in public and go to law, with more immodesty than injustice: your eye became the birth of iniquity. You looked upon a poor man with a proud eye and an insatiable heart, you despised the poor man's plea, and you passed by with disdain one whom you ought to have pitied: your eye was for you a spring and source of sin.

So let your eyes not be the eyes of a wolf lying in wait for prey, but, as is said to the bride: "Your eyes are pools in Heshbon, at the gates of the daughter of many. Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon." What are "pools in Heshbon" but an abundance of rational thoughts, which is at the gates of the church, to which a multitude of teaching is rightly brought?

For the daughter of many is the posterity and offspring of very many teachings, and her nostrils are the fragrance of sacrifices, surpassing all flowers. For what is more sublime than the fragrance of Christ, who made his sweetness rise over the earth? Let this eye, then, foresee what is to come, and if it foresees adversity impending, let it not cease to soften and mitigate it with weeping and tears.

So Jeremiah, placed amid the captivity of the Jewish nation and foreseeing the coming misery of a perpetual captivity, which the Jewish people would have to pay as the price of their faithlessness, said in Lamentations under this same letter: "For this I weep; my eyes have grown dim with weeping, because he who

comforted me has gone far from me." He did not grieve, then, that he had been carried off from his own land, but he saw that the people would be abandoned by Christ and the consolation of the life to come would be lost. This is the captivity that must be mourned, for it seemed deprived of the hope of eternal freedom. In another place, too, under this same letter, he repeated it in Lamentations, saying: "The Lord has accomplished what he planned, his word which he commanded from days of old; he has destroyed and has not

spared, and he has made the enemy rejoice over you and exalted the horn of those who afflict you." Is not the future judgment of Christ plainly announced here, just as it is certainly declared in the present psalm as well? Let the eye, then, foresee what is coming, and turn it aside either by shedding tears or by correcting error. Indeed Jeremiah wept because he perceived the evil case of the impious people, which in stubborn faithlessness denied its own Author.

But David, foreseeing by the prophetic spirit the judgment of Christ, in which no innocent man will be in danger and no criminal will escape, relies on a good conscience and says: "I have done judgment and justice; do not hand me over to those who harm me." He is not praising himself like an insolent boaster, since, being skilled in the law, he certainly

knew that each one should be praised by another's mouth rather than by his own. There is here, I say, no boasting of virtues proclaimed, but a rightful assertion of an innocent life, lest he be thought deserving to be abandoned by the Lord for grave sins and handed over to the power of the wicked. It is a defence, then, not arrogance,

when no eminence of honour is being claimed, but a dreadful misery is being warded off. Peter indeed uses this kind of defence when he says: "Behold, we have left all things and followed you: what then shall we have?" If there had been any taint of arrogant speech in this, he would not have received such grace from the sentence of the Lord and Saviour, that he was declared not only exempt from being judged himself but also one who would judge the merits of others. Nor in a court of law, if someone disclosed what he had done in order to protect his innocence, would his words be taken as boasting rather than as the defence of his case. It is one thing to say that one is worthy of reward, another to say that one does not deserve injury.

And yet that very man who, as they say, was the supreme master of philosophy, when he was accused and asked what penalty he thought he deserved, is said to have replied that he should be entertained daily at a public banquet in the Prytaneum. He laid claim to honour; David guarded against misery. He arrogated glory to himself; David kept humility. For what greater humility can there be than that a man conscious of having kept judgment and justice should fear being handed over to the power of the devil?

He knew that he was a man, no match for the war against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. He knew that Enoch was taken away lest wickedness should alter his heart; that Noah became drunk; that Lot was defiled by incest; that Aaron himself, the first of the priests, was tempted together with his sister Miriam; that Miriam was first spotted with leprosy and afterwards cleansed; that Moses was nearly killed, had not his wife Zipporah warded off all danger from him by circumcising their son and shedding his blood. Warned by these examples, he by no means trusts in his own strength; instead cautious humility draws divine help to itself by prayer, asking not to be handed over to the wicked.

For he knows that the prince of this world is the author of all sins. It is he who tears apart the undivided affections of those close to one another, stirring them up with the goads of anger; he kindles the flame of lust; he fans the desires of avarice, so that the more we seize, the more we seek;

he suggests and supplies the kindling of self-indulgence; he embitters with hatred and inflames with the pursuit of boundless ambition. This vice, alluring at the outset and savage in its progress, could not be checked even by regard for brotherhood: the seeker after heavenly favour, grieving that his brother had been preferred to him, went from sacrifice to fratricide. That the devil is the author of incontinence the apostle teaches: "Lest

Satan tempt you because of your incontinence." We read also that he is the instigator of avarice, as Paul says: "Those who want to become rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil"; and elsewhere: "Put to death, therefore, your members which are on the earth: fornication, impurity, lust, evil desire, and avarice, which is idolatry." For in these things we do the devil's will and carry out his power, since through the desires of this flesh he works the enticement of his deceit.

Whomever, then, he finds in possession of his vices, he will claim as subject to his jurisdiction. Someone commits adultery, indulges in luxury, plunders other people's goods: he is the devil's portion. But the chaste, the continent and the merciful man is Christ's portion. So the devil cannot claim Christ's servant for himself, unless perhaps he catches him fallen into vice. Even then he does not claim him outright, but demands that he be handed over to him as his own.

So David says, "I have done judgment and justice," not to boast but to excuse himself, lest he be deserted by Christ as a sinner. Let the reading from the apostle be an example to us of why anyone is handed over. For the man who had his father's wife, because he acted in this way, was handed over to Satan, as the apostle says. He would not have been handed over, then, had he not done the works of the devil.

Not without reason, therefore, does the prophet refuse to be handed over to the wicked, pleading that he has done not the works of the devil but those of Christ. For Christ says: "Judge for the orphan and do justice to the widow." This, then, is "I have done judgment and justice": in judgment I did not despise the poor, I did not oppress the widow, I did not show partiality to the rich, and in all my works I preserved justice.

The end of judgment is justice. In the one lies the guarding of truth, in the other the fruit of equity; yet neither is a private virtue, but a public one. For to keep the body unstained by union with a man, and by guarding one's integrity to carry the palm of chastity in a body of clay up to the life of the angels, is a private benefit and a public praise. To be frugal and modest and to keep to the measure of sober thrift wins the approval of many, but profits oneself alone.

Fortitude stands out in battle and grows cold in peacetime. Its work is necessary at certain times, but it runs against our wishes, for people would rather not fight than win. Justice alone was born at all times for others rather than for itself, in daily use and for the public good. At its own cost it guards the interests of others, gaining no advantage for itself and very great praise.

This, then, the prophet puts forward to commend his merit, saying: I have done judgment and justice; do not hand me over to those who harm me. Where there is justice, there is mercy; mercy sets free from sin. How then am I handed over to sinners? Like this is the passage in the Song: I have put off my garment; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them? I have put off the garment of the sinner and the earthly veil; why am I judged as a sinner and an earthly man? I have washed my feet, so that no stain of wrongdoing could cling to my footstep. Why do you give wrongdoers power over me?

The second verse follows: Uphold your servant for good; let not the proud slander me. As one conscious of judgment and justice, he goes forward with prophetic authority, so that he does not shrink from calling himself the Lord's servant; for the servant of the Lord owes nothing to strangers. Precious is this servitude, which is paid for with the outlay of virtues. Why he fears being handed over to those who harm him, he plainly discloses: because they are slanderers who hate the truth and attack innocence,

because they are proud. For how proud toward God's lowly servants can he be who exalts himself against God and says: I will ascend into heaven, I will set my throne above the stars of heaven, I will sit on a lofty mountain above the high mountains that lie to the north, I will ascend above the clouds and be like the Most High? What wonder, then, if he can oppress men, who in his stubborn spirit does not yield even to God?

How will he keep the measure of truth and good faith toward man, who with sacrilegious and shameless falsehood promises that he will make himself equal to the almighty Lord? How would he not slander individuals, who provoked the whole earth, shook kings, made the whole world a desert and destroyed its cities, and did not release those who were in captivity?

Let us beware, then, lest he destroy the walls of our soul, lest he tear down the ramparts of our mind, lest he set his throne above the stars. He sets it above the stars when he deceives one of the elect, when he ensnares a just man whose works shine like stars in heaven. Did not Judas the traitor also hear among the rest: You are the light of this world? And did not the devil put out his light?

Moreover, those he could not ensnare he slanders, begrudging them the glory of the heavenly kingdom, so that those whom he could not separate from Christ by his enticements he tries by his slanders to cheat of the fruit of the honor due to them. Let us flee, then, the wicked slanderers, who work sin in us and then themselves compose slanders against us with the most hostile accusations, charging us with what they themselves have done. See, the hand of the Lord is ready to guard and protect you as you flee from your adversaries.

Pharaoh, proud and pitiless, held you in [?] his own land. You fled from him; the hand of the Lord upheld you and freed you from dangers. Pharaoh would not have let you go had you not fled for refuge to the Lord. Pharaoh said: I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go. You see how proud he was. Rightly, then, is he upheld for good who flees from evil. God, then, does not allow us to remain in evil; he upholds us for good and does not allow his own to lie exposed to slanders.

My eyes have failed for your salvation, and for the word of your justice. Consider what these eyes are that fail toward Christ while they await his coming: the eyes of the soul, clearly, not of the body, fixed with the whole intent of faith. For we are taken up with all our eyes in the one we love, and it delights us to see nothing else. No one can say this except one who has turned the whole attention of his mind away from worldly cares and the pleasures of this age.

For how can someone say this who is taken up with the frivolities of the theater? But he says it who said above: Turn away my eyes, lest they see vanity. And what are the eyes that fail for the word of God, if not the eyes of the inner man and the gaze of the soul, which strain to see the Word of God and, through excessive intentness and expectation, fail for the salvation of God, enduring their own failing in order to take on what belongs to the Word?

And because 'the word of God' could trouble many, he therefore added: the word of justice, so that it should not trouble them. It could trouble them, though, because it is written: The elder shall serve the younger — for unless you take it as a mystery, it is an injury to nature — and: I gave you precepts that were not good — does God, then, give bad precepts? —

— and: I am the Lord, who create evils. But the question of the precepts is resolved thus: he ought not to give the weak perfect precepts, which they could not bear. When would a Jew have listened to: Leave all you have and follow me? When would a Jew have listened to: Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me?

Rather, these more perfect precepts were reserved for the gospel. And God did not create evils, but those things that seem harsh to us — blows, death and other things of the kind — which were prescribed for correction [?]; for the law is not laid down for the just, but for the unjust. For if the guilty feared nothing, the innocent would always be afraid.

What, then, are these eyes that fail for the salvation of God? We have said that there is an eye of punishments, which, foreseeing the punishments to come upon sinners, proclaims that repentance must be done. John the Baptist displayed this eye when he said: Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come?

Bear fruits, therefore, worthy of repentance. To John's baptism came the one who had the eye of punishments, but to Christ's baptism comes the one who sees grace; for this is the eye that the shadow of the Lord's passion guards and protects. Aenon, then, is one thing, Ain another: in Aenon is baptized one who is conscious of grave sins, but whoever has a pure eye receives spiritual grace.

And perhaps the eye of punishments belongs to the imperfect soul, while the eye of graces, purer and more sincere, belongs to the perfect one. It is this eye that is signified by this letter, by which the pattern of the just man is directed. For the imperfect soul desires only to escape the judgment on sin, while the perfect soul desires to gain the merit of the heavenly kingdom. We presume, however, that one and the same soul has both eyes, the eye of punishments and the eye of grace: the left eye of punishments, the right of grace, because men cannot be perfect from the start but climb by progress in virtue. First, then, every soul comes, as it were, to the baptism of John,

to put repentance for its sins first; and then, progressing little by little, once it has wept over its sins and been washed by spiritual baptism, it receives the sacrament of Christ. Hence the Church also seems to be proclaimed in the Song of Songs, to whom it is said: You have captured our heart, my sister, my bride, you have captured our heart with one of your eyes. This, then, would be the eye of grace, which has gained for itself a fuller love of Christ.

Many, however, take this passage to mean the two eyes of the Church, one that sees mystical things and the other moral things, because the holy Church not only holds to the discipline of morals but also teaches the secrets of the heavenly mystery. Hence it is said of her: Your eyes are like doves, apart from your silence. For she both sees spiritually and knows that there is a time to be silent and a time to speak, so that she brings forth her word at the proper time, lest by speaking out of season she fall into sin.

Have, then, the eyes of a dove, after the likeness of Christ, for of him we read: Your eyes are like doves upon the abundance of waters, washed in milk, sitting upon fullness. The Lord baptizes in milk, that is, in sincerity, and those are truly baptized in milk who

believe without guile and offer a pure faith; they put on spotless grace. Therefore the bride ascends in white to Christ, because she was baptized in milk. Therefore the powers marvel at her, saying: Who is this who ascends, made white? A little before, she was saying: I am black. Now she is seen made white; she ascends to heaven and, leaning on the Word of God, already reaches the heights. Not without reason is there an abundance of waters where Christ is, so that the human mind longs to be filled. For these waters the deer thirsts, and once it has drunk them it can thirst no more. For these waters the prophet thirsts when he says: My soul has thirsted for you.

Christ, therefore, sits upon the abundance of waters and upon fullness. And so the one who is baptized in milk says: And we have all received from his fullness. Hence the eye of punishments, too, is not foreign to the Church, because, although John baptized in Aenon, he baptized near Salim, where there was an abundance of waters and twelve springs and seventy palm trees.

These springs the Church has: that is, in the Old Testament the twelve patriarchs, in the New the twelve apostles. And so it is said: In the church let us bless the Lord God from the springs of Israel. Whoever attains the sacred mysteries is first bathed in these springs; for these springs, flowing from the eternal spring, have streamed over the whole world.

Where these springs are, there is the ascent of souls. Indeed, Salim has been interpreted as 'the one ascending'; for he truly ascends who lays aside his own sins. By this word, then, the practice of purifying sanctification is expressed. Hence Christ also says fittingly to the Church in the Song: Your teeth are like a flock of shorn goats that have come up from the washing, all of which bear twins, and there is none barren among them. On the surface this is said of goats, but mystically of the Church's flock.

Do not think these animals mean. Listen, indeed, to what the Holy Spirit says of them: Your hair is like a flock of shorn goats that have been revealed from Mount Gilead; your teeth are like a flock of shorn goats that have come up from the washing. You see that this flock feeds on the heights; you hear 'from the mountain'. So where there are precipices for others, there is no danger for goats; where others face danger, there this flock finds its food; there the food is sweeter, there the fruit is choicer.

Their shepherds watch them hanging from a thorny crag, where wolves cannot make their raids, where fruitful trees provide unspoiled fruit. One may see them swollen with rich milk, anxious with a mother's devotion over their tender young. Therefore the Holy Spirit chose them to compare with the assembly of the venerable Church.

And to hear it mystically: the 'hair' in this saying is the loftiness and a certain eminence of just souls, since the sense of the wise man is in his head; for it is certain that wisdom lies in the heights of human thought. And just as goats are shorn to put off what is superfluous, so too the holy Church has a flock of shorn souls, that is, the virtues of many souls. In this flock you could find nothing senseless, nothing superfluous, since faith has made them wise and spiritual grace has cleansed them from every stain of superfluity.

Rightly, then, the souls of the just have been revealed, and revealed from Mount Gilead, that is, from the migration of testimony, because the heavenly testimony migrated from the synagogue to the Church. On this mountain, then, grow incense, resin and other perfumes, which those Ishmaelite merchants, as you have it in the first book of the Old Testament,

were carrying. The Church has these perfumes, which merchants gathered from the Gentiles have brought by faith and devotion. And so, just as goats, refreshed with good food and flourishing in the warmth of the sun, are washed in the river and rise from the river clean and exulting, so the souls of the just come up from the spiritual washing.

These are truly the ones that bear twins, in whom there is no barrenness of any virtue, no sterility of merits. Well do they bear twins, because they double their senses. Hence you have it written in Proverbs: And write these things for yourself threefold, in counsel and knowledge. He first set down a threefold writing and then added two things, counsel and knowledge; but knowledge is twofold, one of incorporeal things, the other of corporeal.

We have spoken of fruitfulness; let us speak of teeth. For many people, when they are sailing or hurrying along a journey by land and see some lovely spot, linger there for the pleasure of it, feasting their eyes and refreshing their minds, and it is not counted a delay to the journey but a delight.

So too it is our pleasure to consider the most beautiful teeth of just souls. For Scripture has taught that the teeth of the just are most beautiful, saying, literally of the patriarch Judah but spiritually of Christ: His eyes are cheerful with wine, and his teeth like milk. In this it proclaimed not the functions of human flesh but the gifts of divine grace. The example teaches, then, that teeth should not be passed over once we have spoken of eyes.

What, then, are the teeth of just souls, if not those that receive food that is shapeless and hard, or often cold, or excessively hot, and now grind it, now warm it, now temper it, according to the quality of the food? They grind what is hard, lest the harshness of the letter in the Old Testament and the rigidity of worldly understanding, unless broken down by a spiritual tooth, should block the passages for wholesome food and, through careless greed, choke the vital organs themselves and, as it were, the throat of the soul.

It is right, then, that you first divide your food, if what you take seems solid, and break it up, and once it is softened pass it, without any harm to the soul, into all its members by natural distribution, so that its whole body may feast on the life-giving juice. Take nothing corpse-like, nothing dead into your mouth, lest it be said: Their throat is an open grave; but drink in the living word, so that it may work in the inward parts of your mind.

These teeth are whiter than milk, because they are the teeth of the just. Indeed, although all our fathers were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, still it is not idly written that all ate the same spiritual food and all drank the same spiritual drink, so that a greater brightness might come to these teeth of the saints. For we know that after the crossing of the Red Sea they were cleansed by the bitter spring of Marah, sweetened by the grace of the wood; then by drinking from the twelve springs; and finally by the stream from the rock pouring forth spiritual water; for the rock was Christ.

Therefore they also ate manna, so that, washed so many times, they might eat the bread of angels, as it is written. Now too, in the mysteries of the gospel, you recognize that although you have been baptized in your whole body, you are afterward still cleansed by spiritual food and drink.

Rightly, then, David, purified in both his inner eyes and his teeth, brings forth words as if lit by the whiteness of spiritual teeth, saying: I have done judgment and justice. For that is the true brightness of teeth, where there rings out the melodious confession of a mind with a good conscience; that is the clean eye which no beam of grave sins

has weighed down, which no speck of slight impurities has troubled. This eye of justice has failed; for whoever clings to Christ is one spirit with him. Balaam, too, asked that his soul might fail among the souls of the just, that is, that he might forget his own error, lay aside what was his own, and take on what belongs to justice and equity. But let us go on to the rest.

There follows: Deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your just ways. He has prepared the way and presumed upon increases to his commendation. Above, he asked not to be handed over to those who harm him; then he asked to be upheld for good, so that the proud might not slander him. That is: 'I do not shun judgment, but the slander of the faithless; for they do not know how to judge, they know only how to slander. I take refuge with you, who know how to render judgment.'

And rightly he does not wish to be handed over to slanderers; for the just man Job suffered much after he was handed over to the one who harms. But that was a hard and great contest, which hardly anyone could easily have won without Job's exceeding patience; and yet he was not handed over entirely, but his better part was exempted. He who says: Do not hand me over, includes the greater things. And we exist more in the soul than in the flesh; for it is said to the just: But you are not in the flesh but in the spirit. He refuses, then, to have his soul handed over, who in his body was wasting away like a spider.

Here, then, with a greater degree of familiarity, presuming on better things, he says: Deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your just ways. He asks that mercy be shown him and that he be taught just ways. Elsewhere too [that is, in later verses] you have this sense: And do not enter into judgment with your servant. For, conscious of our sins, we ought rather to ask for our God's mercy than to implore his justice; the one grants pardon, the other imposes scrutiny.

What hope have men of contending with him from whom hidden things are not hidden, from whom sins cannot lie concealed? And therefore, knowing his power, the one who did not fear man says: Against you alone have I sinned. The just man cannot deny this, because no one is without sin; nor can a king, because, although he has the laws in his power so that he may offend with impunity, he is still subject to God; indeed, he who has been entrusted with more owes more.

This, then, is what he is saying: 'Deal with your servant according to your mercy, because even if I have done some good, as a servant I owe more.' A servant is not discharged by a single deed, for no one who has a servant plowing or tending sheep says to him: Come along, sit down at table, but says to him: Prepare something for my supper, and gird yourself and serve me. Does the servant receive thanks for having done what he was commanded?

So even when we have done what we were commanded, we ought not at once to exalt ourselves but rather to humble ourselves, because if we have done something, we have not thereby fulfilled all the duties of servitude. Who could repay with worthy service such great gifts of nature, the divine benefits of life and of salvation preserved? Who can pay back what he has received? And so, knowing all this, he asks for mercy rather than a hearing, because, he says, no living man shall be justified in your sight.
The fifth verse follows: I am your servant; give me understanding, and I shall know your testimonies. Understanding is a spiritual gift, and so what is God's is asked of the Lord.

Nor does he ask as a stranger, since he confesses himself a servant; well does he say: I am your servant. For a servant does his master's will, a servant seeks the wages of service and hopes for a reward. The servant of the Lord cannot also be the servant of sin, and so he asks that understanding be given him, so that he may guard against sin. He did indeed have understanding, but not so much that he thought he had it in abundance; he seeks a richer understanding.

There is a natural understanding, and there is also an understanding that is not good. That is why Solomon says: But good understanding gives grace. For if all understanding were good, there would have been no need for the addition. Rightly, then, he seeks the grace of his Lord; for he cannot otherwise know his Lord's secrets unless he has received the gift of spiritual understanding. You have this in Jeremiah: Make it known to me, Lord, and I shall know; because unless God makes his mystery known to men, we cannot know it.

The sixth verse follows: It is time to act, Lord; the wicked have scattered your law. Well does he say it is time to act; for there is a time to be silent and a time to speak. But the time to speak has come, and so he declares that it is already the time of the Lord's coming. Since the law has been transgressed, let the end of the law come, its consummation and fullness, the Lord Jesus, to forgive men all their sins, to cancel the bond of their debts, absolve them all and set sinners free.

It is time to act — as when the severity of some illness grows worse and you run to the doctor so that he may come more quickly, lest later he be unable to help. For the doctor is most wanted when a grave sickness has settled on the patient. So when the holy prophet sees in the spirit the transgressions of the people — luxury, self-indulgence, deceit, fraud, greed, drunkenness — he runs to Christ as though interceding for us, knowing that he alone could relieve such great sins; he urges him to come and will brook no delay.

It is time to act, Lord, he says; that is: that you mount the cross for us and undergo death. The whole world is being driven into final peril: come to take away the sin of the world. Let life come to the dying, let resurrection come to those already buried. Let your deed bring help, since even your precepts could not avail. In the law there is precept, in the gospel ministry.

The whole people was blind and did not see its own Maker. The world was lame and wavered on the faltering step of faith. There was no one to apply a poultice, or oil, or a bandage. That woman of the Gospel had spent all her property on physicians. She was a figure of the human assembly that was gathering from the Gentiles, and the physicians of this world could not stanch the flowing blood and deadly discharge of her long-standing affliction.

The power of the ruler of the people had perished, and all his inheritance had died. Seeing this, the prophet says to Christ: "It is time to act, Lord." He does not say "to command" but "to act," because it was not an envoy or a messenger but the Lord himself who was going to save his people. He indeed knew the time and did not delay, but we did not know at what better time he might come to our help.

Or perhaps he wishes to be reminded by us and wishes to be asked. Indeed, if he is asked, he comes even before the time. He came to the fig tree before its season, and he came before the hour, as he says to his mother. She was asking on our behalf and urging him on, saying: "They have no wine, son." Jesus answered: "Woman, what is that to me and to you?

My hour has not yet come." And his mother, who knew his heart, says to the servants: "Do whatever he tells you." Jesus too, who had said that his hour had not come, did what he had put off before, for God made all things in their time.

Whatever he does is not out of season. Everything he has done is timely. To me too he came in his own time, for every time is opportune for salvation, and nothing is untimely when it is a matter of saving those in danger. But he wished to wait a while longer for the synagogue to amend. That is why he came to the fig tree before the time: he came early to the Jews and at the right moment to the Gentiles, early for those who would perish and fittingly for those who would believe.

The seventh verse follows: "Therefore I have loved your commandments above gold and topaz." The law is the herald of Christ. The precepts of the law therefore carry the hope of good things to come. For this is the Lord's commandment: "Take heed to yourself that you do not forsake the Levite all the time you live on the earth." Who is this Levite? You understand,

if you consider who it is that came to serve, who is a priest for ever. Another commandment says: "Observe the month of new grain and keep the Passover to the Lord your God," and further on: "In the place which the Lord your God shall choose for his name to be called upon there, you shall slay the Passover in the evening at the setting of the sun, at the time when you came out of Egypt." So the commandments of God bear signs of the redemption to come and tokens of the resurrection. That is why he records that they are dearer to him than gold and topaz. For what is more welcome than salvation, or more precious than resurrection?

Or else he speaks this way because Christ chose the foolish things of the world, so that, since the world did not know God through wisdom, he might bring salvation to believers through the foolishness of preaching. So he says: "Above the wisdom of the heavenly workmanship and the ordering of the world, above the adornments of the sun and moon and the precious necklaces of the stars, I have loved the obedience of the Lord's passion. For he bestowed more on me by redeeming me than by creating me. Then I was born without awareness, but now I have been saved with my own will."

But not everyone says: "I have loved your commandments above gold and topaz." The miser who broods over his gold and gapes after riches does not say it. He longs for ornaments. The one who says it is the one who can say: "Silver and gold I have none, because I do not seek it, because gold profits me nothing; but the heavenly precept and commandment has redeemed me."

We have stated the gist of the meaning. Now let us set out the story of the topaz stone. We find it written in the history of Xenocrates, who wrote a kind of Lithognomon, a guide to stones, that it is produced or found near the city of the Thebaid called Alabastrum, or Topazion, as some think. It is therefore named after the place where it is produced.

There are others who thought that Topazion was the name of an island. Some Troglodytes, they say, were driven to it when a sudden storm arose at sea, and since they had no knowledge of ships, they could not get back. Then, after staying there a very long time,

they found a stone on the island. Delighted with its colour, they went back home and sold it to Arab merchants who came to them. Philo bought it from these merchants and brought it himself to the mother of Ptolemy the Second, whose name was Berenice. Although she had royal ornaments in abundance, she was astonished beyond measure at its colour and took pains that the beauty of so precious a stone should stay hidden no longer. And so, through her zeal, the stone was sought out and came into more frequent use.

We have told how the topaz stone became known. Now let us speak more precisely about its qualities. In this stone there is a krasis of two colours, that is, a balanced blending. It is leek-green and gold-looking, like chrysoprase, and in both colours it spreads out patterns, as it were. Experts say it spreads them out more fully than chrysoprase. It is also parygrus [?], quite clear, gold-coloured and rich, like something shining, especially when the brightness of the sun strikes it. It is

also very beautiful, and remarkable above all chrysoprases for its size and, as I said, richer to the eye. Its nature is such that if you try to polish and smooth it, it becomes rougher, and it wears away with use. By a certain innate working of nature it is euglyphus, that is, finely marked and wonderful. And so that it might be thought worthy of the greatest pursuit, it is hard to come by, and even when it is found it is seldom in human use, being a stone that a wealthy queen admired.

But enough now. Just as those Troglodytes went back home once they had found, as it were, the reward for their stay, so let us too, having gained the profit of this delay, return to the point from which we turned aside. Nor is it fitting for us to stretch the arms of our discourse any longer toward royal ornaments, when we hold in our hands the cross of Christ. The prophet urges us to prefer it above gold and topaz, for it calls us back from every error and fault and sets us right.

For who among the righteous would not seek the comfort of Christ's death and fellowship in his resurrection? Who would not turn his steps back when he hears that all his past sins are forgiven him? For this used to hold very many back from their zeal for conversion: conscious of their offences, they dared to hope for no pardon, and they thought that the holier the Church's precepts were, the less pardonable sins were.

So in the eighth verse he says: "Therefore I was set right in all your commandments; I have hated every unjust way." He was rightly set right, since he loved, for love covers a multitude of sins. See how much it covers and how much it sets right: "Love is patient, is kind. Love is not envious, does not act wrongly, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own, is not provoked, thinks no evil, does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never fails."

Further on he set down three perfect things, hope, faith and love, and he called love the greater, and rightly so, for love hopes all things and believes all things. Since hope and faith are contained within love, there is no doubt that love is greater. And the prophet is well in agreement with himself. For above he said: "The law of the Lord is blameless, converting the soul." If the law converts the soul,

then surely the one who loves is a lover of the law. Then again, in this same 118th Psalm he put first: "Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord." If he who walks in the law of God is undefiled, then surely he who loves the law of God is converted. So if the law makes a person undefiled, love rightly covers a multitude of sins, because love is the fulfilment of the law.

"I have hated every unjust way," he says. If he who loves the precepts of justice does the things he loves, then surely he who hates iniquity does not do what he detests. And it is with good reason that he who hates every way of iniquity is set right in all the Lord's precepts.

For unless you hate every way of iniquity, you cannot be set right in all God's precepts. It can happen that someone holds back from the horror of cruelty, and yet, deceived by the slippery love of a harlot, once he has set foot on the paths of youthful incontinence, he cannot draw his foot back. For the more alluring vices deceive many, while grim and excessively harsh cruelty repels most people. But youth is freer in love, more careless of falling, more fragile in weakness,

and harder to correct. Another man restrains himself from luxury but is carried off by the lust of avarice. Sins are mostly of this kind: if you avoid one, you run into another, and natural habit aids our weakness. You hate luxury as a thrifty man, but under the pursuit of thrift the greed for possessions often creeps in.

And robbery follows close on avarice itself. How much more tolerable it is to squander one's own goods than to plunder another's! There are those who are so afraid of reducing their wealth at all that they refuse to spend anything even on the needy, and who count mercy as a loss. There are those who, shunning a mean obscurity, are tossed by the gusts of worldly ambition and, like shaken reeds, are carried this way and that, unsure of themselves. There are also those who follow the condition of their forefathers and, content with it as though it were a worthy way of life, do not think that even their ancestral errors should be abandoned. So they do not consider that faithlessness should be exchanged for faith, although changing one's purpose for the better is not fickleness but virtue, not a fault but a grace.

One man, lured by the games of the circus or the pleasures of the theatre, or busy with other vanities, does not come to church often. Another is delighted by the quiet of the countryside, and for that reason seldom comes to church. And so by different habits both run into the same error of indifference to God. But he who hates every way of iniquity is set right and amended in all things. And he did well to say "way of iniquity," for the man who has not entered the ways of iniquity avoids it more easily.
XVII. The letter Phe.

Phe, the seventeenth letter, means in Latin "I have erred" or "I have opened my mouth." Fittingly, then, a tearful passage of the psalm is placed under this letter: "Look upon me and have mercy on me, and let no iniquity have dominion over me. Make your face shine upon your servant." This was so that the light of heavenly mercy might rise for the people that sat in the shadow of death, and that Christ might come, the forgiveness of sins, the redemption of captives, the help of those in distress. But since to those who longed for him he seemed slow in coming, he says: "My eyes have shed streams of water."

In the Lamentations of Jeremiah too there is an even more tearful passage under this letter: "Zion has spread out her hands; there is none to comfort her." She received a fitting recompense. She had neglected to listen to him who spread out his hands, and to come under his wings, so afterwards she herself spread out her hands and could find no one to comfort her.

Jeremiah, before the Lord's coming, seems to be lamenting the captivity that the Babylonians brought upon the Jews. Yet by the prophetic spirit he foresaw rather this other captivity, in which the spiritual Babylonian has bound them in the chains of perpetual error, has made them

exiles from the virtue that was their own, has driven them out of the devotion of their fathers, and has afflicted them with banishment to a distant land. It is this that he laments with pitiable grief. For there is no truer homeland than faith. Faith has brought near those who were far off, and has joined strangers and sojourners by the rights of the heavenly city, as it is written: "So then you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but you are fellow citizens of the saints and members of God's household."

Elsewhere too Jeremiah says under this letter: "All your enemies have opened their mouths against you. They hissed and gnashed their teeth. They said: We have swallowed her up. Yet this is the day we hoped for; we have found it, we have seen it." And here too, just as the Jewish people opened its mouth against Christ, as you have read in the twenty-

first psalm concerning his passion, that they opened their mouth and cursed, you recognize the lot of a fitting recompense: they themselves were to suffer such things from their enemies, and that spiritual sinner, the devil, was to gnash his teeth at them like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour. These people, then, did not say: "Blessed be the Lord, who has not given us as a prey to their teeth," because they did not think they should hope in the Lord. So the devil found the destruction of them that he had counted on. He swallowed them up, since the offended shepherd was not there to draw out of the lion's mouth the legs of the sheep or a piece of its ear.

They would not follow; they would not listen. Therefore, when the shepherd departed, the lion seized their feet and ears in his jaws, because they did not respect the face of the saints and showed no mercy to the nobles, as Jeremiah says for the third time under this letter in Lamentations. Who were the nobles, if not those who lived not this obscure life but in the light of holiness? Mercy is indeed rightly owed to all the needy. But a greater feeling of compassion is stirred when misfortune has cast some from among the rich and noble down to the lowest state and the necessity of want.

Jeremiah, then, laments very tearfully, as one mourning those lost through the sting of everlasting death. But David laments with restraint, as one grieving [?] over error, who did not despair of the remedy of correction, so that he was saddened but not swallowed up.

Then, strengthened by the sobriety of penitence and spurred on by the hope of pardon, he began thus: "Wonderful are your testimonies; therefore my soul has searched them out." It is a moral [?] prayer. Since he was ashamed of his error, he approached God by appealing to the testimonies of God's own mercy. It is as if he said: "At the beginning of my speech I do not dare to speak of my sins, or to lift my eyes to you, the living God.

But you, Lord, have moved me to hope for pardon by the record of your great acts of forgiveness. Wonderful are your testimonies! Abraham's lapse of youthful carelessness did not offend you. Instead you moved him to leave the errors of the Chaldeans and the kinship of his fathers, and when you had called him out, you trained him in the exercises of virtue. The Hebrew people turned away from zeal for their fathers' nobility and preferred the cheap food of Egypt to your divine gifts, yet you not only freed them by making the waves of the Red Sea solid, but also raised them to glory through many triumphs and gave them a fruitful land to possess for their rest.

Cherished in security, that people deserted you. Crushed by the bitterness of war, it called upon you and earned your forgetting of its wrongs against you. Joshua son of Nun recognized that you had come to him as commander of the heavenly host. The people, though triumphant, offended you, so that Midian ruled over them; they prayed to you, so that Midian was conquered. Under King Saul they did not obey you, so that foreigners triumphed over them; with David leading them they served you, so that they won victory over foreigners.

I too, a shepherd, did evil, and by confessing my sin I obtained pardon." So this is a most beautiful verse for encouraging martyrs. In this way the prophetic soul makes progress toward the better, as it believes the wonderful testimony of God and, because it believed, searches it out with diligent inquiry. Do you ask what this progress is? Recognize it from the verses that follow.

"The disclosure of your words enlightens me and gives understanding to little ones." In the Gospel, when John sent his disciples to the Lord Jesus, he said: "Are you the one who is to come, or do we look for another?" Jesus answered that the blind see, the lame walk and the deaf hear, for he had indicated through the prophet Isaiah that this would be the testimony of his coming.

So the things he announced through the prophets he made manifest in the Gospel, and what he himself spoke through the prophets he himself fulfilled in the Gospel. His word, then, was the prophetic word, as you have it written: "Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken."

Understanding, therefore, was given even to those who did not have perfect wisdom, when the dumb speak and the dead are raised. For by these signs those who were untaught and still, as it were, in the cradle of faith, as the people of the Gentiles were, understood that the one who was awaited had come. So he lights up the clarity of faith by the glory of his resurrection and by the power of his divine works, and gives understanding to little ones.

To whom, indeed, if not to those for whom he gives thanks to the Father in the Gospel, in the very thing which he, the Son, was accomplishing: that God had hidden his mysteries from the wise and revealed them to little ones? He was showing that the common people from the Gentiles, or men of lower rank, would believe sooner than the scribes and rulers of the Jews and the rich of this world. That is why the rich have been in want and gone hungry, but the poor man cried out and was heard.

The third verse follows: "I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit, for I longed for your precepts." We find in the Gospel that the Lord Jesus opened his mouth when he proclaimed the beatitudes. But he opened his mouth to give the Spirit to others; David opened his to receive it.

So Jesus says: "Receive the Holy Spirit." Jesus says: "Open your mouth wide and I will fill it." He says this to man, for Christ is fullness. He who fills all things fills your mouth. Write, then, what he says on the breadth of your heart, that is, let your mouth cry out to the Lord.

Your mouth cries out even when it is silent, just as Moses cried out in spirit even when his voice was silent. He was not heard by men, but he resounded before God, for there is a cry of the inner feeling that is heard from heaven. Hannah too cried out silently when she prayed. She did not move her lips, and with the devout voice of her inner mind she stirred Jesus. And so she who prayed in silence went home with her prayer granted, because the Spirit of God was crying out in her, the Spirit who cries even when we are silent: "Abba, Father."

Understand, then, what this mouth is, whether it is the heart or the disposition of the inner man. The soul has members, and so it has a mouth. Open this mouth not only to Christ but also to Christ's disciple, who offered his mouth to be filled by Christ and therefore says:

"Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged." So he urges that we ought to be imitators of him, as he is of Christ. Let the one who is holier open his mouth to Christ, and the one who is lesser to the apostle. Let the prophet be read first, then the apostle, and then the Gospel, in which the words are clear but the precepts stronger. The law says: "You shall love your neighbour," and the Gospel says to you: "You shall love your enemy."

David, then, as a perfect prophet, opened his mouth to Christ, and so he opened his mouth in parables. He opened his mouth and drew in the spirit. Rightly he says: "How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!" The bride of Christ opened her mouth to the bridegroom. She received precepts sweeter than any honey, and so she bore witness, saying: "His mouth is sweetness itself, and he is altogether desirable." Delighted, she held him and would not let him go. "And I brought him," she says, "into my mother's house, and into the inner chamber of her who conceived me."

Perhaps the house is where moral discipline shines out, and the inner chamber is where the loftier mysteries are. Rightly, then, did he long for the Lord's precepts, which were fragrant with the honey of divine grace. Is not the forgiveness of sins sweeter than any honey, and the resurrection of the dead more pleasing than any flower?

The fourth verse: "Look upon me and have mercy on me, according to the judgment of those who love your name." He did well to add "have mercy on me" to "look upon me," because God also looks when he is angry. So he looked upon the camp of the Egyptians, bound the axles of their chariots and cast them all down into the waves. He looked upon Sodom and Gomorrah, and both of them, paying the penalty for their sins, paid the price of offending God. It is also written: "You look upon the earth and make it tremble." And on the other hand: "He looked upon the gifts of Abel, but upon the gifts of Cain he did not look." Angered by this, Cain shed his brother's blood in the crime of murdering his kin.

What it means for God to look upon someone is shown most clearly by this testimony: "For he looked upon the sons of the poor and did not despise their prayers"; for the eye of the Lord does not spurn the gifts of the just. Indeed, when we are angry with someone, we turn our eyes away, as though we judged the one we hate in our heart unworthy of our gaze.

There follows: "Direct my steps according to your word, and let no iniquity have dominion over me." Frequent testimonies of the Scriptures remind us that "steps" are to be understood as the progress of the soul. For who is so dull

of mind as to think that David was anxious about the bodily stepping of his feet and was asking for divine direction to help them? No, as a holy man he longed to have the course of his life directed, as Scripture also testifies elsewhere: "A man's steps are directed by the Lord." Indeed, let us use the testimony of David himself, who says in an earlier psalm: "My steps had nearly slipped, because I envied the peace of sinners."

So he shows that the step of his mind had limped, when he thought the peace of sinners something to marvel at. They do seem to have tranquillity, they do seem to enjoy quiet, but there is no quiet where the mind is restless, and there is no tranquillity of mind where the mind is harried by the goads of a guilty conscience. How can there be security

where there is a battle of conflicting passions and a clash of violent emotions? That is why the Lord, defining what it is to have peace, says: "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give to you; not as the world gives do I give to you." He shows that the peace the world gives does not have the grace of true peace. And wishing to teach that peace does not lie in man, he added: "Peace I leave with you," and again: "My peace I give to you." Indeed the prophet said: "Peace, peace; and where is peace?" It is clear, then, that David spoke of the wavering of his judgment, in which it was the step of his mind, not of his body, that had faltered.

And Moses said: I will turn aside and see this great sight. For in order to see God, he advanced to higher things by a kind of progress in virtue. He was a shepherd of sheep, and he became a leader of citizens. And in the Song of Songs it is said to the bride: How beautiful your steps have become in sandals, daughter of Aminadab! The curves of your thighs are like necklaces, the work of a craftsman. There is no doubt that here too the steps signify the progress of the Church or of the soul: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of peace, who bring good news of good things!

Surely he calls beautiful the progress of gospel preaching and teaching, as it is said elsewhere: Cross over the rivers. That is: run past the flowing and slippery things of this world with a steady step of the mind. That this is said of the soul's step David himself plainly shows later on, when he declares that his soul had crossed the torrent of iniquities.

But let us return to the bride's steps. What does it mean that he added that the Church's steps are beautiful in sandals? We read what was said to Moses: Loose the sandal from your feet. By this he seems to have been warned not to be held bound by bodily fetters. So in the Song of Songs the beautiful one signifies the beauty of the soul, which uses the flesh as a sandal, yet suffers no hindrance in that sandal, but excels in the grace of its gait. The soul, then, shoes itself with the flesh [by the Church's grace],

so that it may pass through the course and passage of this life with grace. This happens if it does not soil its sandal with the mud of the body or plunge it into the abyss of vices, if it chastises its flesh, so that it is not slowed in running or weighed down by the burden of rich fat.

A good sandal for the soul is modesty; a good step is one set in the track of chastity. Wisdom, on the other hand, is the soul's cloak; hence it is written: Honor her, and she will embrace you. Let us therefore use the body as a sandal for the works of the lower virtue: for service, not for command; for compliance, not for pleasure; for obedience, not for discord. And let us set our footstep in the way of wisdom, so that no force of the torrent may hem in our steps.

That is why it was said to Moses: Loose your sandal; it was said also to Joshua son of Nun. But to Christ it was not said; rather it is written, in the words of the Baptist: After me comes a man whose sandals I am not worthy to carry,

because those men, who could not be without sin, are rightly warned to loose their sandal. But he not only did not loose his own sandal; he even loosed the sandals of others, because he not only kept his own body free from sins but also granted forgiveness of the sins of all. So the Church, in imitation of Christ, is beautiful even in her sandals, washed clean of every fault.

And perhaps when she speaks wisdom among the perfect, she is beautiful in her upper members; but when people of lower station or learning also follow the word, do not forget the sequence of the faith, and keep the precepts of the priest, she is beautiful in her sandals. Often the clergy has gone astray, the priest has changed his opinion, the rich have sided with the earthly king of this world: the people has kept its own faith. Hence we may also rightly say of the Lord Jesus

that the Word has beautiful steps even in things that are bodily, when moral questions are discussed. And perhaps the apostles are sent barefoot for this reason, so that their teaching might not be overshadowed but might shine out. So the Church, the daughter of Aminadab, that is, of the willing or well-pleasing one, because the willing and well-pleasing one gathered her together, is beautiful in her sandals as well.

And rightly it is added in the Song: The curves of your thighs are like necklaces, the work of a craftsman's hands, so that the ornaments of the Church's posterity might be celebrated in song. For in the thigh we recognize the emblem of generation, according to the verse: Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty. By this it is signified that the Son of God, when he had emptied himself, girded with the divinity of the Word and shod with human birth, would come forth from a virgin to give salvation to all.

Now "moduli" is the name for the precious ornaments that are usually hung on the necks of matrons. So great an advance of the Church is signified that it is compared to the most precious ornaments and to the torques of those who triumph; for these are the ornaments of warriors. That is why Symmachus said peritrachēlia, that is, "things worn around the neck." So whether it is the generation of Christ from the virgin or the spread of the Church, in outward appearance it has adorned the necks of the faithful as with torques made by a craftsman's hand, but in truth it has crowned them with the spiritual insignia of virtue.

In short, this whole description of the Church's members is full of beauty and praise. For her navel too is proclaimed to be like a turned bowl never lacking mixed wine, because, being shaped in all teaching, it does not lack fullness of knowledge or spiritual drink. And her belly is not only fattened with a heap of wheat, that is, with the stronger food of the heavenly mystery, but is also filled, as with lilies, with the sweetness of moral teaching.

Hence she too, as a queen who has well deserved it, is crowned with the blood of Christ, as it is written: And the adornment of your head is like purple. The blood of Christ is purple; it dyes the souls of the saints, resplendent not only in color but also in power, because it makes kings, and better kings, to whom it grants an eternal kingdom.

And rightly, at such great beauty of the Church, on which the blood of Christ glows red, the Holy Spirit cries out: How beautiful and sweet you have become, O love, in your delights! Beautiful with the grace of virtue, sweet with the delight of grace and the remission of vices, she whom no bitterness of sin troubles, and who is now herself love, having received that very name by loving her Lord. For God is love.

Rightly, then, David asks that his steps be directed according to the word of God, so that they too may become beautiful and iniquity may not rule over him. He was right to guard against this. For he knew that Abraham too, though he directed his steps according to the Lord's precepts, was tested when the chastity of his beautiful wife was assailed, yet was not put to shame; and that when the sacrifice of his only son was demanded, he wrestled with the tender love of a father's heart, yet was crowned. He knew that he himself, assailed by the deadly temptations of wicked iniquity in the fury of Saul, the incest of Amnon, and the parricide of Absalom, had escaped by this alone: that, directing his steps according to the Lord's goodness, he did not depart from a father's affection, groaning within himself over the crime of incest and banishing from himself hatred of the parricide. My son Absalom, my son, he said, Absalom, who will grant me to die for you? His tender love was mindful of nature, forgetful of the offence; earlier he had asked about him: Is the young man alive?

And perhaps we should ask why he first said "young man" and afterward called him "son"; why he did not say either "young man" or "son" in both places. While he was alive, he was a "boy," because he was seeking his father's life by parricide; so he ought not to receive a name of family affection, but one of immaturity. And so the just man kept silent what belonged to the sacred bond and used what belonged to immaturity. But once he was dead, the person's crime vanished in the eyes of his loving father, and the name of nature remained.

There follows: Free me from the slander of men, and I will keep your commandments. Our affliction is not of one kind. There is temptation and there is slander; but temptation is lighter, slander heavier, since temptation can exist [without?] slander, while slander contains temptation within itself. There is also human temptation, which we are able to bear. But slander is grievous. And so the Lord took upon himself the things that are heavier, and when assailed by slanders, he offered a triumphant silence.

Slander is heavier for this reason: it not only fabricates falsehoods, but also discolors deeds done with piety. So Joseph was not only tempted by the offer of adultery and the enticement of his mistress's allure, but was also tested by slanders: it was fabricated that he had wanted to force that very adultery on his mistress, and that when caught he had stripped off his garment so as not to be held by a sign of the fraud and a mark of the crime, when in fact he had left his cloak behind as he fled precisely in order to escape the snares of the woman pressing him and the bonds of her seductive arts.

David himself had experienced what he feared: what slanders he suffered from King Saul! When everyone was terrified, he made sport of the Philistine's onslaught and in single combat took upon himself the whole outcome of the war and the weight of the entire battle, by his own valor alone refuting the disgrace they all shared and turning back on the enemy the reproach of the whole people. And yet, because the young women said: Saul has triumphed over thousands,

and David over tens of thousands, his glory was turned to envy, and he began to be harried by hatred. And to speak of later times: Susanna had a good conscience and yet could not defend herself before men. Two elders, old men, brought false testimony; the number of the priests and their old age took away the girl's voice; only her conscience was free before God. In the end, though condemned by the judgment of men, she was acquitted by the will of God.

Therefore the prophet says: Free me from the slander of men, that I may keep your commandments. For one who is oppressed by slander cannot easily keep the divine commandments; often he is bound to yield to sadness or fear, and to be afflicted either by fear of slander or by grief.

There follows the seventh verse: Make your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your righteous decrees. The Lord illumines his saints and shines in the heart of the righteous. So when you see a wise man, know that the glory of God has come down upon him

and has illumined his mind with the brightness of knowledge and of the understanding of God. He also illumined the face of Moses bodily, and the glory of his countenance was transfigured, and the Jews trembled when they saw it. That is why Moses put a veil over his face, so that the children of Israel would not gaze on it and be thrown into confusion.
