At the same time a mystery was being declared: the veil placed bodily on Moses' face was placed mystically on the hearts of the Jews, because they could not see the true brightness of the law. For the face of Moses is the brightness

of the law, and the brightness of the law lies not in the letter but in the spiritual understanding. So as long as Moses lived and spoke to the Jewish people, he had a veil over his face. But when Moses had died, Joshua son of Nun spoke to the elders and to the people no longer through a veil but with face unveiled, and no one trembled, even though God had said to him too that he would be with him as he had been with Moses and would likewise illumine him, with the glory of deeds, that is, not of countenance. By this the Holy Spirit signified that the true Jesus would come, and that if anyone turned to him and was willing to hear him, the veil would be taken from his heart and with face unveiled he would see the true Savior.

Therefore God the almighty Father, who in the face of Moses blinded the Jewish people, not out of harshness but out of foreknowledge, not out of malice but out of equity and justice (for those who refused to understand the law put the veil on themselves; for the law is spiritual, as the Hebrew said), he, surely, in keeping with what he gives to each of us, where the fault lies not with the giver but with the one who chooses, he, I say, the Lord, illumined the heart of the people of the nations in the face of Christ Jesus through his coming. This is plainly declared by the apostle's example, as we have it written: For God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ Jesus.

So David says to the Lord Jesus: Make your face shine upon your servant. He longed to see the face of Christ, so that his mind might be illumined. This can also be taken of the incarnation, for many prophets and righteous men wished to see it, as the Lord himself declared. But he was not asking for what had been denied to Moses, to see bodily the face of the incorporeal God, if indeed even Moses, so wise and learned, could have asked for this literally rather than in a mystery.

Yet it is human to stretch our desires beyond ourselves, and not without reason did he seek to see the face of him who was coming from the virgin, so that he might be illumined in heart, just as those too were illumined who said: Did not our heart burn within us while he opened the Scriptures to us? But if anyone prefers to take it as said to God the Father, the Son can be understood as the Father's face; for whoever sees the Son sees the Father also.
Yet the face of God illumines inasmuch as his eyes are upon the righteous. Although this must be understood spiritually, nevertheless, since

the story of the illumination of Moses' face has come up, let no one think it could not have happened bodily; let him take note. For through exposure to the sun the appearance of the whole body changes, even in many who are wasted with pallor; and the look of a glowing face spreads over those warmed by the heat of a fire. At daybreak the lands blush, suffused with saffron color, borrowing their appearance from the sun's gift. Necklaces

of gems too, as they glitter, pour onto what is near them the radiance they themselves give off. And do you marvel that the face of Moses was tinged with the brightness of the divine presence? Do you marvel that the mind of the righteous man glows with warmth as the grace of God shines upon it? The prophet had no doubt of it, for he asked first to be illumined, so that he might learn the Lord's righteous decrees.

My eyes have gone down in streams of waters, because I did not keep your law. He has powerfully expressed the feeling of a penitent, saying that his eyes went down in streams of waters, either because through them, as through channels of surging currents, a conduit, as it were, of overflowing tears poured itself out, a continuous and unbroken flood of streaming weeping; or because the eyes themselves went down. For the force of extreme grief has this effect, that with the tears the eyes themselves seem somehow to go down, because the force of the tears is so great that the eyes are thought to dissolve into weeping and pour themselves out in tears.

So the eyes themselves go down, as it were, in streams of waters. By this word the vehement rush of those who weep is [?] more vividly expressed, according to what is written in the Song of Songs: A fountain of gardens, a well of living water, and a rush coming down from Lebanon.

This rush led the Church down from Lebanon; by this rush sins are washed away; by this rush of the pure fountain of the Holy Spirit the bride came from Lebanon, and from the beginning of faith she passed through the world and passed on to the kingdom. According to our capacity, spiritual grace is to some a fountain, to others a well; to others a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed; to others the fountain of gardens which is counted among the Church's dowry; to others a rush coming down from Lebanon, a great rush that never fails.

For the breasts do not fail from the rock, nor the snow from Lebanon, nor the water carried by a strong wind of the virgin Jerusalem. The rush came down from Lebanon when, as the apostles were gathered together with many believers, suddenly there came a sound from heaven, as if the Spirit were being borne with great force, and all were filled with the Holy Spirit, who granted diverse tongues. Good is the rush that knows not how to harm, but knows how to fill.

So if anyone wishes to deserve this rush of grace coming down from heaven, let him too go down with his eyes in streams of waters. Whoever first pours out this rush will deserve that one. She went down with her eyes into these channels of waters who in the Gospel watered the Lord's feet with tears, and so by the price of her faith she bought health for her soul and body, a flow no longer of blood but of spiritual grace.

So David the prophet went down; that is why he obtained grace for his sin. He went down into the channels of waters, that is, he filled them and swelled the currents of running waters with his tears, or else filled empty and dry channels with his weeping alone.

Or, as a certain moral sense of the expression suggests, he went down into the channels of waters, that is, he passed over them; and we could say "he went beyond them and stepped over them." But then the force of the expression is diminished, since a greater force of abundance is conveyed by water going down than by water going up. See, I beg you, what words gain from usage, so that the prophetic utterance

does not lose its force, even though usage itself has been accustomed to serve the sense of the writers with greater elegance. He has expressed this in various ways and often, and almost always with some intensification. For first he said: Every night I will wash my bed; with my tears I will drench my couch. He said again: My tears have been my bread. He said also: And I mingled my drink with weeping. Here he went further, saying: My eyes have gone down in streams of waters.

Following this, Jeremiah in Lamentations expressed the feeling of grief, imitating the force of the descending eye; for this is what you find: My eyes have failed with tears; my eyes have grown dim. Eyes that fail in tears go down, as it were. And elsewhere: My eye is swallowed up.

But it is more to overcome water with tears than for the eyes to be swallowed up by weeping. And elsewhere the same Jeremiah: Their heart cried out to the Lord: Walls of the daughter of Zion, let them bring down torrents, let them flow with tears day and night; give yourself no rest, let not the pupil of your eye be silent. So the eyes that bring down torrents with their tears themselves go down the channels of waters, that is, they fill them up, so that, swelling them with their weeping, they make them overflow with the rush of torrents.

There are, however, manuscripts that read: diexodous hydatōn katebibasan hoi ophthalmoi mou, that is: My eyes have brought down channels of waters. But in my Greek manuscript I read katebēsan, that is: have gone down. In this case the scribe may have erred in either direction, by adding or by dropping two letters.

And indeed he had many things to weep over, whether the incest committed against his daughter or the deaths of his sons. But here he says he wept not for this, but because he did not keep the law of the Lord. A holy man laments guilt more than misfortune. So he wept when Nathan announced to him the Lord's indignation over the death of Uriah, and he acknowledged his sin of transgressing the law.

Then, when his son lay sick, he neither took food nor went up to the royal throne or bed, but lying on the ground he bathed his fasting face with tears, longing to wash away in the child not so much his son's death as the punishment of his own sin. He wept when, after numbering the people, he was suddenly stricken in heart. And so he said: I have sinned grievously, I have sinned foolishly.

He wept, then, first because, puffed up by royal power, he went beyond the measure of the human condition in seeking the number of the people; and then because the price of his error was being exacted from the people. But this punishment had been set by the Lord, not asked for by the king. Yet by entrusting himself to the Lord's mercy he showed good reason for his choice; and at the same time, since the people were suffering on his account, by offering himself for the people he paid for the offence of his pride and showed his loving affection.
XVIII. THE LETTER SADE

There follows the eighteenth letter of Psalm 118, "Sade," which in Latin translation means "consolation." After tears flowing like torrents and the heavy weeping of grief, consolation had to follow. For those who are in grief need consolation; those who have paid the penalty for crimes committed through heavy hardships hope for pardon; and those who have washed away their own faults with weeping and tears earn rest.

Whoever seeks all these things in the divine Scriptures finds them. The first, that we should console those in grief, is taught by her who in the book of Jeremiah cries out tearfully to the captive and exiled Jews: Go, set out, my children, for I am left desolate. I have taken off the robe of peace and put on the robe of my supplication, and I will cry to the Most High all my days. Take courage, children; cry to the Lord, and he will draw you out of the hand of hostile rulers. For I have hoped in the Eternal One for your salvation.

For those who believe in the Lord, then, there is consolation in the Lord's mercy. There is also another kind of consolation, for those who have paid heavy penalties, as you find written in the book of Isaiah: Comfort, comfort my people, says the Lord. Priests, speak to the heart of Jerusalem, comfort her, for her humiliation is complete;
her sin is pardoned, for she has received from the hand of the Lord double for her sins. Even if faith was lacking, punishment had made satisfaction;

those who are not absolved by the commendation of their merits are relieved by paying their penalties. The third is when guilt is washed away with tears, as in the verse: Depart from me, all you who work iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping. This is easily found both in this passage and in many places in the book of Psalms.

So the first consolation in order is that God does not forget to show mercy, nor does he cast off forever those whom he has judged in need of correction. The second is that, once the punishments we have endured for our sins have run their course, we come to pardon.

Hence some philosophers have argued that acquittal harms the wicked and death benefits them, because acquittal gives an incentive to wrongdoing, whereas death puts an end to sin. Who can doubt that this was taken from our own writings? For in the Proverbs of Solomon it says: He who spares the rod hates his son; and the Lord chastises those he loves. And further on: A whip for the horse, a goad for the donkey, and a rod for a foolish nation. For punishment corrects and amends the one who goes astray. If someone is such that he cannot be amended,

he is taken out of the way, so that he may not commit worse sins; for a dead man no longer knows how to go astray. And so Ecclesiastes says: And I praised the dead more than the living, and better than both is he who is not yet born, who has not seen this evil work. The dead man is preferred to the living because he has ceased to sin; the one not yet born is preferred to the dead because he has never known how to sin.

Now let us also speak of those who have paid the penalty for their crimes. Have they not paid the price of their guilt, and is the full punishment no longer owed them? The Lord cries out through Isaiah: Comfort

my people, for she has received from the hand of the Lord double for her sins. Learn where Plato took this from. He went to Egypt for the sake of learning, to come to know the oracles of the law of Moses and the sayings of the prophets. There he heard of the consolation of the people who seemed to have been punished beyond the measure of their sin,

and he carried this passage over into the dialogue he wrote on virtue, veiling it with a certain gift for words. Yet the Lord in the Gospel took up this passage more fully and declared it more openly, saying through the person of Abraham to that rich man of this world: Son, remember that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, while you are tormented. And besides all this, a great chasm has been fixed between you and us, so that those who come from here cannot cross over to you, nor pass from there to here. But now let us hear what the righteous man says as he consoles himself.

You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right. [You have commanded righteousness, your testimonies, and your truth exceedingly.] Truly righteous is the man who, though streaming with tears, wrapped in hardships and paying for his offenses with heavy punishment, is not

overcome by weariness, not broken by fear, not worn out by toil, not ungrateful or sullen. For the common run of people generally take no account of their own offenses and think that they suffer unjustly what they endure. But the righteous man accuses himself at the very opening of his speech and proclaims the justice of the Lord, saying that he suffers what his deserts merit. In calling God just, he first passes sentence on his own injustice, but from the Lord's justice he also hopes for pardon. For the Just One is not always angry: as he avenges guilt, so he moderates punishment; as he punishes sins, so he rewards virtues and the best of merits.

Whoever wishes to give a prize must watch the contest, because no one is crowned without a contest. So he often allows us to be tempted, wishing to give prizes justly to one who wrestles, surely, not to one who sleeps. The crown does not befit those wreathed in flowers, but those covered in dust; victory adorns not those softened by luxury, but those trained by toil.

So the righteous man praises the justice of God in his adversities. But this is not what a parent feels who has lost young children, nor one widowed by the untimely loss of his bride, nor the sick man in pain, nor the shipwrecked in danger, nor the accused in court, nor the captive in the snare. Yet Jeremiah cries out, when for announcing to the peoples the misery of the coming captivity he was sunk into the foul filth of a pit of mud to be put to death: You are righteous, O Lord.

He cries out again when he was in anguish over the pitiable slavery of the conquered people: The Lord is righteous, for I provoked his mouth. Outside he has left me childless, and within there is death. The Hebrews cried out when, because of the virtue of their devotion and the grace of their faith, they were surrounded by the flames of the burning furnace: You are righteous in all that you have done; and so they merited to proclaim the Lord's righteous deeds unharmed by the fire. Daniel

the prophet also, cast a second time into the lions' den and surrounded by the savagery and horror of monstrous beasts, declared with a fearless cry that all things are right in the sight of the Lord. Jonah, shut up in the belly of the beast, scarcely having passage for his breath, a righteous man condemned to the lot of the unrighteous, cried from the belly of the whale in the sea: With the voice of praise and confession I make supplication to you.

David, when he fled from the face of Absalom, driven out by parricidal arms and weapons and having left his kingdom, when he offered himself in place of the destruction of the whole people, said: You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right. What has this innocent flock done? It is I, the shepherd, who have done evil.

With a just God, let the punishment be exacted from the author of the guilt. Abraham himself, the father of faith, when his only son was demanded of the old man for sacrifice, tempered the affection of a father's love by confessing the divine justice, saying: You are righteous, O Lord. For you do not demand what belongs to another, but ask back what is yours; I restore to you the very one you gave. Imitating him, Job, when his children were dead and he was stripped by the loss of his patrimony, tore the garment of his body and said: Naked I was born, naked, he says, I shall also die. The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.

Let us all, then, proclaim the Lord righteous. Whether one is laying out his dying limbs for the tomb, or is struck by loss or by the death of his children, let him say: You are righteous, O Lord. For what of our own do we lose? The apostle cries out: What do you have that you did not receive?

What we have, then, we have received; what we lose, therefore, we give back; we do not lose it. The Lord is righteous in dangers, righteous in losses, righteous in punishments, not only because each person justly pays the price of his own guilt, but also because, while one is punished, very many are corrected. Ananias in the Acts of the Apostles, by defrauding the price he had received from the sale of a field,

committed a crime, though he could have offered nothing and escaped the crime. But so that no one would think the apostles could be cheated with impunity, or would defile the gift of his own mercy with the fraud of bad faith, he was consigned to eternal death, and by a just terror he brought everyone into order to pursue the faith. Pharaoh, drowned with his people in the waves, is an example for the conduct of the world, so that no one may persecute the people of God.

Indeed, God could have made him obedient to his will, but he wished all to be amended by his punishment, and so the Lord says to him: For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth. The Lord was certainly not seeking to increase his own praise, but our correction.

So all the wise say: You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right. For we are not handed over to our adversaries without his judgment, nor do we come into tribulations without his judgment. This is the consolation of the righteous; this is the judgment of the Lord. Indeed, you have it above as well: I remembered your judgments, which are from of old, and I was comforted. You see, then, that the Lord's judgments are consolations.

You have commanded righteousness, your testimonies, and your truth exceedingly. Is it "you have commanded exceedingly" or "exceeding truth"? But exceeding truth is full of praise, and commanding exceedingly is a mark of providence and caution. For he knew they were weak; therefore he admonished them more often, so that they would not forget.

There follows the third verse: Zeal for your house has sought me out, because my enemies have forgotten your words. There is a zeal that leads to life and a zeal that leads to death. Zeal that leads to life is to keep the divine precepts and, out of love for the Lord, to guard his commandments, as Phinehas did, of whom we read in Numbers, where the Lord says to Moses: Phinehas son of Eleazar son of Aaron the priest has calmed my fury from the children of Israel, in that he was zealous with my zeal among them, and I did not consume the children of Israel in my zeal. So I said: Behold, I give him a covenant of peace, and it shall be for him and for his seed after him a covenant of everlasting priesthood, because

he was zealous for his God and did not plead for the children of Israel. Twenty-four thousand of the people lay slain; the punishment was spreading to all, and there was no end to the destruction. Phinehas seized a spear and killed the two who were joined in a union forbidden to them; he redeemed all, softened the Lord's indignation, and gave victory to those to whom the Lord was denying salvation. How saving, then, is the zeal of God!

That vice did not belong to one time only; even now the Midianite woman mingles with the Jew. The Midianite woman is she who is joined by no marriage as a lawful wife, united by no partnership of faith. The Midianite woman is the faithlessness of heretics when it tempts the people of God. Into how many peoples

has this deadly harlot crept, burying a whole people in a common death at a public funeral! Come now too, Phinehas, seize the sword of the word, kill faithlessness, slaughter heresy, lest the whole people perish because of it. Heaven's wrath is pressing: strike the very womb of impiety and the generative organ of faithlessness, so that no unhappy offspring may be formed, so that no adulterous conception may spread the seedbed of transgression and crime,

so that the Lord may establish with you a covenant of peace and a covenant of grace, a covenant of heavenly promises. A priest who strives to keep the chastity of the Church uncorrupted ought to have zeal, and so the chief of priests says: Zeal for your house gnaws at me. And Phinehas was a priest, and the grandson of a priest, and the son of a priest. Zeal is good and useful in a priest, above all so that he may not be negligent or slack. It is better that very many be set free by the condemnation of one or two than that more be endangered by the acquittal of two.

Zeal for your house, he says, has sought me out. You see that the zeal of God is a grace, which seeks out, which comes upon a person, which pours itself into the heart of the righteous. The zeal of God is life. Indeed, the Lord says: Zeal for your house has devoured me. For just as earlier, in Adam, prevailing death had devoured man, so zeal devoured the one whom it made alive in Christ.

Elijah had zeal, and therefore he was caught up into heaven: I have been very zealous, he says, for the Lord. Mattathias Butanus [?] had zeal, who roused the people of God against the sacrileges of Antiochus. Those who have zeal regard as their own enemies all who are enemies of God, even father, brothers, sisters; of all of them they say: They have become enemies to me, as David says. Why say more? An apostle of the Lord, too, was marked by this name, so that he was called Judas the Zealot, as we read in the Gospel.

By zeal for the faith the people of the Gentiles gained eternal life for themselves; through negligence and sloth the people of the Jews lost it. And so it is written: Zeal will seize an untaught people. Since the people that had been instructed in the law had no ardor of faith, zeal betook itself to the Gentiles. So great is its grace that it overcame the privilege of election and surpassed the diligence of learning. Indeed, seizing an untaught people, it made it better.

Thus it worked in the people of the nations, so that they merited the Lord's inheritance, with the same grace by which the Lord worked to join to himself a Church from the nations. Zeal, then, is love. Indeed, love is strong as death, zeal is hard as hell. Hard is the zeal that no allurement of this life can overcome, hard as hell, the zeal through which we die to sin that we may live to God.

The angels too are nothing without zeal, and they lose the privilege of their nature unless they sustain it with the ardor of zeal. Indeed, in the Apocalypse of John the Lord says to the angel of Laodicea: I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, I will begin to spew you out of my mouth. Because you say, I am rich and have grown wealthy and need nothing, and you do not know that you are wretched and pitiable and a beggar and naked and

blind, I counsel you to buy from me gold tested by fire. This is the zeal of God; this is the warmth of faith and the fervor of devotion, which softens and shapes us in Christ like a pleasant food. How great is the Lord's grace, that he places us in his mouth and feasts on certain dishes of our merits, and, if we deserve it, devours us, if he is delighted by the sweetness of our food! Blessed is he whom wisdom has devoured, whom virtue has drunk up, whom righteousness has received. Guilt can have no share in one whom the forgiveness of sins has swallowed up. Where will error find one whom spotless integrity has taken up?

And why should we wonder if angels have it? God the Father himself says: I will be zealous for Jerusalem with great zeal. Because God is great, his zeal too is great, and according to the quality of each one's power, so his zeal is either moderate or great. By zeal Jerusalem is vindicated, by zeal the Church is gathered, by zeal faith is acquired, by zeal chastity is possessed. The Lord Jesus too says: Zeal for your house has eaten me up, rebuking the Jews because they had made the house of prayer a den of robbers, and had also made it a house of trade.

But we ought to be zealous not only for the place where the Church gathers, but also for this inner house of God within us, so that it may not be a house of trade or a den of robbers. For if we hunt after gains, the profits of money and emoluments, we have made a house of trade; if we invade the possessions of others, the boundaries of a widow or of minors, we have made a den of robbers. So let the word of God come and cast out of this house the thieves, the plunderers, the hucksters, so that your heart, your breast, may be clean.

But there is a zeal that leads to guilt, and a zeal that leads to grace. For David himself says: I was zealous at the peace of sinners; and in Ecclesiasticus it is written: Do not be jealous of the wife of your bosom, lest she show against you the malice of wicked teaching; and a woman jealous of a faithful woman is rightly censured. We see, then, that there is a certain measure and discipline of zeal, just as there is a discipline of virtue. And so blessed is he who knows the discipline of zeal and hates those who abandon the Lord's grace, desert their own salvation, and take to themselves the error of deceit.

And therefore he says: because my enemies have forgotten your words. Who are these enemies? If the people of the Jews, how could they be enemies when they were placed under his rule? For David governed all the Jews in his own kingdom. If the Gentiles, how could those who did not know the Lord's law forget the words of God? For no one can forget anything except what he has received.

So those are my enemies who are your enemies, who were not going to receive the Lord when he came to his own. These the prophet declares to be his grievous foes, these his enemies: not those hostile to himself, but those in rebellion against Christ. Indeed, elsewhere he says: And I pined away over your enemies; I hated them with a just hatred. He thought the weapons of faithlessness more grievous than those of battle;

for no enemy of all is more grievous than one who wounds the Author of all. This, then, is why the people of the nations was acquired with great zeal: because God was being denied by his own people. For those who did not keep the memory of the heavenly precepts could hold neither the devotion of faith nor the discipline of virtue. So Adam was cast out of paradise; so the people of the Jews was shut out of the privilege of election.

There follows the fourth verse: Your word is exceedingly fiery, and your servant has loved it. The Lord did indeed send fire upon the earth, not to burn it again with a conflagration like that of Sodom, as it is written, nor to deprive it of the gift of fruitfulness bestowed on it, or of the use or bloom of its greenery; for the Lord is accustomed to approve and increase his work rather than to diminish or condemn it.

Nor was it fitting that innocent elements should pay the penalty for our crime. What wrong had nature done, if its offspring went astray once grown? The birth was not at fault if the progeny slipped into wayward error; the fault lay in the use. What fire, then, did the Lord scatter in the New Testament? One that would inflame the hidden affections of minds with the ardor of divine knowledge, that would kindle the warmth of faith and devotion, that would light up the desire for virtue. Warmed by this fire, Jeremiah says: And there was a blazing fire in my bones. Heated by this fire of heavenly words, Cleopas and that other disciple, who had made the journey together with the Lord from Jerusalem to the village, said: Was not our heart burning within us while he opened the Scriptures to us?

This fire, then, is the word of Christ, and it is a good fire, which knows how to warm and does not know how to burn up anything but sins alone. By this fire that apostolic gold laid upon the good foundation is tested; by this fire that pure silver of works is examined; by this fire those precious stones are made to shine; but hay and straw are consumed. This fire, then, cleanses the soul and consumes error.

Hence the Lord also says: You are already clean because of the word that I have spoken to you. This is the fire that burns before the Lord; for unless one takes up the blaze of devotion, he cannot have the presence of the Lord. Kindle this fire first in your mind, so that the light of Christ may shine upon you.

With this fire the bush was burning and yet was not burned up; for the one word burns to correct the sinner's conscience; it does not burn him up to destroy him. This fire is accustomed to dull, this fire to extinguish the savage blazes of material flames; indeed, the Hebrews, kindled by this fire, could neither fear nor feel the heat of the burning furnace. Rightly, then, does the good servant love the fiery speech of the Lord, through which we put on love, which casts out fear.

He did well to add "exceedingly," because every teacher does indeed inflame the affection of his hearer, but the word of God is above all, piercing to the divisions of the joints and the inmost marrow. Picture the fiery speech of God to yourself, then, in three ways: it cleanses, or it kindles, or it enlightens its hearers. That is why the Lord says: I searched Jerusalem with a lamp; but he found no one in it who was either cleansed or kindled or enlightened, and so he left it in darkness.

Do not wonder that the servant loves the Lord's fiery speech, since the bride loved it too, who says: Your lips are like a scarlet cord; for in scarlet there glows both the appearance of fire and the blood of the Lord's cross. Scarlet are the Lord's lips, which spoke of his own passion.

Indeed, in Exodus scarlet was placed to stand for fire. For the world is made not of scarlet but of four elements; yet in scarlet the figure of fire is expressed, and unless its warmth penetrated heaven and air, seas and lands, all things would dissolve as though their strength were spent. By the cord, then, we recognize the bond of

persuasion; by the scarlet, either the ardor of desire that sparks in the souls of the hearers, or a sign of the passion. Hence the bride says elsewhere: His lips are lilies dripping with rich myrrh. For by myrrh is shown both the ointment of the passion and the grace of the resurrection, which pours the renewed fragrance of life into the bodies of the dead when they are raised. Rightly, then, does the bride, receiving the sweetness of his speech, cry out and testify: His throat is sweetness itself, and he is altogether desirable.
There follows: I am young and despised; I have not forgotten your statutes. This little verse can fit many saints who from earliest youth were trained by hard labors. For Joseph too,

when he was sold by his brothers into Egypt, was younger and despised, sold as he was into the indignity of slavery. And afterward, brought out of prison and set over Egypt, he distributed grain to the peoples. He did not repay his brothers for the wrong they had done him, but returned their money and gave them food; he rescued his father's old age from famine and hunger; and, sending a chariot, he went out to meet him and bowed down to him, while the rest served him amid the insignia of great power. Rightly, then, did he say: I am younger and despised; I have not forgotten your statutes.

He too, younger than his brothers, while he was tending his father's sheep as though sent off to a lowly task, was not presented to the priest, as if he were unworthy to be anointed king; but, sought out by the priest and summoned from the pastures, he received the privilege of royal anointing. Later also, when he went out to war and Goliath, scorning the whole Jewish people with the bulk of his body, challenged them to single combat, while the rest were afraid, he asked the king to give him leave to engage him.

Not even then was he thought fit for so great a contest, for the king said: You cannot go against the foreigner and fight with him, for you are a boy, and he has been a man of war from his youth. Nor would he have been allowed, had he not shown that in his youth he had strangled a lion with his own hands and killed it, after pulling the legs of the seized sheep from its mouth.

He was also despised by the foreigner, because he had come out against an armed warrior with a staff and stones. He replied that he relied not on strength, not on arms, but had come out to battle trusting in the name of the Lord, to take away the reproach of the people who had been challenged. This young and despised man, then, laid the foreigner low, and having won the victory he triumphed among ten thousands, as the singing young women bore witness.

For he bore the type of the one who was to come to earth as one despised, and, without envoy, without helper, without messenger, would set free the whole people of this world by the battle of his cross; the one whom the souls of the saints, renewed through the sacraments of baptism, would applaud, because

he had slain with the sword of his word that true Goliath, now revealed and exposed to us. So the true Goliath lies laid low by the humility of the Son of God; he has lost his head, which he used to turn to many arts and frauds. Souls now secure sing psalms, souls that once wept over the torments of their sins. Resounding on drums, that is, on their own bodies that are dead to sin, they say:

Saul has triumphed among thousands, David among ten thousands. That harsh king, the devil, is indignant and angry because the young women sang that the son of harshness deceived a few, but Christ redeemed the whole world. So Christ, born of a virgin, says: I am young and despised; I have not forgotten your statutes.

The people of the nations also speak, the people who were despised when the first choice was made. They are still raw in faith and young in the zeal of their first devotion, or at any rate their youth has been renewed like the eagle's through the sacraments of baptism. They say: "I am young and despised; I have not forgotten your judgments." I who was despised before am now preferred; I am now set above the chosen. I, once the despised

people of sinners, now share in the venerable fellowship of the heavenly sacraments; I am now received with the honour of the heavenly table. My feasts are not watered by rain; they do not depend on the earth bringing forth its crops or on the fruit of the trees. For my drink I need not look for rivers or springs. Christ is my food, Christ is my drink: the flesh of God is my food and the blood of God is my drink. I no longer wait for the yearly harvests to be filled; Christ is served to me every day. I shall not fear that bad weather or a barren field will lessen him for me, so long as I keep up the diligence of devout worship.

I no longer wish for showers of quails to come down on me, which once amazed me, nor for the manna I once preferred to every other food, because the fathers who ate manna went hungry. My food is the one whoever eats will not hunger. My food does not fatten the body but strengthens the heart of man.

Before, the bread from heaven was a wonder to me, for it is written: "He gave them bread from heaven to eat." But that was not the true bread; it was a shadow of what was to come. The Father kept the true bread from heaven for me. For me the bread of God came down from heaven, the bread that gives life to this world. It did not come down to the Jews, it did not come down to the synagogue; it came down to the Church, to the younger people of God. For how did the bread that gave life come down to the Jews,

when all who ate that bread (that is, the manna, which the Jews thought was the true bread) died in the desert? How did it come down to the synagogue, when the whole synagogue has perished and failed, wasted away by an everlasting fast from faith? Indeed, if they had received the true bread, they would not have said: "Lord, give us this bread always."

Why do you ask, O Jew, that he give you a bread which he gives to all, gives every day, gives always? It is up to you to receive this bread: come to this bread and you will receive it. Of this bread it was said: "All who go far from you shall perish." If you go far from it, you will perish; if you draw near to it, you will live. This is the bread of life. Whoever eats life, then, cannot die. For how will someone die whose food is life? How will someone fail who has a substance that gives life?

Come to him and be filled, for he is bread; come to him and drink, for he is a spring; come to him and be enlightened, for he is light; come to him and be set free, for where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom; come to him and be absolved, for he is the forgiveness of sins. Do you ask who he is? Hear him say it himself: "I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not hunger, and whoever believes in me will never thirst." You heard him and you saw him, and you did not believe him; that is why you are dead. Believe now at least, so that you may live.

But you admire Moses because he led your fathers through the sea with dry feet. Moses did not command; he made a request. He gave no order to the sea; he served the one who gave orders to the waves. You praise Moses because he drowned King Pharaoh with his army. Moses prayed and another commanded; Moses made petition, Christ did the work; Moses was fleeing, Christ

was pursuing; Moses followed the pillar to avoid the darkness of the night, Christ gave the light. You acknowledge Moses, who made the bitter water sweet; you acknowledge Moses, who brought water out of the rock. Yet you do not acknowledge Christ, who laid low the army of that true king of Egypt and drowned it in the depths of the abyss, who frees us every day from the waves of this world so that the storm of this age may not drown us. What good did it do the fathers to cross the Red Sea, when they were not allowed to reach the land of the resurrection?

For everyone who came out of Egypt perished in the desert. Aaron died, Miriam died, and Moses himself died; only Joshua son of Nun was saved, by the likeness of his sacred name. Let the Jew applaud because the rocks poured out water for him when he was thirsty: for me an everlasting spring flowed from the body of God. Christ drank my bitterness, so as to give me the sweetness of his grace.

So the Christian people says: "I am young and despised; I have not forgotten your judgments." It is right for this to be said by the one who has justified God through the sacraments of baptism. For whoever is baptized justifies God, because he confesses his own sins and waits for the Lord to pardon his offenses. David justified God when he said: "Against you alone have I sinned and done evil in your sight, so that you may be justified in your words."

The Pharisees, who refused to be baptized with John's baptism, did not justify God, as you have read in the Gospel. Nor is it enough just to justify God; one must also not forget God's judgments. That means keeping the gifts of spiritual grace undefiled, and preserving the gift of holy forgiveness unharmed and without offense.

This applies to all in general. But each individual Christian also has the special privilege of saying "I am young and despised," if he is humble of heart, gentle and meek. Let him say, then, "I am young and despised": let him first mention the boastfulness that is common to his age, so as to make the grace of his humility all the more commendable. Humility is nothing to wonder at in old age. Old age is drained of strength, broken by infirmities, saddened by pains, panting with sighs, scorched by the heat of cares, and weary of life itself, and so it has forgotten the eagerness that goes with boasting.

Humility is rare indeed among the young, and so it is admirable. While youth is vigorous, while strength is firm, while the blood is hot, while care is unknown and weakness unfamiliar, while joy is constant, then boastfulness is at its height. Then the proud spirit of youth exalts itself; then humility seems cheap and is scorned and cast aside; then submission is thought to be the weakness of a base mind. One must therefore train oneself to a great maturity of character, one that can overcome nature.

Let us consider it this way. In paradise humility failed, and so it came from heaven; in paradise disobedience arose, and so obedience came down with the Savior. The flesh was puffed up, so that no meek submission could be found on earth; the whole inheritance of the transgressor had swollen with pride. When the Lord Jesus came, he first emptied himself. He did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but took the form of a servant; and being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient even to death.

Do not be troubled because it is written "as a man," for he did not take on the likeness of a man but the reality. The apostle himself says elsewhere: "the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." And to bring an example from the Gospel, John says: "We have seen his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth." Because he said "as of the only-begotten," did he mean us to think of a likeness of the only-begotten rather than the reality?

So Christ did not come in vain. A person who was once a proud old man in the former people can now say: "I am young and despised." He says "I am young and despised" in the same way the Church says, "I am black and beautiful." She put "black" first to heighten the beauty; so here too he put "young" first to heighten the humility. She did not say "I am black-beautiful," so that what is black would not be thought beautiful; nor did he say "I am young-despised," so that youth would not be thought contemptible. Rather he says "young" and, remarkably, "humble"—not "proud"—closer to the lowly than to the swollen with pride. So too [?]:

I am black by my earlier sin, but beautiful through confessing my sin, through my zeal for correction and my love of virtue. So although the syllable "and" is, as the grammarians call it, a conjunction, it still makes a distinction, by which things that would be run together are divided and separated. If you say "Ambrose Bassus is inside," one person is understood; but if you state that "Ambrose and Bassus are inside," then of course two are understood.

Let him say, then, "I am young and despised," because Christ redeemed the world as a poor and despised man, because Christ overcame the devil by humility. Let him say "I am despised," because God does not spurn a humbled heart, because Lazarus, that despised man, now rests in Abraham's bosom, while the boastful rich man is tormented in hell. Moses was despised and thought himself unfit when he was sent to free the Hebrew people. Jeremiah was despised,

who said: "Sovereign Lord, see, I do not know how to speak, for I am young." But this despised man is all the more readily chosen; indeed he is told: "Do not say, 'I am young,' for you shall go to all to whom I send you, and you shall speak whatever I command you. Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord." That tax collector was despised, who did not dare to lift his eyes to heaven, and so he was heard more readily than the Pharisee; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

Next comes: "Your righteousness is an everlasting righteousness, and your law is truth." Individuals can indeed do works of righteousness, but not works that last forever. The rich man who had riches in abundance in this world may perhaps have done some works of righteousness,

for which he received his reward in the present life, because those works were not great and did not deserve an everlasting reward. And what of the fact that even when we do some works of righteousness, we do them only now and then, not continually? Many do not seize what belongs to others, yet do not know how to give from their own. Others seize wealth that is not theirs and then usually give some to the poor, in order to win for themselves an appearance of righteousness.

That is not an everlasting righteousness. Many righteous people have often sinned gravely, and so do not have the fruit of everlasting righteousness. It belongs to God alone to possess righteousness forever and in all things, who feeds the just and the unjust. For righteousness must not be shown only in return for kindnesses; true righteousness is the kind that is extended even to enemies. And so the Righteousness of God rightly says: "Love your enemies."

So just as the righteousness of God alone is everlasting, so the law of God is truth. But how are we to take this? Is it that the law of God is truth in the sense that it is true, and everything God has decreed is true, as he says further on, "All your commandments are truth"? Or is it that truth is the law of God, because God does not lie?

With him, then, truth is law and falsehood is transgression. But it can also be taken this way: the law of God is truth, and therefore the law of God is not among the Jews, because they do not accept the truth. The law of God is spiritual, as the apostle said; so those who have not received it spiritually do not have the true law. What is not true is false; what is false kills. So the letter, which kills, is false; the Spirit, who gives life, is true.

Let us also take it this way: the law of God is not a type, not a shadow, not a copy of heavenly things, but the heavenly things themselves. That is why it is written that Christ is the end of the law—not its failure, of course, but the fullness of the law is in Christ, for he came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it. For just as there is an Old Testament, yet all truth is in the New Testament, so also the law given through Moses is a figure of the true law. That law, then, is a copy of the truth: in the copy the blood of a lamb is shed, in the truth Christ is sacrificed.

So it was right that the apostle, after speaking of the sacrifice of calves under the law, added: "Thus it was necessary for the copies of heavenly things to be purified by these, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices. For Christ did not enter a sanctuary made by hands, a copy of the true one, but into heaven itself, and now appears before the face of God on our behalf." And so that we may know that the Lord Jesus gave a new law, you have the Spirit saying: "This is the covenant that I will make with them, says the Lord: I will put my laws in their hearts and write them on their minds, and I will remember their sins and their iniquities no more. Where there is forgiveness, there is no longer any offering for sins."

By this he plainly shows you that all truth is contained in the Gospel, whether because the law of God is written on people's minds and hearts, not on tablets of stone (so those who do not have God's commandments in their hearts do not have the law), or because it grows old among the Jews but is renewed in us.

It is a shadow, not the truth, so that when an offering for sins is made according to the law, no forgiveness of sins takes place; for it is impossible for sins to be cleansed by the blood of bulls and goats. That forgiveness was therefore false until the truth of forgiveness came. What could be plainer, then, than the statement of John the Evangelist, who says: "For the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ"? He set the truth against the law by way of contrast. Since "but" is a disjunction, we must understand that the disjunction was put there because if truth had been in the law, it would not have come through Christ.
We can also understand it this way: Christ is the truth; therefore the truth is law. And if the commandment of the Lord is law, much more is the living and active Word of God law.

Next comes the seventh verse: "Trouble and distress have found me; your commandments are my meditation." Troubles and distresses go looking for the righteous man, and sometimes they find him and sometimes they do not. The one to whom a crown is owed is found; the one who has not proved fit for the contest is not found. Trouble, then, is a kind of grace; indeed, "a troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God." Or is that not grace which produces patience? So he who knew that trouble brings progress was sought out by trouble and found, and did not run away.

Wisdom says: "The wicked will seek me and will not find me." This is not because the Lord did not want to be found by men, since he offered himself to all, even to those who were not seeking him, but because he was sought by such works that those who sought him were unworthy to find him. Simeon, on the other hand, who was waiting for him, found him; Andrew found him. Indeed he said to Simon: "We have found the Messiah," which means Christ.

Philip also says to Nathanael: "We have found him of whom Moses wrote in the law, and the prophets also: Jesus son of Joseph, from Nazareth." And to show how Christ is found, he said: "Come and see." So whoever seeks Christ, let him come, not with the steps of the body but with the footsteps of the mind; let him see him, not with the outward eyes but with the inward. For the eternal one is not seen by bodily sight, since the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal.

Christ, then, is not temporal: he is from the Father before all time, as true God and Son of God, and above time, as everlasting power, enclosed by no end of time; he is above time, as life, whom no day of death will ever find. "For the death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God."

Do you hear what the apostle has said today? "He died to sin," he says, "once for all." Christ died once for you, a sinner; do not sin again after baptism. He died once for all in common, and he dies once for each one, not repeatedly. You are sin, O man; that is why the almighty Father made his Christ sin. He made him a man, to bear our sins.

So the Lord Jesus died to sin for me, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him. He died for me so that he might rise for me. He died once, he rose once. And you, who died with him, were buried with him, and were raised with him in baptism, take care that, having died once, you do not die again. Then you would die not to sin but to pardon. Having risen, take care that you do not die a second time.

For Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death will no longer have dominion over him. So death did have dominion over him? Certainly; by saying "will no longer have dominion," he shows that it once did. Do not throw away so great a gift, O man. For your sake Christ submitted himself to the dominion of death, to free you from the yoke of that dominion. He took on the slavery of death to give you the freedom of eternal life.

So whoever seeks Christ also seeks his trouble and does not run from his suffering. David, indeed, who was worthy to be sought by trouble, himself sought trouble too; for if he had not sought it, he would not have found it. That he did find it, he testifies himself: "I found trouble and sorrow, and I called on the name of the Lord." And elsewhere: "In trouble I called on the Lord, and he heard me and set me in a broad place." Trouble is good, then, for it makes us worthy to be heard by the Lord in a broad place; and to be heard by the Lord our God is a grace.

So whoever seeks trouble does not run from it, and whoever does not run from it is found; for the one who meditates on God's commandments in mind and in deed does not run away. Contests always find the athlete who keeps up his training; but the one who has given up his training surely cannot be found, because he is not worth looking for. So David, like a good athlete, says: "Trouble and distress have found me," because they always found him ready, not running from the battles of distress and trouble but seeking them out.

Next comes: "Your testimonies are righteousness forever; give me understanding of them and give me life." Who is great enough to understand the Lord's testimonies? That is why understanding must be asked of the Lord. Its power is so great that its beginning is the fullness of virtue; for it is written: "Godliness toward God is the beginning of understanding." Godliness is the foundation of all the virtues, [and the discipline?] of human and heavenly things. Godliness is a friend to God and pleasing to parents; it wins the Lord's favor and cherishes family ties; it is the worship of God, the reward of parents, the wage of children. Godliness, I say, is the tribunal of the righteous, the harbor of the needy, the refuge of the wretched, the pardon of sinners.

Whoever has understanding is truly godly. For he understands how easily human frailty slips, and is quick to forgive the one who goes astray. He understands that we have been given a share in a common nature and common use, and so he pays the poor as if it were a debt, and does not deny it as if it were not owed. He understands that misfortunes come in turn, and so he goes out to meet those shipwrecked in this world with the harbor, as it were, of his own kindness. This is the perfect praise among men; this is the full praise in God.

So Solomon too, following his father's teaching, rightly asked the Lord for understanding, saying: "I am a humble child and do not know my going out and my coming in; and your servant is in the midst of your people, whom you have chosen, a people as many as the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted for multitude. Give your servant a [discerning heart?] to hear and to judge your people with justice, and to understand between good and evil." This pleased the Lord,

because he did not ask for a long life for himself or an abundance of royal riches, but for wisdom to understand the judgments and decrees of the Lord. And so he governed so great a people in a peaceful kingdom, because he did not, like Adam, seize the knowledge of the difference between good and evil, but prayed for the grace of understanding it from

Christ. For to be able to know what is divine, you must earn it from the Lord your God. If Adam too had asked, as David asked, he would never have fallen into those inextricable snares of error by which his whole inheritance is strangled. And so he died, and, worse still, by the death of sin, because he seized knowledge before he received the understanding by which he might have been given life.

Understanding, then, gives life, as the Spirit does, because understanding itself is a spiritual grace, and so the Holy Spirit works understanding as his gift. And "understanding is good for all who act on it." This teaches us that we must not only grasp with the mind what we understand, but also carry it out in deeds.
XIX. THE LETTER KOPH

Here begins the letter Koph, the nineteenth, which is interpreted as "enclosure" and, as we find elsewhere, "look." The words differ, but the sense agrees. For someone who is shut in must look around him and not ignore the cause of his danger, especially when it is a deadly crisis. A person is shut in when his inner organs swell or his inner throat swells,

so that the passage of air is blocked and the exchange of breathing in and out is constricted. A woman is shut in when the womb is displaced, so that the vital part of the chest itself is pressed. Severe distress results from this, and unless that chamber for receiving seed is brought back into its place, it usually ends life. So too a person who is anguished in mind and hard pressed by some looming adversity is said to be shut in, by straits of mind no less than of body. For the burning heats and fevers of the soul are greater than those of the body.

A man whose bowels are blocked by a swelling looks for a physician who can ward off the danger and loosen what is bound tight. The physician comes, tries everything and examines the inner parts. You too, then, when you are shut in by the fever of your soul, look at yourself with the inner eye. The force of the disease presses on you, a guilty conscience burns, the weight of sins bears down, and distress cuts off the mind's understanding. Know yourself, and seek the medicine of prayer. Ask that the Physician may come who came down from heaven, who seeks out above all those who are sick, as he himself says: "It is not the healthy who need a physician, but those who are ill." Do you have wounds?

Do not put it off; with him there is no adjournment of healing. Do you have sores? Do not be afraid; he is accustomed to cure with a word, not with the knife. Look, then, with those eyes with which David sought help and earned it. "I lifted up my eyes to the mountains," he says; "I sought where my help would come from, and I found it nowhere but from the Lord." For he who founded the world watches over those who dwell in the world. Look, then, and look always, for the eyes of the righteous are always toward the Lord.

Jeremiah too urges this upon you in Lamentations, under this very letter, when he says to Jerusalem: "Arise and wake in the night, at the beginning of your watch; pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord. Lift up your hands to the Lord for the lives of your little ones, who are fainting from hunger at the head of every street."

Does he not openly show the distress of being shut in, and urge you to provide yourself with a saving remedy through the intent of the heart, where the gaze of the better eye lies? Then further on, again under this letter, he says: "Our time has drawn near, our days are fulfilled, our end has come. Those who pursued us were swifter than the eagles of the sky; they were kindled on the mountains; they lay in wait for us in the desert."

He has shown the utmost confinement, with no remedy except in the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone can bring medicine to those in despair. And as if pointing to him, he says: "The Spirit before our face, Christ the Lord, was taken in our destruction; in his shadow we shall live among the nations." And further on: "You shall drink," he says, "and still be made drunk."

"He has visited your iniquities; he has laid bare your sins." How briefly he has expressed his coming and passion and the forgiveness of all sins! How openly he has declared the gathering of the nations that was to come! Hence that saying of the apostle: "A blindness has come upon part of Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in, and so all Israel should be saved."

Come, Lord Jesus, but no longer in shadow; come now in the Sun of righteousness. If the shadow helped us, if the shadow of your passion protected us, if the shadow of your body saved us, how much more can the open brightness of your power bestow! Through the shadow leprosy was cured; through the shadow too the woman who

touched the fringe of the Lord's garment had her bleeding stopped; through the shadow we saw you, when you had no form or beauty. Your flesh was your shadow, which cooled the heat of our desires, quenched the fires of our lusts, and tempered the blaze of greed and of various passions. And why should I speak of the Lord's shadow, when even the shadow of the apostles healed? For when Peter came by, each person brought out his sick, and the shadow of the passing apostle restored them to health.

Hear that the Lord's flesh was a shadow: "Behold, the Lord sits upon a light cloud and will come into Egypt." And David says: "Protect me under the shadow of your wings." Having emptied himself, then, he became a shade for us whom the sun of iniquity had scorched. So we saw him in a shadow while faith was still in its first stage.

But now he lights up the whole world; and yet we still see him through the shadow of his body, which is the Church, not yet face to face, for the eyes of the body cannot take in the splendor of the Godhead. This shadow too protects the whole world every day. So being shut in has been of benefit; for God has shut up all things in unbelief, that he may have mercy on all. But now let us consider what should be said in this confinement, and where we should begin.

"I cried out with my whole heart; hear me, O Lord; I will seek out your righteous decrees," says David. When we suffer bodily assaults, we usually cry out so that we can call others to our defense. The holy prophet was hard pressed as his persecutors closed in on him. First Saul, hostile to him, pursued him with an armed host; later a parricidal son threatened him, who, not content with his father's exile as a fugitive, sought to take his life. Yet he could suffer less from those whom he saw before him than from those whom he did not see.

For the saints wrestle not only against flesh and blood but also against the principalities and powers of this world and the rulers of darkness, who, like robbers in the night of this age, lie in wait for human affections. So when holy David saw these heavy assaults being made against him, he cried out with his whole heart. For against the devil one must use not loudness of voice but greatness of heart.

Yet there is a voice of the heart, just as there is also a voice of blood, which reaches God; for God says: "The voice of your brother's blood cries out to me." So our heart cries out, not with a bodily sound, but with loftiness of thought and the harmony of the virtues. Great is the cry of faith: for in the Spirit of adoption we cry, "Abba, Father," and the Spirit of God himself cries out in us. Great is the voice of righteousness, great the voice of chastity,

through which even the dead speak; and they do not only speak, but, like Abel, they cry out. But the soul of the unrighteous does not cry out even while he lives, because it is dead to God. There is nothing lofty in it, nothing magnificent, like the voice of those whose sound has gone out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world. Moses spoke with a thin voice, yet he was heard more than all, and he is heard every day in the Church. Only by those, that is, the Jews, is he not heard, who hear with the ear but do not hear. To another prophet it is said: "Lift up your voice with strength."

Hannah, however, did not cry out in her heart as Moses did, but spoke, perhaps because she was asking for children, that is, for good things indeed, but private and not public ones. She did not cry out; but because she was asking of the Lord, and was offering to the Lord whatever son she might receive, she spoke to God. Moses, on the other hand, cried out, because he was praying not for himself but for the whole people. That is why the Lord said to him: "Why do you cry out?" He cried out with devoted feeling and deep understanding, and his cry resounded in heaven, as he asked for miracles worthy of heaven, that the elements of the world might be changed.

Let us go over the course of that passage itself. Pharaoh was pressing on, and, surrounded by countless Egyptian chariots, he was bearing down on the Hebrews. On one side the enemy surrounded them; on the other the sea lying between had hemmed in the people of God. They had no confidence in arms, no hope in their strength. All that could be heard was a wretched complaint, that it would have been better for them to bear the hard burdens of slavery in Egypt than to be consumed by a bitter death in the desert, a complaint that brought no help and gave much offense.

So Moses stood there, sorrowful, troubled, anxious at both the dangers and the complaints of the people, waiting for the fulfillment of the heavenly promises, and silently turning over in his mind by what help the Lord, forgetful of the wrong and mindful of his grace, would come to their aid. The Lord says to him: "Why do you cry out to me?" I do not hear his sound, yet I recognize his voice; I read his silence, and I detect his cry in his works. The people cried out and were not heard; Moses was silent and was heard.

It was not said to the people, "Why do you cry out to me?" for the people, who were crying out things unjust and unworthy of men, were not crying out to God. But it was said to Moses, "Why do you cry out to me?" that is: You alone cry out to me, you who hope in me; you alone cry out to me, you who stir up my power; you alone cry out to me, you who wait for my name to be proclaimed throughout the whole earth.

So Moses cried out in his heart, and every wise man cries out in his heart. Indeed, Wisdom, with a most lofty proclamation, summons people to her mixing bowl, saying: "Leave folly and seek wisdom." This proclamation, which promises wisdom to fools, is one of great loftiness and a great voice. And the Lord Jesus cried out: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink." Truly great were the things he cried out, as he called people to the kingdom of heaven, to that venerable drink by which the flood of eternal life is poured in. And you, when you pray, pray for great things, that is, pray for things that are eternal, not perishable;

pray for things that are divine and heavenly, that you may be like the angels in heaven. Do not pray for money, for it is rust; nor for gold, for it is metal; nor for property, for it is earth. Such a prayer does not reach the Lord. God hears only what he judges worthy of his favors; but he does hear a devout voice, full of devotion and grace.

So we must not only cry out in the heart but cry out with the whole heart. For just as in bodily terms a cry is a good one when one cries with the whole mouth, so spiritually we must cry with the whole heart if we wish to offer great things and obtain from the Lord what we ask. This was the voice the Lord required of the people, a voice the people did not know; and so the Lord said: "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." Whoever draws near with the heart, then, is heard by the Lord. So let the heart cry out first, so that the word can be heard.

But it is not enough to cry out to the Lord; one must also seek out his righteous decrees. He seeks out his righteous decrees who ascribes to divine providence whatever is right in all creatures, and above all in living things endowed with reason. Where else does the turtledove get her devotion to chastity, so that,

once she has lost her mate, she does not know how to indulge in another union, something human beings cannot keep? Where else do so many animals get such sober care for preserving their offspring that, once they recognize the gift of conception, they do not think mating should be repeated, lest an adulterous mixing be made with the seed they have received? The phoenix knows nothing of bodily union and is ignorant of the

allurements of lust; instead it rises again from its own pyre, a bird that survives itself, at once the heir of its own body and the offspring of its own ashes. The eagle, so as not to rear degenerate young, weighs them with careful scrutiny: it holds its still tender chicks in its devoted talons and offers them to the rays of the sun, so that if they happen to turn their eyes away from the force of the glare, it loosens its talon and lets them fall headlong as degenerate; but if they can prove the vigor of their nature by a steady gaze against the sun's rays, it carries them back, a welcome burden, as offspring of worthy stock.

None of the birds of the sky sow or reap, and God feeds them, because they keep the Lord's righteous decrees, claiming nothing as their own and content to relieve their hunger from the fruit-bearing tree, which by the Lord's judgment was given as common food. From these, then, we learn how little the aid of divine providence would be lacking to human beings if we were willing to keep God's justice. Would he who feeds the birds not feed human beings, whom he made in his own image and likeness? Are we not worth more than they? By the privilege of our nature we are worth more, but we are lower through the loss of grace and the injustice of transgression.

The second verse: "I cried out to you; save me, and I will keep your testimonies." He repeats that he cried out to God, and promises to keep the heavenly statutes, which the Lord God established with heaven and earth as witnesses, so that transgressors might be convicted by the testimony of the elements. How can they look up at the heaven that knows of their transgression? How can they expect fruit from the earth, which knows them to be ungrateful? See, then, how great are the things the prophet promises. In crying out, a faithful and ready affection is expressed; in keeping the testimonies, the virtue of self-control and diligence in obedience are made plain.

The third verse: "I came before the ripe hour and cried out; I hoped in your words." The Greek says en aōria, which means "before the hour, before the time." So let whoever prays to the Lord not wait, as it were, for particular prescribed times, knowing that in supplications to the Lord there is no special time, but let him always be engaged in them. Whether we eat or drink, let us proclaim Christ, let us ask Christ, let us think of Christ, let us speak of Christ; let Christ always be in our heart, always on our lips.

But perhaps you will say: How is it, then, that it is written, "There is a time for all things, and a time for every matter under heaven"? But the Lord Jesus is above heaven; he is bounded by no time. Let Arian unbelief shut its mouth: "A time," it says, "for every matter under heaven"; how much more is time under God, not above God! Generation from the Father has no time; for the work does not come before its maker, but the maker is above the beginning of the work. Perhaps they will object that he said, "My time has not yet come," and again said, "Father, the hour has come." But this hour is the hour of the passion. There is also a time of the virginal conception: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb," for the Virgin was under time and therefore conceived at the appointed age.

So let whoever prays pray always, and if he is not always praying, let him always have the disposition of one who prays ready. The Lord Jesus spent whole nights in prayer, not because he needed the help of prayer, but to set you an example to imitate. He spent the night praying for you, so that you might learn how to pray for yourself. Repay him, then, what he offered on your behalf. Listen to the prophet saying above:

"At midnight I rose to give you thanks." You too, rise at least at midnight, if you cannot always keep watch the whole night, so that while you pray at night, the splendor of the true Sun may shine into your breast; for every soul that thinks of Christ is always in the light, and it is day if Christ breathes upon you. But since the following verse expresses clearly the time for prayer, I think that in this verse we should understand the time rather of actions and works than of prayer.

Whoever, while still in youth, takes on the gravity of old age, governs the years of youth with a veteran's self-control, and settles the heat of a body in its prime with a gray-haired maturity of character, runs ahead of the ripeness of age. For what praise can there be if someone turns to the duties of devotion late, with a body worn out by pleasures and already cold with the chill of old age, his vigor laid aside and he grown sluggish? There is no

crown except where the struggle of the contest has been harder, a crown few can reach, and not all who have entered the stadium can attain. That man is praiseworthy who [?] within himself before the contest, who restrains his resisting flesh by the command of the mind, disciplines it with sparing frugality and brings it into subjection, lest it run riot with unbridled freedom and, untamed [?] and burning with desire, break the reins of the governing mind.

So an old man is "at the hour" if he carries out the duties of sober maturity; a young man runs "before the hour" if with the weight of an old man he suppresses the incitements of pleasures and extinguishes the allurements of burning desire. For "the Lord is good to those who wait for him," says Jeremiah, and: "It is good for a man who has borne a heavy yoke from his youth; he will sit alone and keep silent, for he has borne the yoke of the word."

For whoever has borne the yoke from his youth and has willingly bowed his still tender neck to the reins of mature restraint will sit alone, removed from the clamor of passions that harass him, and will keep silent in peace, no longer needing to quarrel with the body or to fight it out with various desires; for the soul that seeks God, and has made all the delights of youth its captives, has borne the yoke of the word.

Hence perhaps we can also take that saying about the Lord, "He will not cry out or contend, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets," not only of his silence in his own defense, his contempt for acquittal and his endurance of the passion, but also of the suppression of all bodily pleasures. That is why it is also written elsewhere that he committed no sin. Rightly, then, he kept silent when placed in danger of death, since he did not fear the sting of death.

"I hoped in your words," he says. The Greek says epēlpisa, which means always to grow in hoping and to add hope to hope. The righteous man always hopes, and even when placed in adversity and afflicted with frequent hardships, he does not know how to despair; rather, the heavier the things he has endured, the more he hopes, and he makes progress in hoping, according to that oracle: "Comfort, comfort my people, says the Lord. Priests, speak righteousness to the heart of Jerusalem; comfort her, for her humiliation is complete and her sin is forgiven, for she has received from the hand of the Lord double for her sins." How quickly he declared that the fullness of humiliation is the forgiveness of sin, and gave again the reason for comfort: that the mark of reconciliation is all the greater, the heavier the penalty has been compared with the fault.

Job, though weighed down by so many bitter misfortunes, heaped up his hope with devoted feeling, asserting that the case of the wicked is distinct from that of the godly; their light will be put out, but, according to Solomon, the righteous always have light. From this we gather that the righteous man always hopes in the words of God and adds hope to hope. Isaiah expressed this more clearly when he said:

"Expect tribulation upon tribulation, hope upon hope." He was speaking to those who had been weaned and taken from the breast, that is, to those who had passed beyond the first nourishment of infancy and were now fit for stronger food. Let the patriarch Isaac serve as an example: once weaned, he became so great that, while still in the first stages of his early years, he did not in the least shrink from the sword of his father about to strike him. Abraham had several sons, but he weaned no other; in this one case alone do we read that he made a great feast. And Scripture rightly called it a "great feast," because it was a type of him on whom the hearts of the saints always feast.

The fourth verse follows: "My eyes went before the morning to meditate on your words." Above he said, "I came before, en aōria," that is, "before the hours, before the time"; here he says "morning," indicating another time for praying and singing psalms to the Lord, so that the former corresponds to his saying, "At midnight I rose," and this one to the saying, "Go before the rising sun." For it is a serious thing if the rays of the rising sun find you lying idle in bed, to your shameless disgrace, and the bright light strikes your sleepy eyes, still weighed down with torpor.

Such a long stretch of time passed in an idle night, without any act of devotion or the offering of a spiritual sacrifice, accuses us. Do you not know, O man, that you owe God the firstfruits of your heart and voice every day? Your harvest is daily; your fruit is daily. So go out to meet the sunrise, so that the dawn may find you already prepared, and the first gleam of day may not have to rouse your eyes still heavy with damp sleep.

"On my bed through the nights I sought him whom my soul loved," says the Church. That is why she deserved to find him and to win his favor, because she sought him even on her bed; she sought him through the nights. Therefore, having gained possession of him, she says to the Bridegroom in a later passage: "Come, my brother, let us go out into the field; let us rest in the villages; at dawn

let us rise and go to the vineyards." Do you notice how the bride invites the Word of God to come to earth and take away the sins of the world? This field was once deserted, overgrown with the brambles of our offenses and bristling with thorns. It was a stronghold in which Adam, banished there, held the heirs of his posterity bound in perpetual exile.

So the Church leads Christ there to set Adam free. Then, once the exiles were released, the field of this world began to have suitable cultivators, and what had once been barren became fruitful by the planting of the eternal vine. Yet even so the Church does not wander off, rejoicing in its spiritual branches, but calls Christ to these vineyards, where there are people singing psalms and praying, where innocent fruit endures night and day.

"There," she says, "I will give you my breasts. The mandrakes have given forth their fragrance." Many distinguish a kind of sex among mandrakes, holding that there are both male and female ones, but that the female ones have a heavy smell. This signifies, then, that the nations, which formerly stank when they were weaker through a certain unmanly feebleness of unbelief, began to bear fruit of a good fragrance once they believed in the coming of the Lord.
