We read also that holy Rachel received mandrakes from her sister Leah, in return for allowing Leah to sleep with holy Jacob that night. Reuben, the firstborn, had brought the mandrakes to his mother Leah, who

with her weak eyes represented the synagogue, because with the dull gaze of a feeble mind she could not see the grace of Christ. This shows that the synagogue yielded to the Church the fruits it had earlier received from the firstborn Son of God. But because Leah, having obtained that night with her husband, bore an heir of her posterity, the mystery is fulfilled, since through the faith of the apostles a remnant of the Jews has been saved by the election of grace.

Hence the Church says: "New and old, my brother, I have kept for you. Who will give you to me as a brother, nursing at my mother's breasts? Finding you outside, I will kiss you, and indeed they will not despise me. I will take you and bring you into my mother's house and into the inner chamber of her who conceived me; you will teach me."

Having, then, the instruction of the New and Old Scriptures, and aware that she is not to be despised, she not only holds fast the Word by prayers in the secret of the heart, but also kisses him with the voices of the choir singing psalms, as though with kisses of grace.

So, pleasing with the fragrance of pomegranates, that is, of diverse and countless fruits and above all of faith, and supported by the riches of wisdom, glory and eternal life, which are at the left and right hand of the Bridegroom, she rouses Christ through holy souls with the applause of congregations singing praise, saying: "[?] daughters of Jerusalem, why do you stir up, and why do you awaken love, until it pleases?"

So the daughters of Jerusalem marvel at her: that is, the holy souls of the patriarchs and prophets and of the righteous of old, or the heavenly powers. They say: "Who is this who comes up made white, leaning on her brother?" This means that with such solemn rites the Church shines, and she who was dark before by day is now bright in the night and glows.

The Lord himself, delighted by so great a gift from those who sing psalms, also says: "Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a signet upon your arm, for love is strong as death. Jealousy is cruel as the underworld; its wings are wings of fire and flame. Many waters cannot shut out

love, and rivers will not overwhelm it." When he hears such devotion from the Church, he judges that there are now peoples fit to carry his seal in their heart and on their arm, as we may. For God the Father has set his seal on him, and the one who has received his testimony has set his seal to this, that God is true. Therefore those who work for the food that endures

to eternal life are sealed in the image and likeness of Christ, who is the image of the invisible God. So, just as God is true, you too should set the seal of truth on your mind and on your work. Let your mouth not speak a lie, and let your hands not do the works of men that belong to this deceitful world, but the works that are God's: let them give generously to the poor, lift up the weak, and honor the dead with burial in a tomb. By these works love is sought, so that no one can be torn from Christ, even

by the danger of death. So the apostle says: "Who will separate us from Christ? Will tribulation, or distress, or persecution?" And further on: "For I am confident that neither death nor life, nor angels, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus."

In this way, too, the jealousy of love is cruel, and its wings are wings of fire. It has wings like a dove, for "the feathers of the dove are covered with silver." With these the one who loves flies away, saying: "See, I have fled far away and stayed in the wilderness." But the wings of love are wings of fire, with which it kindles the ardor of love. Glowing with this heat, the Lord made his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire, but one that burns without consuming.

We also read of the wing of the temple, onto which the devil, tempting the Savior, made him climb; it was at the top of the temple. So there are pinnacles of devotion, there are heights of love, which have always kindled the warmth of grace in human hearts, so that many waters cannot quench or shut out love, and no rivers of worldly storms can overwhelm it.

Since, then, such great grace in the Church and such great rewards for devotion invite us, let us anticipate the rising sun and run to meet its dawning, before he says: "Here I am." The Sun of Righteousness wishes to be anticipated, and waits to be anticipated. Hear how he waits and longs to be anticipated. He says to the angel of the church in Pergamum: "Repent, or else I will come to you." He says to the angel of Laodicea: "Be zealous, then, and repent. See, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him."

[?] he could enter; after all, when he rose again with his body, no bolts on closed doors could keep him out: suddenly, without warning, he poured himself into the apostles' inner room. But he wants to put the zeal of your devotion to the test; the apostles he had already proved. Or perhaps in time of persecution he comes first; where there is peace, he longs to be met first. Certainly, rise before this sun that you see. "Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you." If you rise before this sun, before it comes up, you will receive Christ giving you light. He will first shine in the secret places of your heart.

When you say, "In the night my spirit keeps watch for you," he will make the morning light shine for you in the hours of night, if you meditate on the words of God. For while you meditate there is light, and seeing a light not of time but of grace, you will say: "For your commandments are light." And when day finds you meditating on the divine words, and so pleasing a work of prayer and psalm-singing has delighted your mind, you will say again to the Lord Jesus: "You will make the goings-out of morning and evening a delight."

The Jewish people, who had Moses as their teacher, go over the divine Scriptures every day through their elders, who are chosen for this task, night and day without any break; and if you ask an elder about anything else, he knows nothing but to echo the text of the divine Scripture. There is no talk there of worldly matters; Scripture alone is woven together there; one mouth takes over from another in turn, so that the sacred sound of the heavenly commandments never ceases. And you, Christian, whose teacher is Christ, do you sleep? Are you not afraid that it may be said of you: "This people does not honor me even with their lips"? The Jew honors him at least with his lips; you not even with your lips. If the heart of one who at least honors him with his lips is far from God, how can your heart be near, when you do not honor him even with your lips? How long will sleep hold you, how long worldly things, how long the cares of this life, how long earthly things!

At least divide your time between God and the world. Or, when you cannot do the business of this world in public and the darkness of night prevents you, give your time to God, devote yourself to prayer, and sing psalms so that you do not fall asleep. Cheat your sleep with a good deception. In the morning hurry to church and bring the first fruits of your devout prayer. Afterward, if worldly necessity calls you, you will not be kept from saying: "My eyes were early in the morning to meditate on your words," and you will go out to your affairs with a clear conscience.

How delightful to begin with hymns and canticles, with the Beatitudes that you read in the Gospel! How fortunate that the word of Christ should bless you, and that while you repeat the Lord's blessings you should take up the pursuit of some virtue, so that you may recognize in yourself too the merit of the divine blessing!

The fifth verse follows: "Hear my voice according to your mercy, O Lord; according to your judgment give me life." A man, even if he is holy and righteous, ought always to pray that the Lord may hear him according to his mercy, not according to the merits of any virtue, because virtue is rare and sins are many; and according to his judgment, so that he may bring help to the weak. And we ought to pray this above all when we are pressed by adversity. So it is not without reason that holy David put first his plea for divine mercy.

For there follows: "Those who persecute me have drawn near unjustly, but they have gone far from your law." The Greek puts it this way: "Those who persecute me with iniquity have drawn near," that is, those who were persecuting me with iniquity. The nearer they drew to me, the further they separated themselves from your law, since whoever persecutes his brother is cut off from the law; for the law says: "You shall love the Lord your God; you shall love your neighbor." So let me not hate my brother, lest it be said to me: "If you do not love your brother whom you see, how can you love God whom you do not see?" Do you not know that your brother was bought with the blood of Christ? So if you do not love your brother, you do not love what Christ bought.

So the persecutor draws near to me in order to harm me, but he sets himself apart from the law—for what share has righteousness with iniquity?—and whoever separates himself from the law of God separates himself also from eternal life, for the law is life. Indeed, the prophet, pointing to the law of God, says:

"See, this is life," since whoever does what belongs to the law will live by it, which certainly applies to the spiritual law. And perhaps the one who draws near to me to harm me, as he is separated from the law, is separated from Christ, because Christ is life. But if I cling to Christ, he does not even draw near to me, because even if he has power over my body, he will not be able to harm my soul. Indeed, how far the persecutors of the martyrs are separated from their merits!

But perhaps you will say: "How do the saints cling to God?" And so there follows: "You are near, O Lord, and all your commandments are truth." The Lord is near to all, for he is present everywhere. We cannot flee from him if we offend him, nor deceive him if we do wrong, nor lose him if we worship him.

God watches all things, sees all things, stands by each one, saying: "I am a God who draws near." And how can God be absent anywhere, when you read of the Spirit of God: "The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world"? For where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is the Lord God. "I fill heaven and earth," says the Lord. Where, then, is he lacking who fills all things, or how have we all received from his fullness, unless he draws near to all?

So David, knowing that he is everywhere and fills heaven and earth and sea, says: "Where shall I go from your Spirit, or where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into the underworld, you are present. If I take my wings before the dawn and dwell in the farthest part of the sea, even there your hand will lead me and your right hand will hold me." How quickly he showed that God is everywhere, that wherever the Spirit of God is, there God is, and that where God is, there his Spirit is present!

In this passage the bond of the undivided Trinity is expressed, since the Son of God spoke these words through the mouth of the prophet, speaking in the person of the man who through the incarnation came down to earth, through the resurrection ascended into heaven, and through the death of his body entered the underworld to set free those who were bound. Or if you refer it to the prophet, you notice that it expresses that Christ, the hand and right hand of God, is present everywhere, where God the Father and the Holy Spirit of God are.

We cannot doubt about the sun that, as it advances, it spreads its rays over the whole world and pours its light on all; even those who cannot see it still feel from the warmth of the air itself that it is present. For where is its heat lacking? Where do its rays not reach, when it scatters the darkness of night or clouds and lights up the earth? It gleams in the sky, it glows red on the sea, it burns on the earth. So you do not doubt that the sun shines everywhere; do you doubt about God, that the radiance of his glory and the image of his substance shines everywhere?

What does the Word of God, the eternal radiance, not penetrate, when he lights up even the hidden places of the mind that this sun cannot penetrate? For the Word of God is a spiritual sword, reaching even to the dividing of soul and of joints and marrow. Of this the righteous man says to Mary: "And a sword will pierce your own soul too, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed."

So he penetrates the soul and illuminates it as the brightness of eternal light. But though his power is spread through all and in all and over all—since he was born of the Virgin for all, both good and bad, just as he commands his sun to rise on the good and the bad—yet he warms the one who draws near to him. For just as a man who closes the windows of his house and chooses a dark place to stay shuts out the brightness of the sun, so whoever turns away from the Sun of Righteousness cannot

see his radiance; he walks in darkness, and amid light for everyone he is himself the cause of his own blindness. So open your windows, that your whole house may be lit by the brightness of the true sun; open your eyes, that you may see the Sun of Righteousness rising for you. But take care that no speck of straw troubles them. If there is any dirt in the eye of your mind, you will not be able to see; if there is any disease, it will grow worse, for light strikes the clouded sight of the eyes and stirs up greater pain. So let your eye be sound, lest your whole body begin to be full of darkness and stumble in the light, like the steps of the blind.

If someone shuts the doors of his house, is it the sun's fault that it does not light up his house? So if someone decides that his own mind must be barred with the bolts of his sins, and foolishly turns the radiance of the Word away from himself and brings upon himself the blindness of folly,

can he complain that the Sun of Righteousness refused to come in, or accuse the heavenly light of weakness? The Word of God knocks at your door. "If anyone opens to me," he says, "I will come in." So if someone does not open, is the fault not that of the one who does not open rather than of the one who does not come in? Nothing indeed is barred to God, nothing closed to the eternal light; but he disdains to open the gates of malice, and he will not enter the chambers of wickedness.

Since the vital power of our soul shrinks from a rotting part of the body, so that decayed limbs cannot feel its grace, would God deign to dwell in certain members of a corrupt soul? Yet the vital power of the soul is spread through the whole body; whether hand or foot or finger, each shares in sensation. Can the wisdom of God be absent anywhere, can his majesty be absent anywhere?

Certainly he does not hold back those who flee, he does not force [?]; but neither does he scorn those who draw near. His power, his Word, God, is near to all; for in him all things hold together, and he is the head of the body, the Church, in whom all fullness dwells. But many are separated from him by their sins; of them it is said: "See, those who go far from you will perish."

So the holy man says: "But for me it is good to cling to God"; and the apostle says that God is not far from each one of us: "In him," he says, "we live and exist and move." For, supplying the grace of life to all, he is at hand to all by the gift of his goodness; but he is nearer to those who are of a contrite heart.

The ancient history also teaches this in figures. Moses was on the summit of Mount Sinai, and he was alone. The people were in the valley at the foot of the mountain; the elders were partway up the mountain, above the merits of the common people, but separated by a very great distance from the merits of Moses. Not all were at the top, nor all at the bottom—only the people were there; Moses alone was on the summit of Mount Sinai, which in Latin translation means "temptation." You too, if you climb above temptations and bring your prayer with a contrite heart, will be nearest to God; if you are pure in heart, you too will see God, for "blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God."

So the one who is nearest to God says: "You are near, O Lord, and all your commandments are truth." The Jew cannot say this, since he does not receive the Lord Jesus; for he has separated himself, and believes not in the truth but in the shadow. How can he say "Your commandments are truth," when grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, since he does not acknowledge the one who redeemed the whole world by the truth and fullness of his circumcision?

The eighth verse is: "From the beginning I have known of your testimonies, that you have founded them forever." "From the beginning," he says, "I have taken up knowledge and faith concerning your testimonies, that they are founded forever." For the testimony is faithful and gives wisdom to the little ones. If Adam and Eve had known that the more cautious commandments had been given to them as to little children, so that they should not claim for themselves the knowledge of good and evil, which they could not define with right discernment, they could have kept their dwelling in paradise forever. If

men considered that the blood of a man cries out to God, they would keep their hands from killing a man. If they kept the commandments that the Lord gave with heaven and earth as witnesses, saying, "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth," knowing that whatever crime they commit against the law of the Lord, they will be convicted of having done it by the testimony of angels and powers, and also of holy men, they would lay their foundation upon these testimonies, because they are eternal and everlasting. So let us too build our work upon the foundation of the heavenly testimonies, so that it may not burn like wood or straw, but be proved like gold, and remain resting on an eternal foundation.
20. THE LETTER RESH

Here begins the letter Resh, which in Latin translation means "head" or "primacy." The head—if we consider the form of the human race—is what nourishes all the members, directs them, and fills them with the senses; for "the senses of a wise man are in his head." From there the courses of the veins, the passages of breath, and the powers of the blood are channeled into every part of the whole body; it surveys all things, it adorns all things. When the head is taken away, the body has no name, it is not recognized, and no use of life remains to it.

For this reason those who are condemned for some crime are deprived of what is the ornament of the whole body; and because they have been found to have committed, by a shameful or wicked offense, the filth of brutish savagery or the horror of bestial cruelty, they are ordered, as men who have fallen away from the standard of human restraint, to strip off the form of the human condition as well. For when the head is cut off, the trunk of the remaining body is likened to the bodies of beasts, and the one who could not keep to the rule of wisdom is robbed of wisdom's citadel. So the body is buried without its beauty; for in the head is the vigor of life, in the head is the grace of comeliness.

It is said that the snake, when threatened by danger, always hides its head and, coiling itself into a circle, exposes the rest of its body and protects this alone, because while the head keeps its vigor it is able to restore its other limbs if they are crushed. You too, keep this head in the moral sense; and keep it also in the mystical sense. The mystical head is Christ, because all things hold together in him and he is the head of the body, the Church. Whoever loses this head cannot have the use of life; by this alone we differ from the beasts,

having been formed in the image of God and in the likeness of his virtues by their power. Faith sets us apart from comparison with irrational cattle. Keep this head, you human serpents. Even if all your limbs are cut, your whole body burned in flames, plunged into the deep, torn open by beasts, yet if this head is guarded, life is whole and salvation is safe; for no one can perish from whom Christ has not been taken away.

The head is also the sum of our effort and work, the sum of our business, the sum of our hope, the sum of the virtues. And the whole sum of our effort is that we should be more humble and follow the truth, which the one who exalts himself does not see, "puffed up in vain by the mind of his flesh, and not holding fast to the head." What this head is he clearly expressed when he said: "from which the whole body, supplied and knit together by its joints and ligaments, grows with the growth that is from God."

And in the book of Isaiah the Lord says through the prophet: "I will take away from Judah head and tail, beginning and end." Judah lost the head it held, since it did not receive the Lord Jesus. Where there is faith, we have both beginning and end; where there is unbelief, there is neither beginning nor end. The Church, which has Christ, has a beginning, for Christ is the beginning of the Church, the firstborn from the dead. She also has an end, because he is the first and the

last; he is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. The synagogue has neither beginning nor end, because it neither found at the beginning what to follow nor at the end what to hope for. So the one who is puffed up does not hold fast to the head, that is, to that humility of Christ by which he came down even to the cross and came down even to the underworld. That is why the Jew did not believe: because he despised the one who said, "Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart." This humility is the head of all the virtues; it nourishes, as it were, the whole body of our actions.

Though someone may be weak, poor, and of low birth, yet if he does not exalt himself and put himself forward, he commends himself by his very humility. Let someone be very rich and noble: if he boasts of his noble birth and his wealth, he is cheapened by his own arrogance. Let someone be eloquent and strong, who, swollen with pride in his eloquence and strength, claims a great deal for himself: is not the unlearned and feeble man often preferred to him because of his modesty?

Indeed, the Pharisee in the Gospel, although he was abstemious, sparing of what belonged to others, generous with his own, and no shirker of fasting, as he himself said, nevertheless lost through his boasting even what he could have had; all those kinds of virtue, discolored by a single vice, could do him no good. The tax collector, who could list nothing that might win approval, nevertheless, because of his humility, went down from the temple justified rather than that Pharisee, as it is written in the prophet, that "he will save the humble in spirit."

That this letter expresses "head" we are also clearly taught in the Lamentations of Jeremiah; for with this letter set at the beginning the prophet says: "The breath before our face, Christ the Lord: under his shadow we shall live among the nations." This, then, is truly the head, which is the head of all.

We have spoken about "head". Let us also speak about "primacy", a word which, though it differs in sound and letters, still comes to the same meaning. For we read in the Old Testament of the birthright that Esau gave up to his brother along with the rights of the firstborn. That is why he was called Edom, which means earthly and cunning. These are the brothers for whom their father Isaac asked the Lord, praying that he would give him heirs of his line from his wife Rebecca,

who for twenty years had given no [?] sign of bearing children. The Lord heard him, and Rebecca conceived. When the little ones seemed to be tossing about in her womb, she asked the Lord and received the answer: "Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be separated from your womb; one people shall overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger." Is the mystery not plain? Two peoples are signified: the elder people of the Jews, and the younger Christian people, which received the elder brother's birthright for a dish of cooked lentils.

This sign clearly shows that the elder, earthly people lost the birthright it had through greed and lack of restraint, while the people of the Church, through sobriety and self-control, seized a birthright that was not theirs by order of age, both by confession and by a holy theft of the father's blessing. What, then, did the Christian people seize, if not the Lord Jesus? For from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force, as the Lord himself declared. It is a good fraud that steals eternal life. But since we think enough has been said about the interpretations of this letter, let us consider what the prophet set beneath it.

The first verse, then, is: "See my humility and rescue me, for I have not forgotten your law." Perhaps someone may say: "The prophet is boasting of himself." Even if he boasts, he boasts in his weaknesses, as the apostle also does when he says: "I will boast in my weaknesses." One person boasts in his riches, another in the titles of his nobility and lineage, another in his offices and honours. The righteous man boasts in humility,

for it is a good glory to be subject to Christ. And so that you may know that he does not want to boast but to call down the Lord's grace upon himself, the same prophet says elsewhere: "See my humility and my toil." He speaks, then, as one who has humbled his heart and as one who has laboured greatly. There he asks for his sins to be forgiven; here he prays to be rescued.

Picture a priest anxious for the safety of a minister whom he knows God has approved. Picture a father praying for a son who lies gravely ill, or a woman grieving for her son or her husband, bowed over her prayers, pouring out floods of tears night and day, humbling herself and lying prostrate on the ground, fasting again and again, and, what is harder than all this, worn out by grief of mind and heart and numbed as the sickness and danger drag on. Picture them saying to the Lord: "See my humility and rescue me."

Consider also that divine Scripture and our Lord anoint us every day with a kind of spiritual oil of heavenly precepts and train us. Eager to call as many as possible to take up the contest, the Lord has set out crowns of various kinds as prizes. Consider, I say, Christ's athlete, worn out by countless bouts and still resisting though his strength is nearly gone, shaken by the weight of the danger, when he sees that his wrestling is not only against flesh and blood but also against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Picture him saying: "See my humility and rescue me, for I have not forgotten your law." For one who has fought according to God's precepts could not forget them.

Look also at someone undergoing martyrdom: afflicted with torture after torture, thrust into darkness, broken by the heavy weight of chains, his legs stretched in the stocks, torn open on the rack, furrowed by iron claws, burned with red-hot plates. He is a man of persevering faith, but his spirit is now weary because the crown of a holy death is so long delayed, and he says: "See my humility and rescue me, for I have not forgotten your law." The testimonies of Scripture teach us that "humility" can be spoken of not only in our pursuits and resolutions but also in our trials. For we read: "Acceptable men in the furnace of humility"; the Greek says ταπεινώσεως, that is, "of humility". I mention this because very many Latin copies have "in the furnace of affliction". The Latin makes a distinction; the Greek does not, for ταπείνωσις is used both for the humility that is a virtue and for the humility of affliction. It does not matter if the Latin distinguishes them, for the Greek was not translated from the Latin; the Latin was translated from the Greek.

So too the Hebrews, as long as they were in Egypt, were in an iron furnace, that is, in the furnace of trial, the furnace of affliction, when they were oppressed by harsh commands. That is why it is written that God brought them out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt. The furnace was of iron because no one's works of virtue yet shone in their fullness in Egypt. No one's gold had been proved there, and no one's lead of wickedness had been burned away. It was a harsh furnace, the furnace of everlasting death, which no one could escape, which consumed everyone, and in which there was only grief and mourning.

But the furnace in which Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael sang a hymn to the Lord was a furnace of gold, not of iron, and through it wisdom shone out to the whole world by the faith of their devotion. This furnace too was in Babylonia, where there was no spiritual gold except perhaps gold held captive, for the Lord led captivity captive. This was the gold in these saints, who were captives among the Babylonians in body but free before God in spirit, loosed from the chains of human captivity and bound to the yoke of spiritual grace. And perhaps the same furnace is of iron to the weak and of gold to those who persevere.

All who wish to return to paradise must be tested by fire. For it is not written idly that when Adam and Eve had been driven out of their home in paradise, God placed at the exit of paradise a flaming sword that turned every way. All must pass through the flames, even John the evangelist, whom the Lord loved so much that he said of him to Peter: "If I want him to remain thus, what is that to you? Follow me."

Some have had doubts about his death, but we cannot doubt that he passed through the fire, because he is in paradise and is not separated from Christ. Or take Peter, who received the keys of the kingdom of heaven and walked upon the sea: he too must say, "We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into a place of refreshment." But for John the fiery sword will quickly be turned aside, because no wickedness is found in one whom righteousness loved. If there was any human fault in him, divine love burned it away, for his wings are like wings of fire.

Whoever has had the fire of love here will have no cause to fear the fire of the sword there. To Peter himself, who so often offered his life for Christ, the Lord will say: "Pass through, sit down at table." But Peter will say: "You have tested us with fire, as silver is tested with fire." For if many waters could not shut out love in him, how will fire shut him out? He will be tested as silver; I shall be tested as lead. I shall burn until the lead melts away.

If no silver is found in me, woe is me! I shall be thrust down into the lowest hell or burned up entirely like stubble. If any gold or silver is found in me, not through my own deeds but through the mercy and grace of Christ and through the ministry of the priesthood, perhaps I too shall say: "For those who hope in you shall not be put to shame."

By that fiery sword, then, the wickedness that sits upon the talent of lead will be burned away. That is why only one could not feel that fire, Christ, who is the righteousness of God, because he committed no sin: the fire found nothing in him that it could burn. And so for him alone the everlasting gates were lifted up, so that the King of glory might enter, not a man on trial.

Here, indeed, his flesh tasted death, for otherwise it could not have risen again. What I have read I take as settled; what I have not read I reverently leave to those who know. I confess one thing: whatever that flesh underwent, it underwent so that by its footsteps it might open the way again for others, either to triumph through the suffering of martyrdom or to pass into paradise. So let no one claim anything for himself; let no one boast of his merits or his power. Let us all hope to find mercy through the Lord Jesus, since we shall all stand before his judgment seat. From him I shall ask pardon, from him forgiveness; for what other hope do sinners have?

Whoever here thinks himself gold has lead, and whoever thinks himself a grain of wheat has stubble that can be burned up. Many here seem to themselves to be gold. I do not envy them, but even gold will be tested; it will be burned so that it can be proved. For it is written: "As gold in the furnace I will prove them." Let them take note, then, that all will be tested. So let the many who think themselves gold also pursue humility, so that they may burn away their faults.

But here such talk is empty boasting. That is why a wiser lump of gold says to the many who think themselves lumps of gold: "The furnace will test us all." Since, then, we are to be tested, let us so conduct ourselves that we may deserve to be approved at God's judgment. While we are here, let us hold fast to humility, so that when each of us comes to God's judgment, to those fires through which we must pass, he may say: "See my humility and rescue me." For if he has been proud, arrogant or stubborn, he will not be able to say this. No one will say, "See my pride", but rather, "See my humility", so that by its grace he may deserve to be rescued from that fire.

There is, then, a humility of toil and weariness, and there is also a humility of virtue and of resolve, which the righteous man keeps even in good and prosperous times and when he is at leisure. Though no toil has broken him and he is uncertain about the outcome of no contest, he shows a humble disposition towards everyone. He does not try to exalt what is his own, but rather to play down the value of his work and the grace of his merit.

Hear a righteous man humbling himself: "I am," he says, "the least of the apostles." That chosen vessel of God, that teacher of the Gentiles, calls himself the least, unworthy of the name of the office his works displayed. He claims nothing for himself but ascribes everything to the grace of God. This is surely what befits a righteous man.

It was by this humility that Abraham came to be called the father of faith. When he was given a share in conversation with God, he said that he was earth and clay. The Lord himself also says: "But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by men and despised by the people." He said this when speaking of the suffering of his body, he who sought not his own interests but those of others.

The apostle wants us to become his imitators, and he urges us, saying: "Have this mind in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant." So if we wish to follow Christ, let us not seek noble birth or riches. He emptied himself though he was in the form of God; though he was rich, he became poor. Do not you, then, look down on the common man because you are noble; do not despise the slave because you are powerful; do not scorn the poor man because you are rich. Are you nobler, more powerful or richer than Christ?

For your sake he took on the very things you despise. For your sake he humbled himself even to death, death on a cross, to undo the fall caused by your pride, so that what we had lost through the disobedience of the one man Adam we might recover through the obedience of the one Lord Jesus. "Therefore," he says, "God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, because the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father."

Consider, O man, what you are reading. The apostle was not labouring to prove Christ's power but to proclaim his obedience, and to show how great is the grace of humility and how great its reward. If you take it with simple ears, humility exalted even Christ;

but by that humility Christ was seeking not his own interests but yours. So listen with sharper ears: in the moral sense it benefited you; in the mystical sense it redeemed your salvation. Understand it however you like, it is your salvation. If you think his humility benefited Christ, whom will it not benefit? If it exalted him, whom will it not raise up?

The Lord became the servant of all, and the maker of all was beaten. He washed feet, was crucified, and died. Yet in all this I see no loss to his divinity; I recognize an advance in his work. He who had nothing to add to his power found something to add to the honour of his majesty. I dare to say that the gift of his handiwork would have been lost if humility had not recovered it.

So he redeemed us, but he also won us for himself. Humility, then, brings no loss. He who emptied himself is full; he who did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, taking the form of a servant, is in the glory of God the Father. I have received him whom I did not know; I have recognized him whom I did not recognize; I confess him whom I denied. To him I bend the knee of my body; to him I bend the knee of my mind; I worship him from whom I once fled.

We give you thanks, Lord Jesus, that you created us and, once created, set us over wild beasts and dumb animals. Greater still are the gifts of your visitation: you honoured those you visited with fellowship in your majesty, saying, "I will declare your name to my brothers." For when you took up a body, you became our brother, and yet you did not cease to be Lord.

Greater still is the grace of redemption: when we were in peril, you redeemed us by your own death, as it is written: "It is expedient that one man should die for the people." You raised the dead, saying, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up"; for in that temple of the Lord's body, resurrection grew for all.

You made those who rise again equal to the angels, as you said: "For women who do not marry and men who do not take wives will be like angels in heaven." Finally, you placed us at the right hand of God, on that throne of the Son of Man, as you yourself deigned to say: "But from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God."

So the apostle, marvelling at the gifts of God's goodness and showing at the same time that the generosity of the Father and the Son is one, says: "But God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us." You hear, O man, in what you ought to be rich and what virtues you ought to have: to show forth the love of God in yourself, and to imitate the sweetness of heavenly love.

And he added: "Even when we were dead in our sins, he made us alive together in Christ, by whose grace you have been saved, and raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus." In Christ, certainly, the flesh too is honoured. He, then, who sits at the right hand of God was humbled for our sake, and so he says to us: "Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart."

He did not say, "Learn from me, because I am powerful", but "because I am humble of heart", so that you may imitate him and say to him: "Lord, I have heard your voice; I have fulfilled your command. You told us to learn humility from you, and we have learned it not only from your words but also from your deeds. I have done what you commanded: see my humility."

A good athlete shows his limbs to prove the discipline of his way of life. He also shows them when, after some especially hard bouts, he is made to compete again, so that the judge, seeing his exhausted body, will not make him fight. So you too, show the humility of your heart, so as to display the honours of virtue; show also the contests your heart has fought, so that you may say, "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race," and the judge of the spiritual contest, seeing this, may award you the crown of righteousness, because you have kept the rules of the contest.

Next comes the second verse: "Judge my cause and deliver me; for your word's sake give me life." The innocent hurry to judgment and want to be vindicated quickly by the one who will rule on their innocence. This is the custom even in the world, and in this the world shares something with the saints. But the man who is righteous before God has another reason not to fear judgment: his case is heard before a merciful

judge, and before his Redeemer he wishes and hopes to be acquitted quickly, for the acquittal of the saints comes early. That is why the Lord, speaking through Ezekiel to the angels who carry out his vengeance, says: "Begin with my saints." The Lord does not want the saints to share a common judgment with the devil's companions, for the devil and his servants will not be scourged with men.

Where the guilt differs, the punishment is kept separate. So Scripture says in another place: "It is time for judgment to begin with the house of God." For those he pities he chastises quickly, so that they may not be tormented any longer by waiting for the judgment to come, nor be worn down any longer by the wretched state of guilt, and so that each may pay even double for his sins and at last be acquitted. For the punishment of the guilty is a kind of release from their offences.

In this world we see the guilty, bound in chains, led along in a kind of wretched parade, and sometimes the innocent suffer this too, so that it would be easier to die than to undergo such punishments. Those with a clear conscience certainly long to be heard. Even those weighed down by grave crimes long to get through their penalty by a quick death, so as to gain some shortening of their punishment.

There is also hope in the judge's mercy. The confinement of prison is harsher than exile itself, and not all who are banished are shut out from returning forever. If a human trial can achieve this, how much more should all seek the judgment of Christ! The devil's judgment is postponed so that he may always remain a defendant under punishment, always bound by the chain of his own wickedness, and bear forever the judgment of his own conscience.

That is why the rich man in the Gospel, sinner though he is, is pressed by painful torments, so that he may escape the sooner. The devil, however, is shown never to have come to judgment and not yet to have been subjected to punishment, except for what he himself pays in perpetual fear, conscious as he is of such great crimes, so that he may never be secure.

Or rather, to speak more accurately, the saint comes to judgment and the ungodly does not, since the ungodly do not rise in the judgment. The one asks to be acquitted, the other to be released after being punished; but whoever has not believed is not judged, but is punished by the judgment of his own ungodliness. Before our emperors, barbarians are not punished as criminals for what they did among their own people, since they are not subjects; rather, they are held under the graver name of enemies and are punished without any inquiry into a private

crime. In the same way Christ chastises his own, whom he loves, but those who are strangers to him, bound as it were by a general condemnation for their ungodliness, he hands over to eternal punishment; for the last enemy to be destroyed is death. And yet the prophet modestly teaches by his own example that even one who has no confidence in his works may still hope for a more lenient sentence for the sake of the word.

One man wants to live for the sake of riches, another for the sake of his children. This man asks to be given life for the sake of the word of God, just as Simeon waited for the coming of the Lord. So when he received the Lord in the temple, he said: "Now you dismiss your servant in peace, for my eyes have seen your salvation," declaring that he had had no other desire to live except to see Christ. At last he saw him, and he asked to be released from the chains of the body.

We can also understand "Judge my judgment" as if the case to be pleaded about our own judging were more serious for us than the case about our error. For pardon is more easily given to one who errs than to one who judges another wickedly. The same standard of judgment that you thought should be passed on another must come back upon you.

Next comes the third verse: "Salvation is far from sinners, because they have not sought out your righteous ways." Those whose judgment comes late have their salvation far off. But they are the authors of their own danger, because they did not draw near to the Lord. They became far off because by their own will they separated themselves from the grace of salvation. Salvation did not flee from them; they distanced themselves from salvation. Salvation came to the Jews, but they did not receive it. How did they not receive it? Listen: Jesus is salvation, and Jesus was called the Son of Man. The Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost, but the Jews asked for a robber to be released to them and rejected Jesus.

Who makes himself far from the Lord, if not the one who does not seek out his righteous ways? But whoever seeks them is near and clings to God. That is why the apostle says to those who seek God's righteousness: "You who were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ." The blood of Christ is righteousness; and so he himself says to John: "Let us fulfil all righteousness."

Next comes the fourth verse: "Your mercies are very many, Lord; give me life according to your judgments." Even though salvation is far from sinners, let no one despair, because his mercies are many. Those who are perishing through their own sin are set free by the Lord's mercy: "I will have mercy," he says, "on whom I will have mercy." He appeared openly to those who were not seeking him, called those who were fleeing, gathered the ignorant, and gave himself up to suffering for all. Is he not, then, abundantly merciful? A man's mercy reaches his neighbour, but the Lord's mercy reaches all flesh, so that all flesh, endowed with that compassion of the Lord, might ascend to God.

But how is it that, after saying the Lord's mercies are many, he asks to be given life according to his judgments, especially when he himself says elsewhere, "And do not enter into judgment with your servant"? The answer is that there is one judgment concerning the benefits of Christ, which we cannot repay (for who can repay the debt of our nature, the debt of salvation and grace?), and another judgment in which we are assessed with our frailty taken into account. Yet in this very judgment, judgment is joined with mercy, so that the truth of judgment is tempered by the Lord's compassion.

Or perhaps, because he had said, "Judge my judgment," he therefore added that the Lord's mercies are very many; for it is a grave thing to pass judgment on another. Hence it is also written: "Do not judge, so that you may not be judged." For since each person is conscious

of his own sins, how can he pass judgment on another's sin? Let him judge another's error who has nothing in himself to condemn; let him judge who does not do the same things he thinks deserve punishment in another, lest in judging another he pronounce sentence on himself; let him judge who is led to his verdict by no hatred, no resentment, no fickleness. You heard today what the true and just Judge said: "I can do nothing of myself."

Some heretics used to raise questions from this passage, as though the Son were weak because he does nothing of himself, as though even according to his divinity he were subordinate and subject to the Father's command. They do not notice that

by this very passage the unity of the divine power is all the more clearly proved, where they think there is a difference of power between Father and Son. The Son does nothing of himself because, through the unity of their working, neither does the Son act without the Father nor the Father without the Son. Indeed, the Father says to the Son: "Let us make man in our image and likeness," declaring that the work is shared where the counsel is shared. What does he do without Wisdom, who made all things in wisdom, as we read:

"In wisdom you have made all things"? Indeed, Wisdom said: "When he made the heavens I was with him, and I was the one in whom he delighted"; and the evangelist says: "All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made," to teach that the Son is not only the maker of all things but also a partner in the Father's work.

Yet I think this passage should be referred to the pattern of judging. For the gospel is not only teaching about faith but also instruction in morals and a mirror of upright living. I find in the gospel that the Lord Jesus took on the dispositions and duties of many, to teach us how we ought to conduct ourselves in those duties. He took on the role of shepherd and said: "The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep"; and so for his rational flock he did not withhold himself from bodily suffering, so that, laying the weary sheep on the shoulders of his cross, he might restore it by carrying a loving burden.

He took on the role of advocate, for we have him as our advocate with the Father. He spent whole nights in prayer for us, to teach us by his example how we ought to beg pardon for our sins. For he did not spend the night in prayer as though he could not otherwise reconcile the Father to us, but to show what an advocate ought to be, what a priest ought to be: one who should stand as intercessor for Christ's flock not only by day but also by night.

Or did he need help to obtain what he could himself do, the very thing he was asking for, as he himself said: "I am going to the Father, and whatever you ask of him in my name, I will do"? Indeed, elsewhere, when he was raising Lazarus, he says: "I knew that you always hear me." Nor did he spend the night in prayer as one who was weak, since he knew that he is always heard; and he cried out: "Lazarus, come out!" Resurrection spoke, and death withdrew.

He also took on the condition of a defendant: he stood accused before a judge, and the Lord of all did not disdain the lowliness of a provincial governor. When questioned, he kept silent, showing that the defense of innocence lies not in loud shouting or in the pleading of courtroom advocacy but in integrity of conscience, and that what we should seek is not the safety of the body but the purity of the soul. Indeed, he who acquitted Susanna while she kept silent offered himself to death: in her case so that no one should despair, in this case so that he should not refuse the sacrifice

for the redemption of the whole world. Finally, when he was struck, he did not revile, he did not strike back; the Lord of heaven and earth laid aside the desire for vengeance and uttered a word of humility, saying: "If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness to the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me?" As though he were weak, he laments the injury of the blows, and though he could have avenged himself, he preferred to complain rather than to punish.

So here too he took on the role and the purpose of a judge, saying: "I can do nothing of myself." For a good judge does nothing by his own whim or according to his private will, but pronounces according to the laws and rights. He obeys the decrees of the law and does not indulge his own will; he brings nothing prepared and premeditated from home, but judges as he hears and decides according to the nature of the case. He complies with the laws and does not oppose them; he examines the merits of the case and does not alter them.

Learn, you judges of this world, what disposition you ought to keep in judging, what sobriety, what sincerity. The Lord of all says: "I can do nothing of myself." Elsewhere I read: "He cannot deny himself." He cannot—not, of course, through weakness but through integrity; not through inability to act but through scrupulousness in judging. What can he not do who can do all things, except what he does not wish to be able to do? He does not wish to be able to do what

he would condemn; he does not wish to be able to act against faith; he does not wish to be able to act against truth. Finally, hear him saying why he cannot do anything of himself: "As I hear," he says, "so I judge"; that is: "I do not decide by my own power what pleases me, but by the conscientiousness of a judge what is just; and therefore my judgment is true, because I indulge not my own will but equity." Hear what the heavenly Judge says: "I can do nothing of myself; as I hear, so I judge."

And Pilate said to the Lord Jesus: "I have power to release you and I have power to crucify you." You usurp, O man, a power you do not have, when God, who has power over all things, denies that he has it. Hear what Justice says: "I can do nothing of myself." Hear what the judge of equity declares: "As I hear, so I judge." Hear what the judge of iniquity says: "I have power to release you and I have power to crucify you." By your own voice, Pilate, your very own, you are bound; by your own sentence you are condemned.

It was by power, then, not by equity, that you handed the Lord over to be crucified; by power you acquitted a robber but killed the Author of life. Yet not even this power that you claim to have did you have of yourself. Indeed, the Lord Jesus says to you: "You would have no power over me at all unless it had been given you from above." It is an evil power to be permitted what does harm; that power belongs to darkness—not to fail to see the truth, but to spurn it.

Hear what the true Judge says: "I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me." He speaks as a man, he teaches as a judge, since one who judges ought not to obey his own will but to hold to what the laws prescribe. Take a judge of this world: can he go against the terms of an imperial rescript? Can he overstep the rule of an imperial decree? How much more ought we to keep the pattern of divine judgment!

Christ says: "I do not seek my own will"—that is, a human will, which is steered by hatred, or driven by partisanship, or bent by favor, or corrupted by the lies of others, for "every man is a liar"—"but the will," he says, "of him who sent me"; that is: "I have come to teach the pattern of divine judicial inquiry, so that in judging, the safeguarding of truth may matter more than obedience to one's own will." So here too what is expressed is not weakness of power but a pattern of justice.

The judgment of the Son of God is just, then, because it is according to God's will, not according to human feeling. For God is full of mercies, and his mercy is joined with judgment and his judgment with mercy; he neither shows mercy without judgment nor judges without mercy. Indeed, it is written: "His mercy is in the scales;

but the sons of men are liars in the scales, so as to deceive." So God examines and weighs the merits of each person, and just as he gives grace by measure, so that it may not exceed the measure, so he gives mercy by measure. Hence he says: "Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will they give into your lap. With the same measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you." Likewise each person's works are weighed in the balance, so that if the good outweigh the bad, a reward is bestowed; if sins outweigh virtues, a harsher

punishment binds the guilty. You have this expressly stated in the letter to Timothy, where the apostle Paul says: "The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others follow after them. Likewise good deeds too are manifest, and those that are otherwise cannot be hidden."

Everything, then, is done by the Lord our God with a certain measure and weight. "Who has set the rocks in the balance?" Scripture says; and just before: "Who has measured the water in his hand and the heavens with his palm?" He who examines our deeds surely bestows his own gifts only after examination, and decides all things by a sound weighing. He weighs mercy, he weighs vengeance; in both there is a fixed weight and a fitting measure. Hence David too says: "And you will give them tears to drink in measure," lest, without the restraint of measure, they be crushed by a heap of punishments and be unable to bear it.

And elsewhere the same prophet says: "In the hand of the Lord is a cup full of pure wine, well mixed, and he has tipped it from this side to that; yet its dregs have not been emptied out." And Jeremiah says: "Babylon is a golden cup in the hand of the Lord, by which the nations were made drunk"; that is, punishment has been paid in full by the nations, so that they might no longer exult over having harassed God's people with most bitter devastation.

The sense of David's verse, then, is this: the punishment owed to the ungodly is prepared and full, and the Lord tips it toward the faithless; yet in his compassion he does not see fit to pour it out to the dregs, lest they be unable to bear the full measure of torment. So he tips the cup but does not empty it: tipping it belongs to his censure, not emptying it to his mercy.

So the Lord our God tempers even judgment with mercy. For which of us can stand without God's compassion? What can we do that is worthy of heavenly rewards? Which of us rises so high in this body as to lift up his soul so that it clings to Christ unceasingly? By what merit, pray, is it granted to a human being that this corruptible flesh should put on incorruption and this mortal nature put on immortality? By what labors, by what sufferings can we lighten our sins? "The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the glory that is to come." It is not according to our merits, then, but according to God's mercy that the pattern of the heavenly decrees proceeds toward humankind.

There follows the fifth verse: "Many are those who persecute me and afflict me; I have not turned aside from your testimonies." It is no great thing not to turn aside from God's testimonies when no one afflicts you, no one persecutes you. For who, with prosperous events going his way without any setback, would become ungrateful? Who, abounding in riches

and strong in constant health, would not credit God's grace for what has been granted him? Indeed, when the Lord was praising holy Job, the adversary said: "Does Job worship the Lord for nothing? Have you not given him everything? Stretch out your hand against all that he has, and see whether he will not curse you to your face." So Job was proved all the more when, having lost his wealth and his children, he did not withdraw from the worship of the Lord or from gratitude to him.

But the persecutor is not just one; he has many servants. Yet let him not frighten you. For "through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God." If there are many persecutions, there are many trials; where there are many crowns, there are many contests. So it is to your profit that there are many persecutors, so that among many persecutions you may more easily find the way to be crowned.

Let us take the example of the martyr Sebastian, whose feast day is today. He was a native of Milan. Perhaps the persecutor had already left, or had not yet come to these parts, or was milder here. Sebastian noticed that here the contest was either nonexistent or lukewarm. He set out for Rome, where bitter persecutions were raging against zeal for the faith; there he suffered, that is, there he was crowned. And so there, where he had come as a stranger, he established a dwelling of everlasting immortality. If there had been only one persecutor, this martyr would certainly not have been crowned.

But what is worse, the persecutors are not only those who are seen but also those who are not seen, and these persecutors are far more numerous. For just as a single persecuting king used to send orders for persecution to many, and in the various cities or provinces there were different persecutors, so too the devil directs many of his servants to carry out persecutions not only outwardly but also inwardly, in each person's soul.

Of these persecutions it was said: "All who wish to live godly lives in Christ Jesus suffer persecution." He said "all"; he excepted no one. For who can be excepted, when the Lord himself endured the trials of persecution? Avarice persecutes, ambition persecutes, self-indulgence persecutes, pride persecutes, fornication persecutes. Hence the apostle too says: "Flee fornication"; for why would you flee it, unless it were pursuing you? For there is an evil spirit of fornication, an evil spirit of avarice, an evil spirit of pride.

These are the grievous persecutors, who without the terror of the sword often crush a person's mind, who conquer the souls of the faithful by enticements rather than by terrors. These are the enemies you must beware of, these the harsher tyrants, by whom Adam was taken captive. Many who were crowned in public persecution have fallen in this hidden persecution.

"Fighting without," he says, "fears within." Do you notice how grievous is the struggle that goes on inside a person, when he is in conflict with himself and battles his own desires? The apostle himself wavers, is held fast, is bound. He declares that he is taken captive in the law of sin and vanquished by the body of death, and that he could not have escaped had he not been set free by the grace of the Lord Jesus.

But just as there are many persecutions, so there are many martyrdoms. Every day you are a witness of Christ. You were tempted by the spirit of fornication, but in fear of Christ's coming judgment you did not think the chastity of mind and body should be defiled: you are a martyr of Christ. You were tempted by the spirit of avarice to seize the property of a weaker man, to violate the rights of a defenseless widow, and yet, contemplating the heavenly precepts, you judged that help should be given rather than injury inflicted:

you are a witness of Christ. Indeed, these are the witnesses Christ wants standing beside him, as it is written: "Do justice for the orphan and vindicate the widow; and come, let us reason together, says the Lord." You were tempted by the spirit of pride, but seeing the poor and needy you had compassion on them with a devout heart and loved humility more than arrogance: you are a witness of Christ;

and what is more, you have borne witness not only in word but also in deed. For who is a richer witness than one who confesses that the Lord Jesus has come in the flesh by keeping the precepts of the gospel? For whoever hears and does not act denies Christ; though he confesses him in word, he denies him in deeds. How many there are who say: "Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons, and work many mighty deeds?" On that day he will answer: "Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity!" He, then, is a witness who bears witness to the precepts of the Lord Jesus with deeds to back his words.

How many, then, are Christ's martyrs in secret every day, confessing the Lord Jesus! The apostle knew this martyrdom and this faithful witness to Christ, for he said: "For this is our boast, the testimony of our conscience." How many have confessed outwardly and denied inwardly! For many, in order to marry a woman whose Christian parents were refusing her to a pagan husband, feigned the faith for a time and are found out to have confessed outwardly what they

denied inwardly. Or do we think that the Lord our God was so severely angered against the Jewish people, so that twenty-three thousand of the people were put to death because they had intercourse with women of the Midianite nation, merely on account of fornication, and not rather because through intercourse with foreign women they were driven to abandon the faith and deny the Lord?

"Do not believe every spirit," Scripture says, "but know by their fruits whom you ought to believe." Someone comes into the church while seeking office under Christian emperors; with a feigned heart he pretends to offer prayer; he bows down and prostrates himself on the ground, though he has not bent the knee of his mind. A man sees him and thinks him a Christian; a man sees him praying humbly and believes him; but God hears him denying. He goes away approved by man but condemned by the Judge.

How much more tolerable it would have been for him to deny before man and confess to God! Yet even this is blameworthy, for perfect confession requires both the devotion of the heart and the profession of the voice: "For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation."

So in the inward persecutions be faithful and brave, so that you may also be approved in these public persecutions. In the inward persecutions too there are kings and governors, judges terrible in their power. You have an example in the temptation the Lord endured. All the kingdoms were shown to him, and it was said to him: "All these I will give you if you fall down and worship me." It is also read elsewhere: "Let not sin reign in your mortal body."

You see, O man, before what kings you have taken your stand, before what governors of sins, if guilt reigns in you. As many sins and as many vices as there are, so many kings are there; and before these we are brought, and before these we stand. These kings too have a tribunal in the minds of a great many. But if anyone confesses Christ, he at once makes that king a captive and casts him down from the throne of his mind. For how could the devil's tribunal remain in one in whom Christ's tribunal is raised up?

"Many, then, are those who persecute and afflict me." Perhaps it is Christ who says this, and says it in the voices of individual believers, for it is he whom the adversary persecutes in us. If you shun the persecutors, you cast Christ away, who allows himself to be tempted in order to conquer. Wherever the devil sees him, there he lays ambushes, there he brings up the siege engines of temptation, there he weaves snares, to shut him out if he can. But where

the devil does battle, there Christ stands by; where the devil lays siege, there Christ is shut within and defends the enclosure of spiritual walls. So whoever runs away from the persecutor also rejects the defender. But when you hear, "Many are those who persecute and afflict me," do not be afraid, you who can say: "If God is for us, who is against us?" Yet the one who says this is he who does not turn aside from the Lord's testimonies by any crooked path of vice.

There follows the sixth verse: "I saw those who did not keep the covenant, and I pined away, because they did not keep your words." Blessed is he who pines away in the love of God, who sees those who do not keep the covenant. One man pines away because of sinful loves; he wastes away while he is kept waiting in his love for his beloved, and while the fulfillment of his burning

desire is delayed, his spirit fails, and the strength of his body is diminished by a disfiguring pallor and the wasting of weary limbs. Another, who covets money, pines away in wretched, greedy longing until he gets it. Another, immoderately impatient to seize office, is consumed by no small wasting of mind if he must sigh long after what he desires. Not such is he who says: "How my flesh has wasted away in a desert land, trackless and without water!" For he chastised his flesh and made it waste away, while, intent with untiring desire on the knowledge of God and anticipating the light of day with eager expectation, he longed to pay his homage to the Lord before dawn with canticles and hymns.

The man of peace, then, pines away when he sees others break covenants, destroy the harmony of agreements, revive quarrels out of peace, and return from goodwill to tumult. This is certainly not done by one who keeps the Lord's precepts, by one who hears him saying: "My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you." So whoever keeps the covenant obeys Christ's commands; but whoever does not keep it despises Christ's precepts and, what is worse, disdains and neglects them once he knows them.

There follows the seventh verse: "See that I have loved your precepts, O Lord; in your mercy give me life." Here too he invites the Lord to look upon a heart full of love for him. No one says "See" unless he judges that, if he is seen, he will be pleasing. And he does well to say "See," and says it in keeping with the law, for the law commands that every person present himself three times a year in the sight of the Lord.

The saint presents himself every day, appears every day, and does not appear empty-handed; for he is not empty who has received of his fullness. David was not empty, who said: "Our mouth was filled with joy," for joy is a fruit of the Holy Spirit. And just as we have all received of the fullness of the Word, as John said, so the Holy Spirit too has filled the whole world from his own fullness.

Zechariah was not empty, who was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied the coming of the Lord Jesus. Paul was not empty, who preached the gospel in abundance and was filled, receiving from the Ephesians a fragrant offering, a sacrifice pleasing to God. Nor were the Corinthians empty, in whom the grace of God abounded, according to the testimony of the same apostle.

So David offered himself to God every day, and he did not come empty-handed. He could say, "I opened my mouth and drew in the Spirit"; that is why he said, "See how I have loved your commandments." Hear how you ought to offer yourself to Christ: not in things that are seen, but in things hidden, in secret, so that your Father who sees in secret may reward you and repay your faithful devotion.

"I have loved your commandments," he says. He did not say "I have kept them" or "I have guarded them"; for the imprudent did not keep the Lord's commandments. Some manuscripts have asynetountas, that is, "the foolish," "those who do not understand." So those who do not understand are not wise, and these do not keep the commandments. But one who is perfect in understanding and perfect in wisdom loves them, which is more than keeping them.

For keeping is mostly a matter of necessity and fear, but loving is a matter of charity. One who preaches the gospel keeps the commandment, but one who preaches it willingly receives a reward; how much more is one who loves rewarded! We can fail to love what we will, but we cannot fail to will what we love. Yet although he looks for the reward of perfect charity, he also asks for the support of God's mercy, that in it he may be given life by the Lord. So he is not an arrogant man demanding a reward that is owed him, but a humble man pleading for God's mercy.

There follows the last verse of this letter: "The beginning of your words is truth; all the judgments of your justice are for ever." Since the beginning of God's words is truth, truth is certainly the foundation of faith. For first we must believe that the oracles of the most high God which we read in the divine Scriptures are true;

second, we must learn their power through fuller knowledge. For just as the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, while love is the fullness of wisdom (for the law is wisdom, and love is the fulfilment of the law), so the fullness of God's words is wisdom and the knowledge of justice. For just as there is a kind of progress from the fear of the Lord to the grace of charity, so there seems to be a kind of progress from truth to the judgment of divine justice.

You came to church and heard that God is one, which is where the law begins, as you have it written: "Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord." Believe that there is one God, not many gods. But when you begin to read that the Lord Jesus, the Son of God, came in the flesh to redeem the whole world, distinguish wisely: there is one God the Father, from whom are all things and we in him, and one Lord Jesus, through whom are all things and we through him.

Recognize that he came so that our hearts might be shaped along the paths of virtue, that we might learn gentleness of character from the example of his life, and that guilt might be wiped away by grace; then you have advanced from confessing the truth to knowing justice. Faith is the beginning of the Christian, but justice is the Christian's fullness; faith lies in the confession of the peoples, justice in the suffering of martyrdom.

Knowing, then, that all the judgments of God's justice will stand for ever, let us take care that our works do not displease him and we come under eternal judgment, and that, if we have done anything good, we are not undone by complacent pride. "We must all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done, whether good or evil."

You see that Paul too will stand there, as he himself says. Beware of bringing wood, beware of bringing straw with you to God's judgment, for fire will burn them up. Beware lest, while you have one or two things that will be approved, you bring [?] in many more works what will give offense. If anyone's work is burned up, he will suffer loss, yet he himself can be saved through fire.

From this we gather that the same man is saved in part and condemned in part. Knowing, then, that there are many judgments, let us examine all our works. For a just man, the burning of any of his work is a heavy loss [?]; for the wicked, it is a wretched punishment. Let all at the judgment rather be full of grace, full of blooming crowns, lest perhaps, when our deeds are weighed, guilt should tip the scale.
XXI. THE LETTER SIN

Here begins the letter Sin, which in Latin means "upon a wound." What is "upon a wound" but a remedy that soothes the pain of the wound? Oil is poured upon a wound to soften all its harshness; a poultice is put upon a wound, and a bandage upon a wound, and by these every wound is tended.

So where there is hope of restoring health, remedies are applied to wounds. But where "the whole head is in pain and the whole heart in sorrow, there is neither wound nor scar nor inflamed sore"—that is, where not a part but the whole is in danger and is being consumed by a kind of wasting of the whole corrupted body—there one cannot apply a poultice, or oil, or a bandage. It is far better, then, to have a wound which you can tend and bind up than for death to creep within with no wound to show.

But there is not only a wound of the body; there is also a wound of the mind, which is soothed by the oil, as it were, of gentler address and the sweetness of peaceable speech. There are compresses of words, there are remedies of heavenly commandments, by which all the poison of wickedness is removed. There are bonds of the law which do not chafe but rather set free those bound by them, and there is a spiritual poultice by which certain bruised members of the soul are made firm again.

Let us consider, then, what is the wound and what is upon the wound. "Princes have persecuted me without cause" is the wound; "I will exult in your words like one who finds much spoil" is what is upon the wound, because the hardness of the wound is healed by the Lord's words.

In the Lamentations of Jeremiah, too, you have written under this letter: "You have heard their reproach, O Lord, all their counsels against me, the lips of those who rise up against me, and their plotting against me all the day, their sitting down and their rising up"; that is the wound. But he added: "Look upon it before their eyes; render them their recompense, O Lord, according to the works of their hands"; that is upon the wound, since vengeance often eases the pain of a wound.

And further on the same Jeremiah says: "Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Edom, you who dwell in Geth; to you also the cup shall pass; you shall drink and be drunk"; that is upon the wound. For the Lord's cup is the forgiveness of sins, in which is poured out the blood that redeemed the sins of the whole world. This cup made the nations drunk, so that they no longer remembered their own pain but forgot their old error.

Good, then, is spiritual drunkenness, which does not know how to make the body's step unsteady, but knows how to lighten the step of the mind. Good is the drunkenness of the cup of salvation, which removes the sorrow of a sinful conscience and pours in the joy of eternal life. That is why Scripture says, "And your cup that makes drunk, how glorious it is!"

So the remedy is upon the wound, because the physician is the Lord Jesus himself, who healed our wounds, pouring in wine and oil and binding up the wounds of that Adam who was wounded by robbers as he went down from Jerusalem. Let each one take care, then, not to go down from Jerusalem;

for each one goes down by his sins and goes up by his merits. Or, since we are frail, let one who has gone down run to that Samaritan, the guardian of his own work, the guardian of law and grace, so that he may find a remedy for his wound, for he lays the bandage of heavenly words upon the wound, saying, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near." Good is the bandage that joins the broken bones of your soul, restores them to firmness and their former strength, and makes the torn limbs whole without the blemish of any scar.

We think enough has been said about the meaning of the letter, as far as our capacity allows. Let us set about considering the verses of the holy prophet, which he set down by the revelation of the Holy Spirit: "Princes have persecuted me without cause, and my heart has trembled at your words." If we go back to the ancient history, Saul and Absalom and many foreign

princes persecuted holy David, but none of them could triumph over him. There are also the princes of this world and the rulers of darkness, who try to overpower you within your own breast and carry on a cruel persecution inside you, promising kingdoms of the earth, honors and riches, if you give in with a weak mind and decide to obey their commands. These princes sometimes persecute without cause, sometimes not without cause.

They persecute without cause the one in whom they find nothing of their own and whom they strive to subdue; they do not persecute without cause the one who has given himself over to their power and has entered wholly into the possession of the world. For they claim dominion over their own as of right, and demand from them the wages of iniquity.

A martyr rightly says this, since he endures the torments of persecution unjustly: he has stolen nothing, violently oppressed no one, shed no one's blood, never thought anyone's marriage bed should be violated; he owes nothing to the laws, yet is forced to suffer punishments heavier than robbers'; he speaks what is just and is not heard, he speaks what is full of salvation and is attacked, so that he can say, "When I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause." He suffers persecution without cause, then, who is attacked without any crime: he is attacked as guilty when in such a confession he deserves praise; he is attacked as a sorcerer because he glories in the name of the Lord, though piety is the foundation of all virtues. Truly he is attacked in vain who, among the impious and faithless, is accused of impiety, though he is a teacher of the faith.

But one who is attacked without cause ought to be brave and steadfast. How, then, did he add, "and my heart has trembled at your words"?
