Trembling belongs to weakness, to fear and dread; but there is also a weakness that leads to salvation, and there is also a fear proper to the saints: "Fear the Lord, you his saints," and, "Blessed is the man who fears the Lord." Why "blessed"? Because "he will delight greatly in his commandments."

Picture, then, a martyr set amid dangers: on one side the savage beasts roar to strike terror, on another the hiss of red-hot plates and the flame of a blazing furnace seethe, on another the dragging of heavy chains resounds, and here stands the bloody executioner. Picture him, I say, looking around and seeing everything full of tortures, then thinking of God's commandments—that everlasting fire, that endless burning of the faithless, that misery of punishment ever renewed—and trembling in his heart lest, while yielding to present things, he hand himself over to everlasting ruin, and being troubled in mind as he gazes, as if seeing it before him, on that terrible sword of the

judgment to come. Will you not rank this trembling equal to the confidence of a steadfast man? The confidence of one who longs for eternal things and the trembling of one who fears divine things lead to the same result. Still, let the one who hopes be the stronger, let the one who is confident be the stronger.

O that I might deserve to be such a man that, if a persecutor should fall upon me, I would not consider the bitterness of my punishments, not measure the torments or the penalties, not think of the cruelty of any pain, but count all these things light, and tremble only lest Christ deny me, lest Christ shut me out, lest he drive me from the council of priests if he judges me unworthy of that fellowship! May he see me rather, though shaken by terror of bodily punishments, yet trembling still more at the judgments to come! Even if he says to me, "O you of little faith, why did you doubt?", he will still stretch out his right hand, and when I am tossed by the mass of the rising waves of this world, he will make me firm in the faithful harbor of the mind.

The second verse follows: "I will exult in your words like one who finds much spoil." Good, then, is trembling at God's words if it produces exultation; for one who trembles at God's words afterwards exults in God's words. So one who keeps God's words in his hall, that is, in his heart, shuts the speeches of princes out of his heart: fear shuts out fear. For if someone who enters the baths sheds the heat of the sun, and heat drives out heat, how much more does the terror of divine judgment drive out this human terror, and the fervor of eternal grace the fervor of worldly favor!

So one who has the word of God exults; for he has much spoil, taken from the Jews, he has the stripped armor of a fallen enemy. Just as David took Goliath's sword and cut off his head with his own sword, so the true David, the humble and meek Lord Jesus, cut off the head of the spiritual Goliath with his own weapons. For the nations were the devil's weapons, and wounded by the faith of the nations, he lost the head he had.

The fallen one was stripped of his spoils and his goods were plundered, because the strong man was bound. The devil's vessel was the flesh of sinful man; but after we believed in Christ, our flesh began to be a vessel of election, as you have it of the apostle Paul, who was sent to the Gentiles, in the words the Lord Jesus spoke to Ananias: "Go, for he is a vessel of election to me."

Rightly, then, was Christ's name called "Quickly strip off the spoils, swiftly divide them," because, "before the child knows how to call father or mother, he will take the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians." So the king of the Assyrians—that is, of those whom faithlessness had made empty—lost the spoils he held.

And that you may know again that Christ claimed back from the devil the spoils he had seized in Adam: "the Sabeans, men of stature," passed over to the Lord Jesus bound in chains and began to worship him, because "he led captivity captive." He took away the devil's head so that he himself might be the head of the slain body. Rightly now do the nations carry the royal head throughout the whole world, because they are members of Christ.

You have learned about the nations. Learn also about the Jews, from whom the Lord Jesus took the spoils: that is, he took the kingdom of heaven away and gave it to a nation producing its fruit. He took away the strength of bread and the strength of water; the prophet, the wonderful counselor, the wise architect and the intelligent hearer he took from them and gave to us;

rightly do I exult, "like one who finds much spoil." Without labor of my own I have found spoils I did not have: I have found the Heptateuch, I have found the books of Kings, I have found the writings of the prophets, I have found Ezra, I have found the Psalms, I have found Proverbs, I have found Ecclesiastes, I have found the Song of Songs, I have found Christ the wonderful counselor, I have found Paul the wise architect, I have found the intelligent hearer, the Christian people, who know how to hear what is read;

for he truly hears who understands what he hears. The law is spiritual; the Jew who hears it in a bodily way does not hear it, but he hears it who hears in the Spirit. They have the books, but not the meaning of the books; they have the prophets, but they do not have the one of whom the prophets prophesied. For how can they have him whom they did not receive?

That is why he appeared to me with Moses and Elijah: because he withdrew from them. One who has the word of God has much spoil; he has the resurrection, he has justice, power and wisdom, he has everything, because in him all things hold together. The Hebrews despoiled the Egyptians and carried off their vessels; the Christian people possess the spoils of the Jews, and we have everything that they did not know they had. They carried off material gold and silver; we have received the gold of the mind, we have acquired the silver of heavenly speech.

The third verse follows: "I have hated and abhorred injustice, but I have loved your law." Rightly does one who has the weapons of justice hate injustice. The Hebrew, though he had these weapons—that is, the law and the prophets—abhorred a dead body, because the law says, "Whoever touches a dead body shall be unclean," and he refused the dead the last duties of humanity; but in the eyes of the law no one is dead except the unjust man.

This is uncleanness for the righteous: iniquity. For what is more unclean than to stain the mind, the most precious thing given to man, with shameful crimes and to make it savage with cruel schemes? What good does it do them to shrink from looking at a dead man? Would that their life did not defile anyone who comes near, since their death can contaminate no one! Death harms no one; would that life did no harm!

The contagion of filth is partnership in iniquity. How, then, can one defile who can no longer be wicked, since, even if he was, he has ceased to be? Flee iniquity, then, lest it seize you; flee injustice, which makes the living dead already.

But no one flees iniquity except one who loves equity; and so he says, "but I have loved your law." In the law there is equity—if you take the law spiritually, if you rise with Christ and contemplate there that holy heavenly altar, not the earthly altar which was destroyed by the ravages of the enemy; if you look to that Jerusalem which is in heaven, not this one which the Jewish people thronged on earth, which, because of the faithlessness of its inhabitants, was conquered by the Roman army, set on fire and burned; if you gaze on that high priest of whom it is written: "Having therefore a great high priest who has gone out from the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our faithful confession." He is our advocate with the Father every day, so that for those with whom, in the days of his flesh, he suffered with merciful compassion, he may work the forgiveness of sins every day. For what other hope is there for the human race, unless the offenses of all the living are forgiven? He alone, then, is the chief of priests, before whom stand the godly priests who have entered that most high heavenly sanctuary by the merit of their own blood. That law, then, is to be loved in which the true Hebrew is free from all slavery to vices, in which there is the great Sabbath and the undisturbed rest of the departed, in which the seed of a dead people is raised up, not by intercourse but by a brother's redemption. According to this law, then, the saint hates injustice, not the unjust man, who can often be converted; and he loathes not the remains of the dead but dead iniquity.

The fourth verse follows: "Seven times a day I have spoken your praise for the judgments of your justice." The number expresses the zeal of holy devotion, but I think rather that it declares a disposition that is pure, quiet and free of every burden of sin, so that prayer may be offered without any fire of angry cursing or shameful

desire, that we may ask for nothing that harms another, nothing that stains us with worldly requests. Let us praise in hymns and songs, always confessing that what we sing in God's praises is true and just. Let our judgment not be wavering and doubtful, nor the bent of our mind divided; let it not be taken up with material business and turned aside from carrying out our spiritual purpose. Let the justice of God always be acknowledged as just with a tranquil mind, not with idle leisure.

The fifth verse follows: "Great peace have those who love your name, and for them there is no stumbling block." We said above that charity casts out fear; now we say that it casts out every disturbance. For in one who loves God there is a deep tranquillity of a steadfast mind. "Many waters," it says, "cannot shut out love, and rivers will not overflow it." The many waters are the various passions, and the rivers are worldly desires stirred up by bodily impulses; yet they cannot overthrow the wall of charity.

And so one founded on charity says, "Our soul has passed through the torrent." Could the water of the sea shut out Moses' charity? So that the course of the Psalms may support you in the literal sense as well: surely, because he loved God, he believed the way through the sea was safe for him; but those who did not love God were drowned in the waves and met an end worthy of their sacrileges.

Elijah and Elisha crossed the Jordan on foot, and this was the reward and grace of their great charity. So, in order to cross the waters of the river Jordan, they had first crossed the flood of our passions with the step of the mind. Of this water the Lord says, "If you pass through water, I am with you, and the rivers will not overflow you." He is always present to his just ones when they are worn down by any adversity, provided they pass through with a steadfast mind, not doubting, not troubled by uncertainty of faith.

Pass through, then, you too, with the love of a faithful soul. If you want the divine presence to be with you, let there be not only peace but great peace in your soul; let no battles of conflicting desires assail you, let neither anger nor lust goad you; and if there is a fight, let it be outside, not within. Fight against your persecutors, though even to them you must often yield in silence, because they conquer for your sake.

Their power is your victory; indeed, they are triumphed over at the very moment they believe they have won. So let avarice not assail you, let greed not harass you, let sadness not cast you down, let lust not inflame you, let pride not puff you up, let ambition not bend you, let fear not dismay you. Let great peace abound, which surpasses all understanding, in the words of the apostle, than which nothing more beautiful could have been said.

For the highest end of wisdom is that we be tranquil of mind, and that our feelings not slip and be disturbed by the invented tales of the poets. The highest end of justice is that iniquity cannot move the mind of the just man. This is the end of all virtue, and even of bodily courage: to restore peace when war is over. So even the courage of fighting usually serves peace; let no one, then, disturb a peaceable heart.

Many things arise to disturb a person. Often a wife, deceived by the serpent's snares, tries to unsettle her husband's mind; a father often mocks his son's faith; a husband tries his wife's resolve with reproaches. But in all these things the righteous man prevails and says: Who will separate us from the love of Christ?

Tribulation, or distress, or persecution? How often good deeds are counted as crimes, how often virtue is treated as a disgrace, how often kindness itself goes unthanked! A righteous man has sold his possessions, distributed them to the poor, and kept nothing for himself, yet he is often despised in the very church because he has ceased to be rich, as it is written: If a man gives all his

possessions out of love, he will be scorned with scorn. So let him not be troubled, for he sought neither the reward nor the favour of this world, but of eternal life. Let him not resent it that people defer to money more than to good works. For if he were honoured in this world for his good work and gained the fruit of his effort here, it would be said of him: He has received his reward. A good work does indeed win favour here as well, but that is only a small portion of the salvation to be earned.

Keep your reward for the future, and count the reproaches of this world as increases to your reward. Always think of the apostle's saying, that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to come. So let the righteous man be broken by no injuries, troubled by no dangers, shaken by no storms, whether death assails him or life, or the angels of heaven. Let him be neither cast down by adversity nor lifted up by prosperity; let his heart never be weak. Death tempts, and life tempts too: beware of stumbling.

Whoever has the peace that surpasses all understanding is great; he is not one of these little ones. Therefore he ought not to suffer stumbling, for it is the little ones who are unsettled by a stumbling block. That is why the Lord too says: Whoever causes one of these least little ones to stumble. He called those whom stumbling blocks disturb not only little but even least, and so, as you have read, whoever disturbs the infancy of a weak mind is liable to a heavy penalty. For just as he incurs the heavier punishment who persuades a little child to commit a crime and drives its unwary years headlong, so too does he who ensnares one who is feeble, foolish and improvident, whether by persuading him to error or by unsettling his heart. Do you want to know how weak the one who stumbles is? I will not eat meat, he says, lest I cause my brother to stumble. What weakness, what infancy of soul, that even his brother's food unsettles him! Where can a person not find a precipice, when there is danger even here?

And what is worse, weakness of this kind creeps into many. You see a righteous man in want, and you are tempted; you see a wicked man rich, and you are tempted; you see a holy man without children, and you are tempted; you see an unjust man abounding in children, honours and worldly praise, and you are tempted. How many pits, how many snares — and, what is graver, snares that strangle so many! In the city of Sodom scarcely one man, Lot, was found who was not tempted, and even his wife could not escape the snares of temptation.

The people of the Hebrews crossed the sea, but could not get past temptations. All were tempted except Joshua and Caleb, who alone of the elders were found worthy to enter the land of promise, because they remained untouched by temptation. Neither Aaron nor Miriam entered, because they too were tempted; nor did Moses enter, because he was the leader of a people that was tempted. He was a type of the law, which could not shut out temptations. It could not

lead into the land of resurrection, because that grace was reserved for the gospel. The law could not give peace; that is why Moses was always at war as long as he lived, and the people of the law are always in the uncertainty of war. But Joshua son of Nun settled the spirits of the people in deep peace, since whoever is under the law is tossed about by uncertainties, whereas whoever is under the gospel hears him who says: Peace I leave with you, my peace I give to you. And so for those who love there is no stumbling block.

Take it another way: the Lord's cross is a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks. It is a stumbling block to the faithless, because the Jew says: 'So this is God, who appeared as a man? This is God, who fasted? This is God, who was beaten? This is God, who was crucified, who could not come down from the cross and free himself?' Indeed, this is what they said at the time of the Lord's passion: Let him come down from the cross and we will believe him. He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he wants him.

Do not let these things tempt you or disturb you; do not let thoughts of this kind work their way into your mind. Where there is peace, and great peace, there the cross of Christ is not a disgrace but salvation. The Lord's cross was no disgrace to Peter; it gave him such glory that he honoured Christ with his feet

turned upward, fearing that if he were crucified in the same posture as the Lord, he might seem to have aspired to the Lord's glory. So the cross is a disgrace to the faithless, but to the faithful it is grace, redemption and resurrection, because the Lord suffered for us, because he redeemed us with that blood and by that resurrection called us back to paradise. How can anyone who believes this be disturbed, when the hope of the heavenly kingdom rises before him?

Next comes the sixth verse: I looked for your salvation, Lord, and I have done your commandments. Whoever waits hopes [?]; so hope comes first, and salvation follows. Hope thus runs ahead of its fulfilment. That is why he who waited for salvation from the Lord did the Lord's commandments. Hence in the gospel the Lord calls those who have done his commandments friends, not servants. For whoever loves acts, and whoever has acted is rightly rewarded with the recompense of love.

Next comes the seventh verse: My soul has kept your testimonies and has loved them exceedingly. We said above too that to love is more than to keep, because keeping is sometimes a matter of necessity or fear, while loving is a matter of charity. So here, having said 'I have kept', he added 'I have loved', so that it would be the keeping of one who loves, not of one who fears. Whoever loves exceedingly keeps exceedingly.

Next comes the eighth verse: I have kept your commandments and your testimonies, for all my ways are in your sight, Lord. Blessed is he who can say: All my ways are before you — who has no wish to hide any of his thoughts or any of his deeds. Adam hid his way; Eve hid hers after her fault; Cain hid the murder of his brother. Concealment lies in our intention, not in its success; yet whoever conceals is full of faithlessness, even though nothing is hidden from God. That is why the Church in the Song of Songs

showed him her secrets, saying: I will take you and bring you into my mother's house, into the inner chamber of her who conceived me. For although God sees all the hidden things of the heart, it is still good for each of us to open and lay out our soul before him, and to go out to meet him as one goes to meet light or warmth. And not without reason does the Church glory, saying: I was in his eyes as one who finds peace, since she was not afraid to disclose her ways.

This, then, is the voice of the righteous, for the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous. And so it is fitting that this be said to the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the way and the truth, by those who long to find that true way by faith, conduct and deed: All my ways are before you, Lord. For no way can be good except the one you have judged worthy to be lit by the visitation of your light. To you be honour, glory, praise and everlastingness, from ages past, now and always, and for all ages of ages. Amen.
XXII. THE LETTER TAU.

The letter Tau begins, which in Latin translation means 'he has erred'; another interpretation gives 'he has completed'. What does 'he has erred' mean? It is the twenty-second letter, the last among the Hebrews. Now we have said that this psalm, the hundred and eighteenth, signifies the progress of a person who, schooled in the teachings of moral instruction, would put off all the infancy of an untrained mind and take on the knowledge of seasoned counsel and the maturity of an elder's prudence.

Where there is error, fault is indicated. Here, then, is progress: that fault should come to an end. But why is it interpreted this way? 'He has erred,' it says — not 'he errs' but 'he has erred'. To have erred belongs to past time, to err to the present; whoever has erred has ceased to err and condemns his former error. For 'he has erred' is said of one who is no longer in error. One who still remains in error is not said to have erred, but to err; to err belongs to one who persists in vice, to have erred to one who is correcting his lapse.

Indeed the corrector of morals says: For we too were once foolish, unbelieving, erring in desires and pleasures. He would certainly not have said, We were once foolish, unless he had afterwards gained the discipline of wisdom, nor would he have said, We were erring, unless he had laid aside his former error.

Then, to show that the lapse had been wiped out and that no trace of the offence remained, he says: But when the kindness and humanity of our Saviour appeared, not by works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit. So, having laid aside his old error and been renewed by the Holy Spirit and by a thorough reform of his conduct, he says: For we were once erring. You see, then, that to have renounced error is a mark not of vice but of progress.

Finally, let the Lord Jesus himself teach you, if you think human counsels or opinions are not to be believed. For in his gospel he himself declared that the shepherd left the ninety-nine sheep and went looking for the one that had gone astray. It is the hundredth sheep that he says went astray; let the perfection and fullness of the number itself instruct and shape you.

Not without reason is it preferred to the rest, because it is a greater thing to have called oneself back from vice than to have been all but ignorant of vices themselves. For souls steeped in vice to throw off the reins of their desires and amend themselves belongs not only to perfect virtue but also to heavenly grace. To amend what is to come is a matter of human effort; to forgive what is past belongs to divine power. And so the shepherd lays the sheep he has found on his shoulders. Surely you recognize the mystery:

how the weary sheep is restored, because the weary human condition cannot be revived in any other way than by the sacrament of the Lord's passion and of the blood of Jesus Christ, whose sovereignty is upon his shoulders; for on that cross he bore our infirmities, so that there he might cancel the sins of all. Rightly do the angels rejoice, because he who erred no longer errs; he has already forgotten his error.

So it is not error but completion, as the other interpretation teaches; and completion is the perfection of discipline. Hence Jeremiah too, in his Lamentations, says under this letter: Your iniquity has come to an end, daughter of Zion; he will no longer drive you into exile.

He has visited your iniquities, daughter of Edom; he has uncovered your sins. Do you notice that iniquity could not come to an end without God's visitation, and that correction could not be complete except through the grace of the Lord and Saviour? And how iniquity comes to an end, hear the Church saying: I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them? So the garment of the old man, woven through with the vices of error and laid aside in the washing of regeneration, she does not know how she could put on again;

for through her zeal for correction, forgetfulness of sins had grown in her. So great is the power of completed amendment that one returns to a kind of spiritual childhood, which knows nothing of the ways of error and could not commit a crime even if it wished, because it has lost the habit of knowing how to sin. I think enough has now been said about the interpretation of this letter. Let us now learn from what follows what the mind of the completed man is.

So he says: Let my prayer draw near in your sight, Lord; according to your word give me understanding. A good life makes prayer fly and gives spiritual wings to petitions, on which the prayer of the saints is carried up to God. The Spirit too, in whom we pray, lifts up the prayer of the righteous, especially when a compassionate heart commends it with contrition. Such is the confidence of the completed man. Indeed, earlier in this psalm David himself sought a lamp for his feet, so that as he walked this earthly road he might not go astray.

But now, as one already placed at the end with his journey completed, he rises wholly above the business of travelling and directs his prayer to heavenly things. He sends it into the sight of the Lord and Saviour, giving it the breezes of righteousness, the winds of wisdom, the oars of devotion and faith, and the supports of innocence and purity; for prayer is weighed down by sin and moves far from God, and it is weighed down the more, the more wicked the life of the one praying. But the prayer of the innocent ascends, and so does the groaning of a compassionate heart, if they hate the mud of Egypt and refuse to labour at earthly things. Indeed, you have read that the voice of the Hebrews,

who could not bear the harsh commands of the Egyptians and refused works as filthy as they were heavy, unworthy of the nobility of their race, ascended to the Lord our God. Their prayer ascended because, although they worked, they worked unwillingly. And so God's mercy descended to them, because their devotion ascended to God.

It ascended, then, but not bodily; so great a prophet was not asking that his prayer draw near in a bodily way. Whoever thinks so is certainly confining God to some fixed place and seat, or imagining some wider place in which God is, when in fact he, invisible, ineffable and incomprehensible, fills all things, and the fullness of the Godhead dwells in him.

I have read that Moses drew near to God when he received the law; but David, with his usual modesty, asks not that he himself but that his prayer may draw near to God. So there seems to be a certain distinct order: those who are more perfect draw near to God themselves, while righteous men of the next rank are content if their prayer draws near.

Let us consider from our ordinary way of speaking what it means to draw near. Picture a teacher and a pupil. If the pupil has eagerly either absorbed his teacher's genius or attended to his instruction, so

that he seems to come very close to the likeness of his work and teaching, do we not usually say that he has drawn near to his teacher? So you too, if you show yourself an imitator of Christ, like the one who said: Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ — if you know no deceit, hate lying, follow truth, do not shrink from justice, and love chastity — you have drawn near to Christ, and through Christ to God. He is the way by which one comes to the Father, he who is always with the Father.

We have learned what it means for prayer to draw near, namely, 'let it be lifted up by our deeds'. If you lift up your deeds, you have lifted up your prayer. Whoever knows how to lift up his hands directs his prayer into the sight of God, as you read further on: Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight, the lifting up of my hands as an evening sacrifice. This kind of prayer leads to life; another kind leads to sin: And let his prayer become sin. You too, if you ask for worldly things, if you request shameful things, your prayer is directed not to God but into sin. So understand what you are asking for.

According to your word, he says, give me understanding. Notice what he asks. He did not say 'understanding' in general, but understanding according to the word of God; for there is an understanding that leads to death, just as there is a prudence that leads to destruction: The children of this world are more prudent in their generation than the children of light.

But this prudence, which belongs to the world, does nothing to help toward eternal life. It is concerned with honour and petty gains, intent on piling up profits, not on acquiring merits. In short, it is concerned with the elements of the world, a wisdom more showy than true, like all philosophy, which seeks what belongs to others while ignorant of what is its own, examines the regions of the sky and probes the expanses of the world, which can be of no use to it, and knows nothing of God, whom alone it ought to seek.

That is why the truly wise man says: If anyone among you seems to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise; for the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. We must strive, then, to be fools in this world and to have nothing to do with philosophy, so that no one may lead our faith away from the truth by means of the elements of this world, and no one may plunder our teaching by means of philosophy.

For this, we know, is how the Arians fell into faithlessness: they thought the generation of Christ should be worked out from the ways of this world. They abandoned the apostle and follow Aristotle. They abandoned the wisdom that is with God and chose the traps of disputation and the snaring of words according to the discipline of dialectic, though the apostle cries out: Let no one plunder you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human traditions, according to the elements of this world, and not according to Christ.

Would that I could imitate that foolishness by which I might be wise! I mean the man who has ample possessions but cares nothing for their produce, being intent on God; the man who rejects even honours offered to him and does not seek the teaching of philosophy, and who, even if he knew it before,

pretends not to know it and unlearns it by not seeking it; who does not seek his own interests but bestows his own goods on others, and gains eternal things for himself! Such a man can say: According to your word give me understanding — that is, not according to the philosophers, not according to the advocates, not according to the merchants of this world, not according to the architects of houses, but according to your word, which is the foundation of true wisdom and of good works, so that on it the prophet may build the gold of his heart, the silver of his speech and the precious stones of his works, and his work cannot slip and perish.

Next comes the second verse: Let my petition also come in before you; according to your word deliver me. Observe the order. First he said: Let my prayer draw near; next he asked for understanding according to the word; third he says: Let my petition come in before you. Does not the Lord invite us in, as is the custom among us, and deign to receive us with kindness?

When you want to meet one of the leading men, do you not first approach his house, then seek to be informed and instructed so as to learn the mind of the master of the house, and then beg to enter his house, so that no one may rebuff you and shut you out? So you too must knock at that heavenly palace — knock not with your bodily hand but with what we might call the right hand of your prayer. It is not only the bodily hand that knocks; the voice knocks too, for it is

written: The voice of my brother knocks at the door. We knock with a finger too; indeed Thomas was found worthy to open the door of the resurrection with his finger. And to you Jesus says: Put your finger here and place it in my hands and my side, and do not be unbelieving, but believing. So knock with your finger, if you cannot with your whole hand. Knock at the door; Christ is the door, who says: If anyone enters through me, he will be saved.

When you have knocked at this door, then, see how you enter, lest, though you have entered, you remain out of the king's sight. Many people enter palaces and do not immediately see the earthly king, but wait upon him again and again in the hope of one day being granted a sight of him. Nor do they presume to obtain an audience; but when summoned they are presented, and they pour out their petition so as to be received with goodwill, taking care that the opening of their speech does not falter or give offence. How much more must we ask God that our prayer may enter the door of his mercy! Indeed Paul too asks that a door for the word be opened to him, so that he may speak the mystery of Christ.

But since the Greek has εἰσέλθοι τὸ ἀξίωμά μου, that is, 'let my dignity come in' — although the copyist may have erred and it may have been ἀξίωσις, that is, 'entreaty' — let us nevertheless explain this reading too, as best we can. Surely, when you petition a man who is a king, you ask him to take account of your rank and to let consideration of your dignity move him, so that he either shows mercy, if pardon is to be sought, or grants you the deference due to your rank. What more need I say? Everyone who comes to petition enters in such a way that deference is paid to dignities. Rightly, then, does the one devoted to God also say: Let my dignity come in before you. The Christian too has his dignity, since he serves as a soldier of so great an emperor.

There are very great dignities of true faith as well, and with Christ too there are various ranks of honour: God appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers. But these are the dignities of those who hold office. There are also the dignities of private persons, such as piety, justice, sobriety, chastity and discipline.

There are also dignities of prayer: if you pray for a widow, if you pray for an orphan, if you pray for a merciful man or for one who is exceedingly devout and faithful, if you pray in tribulation, if you pray with grief, if you who pray share with compassion in another's sorrow. Your prayer enters into God's grace and enters his house if the church prays with you, if the whole people implores him, so as to win the Lord's favour.

And what does he ask for? To be rescued, to be set free, because he has long been fighting against the spiritual forces of wickedness and against the temptations of this world, and because it is heavy enough to endure a long campaign over the lengthy course of this life. Indeed he also says further on: Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged! For he groans because he must keep tireless watch with unbroken toil; therefore he asks to be freed from so many adversaries, and has no wish to share the company of earthly men.

The third verse follows: "My lips shall pour forth a hymn, when you have taught me your righteous decrees." The one who pours forth a hymn is the one who can say, "For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God." And the one who has tasted the many sweet commandments of the Lord pours forth well. The one who has poured forth the Word pours forth a hymn. Indeed, David earlier poured forth a good word; here he pours forth a hymn.

For he had tasted the good bread that came down from heaven, the good bread of which, if anyone eats, he will not die for ever. The word of God has its own banquets: some more solid, such as the Law and the Gospel, others sweeter, such as the Psalms and the Song of Songs. The Church, or the devout soul, poured forth a hymn when God the Word said to her, "Let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet." She poured forth a hymn when he said to her, "Your lips drip the honeycomb, O bride; honey and milk are under your tongue."

But no one can pour forth a hymn until he has learned the righteous decrees of God, and learned them from the Lord his God himself. That is why David asks particularly that God should teach him. For he had heard and come to know in the Spirit that there is one Teacher, and so everywhere he begged that God himself should become his teacher, so that he might learn God's righteous decrees from him.

For how can someone sing who is gripped by dread and fear of punishment? How can someone sing who is conscious of grave sins, unless he is first made secure of pardon? Indeed, further on you have, "How shall we sing the Lord's song in a foreign land?", a land where he is assailed, where he is taken captive under the law of sin, where he weeps and laments the hardships of his captivity.

So you too, eat the food of the heavenly Scriptures. Eat, so that it may remain in you for eternal life; eat every day, so that you do not go hungry; eat to be filled; eat so that you may pour forth the rich fare of the heavenly words. Spiritual banquets do not harm those who are filled with them, but do them good. That is why the prophet wished to be filled, when he says, "Let my mouth be filled with your praise, that I may sing your glory." When someone sings the glory of God, his heart pours forth a hymn to the Lord.

The fourth verse follows: "My tongue shall speak your word, for all your commandments are righteousness." Whoever has learned the righteous decrees of God speaks the word of God, and whoever speaks the word of God does not speak an idle word. To speak of the works of men is an idle word. That is why the saint says that grace was given him by the Lord, so that his mouth should not speak of the works of men; for that is an idle word, and not only idle but dangerous too, since for it

we shall have to give an account. "For every idle word you speak, you will give an account for it." For it is no small danger when you have so many utterances of God, and the works of God that he did in Genesis, in Exodus, in Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy, in Joshua, in the book of Judges, in the books of Kings and of Ezra, and that he did in the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles, if you pass these over and speak of the things of the world and listen to the things of the world.

"Hedge your ears with thorns." If only you would hedge in your tongue as well, so that you do not speak! But what is worse, your tongue is surrounded by thorns, which prick and wound anyone who speaks of worldly things. That is why the adversary often floods even those who are praying with worldly thoughts. If, then, we ought not to listen to what is alien or superfluous, how much more ought we not to speak slander, when the venerable Scripture says to each of us, "Bind up your

silver and gold, and make a yoke and a weight for your mouth"! Bind up your thoughts with faithful silence, bind up your words, put a yoke on your mouth so that it does not toss about with the untamed neck of its words; put a weight on it, so that we may weigh everything we say with careful judgment. Yet with what thorns does Scripture tell you to hedge your ears, if not with a contrite heart and the fear of judgment? These prick to our health; they goad, they do not wound—although the wounds of a friend are also beneficial.

"All your commandments," he says, "are righteousness." For they are commandments of righteousness, and so they cannot be without righteousness. It is God's commandment that you should love your God. Hence Paul says, "For he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. For it is written: You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not covet; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word." If every commandment is summed up in that word, and that word is righteousness—for what is so righteous as to love your God and love your brother?—then surely all the commandments of God are righteousness.

For just as one who can kill his brother surely does [not] love his brother, as one who commits adultery with his brother's wife surely does not love his brother, as one who steals, one who covets what belongs to another, surely does not love the man he longs to defraud, so too one who proudly despises his brother, who tries to disgrace him, who feeds on wrongs done to him, is a stranger to the fellowship of love.

The fifth verse follows: "Let your hand be there to save me, for I have chosen your commandments." He seems to be praying for the coming of the Lord, for Christ is the hand of God. We read that he is the right hand of God, of whom he said above, "The right hand of the Lord has done mightily, the right hand of the Lord has exalted me." Why then did he say "hand" here? Perhaps not only for the elegance of variety, which the Scriptures do not usually neglect, but also because of a certain distinction between hands: "right hand" is used there, where it is written that he exalted him by power, and "hand" here, where we are to understand that he preserved him through humility.

"The hand of the Lord" can also be understood as in common usage, when people say, "That king's hand is great," meaning his army is great, or "That man's hand is weaker." So here too we may understand: "Let your aid and support be present, so that you send your angels, your help, the reinforcements of your power, to set your people free." This is the hand of God of which it is written: "Are they not all ministering spirits, sent to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?" So the one who has chosen the commandments of God has the confidence to demand divine help for himself with authority.

The sixth verse follows: "I have longed for your salvation, O Lord, and your law is my meditation." One person delights in a long life here and longs to prolong the life of this body to the very end of worn-out old age. Others are broken by the weakness of illness, and none of them can say, "When I am weak, then I am strong." They think themselves happy if they enjoy the comfort of unimpaired

health, these people for whom weakness does not serve salvation. None of these either can say, "I have longed for your salvation, O Lord"; for they seek their own health rather than the salvation of God, obeying physicians rather than the Scriptures. But the precepts of medicine run counter to those who are devoted to the knowledge of God:

they call them back from fasting, they do not allow them to keep vigil, they draw them away from all concentrated meditation. So whoever gives himself over to the physicians denies himself; but whoever seeks the salvation of God follows Christ, who is called the salvation of God, seeking not the things of the body but the things that are eternal, even while he lives in this body. And whoever seeks the salvation of God surely meditates on the law day and night. His meditation on the divine decrees is unceasing, and no care for this body turns him away from devotion to learning.

The seventh verse follows: "My soul shall live and shall praise you, and your judgments shall help me." He delights in the prospect of the reward of the life to come, certainly not of the present life. For how can this be called life, of which it is written, "And you have brought me down into the dust of death"? How many living people are in hell!

Paul himself, who truly longed for the salvation of God, desired to be set free from the body of this death, saying, "For I desire to depart and to be with Christ, for that is far better; but to remain in the flesh is more necessary" than desirable. How then does the soul live while wrapped in the shroud of death? Or what life is it that lies in shadow?

We are in the region of the shadow of death; our life is hidden, not free. It will be free in the land of the living, where the righteous man takes up the confidence of pleasing, so that he may please the Lord in the land of the living. There, then, our soul will live, where it will be clothed with nothing mortal, nothing weak [?], and will owe no debt of punishment.

There it will praise the Lord, when, having laid aside the body of weakness, it has begun to be conformed to the glory of the body of Christ. For while we are in sin, how can we praise fully? For God said to the sinner, "Why do you recount my righteous decrees?" Placed here, we are in shadow; in shadow we live, in shadow we praise. In shadow we cannot praise perfectly. We are in a foreign land; indeed, you heard him say further on, "How shall we sing the Lord's song in a foreign land?"

The judgments of God help the saints when the reward of eternal life is granted for good works. Blessed is he who says, "And your judgments shall help me." I who am weak, I who am a sinner, fear the judgments of God because of my consciousness of my sins; they bring me terror, they harass me; but they help the saints. And yet they will help the sinner too, though in a different way.

The saint will be helped as he is proved; the sinner will be helped as he is humbled, as he is chastised, so that he may pay for his sins twice over, as his work is burned up so that he himself may be saved, yet as through fire. Perhaps the sense also fits this way: if I am found worthy of judgment, I shall be worthy to be stripped of fellowship with the ungodly, since the ungodly do not rise to judgment; and the judgments will help me, since whoever believes in the Lord is not judged. His faith will benefit him and will plead for his pardon, even if there is some fault in his works.

The eighth verse follows: "I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost; give life to your servant, for I have not forgotten your commandments." The Greek has "seek your servant," that is, zētēson, and a scribe could have made a mistake and written zēson, which means "give life." Both senses indeed hold good, but "seek your servant" is more fitting in this place, since the sheep that has gone astray must be sought by the shepherd so that it does not perish. That is why he says, "I have gone astray."

You too, tell your iniquities, so that you may be justified. In admitting that you have fallen, you share common fellowship with everyone, for no one is without sin. To deny this is sacrilege—for God alone is without sin—but to confess it to God is the remedy that brings release from punishment. "I have gone astray," he says; but one who has strayed from the way can return to the way, can be called back to it. And he beautifully added, "like a sheep that was lost"; for one who recognizes his straying is not lost.

"Seek your servant," he says, "for I have not forgotten your commandments." Come then, Lord Jesus, seek your servant, seek your weary sheep. Come, Shepherd, seek, as you sought the sheep of Joseph. Your sheep has gone astray while you linger, while you go about on the mountains. Leave your ninety-nine sheep and come to seek the one sheep that has gone astray. Come without dogs, come without evil workers, without the hireling who does not know how to enter by the door. Come without a helper, without a messenger; I have long been waiting for you to come. For I know that you will come, since I have not forgotten your commandments. Come not with a rod, but with love and a spirit of gentleness.

Do not hesitate to leave your ninety-nine sheep on the mountains, for while they are on the mountains the ravening wolves cannot attack them. In paradise the serpent did harm once; he lost his prey there after Adam was driven out, and he can do no more harm there. Come to me, whom the attack of savage wolves torments.

Come to me, who, cast out of paradise, have long been assailed by the venom of the serpent's wound, who have strayed from those flocks of yours on high. For you had placed me there too, but the wolf by night drove me away from your folds. Seek me, for I am searching for you; seek me, find me, take me up, carry me. You can find the one you seek; you deign to take up the one you have found, and to lay upon your shoulders the one you have taken up.

A loving burden does not weary you; carrying righteousness is no burden to you. Come then, Lord, for though I have gone astray, I have not forgotten your commandments; I keep my hope of healing. Come, Lord, for you alone can call back the straying sheep, and you will not grieve those you leave behind; for they too will rejoice at the sinner's return. Come, to bring salvation on earth and joy in heaven.

Come then and seek your sheep, not through servants, not through hirelings, but by yourself. Take me up in the flesh that fell in Adam. Take me up not from Sarah but from Mary, so that she may be a virgin uncorrupted, a virgin by grace, untouched by any stain of sin. Carry me on the cross, which is salvation to those who stray, on which alone the weary find rest, on which alone all who die shall live.
Yet "give life" can also beautifully be said, because one whom Power has carried on its shoulders cannot die.

So the soul says, and the Church says, "I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost"; but she also says, "I sought him whom my soul loved." This amounts to saying, "Give life to your servant, for I have not forgotten your commandments. I have sought you, but I cannot find you unless you are willing to be found. And you do wish to be found, but you wish to be sought for a long time, to be searched out more diligently."

Your Church knows this: that you do not want her to seek you while asleep, you do not want her to search for you while lying down. And so you knock at the door to rouse her from sleep; you test whether her heart is awake while her flesh sleeps. You wish to raise her as she lies there, saying, "Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead." You put your hand through the opening so that she may rise, and if she is slow to rise, you leave her. You want her to seek again, and to ask many, and not to forget to seek, not to forget your words, so that if she holds fast to them, you may offer yourself to be seen and not shrink from being held.

And when she has been found worthy to embrace you, she will show her fruits, she will show that she has not forgotten your commandments, and she will say to you, "Come, my brother, let us go out into the field; and at our gates is every fruit of the trees; new and old, my brother, I have kept for you."

This is to say, "I hold all the commandments of the New and the Old Testament." Only the Church can say this. No other congregation says it; the synagogue does not say it, holding neither the new according to the letter nor the old according to the spirit. The Manichaean heresy, which does not accept the prophets, does not say, "I have kept the old for you." Rightly [?] is she seen made white, who shines with the grace of both testaments.

The Bridegroom answers her: "Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm." You who have kept the new and the old for me are my seal; you are in my image and likeness. In you shines the image of righteousness, the image of wisdom, the image of virtue.

And since the image of God is in your heart, let it be [?] in your works as well; let the likeness of the Gospel be in your deeds, so that in your conduct you keep my precepts. The likeness of the Gospel will be in you if you offer the other cheek to the one who strikes you, if you love your enemy, if you take up your cross and follow me. That is why I carried the cross for you, so that you would not hesitate to carry it for my sake.

The daughters of Jerusalem heard that the Lord Jesus was now joining the Church to himself; and because, considering the greatness of the Word, they judged her unequal to so great a marriage and feared that she might not be able to bear the weight of the union, they make excuses, saying, "Our sister is little and has no breasts."

For this is how those who wish to postpone a wedding usually make excuses: they plead the weakness of immature age and add that she has no breasts, which signify the marriageable time of life. This is the common sign for all virgins who are to marry: when their breasts begin to grow, they are then judged fit for union.

Troubled, then, that the Bridegroom in the eagerness of his love is pressing for the wedding, they say, "What shall we do for our sister on the day when he speaks in her?" Or, as Symmachus has it, "when he speaks to her"; that is, at the celebration of the betrothal there usually takes place a conversation and the confirmation of the marriage.

"What then shall we do," they say in their distress, "since the spiritual union is being pressed upon us?" They cannot make excuses against so great a marriage, for there is no one who does not think blessed the union of the soul and the Spirit, or of Christ and the Church. But because the fullness of the Word, or of the Holy Spirit, flashes and shines, and nothing can equal it, they wish to postpone it, so that by that delay the soul or the Church may become more perfect.

So they say, "If she is a wall, let us build shelters upon it; and if she is a door, let us carve cedar panels upon it." The soul of the saint is a wall. The Church too has her walls, she who, now more perfect, says, "I am a fortified city."

This is the wall that has twelve apostolic gates, through which entrance into the Church lies open to the people of the nations. But although a wall encloses the circuit of the whole city, it is better fortified when it has shelters prepared, in which the city's defenders can find safe support for keeping watch and guard. But because this city is a city of reason and all its hope is in the word of God, it needs ramparts not of iron but of silver, accustomed to drive back the attacks of the enemy with heavenly words rather than with the pleasures [?] of the body. Supported by that defense, shining with that splendor, she is judged more fit for union with Christ.

And since Christ is the door, who says, "If anyone enters by me, he will be saved," the Church too is called a door, because through her the way to salvation lies open to the peoples. But so that she may not be corrupted by the moths and worms of the heretics, the daughters of Jerusalem—whether angels or the souls of the righteous—say, "Let us build cedar panels upon her," that is, the good fragrance of lofty faith. For the fragrance of this wood is sweet, and neither worm nor moth can corrupt it.

That is why this wood is chosen for raising the gables of roofs and for shaping the letters of the alphabet with which children are first introduced to the study of liberal learning. This wood, then, is lofty in its grace, light as a burden, sweet in its fragrance, useful as an instrument of knowledge, fit for the service of eternal understanding.

But just as Christ, loving his bride, was pressing for the solemn rite of the spiritual union, so the Church too, already captivated by the beauty of the Word, was hastening to the wedding. And so, impatient of the delays and postponements that the daughters of Jerusalem were eager to contrive, she says, "I am a wall, and my breasts are towers"; that is, "Do not doubt whether I am a wall"—for they had said, "If she is a wall"—"I am a wall," she says, "and I do not have small breasts; my breasts are like towers.

How can you say that I have no breasts? I have understandings of wisdom like towers, in which there is abundance, as it is written: 'and abundance in your towers.'" By these breasts, that is, these understandings, she judged herself fit for so great a marriage; but the daughters of Jerusalem could not yet judge so, because they did not see the abundance of her understanding.

And she added, "I was in his eyes as one finding peace"; that is, "You deliberate about my understanding, though I have found the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding and guards both hearts and minds in Christ Jesus. Such," she says, "was I in the eyes of the Bridegroom, like one who has peace." For it is written, "Those who rightly seek peace shall have it." [?] So, as the beloved and his beloved hastened, the spiritual union was celebrated, sought by mutual consent.

And so, as if singing a wedding song, the Spirit exulted in the prophet, saying, "Solomon had a vineyard in Belamon; he gave his vineyard to those who keep it." The Spirit therefore proclaims: the congregation of the peoples has been planted and founded on the root of the eternal vine, and with gentle heart has bowed its spiritual neck under the yoke of the Word; and it has been planted in the multitude of the nations.

For this is how "Belamon" is to be understood, as Symmachus, Aquila and other translations have shown in Greek. The old union, which could not bear fruit, was repudiated; the vineyard was given to new and faithful cultivators, who could not only produce fruit but also keep it. So one sheep went astray, but once called back it filled the expanse of the whole world; straying had led one sheep away, but the grace of the Lord gathered a multitude of peoples. Man went astray, but the Church is now a wall, and a strong wall. Adam went astray; David, who did not forget the commandments of God, is a wall.

So this vineyard, guarded and fenced with a spiritual defense, gives a thousand fruits to Christ and two hundred fruits to its keepers. And so the Church says, "My vine is before me; a thousand for Solomon, and two hundred for those who keep its fruit."

Perfection and fullness belong to Christ, a portion to the servants. You have this mystery in Genesis, where Joseph gave five portions to his younger brother Benjamin and one each to the other brothers. So to the Lord is offered the portion and privilege of the five senses, which he himself surely bestows on the one he loves, just as he loved Paul, to whom he gave preeminence in wisdom for calling the Gentiles.

Delighted, then, by these fruits, the Church says to Christ, "You who sit in the gardens, friends are listening to your voice; let me hear your voice." For she delighted that Christ was sitting in the gardens and that the friends placed in the gardens were listening to his voice. But because those friends were heavenly beings—archangels, or dominions and thrones—while human beings had been driven out of paradise for disobeying the heavenly commandments, and so the Church could not yet hear his voice as she longed to, she says, "Let me hear your voice." So we too, if we want him to sit within us, should be gardens enclosed and fortified; let us bear the flowers of virtue and the sweetness of grace, so that we may be able to hear the Lord Jesus as he converses with the angels.

But it was to come about that the Church, once she had reached her fullness, would be tried by various persecutions. So while she is delighting in the grace of the Word, she suddenly sees the snares of the persecutors. She feared more for her bridegroom than for herself, or else it is Christ in us whom the persecutors seek above all, and so she says: "Flee, my brother, and be like a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of spices."

He flees for the sake of the weak, who cannot bear heavier trials. That is why it is written that we should flee from city to city, and if they persecute us in this city, we should flee to another. So, as we have said, let him flee for the sake of the weak. Or let him flee from the weak and pass over to the mountains of spices, those who by their martyrdom can give off the fragrance of the blessed resurrection. The mountains of spices are the saints. Christ takes refuge with them, because his foundations are on the holy mountains.

So he takes refuge with those who are his firm foundations. In us he flees, but in them he stands at a secure post. Paul, then, is a mountain of spices, for he can say: "For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God." David is a mountain of spices, for the fragrance of his prayer rose up to the Lord, and so he said: "Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight."

Symmachus and Aquila, however, translated it so that Christ says to the Church: "You who sit in the gardens." That is: "You now sit in gardens worthy of the paradise above. So let me hear your voice, to which the friends are listening; I too long to hear it." The Church began to be in gardens after Christ suffered in a garden.
